angel-post-03-time-as-geology-not-arrow:
Chapter 3. Time as Geology, Not Arrow

← Chapter 2 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 4 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 3

Most histories are shaped like an arrow. They start early and end late, and the reader is carried from cause to effect along a line that runs one direction only. Angel in the Forest does not move like that, and the difference is not a stylistic quirk. It is the structural heart of the book, and it is the place where Young comes closest to an idea this study keeps circling: that the past is not behind us but beneath us, laid down in layers we are standing on right now.

Notice first how the book is built. It opens in the summer of 1940, on the ferry. Then it goes back to Rapp's Pennsylvania, comes to the Wabash, tells the Rappite story and the Owenite story across their thirteen years. But it never stays back there. Chapters keep surfacing into 1940. There is a chapter called "The Children of the Ozarks, 1940." There is one called "Glaucas, 1940." The last full chapter, "Farewell to New Harmony," is set on a summer day in 1940 in the town graveyard. The present is threaded all the way through the past, so that you are never allowed to sink into the nineteenth century and forget where you are standing. Every time the history gets going, the ground of the present pushes back up through it. The book will not let time behave like an arrow because Young does not believe time is an arrow. She believes it is a column, and she drills you up and down through it until you can feel the whole depth of it under your feet.

The past you can still buy

The evidence that the past is underfoot rather than behind is scattered through the 1940 sections as a plain, concrete fact.

The Owenites planted golden rain trees. The Owenites failed and scattered, their New Moral World never arrived, and yet the trees kept seeding, and in 1940 the shoots are still for sale in the town shops, six for twenty-five cents, guaranteed to grow. The failed future is literally still propagating. You can carry it home in your hand.

Father Rapp's angel came down, so the story went, and left its footprints pressed into a slab of stone. Rapp is gone. The angel is gone. The stone endured all through the nineteenth century, weathering slowly, until by 1900 the right footprint was still whole but the left had begun to wear away. And the children of New Harmony played hopscotch on it. The holiest sign the first utopia produced, the print of an actual angel, has become a worn square in a children's game, still there, still stepped on, its meaning half rubbed off by weather and feet. That is the past exactly: not gone, not preserved, just underfoot and repurposed by whoever is standing on it now.

And the one unbroken line in the whole town is the undertaker's. Every utopian scheme failed. The only dynasty left in New Harmony in 1940 is the business of burial. Young draws him almost fondly, a man always on his way from the grave to the cradle, holding mortgages he will not foreclose, on whom the entire town depends. He is the figure of accumulation itself, the one whose work is to handle each layer as it goes down. The utopias promised to end death and were themselves buried. The undertaker remains.

The chapter where the sacred is the depth

The book's clearest statement of all this is a chapter called "An Adult View," and it is one of the most extraordinary passages in American prose. In the middle of a history of two communities, Young stops and narrates the entire geological and evolutionary past of the Wabash valley, and she does it in the language of scripture.

She calls it the Book of Nature, written, she says, on leaves of sandstone and limestone, no everlasting material. For thousands of years, she tells us, what is now Indiana was a plain of granite under a deep, tideless salt sea. Transparent fishes appeared and left their fins printed on the rock. The waters withdrew, she writes, without the benefit of Noah. Pterodactyls rose out of the mist. The sea came back, glassy as death, and each time that Lazarus of birds and flowers rose again to new life. Glaciers came down from the north like crystal rivers, and what could not move was destroyed. When the ice pulled back it left rich soil, and elephants browsed the Wabash hills, and where New Harmony now stands there was a crocodile whose open mouth made a dormitory for small birds. It was, she says, an Adamless Eden. And then the line the whole chapter turns on: when man finally arose, he was already old and corrupt, like the earth before him, a creature with a history. There was never a first dawn.

Read what she is doing with the borrowed words. Book of Nature, Noah, Lazarus, Eden, resurrection: she takes the entire vocabulary of the sacred and pours it, not upward toward heaven, but straight down into the rock and the fish and the ice. The holiness in this passage does not point past the world to something above it. It points deeper into the world, into the sheer unimaginable depth of what is actually beneath the cornfields. This is what the sacred looks like from inside the philosophy. Not a truth located somewhere else, but the ordinary ground revealed to be layered thousands of feet deep with everything that ever lived here, and that depth treated with the reverence usually reserved for God. The salt sea is scripture. The glacier is scripture. And "there was never a first dawn" is the flat refusal of the whole arrow model: no clean origin, no starting line, no moment before the layers began. The present is not the point the arrow was aimed at. It is only the most recent layer, and a thin one.

Oil, dinosaurs, and the preacher who could not hold it

Young keeps the geology pressed against the present in the smaller chapters too, and never more sharply than in the talk of the farmers around Glaucas, the barefoot sewer cleaner who goes down under the town and comes back up. The farmers talk, among the price of corn and sheep's lice and Byrd's polar expedition, about the oil under the fields, and they say it is made of the melted bodies of dinosaurs that once roamed these hills. The town runs, in other words, on the liquefied deep past. The engine of the present is the rendered flesh of the ancient dead, pumped up from below.

The preacher will not have it. He says the oil talk is propaganda against the word of God, because there could not have been a garden of Eden and dinosaurs too, and glacial ages, and monkeys for ancestors. He is right that they do not fit together in a single tidy story. His mistake is thinking they have to. He needs one truth and has to throw out the others to keep it. Young does the opposite. She holds Eden and the dinosaurs and the glaciers all at once, in the same breath, without letting any of them win, which is the discipline this philosophy calls witness: staying in the room with contradictory truths instead of forcing one to defeat the rest. The preacher wants an arrow with a clean beginning. Young gives you the column, oil and Eden and ice all stacked and all real, and lets you feel the strain of holding it.

The graveyard hill, and the sensation of the whole

By the time you reach the last chapter, the book has drilled you so thoroughly through the layers that its final image lands with a particular force. On the graveyard hill above New Harmony, on a summer day in 1940, a barefoot pregnant woman the town calls Fuzzy Wuzzy sits with her children, eating raw hamburgers out of a paper sack, overlooking, Young writes, all time and space. Her children toss a ball above tombs inscribed on one side "All die at sunset" and on the other "The spirit of man is immortal." A dead sparrow lies at her feet. The baby turns in her stomach.

She has no idea what she is sitting on. Beneath that picnic is the whole column the book has shown you: the failed Owenites and their rain trees, the celibate Rappites and their angel, the elephants, the crocodile where the town now stands, the salt sea, the granite. She is a living crossing point, the exact place where all of that accumulated past presses up from below and the child not yet born presses forward from above, and she is simply eating her lunch. But the reader is not innocent anymore. The reader, drilled up and down through the layers for four hundred pages, feels the entire depth under that hill. That is the sensation this philosophy points at when it says you are the place where time crosses itself: the moment of finally seeing the structure you were always standing inside. Young does not tell you about it. She builds the book so that you feel it, from underneath, at the last possible moment.

What geology knows that a timeline does not

A timeline gives you sequence and causation, one thing leading to the next, and it quietly promises that the story is over, that the present is where the arrow finally came to rest. Geology promises nothing of the kind. It says the present is a surface, and under the surface is everything, undestroyed, pressing up, still for sale in the shops and still worn into the hopscotch stone and still burning as oil in the engines. Nothing arrived. Nothing concluded. The Rappites did not fail into the past; they failed into the ground, where they still are.

This is why Young could not have written a normal history of New Harmony and said what she needed to say. A line would have let the reader believe the utopias were finished, safely behind us, a closed case with a lesson attached. By refusing the line and building the column instead, she keeps the failed futures exactly where they actually are, which is beneath our feet and holding us up. The past does not go away. It accumulates. And the honest shape for a book about it is not an arrow but a core sample, drilled straight down through the layers, every one of them still there.
angel-post-06-two-utopias-one-structure:
Chapter 6. Two Utopias, One Structure

← Chapter 5 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 7 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 6

On paper, Rapp and Owen could not be more opposite. One was a German peasant, the other an English cotton lord. One built his community on Scripture, the other on science. One was a tyrant who demanded submission, the other an egalitarian who dreamed of liberation. One enforced total celibacy, the other invited free love. One promised heaven, the other promised rational happiness on earth. If you were looking for two men who represented opposite answers to the question of how human beings should live, you could hardly assemble a cleaner pair.

Young put them on the same ground they inhabited in New Harmony, in the same half-mile square, one after the other, and the reason she did is to show that underneath the opposition they were the same error, made twice.

One fixed account, handed down before the people arrive

Both communities rest on a single, fixed account of what a human being is, settled in advance and imposed from above.

Rapp's account is theological. Man is fallen, the fall was sexual, the path back is renunciation, and the destination is the sexless angel. Owen's account is mechanistic. Man is nothing but the product of his circumstances, the path is correct social design, and the destination is rational happiness. These accounts contradict each other on every point of content. What matters is that they are identical in kind. Each is a complete and closed answer to the question of human nature, worked out before a single actual person walks through the gate of their utopia, and each is held by its author to be not one possible view but an absolute truth. And so neither account can make room for the people who actually show up. Rapp cannot see anyone who is not becoming an angel. Owen cannot see anyone who is not a machine awaiting adjustment. The specific blindness differs. The structure of their blindness is the same: a total theory of the person, and then an inability to perceive the persons who exceed it.

The Committee and the celibacy edict are the same instrument

Both communities require the individual to be pruned back for the sake of the group's coherence, and the pruning is the same operation whether it is done with a scalpel or with a clipboard.

In Rapp's community this is overt and brutal. The edict of celibacy, enforced on everyone, backed by the threat of the most drastic measures, is the suppression of individual difference in its rawest form. In Owen's community the same operation is gentler and looks nothing like it, which is exactly why it is worth noticing. There is a Committee that decides what counts as correct behavior, and when Thomas Pears is dismissed, the real reason, as Young sees it, is that the Committee objected to his soul, to his idea of the pursuit of happiness. That is the celibacy edict in a business suit. A central body has decided what a member is permitted to be, and a man who wants something the account does not authorize is corrected out of the way. Celibacy and free love are opposite rules. They are enforced by the same machine, a body that decides in advance what a person is allowed to want, and removes whatever does not fit.

The transfer, where the sameness becomes literal

The proof of all this is not an interpretation Young imposes. It is a fact of the historical record, and it is one of the most brilliant things in the book. In 1825, Robert Owen bought Harmony from George Rapp for a little under a hundred and fifty thousand dollars. He bought the houses, the factories, the lands, the goods in the store, the horses and cows and steers, the orchards, the furnace, the fire engine, the wharf. Rapp took almost nothing with him. In Young's grim detail, he took all but the castrated dogs, which he carried away.

So the physical place is perfectly continuous. The same granaries, the same workshops, the same dormitories, the same geometrical streets laid out in the shape of the New Jerusalem. Nothing material changes hands except the ownership. What is replaced is only the invisible thing, the entire metaphysical superstructure. The cruciform church where celibates had prayed for the angelic state became a dance hall where the Owenites danced in rational patterns feeling the confluence of beauty and truth. The dormitories that had enforced chastity filled with free love. The identical buildings now housed the exactly opposite belief. And then, in those same buildings, the Owenite community failed along the same arc the Rappite dream had traced, coming apart from within, its people strangers to one another, its fields going to weeds.

This is the argument made visible. Strip the two metaphysics off the top and what remains is one infrastructure and one collapse. The continuity of the place demonstrates that the difference in doctrine, enormous as it looked, made no difference at the level where these communities actually broke. Both were single fixed accounts pressed onto the same plural humanity in the same square half-mile, and both broke on the same rock. Rapp himself confirms the pattern without meaning to: when he moved to Pennsylvania he simply rebuilt Harmony and called it Economy, laid out exactly like the town he had left, because for a man who holds one fixed account, every new place is only the same place again.

The error is the certainty, not the content

The philosophy this study follows would say that the mistake in both cases is not being religious and not being rational. The mistake is the moment either man looked at his own constructed account of human life and called it simply the way things are, the given world, reality itself. Rapp did this with heaven. Owen did it with reason. The content is interchangeable, and that interchangeability is the whole point. Once you have mistaken your construction for the bedrock, the people who do not match it stop looking like people with a different view and start looking like defects to be repaired. That single move, treating a made thing as a found thing, is the error, and it is one error, not two. Young placed the utopias side by side so that the shared move would show through the opposed vocabularies.

Three men, one mistake

The reason to be sure this is structural and not just a quirk of utopian dreamers is Owen's own conservative partner, William Allen. Allen was a Quaker who entered the New Harmony partnership reluctantly, by his own account only to have the strength to oppose the infidel plans of Robert Owen. And Allen held a view that is the mirror image of Owen's radicalism while being the identical error underneath. He believed that the existing order, the whole division of society into governors and governed, rich and poor, learned and unlearned, was God's plan, the handwriting of God on every wall, and therefore not to be tampered with. Where Owen was certain the correct account of human life required tearing the old order down, Allen was certain the correct account required leaving it exactly as it stood.

Line the three of them up. Rapp is certain the true account of man is renunciation toward heaven. Owen is certain it is a rational redesign toward happiness. Allen is certain it is the existing hierarchy as divine arrangement. Three incompatible theories of human nature, and each man holds his own to be the truth rather than one construction among possible others, and each is wrong in the same way. Allen matters because he proves the error has no political home. It is not a disease of radicals or of conservatives. The revolutionary who imposes a new total account and the conservative who defends the existing order as God's own plan are performing the identical act: taking one built version of reality for the given world, and refusing to see the seams. The mistake is not left or right. It is the certainty itself.

And yet the building was not the error

Here the philosophy makes a turn that keeps all of this from collapsing into mere futility. The certainty was the error. The building was not.

Both communities failed, and both left something real behind that outlasted them. The Rappites' relentless productivity fed into the commerce of the whole Mississippi valley. Owen's experiment, for all its collapse, seeded the free schools, the public education, and the property and social rights of women that his son Robert Dale would spend a career fighting for, calling the temple of freedom not marble or carved pillars but a humble schoolhouse. Further out, Owen's labors ran into the British labor movement itself. None of these outcomes needed the original metaphysics to be true. The angel was a fiction and the science of society was a fiction, but the granary held real grain and the schoolhouse taught real children.

That is the distinction the book is built to hold. What was wrong in Rapp and Owen was the fixed certainty, the account of human nature mistaken for reality and enforced against actual people. What was worth something was the labor, and the labor survived the doctrine. You can build seriously, pour a life into the work, and still hold your account of things as a construction rather than the bedrock, and when you do, the building can leave something real behind precisely because you never needed it to be eternal or true forever to be worth doing. The lasting things came out of Rapp and Owen almost sideways, from the work rather than the creed, from everything they did that did not depend on their being right.

Two utopias, three certainties, one structure, one error. And the way past it is not a fourth and better account of human nature waiting to be found. It is the refusal to hold any account as the final one, the willingness to keep building on ground you know to be provisional, without ever again mistaking the scaffold for the earth.
angel-post-09-the-body-the-utopia-cannot:
Chapter 9. The Body the Utopia Cannot Hold

← Chapter 8 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 10 →

Two communities tried to build heaven on the same bend of the Wabash, one after the other, and both of them failed. The reasons usually given are organizational. Rapp’s people were held together by one old man’s will and could not survive without it. Owen’s people were held together by an idea, and the idea could not survive contact with actual farming. Both explanations are true. But Marguerite Young keeps her eye on something the organizational account leaves out, and she keeps it there with a patience that starts to feel like a thesis. Both utopias failed, in part, because neither one could find room for the bodies of the people living inside it.

This is easy to miss, because Young never states it as an argument. She states it as weather, as illness, as a list of what people ate and what killed them. But the accumulation is the argument. A community is a theory about human nature made concrete, and if the theory has no place for the body, the body does not go away. It goes on getting sick, getting old, wanting things, and dying. The utopia can refuse to speak about this. It cannot make it stop.

The Rappite body

Father Rapp’s Harmony ran on celibacy, and Young looks at what that costs without ever reaching for outrage. This is one of the harder things she does. It would be easy to write the Rappites off as monsters, or as fools. She does neither. She holds two facts together at once: this was a community of real spiritual intensity and staggering productivity, and it was killing its members at the level of the cell.

The productivity is not incidental to the celibacy. It flows from it. Young repeats Byron’s sly note that before the total edict, Rappite babies had arrived “never at harvest,” the implication being that harmony “was a form of economy.” Reproduction is inefficient. It distracts. It produces individuals, and individuals have wills, and a will is exactly the thing a perfectly harmonious economy cannot afford. So the community switches off reproduction the way you would switch off an expensive machine. The producer, Young writes, is forced to “lop off his own branch of the tree of life” so the corporation’s books can show a steady increase in earnings. That is the logic in one line. The body is a cost. Cut it.

The images pile up, and they are all bodily. The mills and furnaces of Harmony, “the power of which was derived from a treadmill operated by castrated dogs.” A town laid out with a cocoonery and a brewery and a hattery and, Young notes, “everything but a maternity ward.” The whole reproductive drive of the settlement redirected into labor, the dogs on the wheel a small exact figure for what has been done to everyone.

And then, when the body does assert itself, the story turns terrible. John Rapp, Father Rapp’s own son, could not keep the vow. His wife began to “swell out like the yeast of bread,” and there was no hiding it. Young describes John’s happiness with real tenderness. He had seen a droplet of milk on his wife’s breast, he whistled like a mockingbird, he was, she says, “the poor fool.” The community read that happiness as a crime against everyone who had stayed temperate. Father Rapp decided the offender must be punished. The punishment was not a flogging. It was emasculation, and the victim died “crying like a stuck pig,” somewhere near the piggery. The reason Young gives, in the community’s own logic, is the coldest sentence in the section: “Community must be preserved, at any cost to the finite destiny of finite man.”

This is what it looks like when a theory of human nature meets a human body and decides the body is the thing that has to give. The infant daughter survived, Young tells us, and grew up with a twinkle in her eye. The body wins in the long run. It always does. But the cost of the theory was a man’s life, and Young makes you sit with the fact that the community that killed him was, by every economic measure, a success.

The Owenite body

The Owenites were the opposite of the Rappites in almost every way, and their failure has the same shape. Where Rapp had one will, Owen had a program: a science of society, rational and generous and confident. What the program had no vocabulary for was the ground it stood on. New Harmony sat on broken river bottoms, and the breaking up of those bottoms released the germs of malaria, and people died. Babies died of whooping cough. The streets were mud. The dancers, walking home from the balls that filled almost every night, “were soon black from head to foot,” which is a lovely small joke and also a plain fact about mud and about bodies that have to walk through it.

Young gives the Owenite body a face, and it belongs to Mrs. Pears, who is miserable and correct about being miserable. Her eyes had gone bad from sewing, so bad that “she could hardly see to lift her hand before her face.” She missed Pittsburgh. She watched a neighbor lose a child, and watched the babies dying, and understood in her plain, unphilosophical way that the rational program had nothing to offer any of it. Owen’s system was addressed entirely to the mind. It had elaborate views on education and property and the formation of character. It had no answer for a woman going blind with a needle in her hand, or a child drowning in its own cough. The body was simply outside the frame. It was left to rot in the bottomlands while the committee debated the future of the human race.

The man in the storm

The clearest single image of the problem is old Greenwood, who Young says would have been “more at home among the Rappite candidates for heaven than among the Owenites,” and who does something during the second summer that nobody around him can explain. In a green-lit thunderstorm, with trees falling and lightning scrawling the sky, Robert Dale looks out the window and sees an old man walking the flooded streets, calm, going nowhere, carrying “a slender iron rod, ten or twelve feet long,” upright like a musket. Where was the war?

There was no war. Greenwood was old and in pain and he wanted to die, and when Robert Dale asks him afterward why he did not come in out of the rain, he says he thought it might be a chance to slip off and be laid quietly in the corner of the orchard. He did not want the responsibility of destroying himself, so he had prayed that God, who had struck the Rappite house and the young colt and the trees, might strike him too. If God had only seen fit to do it, he says, he would have been at rest that very minute, all his pains gone, no more burden to anyone or to himself.

This is the tenth pillar’s opposite and the ninth pillar’s proof. Greenwood is carrying a bodily truth. I am old, I hurt, I am ready to be done. And the community he lives in has no legitimate place to put it. New Harmony is a rational utopia. It does not have a language for a man who simply wants to stop. So the truth has to leave his body sideways, through an iron rod in a lightning storm, dressed up as an accident that God might arrange. When a community has no noun for what you are living through, you do not stop living through it. You are just erased from the official account of what is happening, and you have to smuggle your own experience out under cover of weather. Greenwood in the storm is a philosophy of language compressed into one drenched old man.

Contraband: the sacred body

And then, buried inside the Rappite section, the most surprising thing in the book. Frederick Rapp, the adopted son, was a pantheist inside a community built on denying nature. He believed, Young writes, that God is everywhere, inhering in “the feathery catkins of the willow, the pyramids of the horse-chestnut.” The whole physical universe was the body of God, and God was “a huge animal without eyes,” because there is nothing outside God for God to look on, “not even one small, wet violet.”

That theology does not point up toward heaven, or out toward some transcendent truth. It points down and in, into the actual willow, the actual violet. The divine is not the opposite of the physical world. It is the physical world, all of it, seen. This is the sacred exactly as Radical Immanence describes it: not a signpost to something beyond the ordinary, but the ordinary itself given its full weight. The bus, the cup of tea, the wet violet. Frederick found the tenth pillar a century and a half early, and he found it in the last place you would look, in the heart of a community whose entire economy ran on the conviction that the body is a cost and the physical world a snare.

That is why it reads like contraband. Frederick’s eyeless God is everything Father Rapp’s Harmony refused. Harmony said the body was the obstacle to the spirit and cut it away, castrated the dogs and the son alike. Frederick said the body of the world was where God actually lived. He kept carving his golden rose and playing his flute in the middle of a machine designed to prove him wrong, and Young lets his heresy stand as the truest thing anyone in the Rappite chapters believes.

What Young shows

There is a long tradition of arguing that utopias fail because they suppress the body, and it would be easy to file Young under it and move on. Plenty of critics have made the general case that any plan for a perfected society ends up at war with appetite, with sex, with the stubborn animal facts of the people it means to perfect. Young knows this. But she is not making the general case. She is doing something harder and more useful. She is showing you the specific bodies. John Rapp near the piggery. Mrs. Pears blind at her sewing. Hectorina Grant’s dead child. The dancers black to the knee. Greenwood in the rain with his rod. She does not argue that the body defeats the utopia. She just keeps the body in the frame until you cannot unsee it, and then the defeat is obvious.

Both communities had a theory of what a person is. Rapp’s person was a will to be dissolved into the general harmony. Owen’s person was a mind to be correctly educated. Neither theory had a place for the thing that gets malaria, wants its wife, goes blind sewing, grows old and hurts and wants to be laid in the orchard. And the thing without a place in the theory was the thing that was actually there, in the mud, the whole time.

Radical Immanence starts where both utopias refused to start. It says the body is not the obstacle to the sacred but the location of it. It says a philosophy that cannot describe an old man’s readiness to die is not more spiritual than one that can, only more dishonest. The people at New Harmony were not failing at utopia when they got sick and grieved and wanted things. That was the truth the utopia was built to deny. Young’s method is to refuse the denial, to stay in the room with the body until the body has had its say. The wet violet outlasts the harmony. The daughter with the twinkle in her eye grows up. The sentence does not end where the theory wanted it to.
angel-post-14-the-sacred-without-transce:
Chapter 14. The Sacred Without Transcendence: Young’s Secular Theology

← Chapter 13 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters

Both utopias in this book believed in transcendence. Rapp’s people believed in a heaven above, a New Jerusalem descending from the sky. Owen’s people believed in a perfected future ahead, a New Moral World that reason would build. One pointed up and one pointed forward, but both located the real, the meaningful, the sacred, somewhere other than here. And both failed. The obvious conclusion, the one a colder writer would draw, is that meaning was a delusion all along, that with heaven and progress both exposed as lies there is nothing left but mud and malaria and the indifferent river. Young does not draw that conclusion. This is the most important thing about her, and the hardest to say without sounding sentimental, so I will try to say it carefully. She removes both guarantees, the God above and the Progress ahead, and what she finds underneath them is not emptiness. It is the ordinary world, and it turns out to be enough. Not enough as a consolation prize. Enough, full stop.

The footprint

Consider the angel’s footprint. Somewhere in old Harmony the Rappites left a slab of stone with a footprint pressed into it, said to be the mark of an angel who descended to the earth. By 1940 the weather had worn part of it away, so an odd-jobs man from twenty miles up the river was hired, at fifty cents an hour, to chisel it back into shape. Young watches him work. He chews a straw. He wears a hat with holes cut for air. He has no opinion on whether an angel was ever really there, but he reasons, sensibly enough, that if there had been no angel he would not be putting the footprints back, would he? The work means shoes for his baby, whose toes stick out. Everything in this scene is available for mockery, and a lesser writer would take it: the manufactured relic, the credulous restoration, the whole apparatus of a miracle being re-carved by a man who needs the wage. Young does not mock it, and if you read her carefully you see why. The footprint is real. It is an actual stone with an actual shape cut into it, and people actually come to look. The meaning of the footprint is made, not found, made by the Rappites who first carved it, made again by the man re-carving it now, made a third time by the pilgrim who stands before it. Young’s whole theology is in her refusal to say that a made meaning is a false one. The meaning is real precisely because it is made, here, by people, in this world, with a chisel, for shoes. There is no angel. There is a footprint, and there are the human hands that keep it, and that is not less than the sacred. It is where the sacred actually lives.

The golden rain trees

Or consider the golden rain trees. The Owenites planted them as a sign of the New Moral World that was coming. The New Moral World did not come. But in 1940, in the shops on Brewery and Church Streets, you could still buy the trees, six shoots for twenty-five cents, “guaranteed to grow in any temperate latitude.” The sign outlived the thing it was meant to signify. The utopia is dust and the tree is still in bloom, still for sale, still growing wherever the climate allows. There is a entire argument in that fact, and Young lets the fact carry it. The Owenites thought the trees pointed forward to a redeemed future. The trees did not care about the future. They were only ever trees, and being only trees, they persisted, while the redeemed future that was supposed to give them meaning quietly failed to arrive. And here is enormous. The trees did not lose their meaning when the New Moral World failed. They gained a different one. They became themselves, ordinary golden-flowering trees a person can plant in a yard for a quarter, and that ordinary fact is more durable than any moral world, and quietly more beautiful. The sacred survived, not in the sign’s pointing forward, but in the tree’s staying put.

A God that cannot see itself

Behind all of this stands the one theology in the book that Young clearly loves, the heresy of Frederick Rapp, the pantheist hidden inside the community that denied the flesh. He believed God was everything, and therefore that God was “a huge animal without eyes,” because there is nothing outside God for God to look at, “not even one small, wet violet.” This is Young’s own sense of the sacred, handed to a minor character to say. A God with no outside is a God that cannot transcend anything, because there is nowhere beyond it to stand. A God that is everywhere is a God with no special address in the sky, no elsewhere it points to. It is immanent all the way down. It is the willow and the horse-chestnut and the wet violet, and it is nothing in addition to them, nothing behind them, nothing they are a sign of. The sacred here is not a light shining through the world from somewhere else. It is the world, attended to closely enough that its own strangeness becomes visible. Not one small, wet violet is left out, and not one small, wet violet points anywhere but at itself.

The ferry

You can find this theology already at work in the book’s first paragraph, before a word of history has been spoken, if you know to look for it. The book opens on a ferry. “You come to old New Harmony by a creaking ferry.” There are sandpipers migrating between the two shores, building not nests but holes in the mudbanks, so that the hills seem coated with golden birds. There are, likely enough, two blind mules riding along as fellow passengers, with translucent logs of fallen birch tied behind them. The ferryman, likely enough, will never say a word. A barge turns at the bend of the hills, the bargeman standing with his legs spread wide against a cloudless sky. Read as scene-setting, this is atmosphere, a slow and pretty way into the book. But it is not scene-setting. It is a demonstration. Young is showing you, in the first thing she does, what her whole method comes down to: this quality of attention, this willingness to look at a blind mule and a silent ferryman and a mudbank full of ordinary birds with the same seriousness a believer brings to an altar. The sacred is already fully present on that ferry, before any angel, before any utopia, before any word of history. It is present in the attention itself. Nothing has to descend from the sky to make the crossing matter. The looking is what makes it matter, and the looking is available to anyone.

The crossing point

There is a particular feeling that Angel in the Forest is built to produce, and it belongs to the eleventh pillar, the crossing point. It is the sensation of suddenly seeing the structure you have been standing inside all along. You are on the ferry, in the ordinary present, in 1940 or in your own year, and the whole weight of what made this moment possible comes up through the ground beneath you: the utopians and the Indians one layer below them, the language you are thinking in, the trees somebody planted, the footprint somebody carved and somebody re-carved. And at the same time you feel, faintly, the weight of what you are laying down for whoever crosses this river after you. You are not passing through the world. You are the place where its past and its future cross. Young does not state this as a doctrine. She produces it as an experience, by the slow accumulation of attended-to ordinary things, until the reader feels the crossing point rather than being told about it. That is what the book is for. That is the sensation it was built to leave you holding.

What she gives us to hold

So here is the question the book is quietly answering, and here asking directly. After you take away God, and after you take away Progress, after both the heaven above and the perfect future ahead have been shown to be lies people build and then die inside of, what is left to hold onto? Young’s answer is one word, and it is not a grand word. Attention. That is all, and it is everything. The sacred is not somewhere else, waiting to redeem this world. It is here, in the wet violet and the blind mule and the re-carved footprint and the tree you can buy for a quarter, and it becomes visible only when someone bothers to look at it honestly and without turning away. This is harder than believing in heaven, because heaven does the work for you and attention you have to do yourself, every day, at whatever the wage. And it is more sustaining than believing in Progress, because Progress is always about to arrive and attention is available right now. The two utopias reached past the world for their meaning, and the world killed them for it. Young stayed in the world, on the ferry, looking, and found that the world, looked at closely enough, does not need anything beyond it. The footprint is real. The tree is still growing. The violet is still wet. All the reader has to do which is also the hardest to do is look.

Chapter 5. Robert Owen and the Erasure of the Irrational

← Chapter 4 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 6 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest Chapter 5

Rapp demanded that his people submit to God. Owen demanded that his people submit to Reason. These look like opposite projects, the mystic and the scientist, the celibate order and the free-thinking commune, and Young grants Owen a sympathy she never quite extends to Rapp. But the deepest thing her book shows is that the two utopias failed in the same shape. A total vocabulary was imposed on a plural population, and the people who did not fit the vocabulary were not argued with. They were made invisible. Where Rapp could not see anyone who was not a future angel, Owen could not see anyone who was not a machine.

The right diagnosis and the wrong cure

Owen believed that man is entirely the creature of his circumstances. Change the circumstances, he held, and you change the man completely, because there is nothing to a person except the conditions that formed him. This was not a cruel idea in its origin. Young can see exactly what Owen saw, and so can we. He had run the cotton mills at New Lanark, and he had looked hard at what industrial capitalism did to the people caught in it, the mill children, the skeletal workers, the whole machinery of poverty grinding human beings down. His diagnosis of that suffering was not wrong. The conditions really were making the people. That much he saw clearly, and it is to Young's credit that she lets him be right about it.

The trouble is the cure. If a person is nothing but the product of circumstances, then to fix the person you rebuild the circumstances and treat the human being inside them as a mechanism to be adjusted. The diagnosis that begins in compassion for the mill children ends in a community where the members are handled like parts. Owen's science of society could relieve suffering only by first deciding that a person is a machine, and a machine has no inner life to consult, no grief that counts, no longing that means anything. The reduction that made the reform possible is the same reduction that made the reform unlivable.

This is the point the philosophy makes when it says reality is something we build, not something we simply find. Owen was certain he had discovered the objective truth of human nature, the science of society, as solid as physics. He did not notice that "man is a machine formed by circumstance" is a constructed version of reality exactly as much as "man is a future angel" is. Both men mistook the version they had built for the world itself, and both then tried to force the world to match. Owen's rationalism felt to him like the truth and looked to Young like one more cathedral of belief, this time in the vocabulary of mechanism.

The Pears family, writing home

The clearest view of what this felt like from the inside comes from the letters of Thomas and Sarah Pears, who arrived at New Harmony as believers and wrote home to Pittsburgh in a mounting confusion that Young lets us read almost in real time.

Sarah Pears could not make the new life mean anything. Her eyes had gone bad from endless sewing, so bad she could barely lift her hand before her face, and she wrote that at times she felt like an animated mummy. She cast, in her own phrase, many a long and lingering look back toward Pittsburgh, toward old Sabbath bells and conversation and the things she had loved, and she said she felt like a bird shut in a cage forever, out of humanity's reach. Her husband fared no better. Thomas Pears was made the community's bookkeeper, and when, in the general confusion, he debited and credited the same sum twice, he was dismissed. Young sees the real reason plainly: the Committee, that great God on wheels, had objected to his soul, to his idea of the pursuit of happiness. Having lost the books, he was put to sorting and picking wool, work he compared to being a slave in the South, and he wrote that he had almost taken to singing shanty songs, as if that could carry the humiliation.

The letters are documentary testimony, and Young uses them that way, as the ground-level record of a rational utopia. But they are also something the science of society had no place for. Sarah's homesickness, Thomas's shame, the small grief of a woman who misses her city and a man who has been demoted for having a soul: none of this exists in Owen's vocabulary. Circumstances do not have feelings. A machine does not long for Pittsburgh. The dancers who walked to the community balls through the mud and arrived black from head to foot are a perfect small image of the whole thing, people trying to reach the promised happiness and showing up filthy, and no line in the science of society can hold what that was like for them. Their experience was real and their utopia had no words for it, which meant that inside the utopia their experience did not officially exist.

The declaration that came too late

The high point of Owen's abstraction is the Declaration of Mental Independence, which he delivered on the Fourth of July, 1826, from Father Rapp's own old pulpit, the very spot from which Rapp had preached submission. Owen announced that mankind had always been enslaved by a trinity of monstrous evils: private property, absurd and irrational systems of religion, and marriage founded on property and religion together. He thought the document more important than the one the founding fathers had signed fifty years before. He started a new calendar from the date. He predicted that within twelve months the principles would begin to overshadow the whole earth.

Young sets this against what was actually happening in the town at that moment, and the contrast is quiet and merciless. While Owen declared the liberation of all mankind, the community around him was coming apart. The members, one observer reported, passed and repassed each other daily and remained perfect strangers, ignorant of one another's feelings, situations, and very often names. A large patch of cabbages rotted from neglect while people argued. Pigs and cows wandered in through the widening holes in the fences. The potatoes rotted in the ground. Owen was addressing all mankind from a pulpit while the people fifteen feet in front of him were hungry, homesick, and unknown to each other. The word "ought," as Young puts it, is a different thing from the word "is." People of fifty summers could not reduce themselves to bald sucklings and be born again as rational creatures on command. The declaration was pitched at a level of abstraction so high that it could not reach a single person in the room.

Old Greenwood in the lightning

The book's sharpest image of what Owen's vocabulary could not hold is old Greenwood, and it deserves to be examined closely. During a summer of terrible storms in New Harmony's second year, Robert Dale Owen, the founder's son, looked out a window into the green light of a thunderstorm and saw old Greenwood walking slowly up and down the flooded street, drenched, going nowhere, carrying upright over his shoulder a slender iron rod ten or twelve feet long, held the way a soldier carries a musket, while lightning tore across the sky and trees came down around him. Robert Dale could make no sense of it. He wondered whether the old man had simply lost his reason and lacked the sense to come in out of the rain.

Later Greenwood explained himself, and his explanation is entirely lucid. He was very old, he said, and unwell, and he suffered much, and he had thought the storm might be a chance to slip off and be laid quietly in the corner of the orchard. He had not wanted to take the responsibility of ending his own life, so he had gone out under the lightning and left the decision to God, who had already struck the house and the colt and the orchard trees and might have spared one more blow for him. There is nothing insane in this. It is the plain speech of an old man in pain who wants his suffering to end and will not raise his own hand to end it. But Owen's rational community has no noun for it. In the vocabulary of mechanism and circumstance, a suffering old man who wants to die is a malfunction, an eccentricity, a Fool of Nature. The science of society can register that Greenwood is behaving irrationally. It cannot hear what he is actually saying, because his whole condition, the weariness of a long life and the wish to be released from it, is written in a language the utopia does not speak. This is the violence the philosophy means when it says that when the official vocabulary has no word for your experience, you are not just misunderstood, you are made not to exist. Greenwood stands in the lightning fully present and fully articulate, and the rational world can only see a man too foolish to come inside.

Dublin, and the reply Owen could not hear

The clearest proof that Owen's problem was a problem of language, and not merely of tact, is what happened when he took his science to Ireland. Speaking before an audience of Catholic divines in Dublin, he told them, more or less, that the potato was worthier of study than the garments priests wore and miraculous food from heaven, that the humble potato would not multiply because priests wore its flowers in their hats, and that if more potatoes were raised there would be fewer souls migrating to another sphere. Grow the food, fix the circumstance, and the misery dissolves. It was his whole gospel in miniature.

The Catholic divines gave their answer, and the answer is not stupid. They spoke of the ravens who neither sow nor reap, whom God feeds anyway, and asked how much better than the birds a man might be. They said that no system could strip human nature of its frailties on this side of paradise, that suffering was not an error to be engineered out of the world but a condition through which vision came, and that the greater the suffering the greater the good that might be seen in it. The lowliest housemaid, they said, might have received the most exalted vision of all. And they asked the question that goes straight to the root of Owen's project: what man, merely by the employment of reason, could add one cubit to his stature, or take away an inch?

That is not superstition dressed up. It is a rival theory of the person, one that holds the human being to be more than the sum of his circumstances, and holds suffering to carry a meaning that no rearrangement of conditions could replace. Owen could not engage it, and the reason he could not is the crux of that chapter. He did not lose the argument with the divines. He never entered it, because his framework had already decided that what they were describing did not exist. To Owen there was reality, which was mechanism and circumstance, and there was error, which was everything else, and the divines had simply been filed under error before they opened their mouths. A vocabulary that begins by ruling the opponent out of existence cannot be argued with, only escaped, and no one in that room could escape it.

The same erasure, wearing reason's clothes

Honestly, it took me a while to understand why Young didn’t make Owen’s utopia the answer to Rapp’s. I wanted to believe that there was a reasonable answer to life. Young is fair to Owen. He was kinder than Rapp, his intentions were better, his diagnosis of industrial misery was largely correct, and he never castrated anyone or promised anyone an angel. But the structure of his failure is the same structure, and Young built the two utopias side by side so that we would feel the sameness underneath the difference. Rapp imposed a single vocabulary, the future angel, and could not see the plural people underneath it. Owen imposed a single vocabulary, the machine formed by circumstance, and could not see Sarah Pears missing Pittsburgh, or Thomas Pears demoted for having a soul, or old Greenwood asking the lightning for rest, or the Catholic divines describing a person that reason could not reduce.

Submission to Reason turns out to erase the individual as thoroughly as submission to God, and it does it by the same method, which is a method of language. Both utopias handed everyone a complete account of what a human being is, and then stopped being able to perceive the humans who did not match the account. What the official vocabulary cannot name, it does not correct or convert. It simply makes them disappear, and calls the disappearance reason.
angel-post-04-father-rapp-and-the-constr:
Chapter 4. Father Rapp and the Construction of a Self

← Chapter 3 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 5 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 4

If you wanted to design the most extreme possible attempt to make many people into one person, you could hardly do better than George Rapp's community. Everything this study has been circling, the plural self, the constructed reality, the suppression of difference, has a limit case, and Young found it in the celibate order that built the first Harmony. The Rappites did not merely encourage conformity. They set out to erase the individual so completely that the members would become identical, sexless, and interchangeable, a single angelic type repeated seven hundred times. The interest of Young's account is that she shows exactly what that project costs, and exactly why it cannot hold.

The theology and the machine

Rapp's people believed they were becoming angels. Not metaphorically. They held that the true human state was asexual, that Adam's fall was sexual reproduction itself, and that to climb back toward the angelic condition a person had to give up the body's continuation entirely. From this followed total celibacy, enforced across the whole community, and from that, in Young's flat phrasing, the theology afforded an excuse for the most drastic measures, even emasculation. She does not look away from this and she does not soften it. She lets you see the full brutality of a belief followed all the way to its end.

What she notices, and what makes the chapter more than a horror story, is that the theology and the account book are the same machine. She points out that before the edict of celibacy, Rappite babies had arrived at regular intervals but never at harvest time, and draws the dry conclusion that Rapp's harmony was a form of economy. The suppression of sex was also the suppression of any drain on the corporation. The producer, she writes, is forced to lop off his own branch of the tree of life so that the books may show a steady increase in earnings. Rapp had learned from the new preachers who talked about birth control and soil preservation, and he harnessed the new science to the old religion. From complete birth control, Young writes, it was a short road to the complete death of the individual will and the simplified angelic state, its weakest echo. The angel and the ledger want the same thing: a member who takes up no room of his own, who does not reproduce, who does not want, who sinks, in her exact words, to the level of the general desire. That sentence sums up the entire logic of the community. If the community is to be preserved, the individual must be destroyed. Once you accept that premise, everything that follows, the celibacy, the emasculation, the nameless graves, proceeds with a horrible internal consistency. Young's achievement is to show you that consistency from the inside, so that you understand it even as it appalls you.

This is the political point the philosophy names when it says the demand for a single fixed identity is not natural but a tool. Systems that need to sort people need simple people. Rapp needed future angels, maximally identical, maximally sortable, all facing the same direction. The seven hundred actual human beings underneath that demand were the raw material the machine existed to simplify.

How Young stays in the room

The easy thing would be to file Rapp as a monster or to rescue him as a misunderstood visionary. Young does neither, and her refusal is itself a method. Her Rapp is grotesque and, in his own way, great, a tyrant and a mountebank and also unforgettable, a man she will forgive even his monstrous theories of sex without ever pretending they were anything but monstrous. She holds the two judgments at once and lets neither win.

The clearest case is the angel. Rapp said he had seen an angel descend in the old Harmony in Pennsylvania, and that it left its footprints pressed into a slab of stone. Was the angel real? Was Rapp a madman, or a liar, or a man who genuinely saw something? Young allows the question to float and never brings it down. She does not debunk the angel and she does not endorse it. She keeps it suspended as a permanent condition of the book, because the honest answer is that we cannot know, and pretending otherwise, in either direction, would be a lie about the limits of what a history can settle. Staying in the room with an unresolved thing, refusing to force it into a verdict, is the discipline this philosophy calls the witness, and the angel is where Young practices it most purely.

Frederick, the seam in the leadership

The proof that Rapp's system could not hold its own members is standing right next to Rapp the entire time. Frederick, his adopted son and the community's lord temporal, the number two man in the whole order, was a pantheist and a lover of nature living in the heart of a community organized around denying nature. He believed that God is all, that God is everywhere, that the whole body of the universe was the body of God, a huge animal without eyes, because there is nothing outside God for God to look on, not even one small, wet violet.

Read what that belief actually reveres. Frederick's God exists permanently and inseparably as an essential, natural and intrinsic part of everything, from the catkins of the willow and the buds of the ash, to the mayfly that lives a day and the whale that lives four hundred years, to the flower distended for the bee and the sexual juices and the endless business of procreation. He worshipped exactly the fecundity his community existed to renounce. The harmony he loved was, in Young's phrase, larger than Harmony, the whole teeming reproductive world that Rapp had declared to be the fall. And this man was not an outsider or a dissident. He was the co-ruler. The seam does not show at the edge of the community, among some marginal heretic. It shows at the very top, in the second most powerful person in the order. A schema that cannot contain its own lord temporal without contradiction is a schema that was never holding anything. It was only pressing down, and the pressure was visible in the leadership itself.

The Coming of One

The deepest illustration of all this is the chapter Young calls "The Coming of One," and it deserves to be told in full, because it is the perfect experiment: what happens to a community organized entirely around awaiting a single redemptive figure when one actually arrives.

The Rappites had spent decades waiting for the One, the promised figure who would confirm everything. In July of 1829 a magnificently embossed letter reached them from Frankfurt, announcing Count Maximilian de Leon, the Great Ambassador and Anointed One of God, descendant of the Stem of Judah and the Root of David, child of Abraham and Isaac and Solomon, enemy of Cain and Herod and Pontius Pilate, came to America as the last hope of salvation. Rapp, flattered, invited him. It took two years for the Count to cross. When he finally rolled into Economy on a fine autumn day in 1831, the whole community lined the streets with offerings of late flowers while the band played from the church tower, and the herdsmen blew their horns three times as if to welcome a heavenly host.

Out of the curtained carriage stepped the long-expected One: a corpulent, fat gentleman, nothing ethereal, in purple and green broadcloth, blond curls draped over his collar, a golden book in his green-gloved hands. Three chins. Kid gloves. Peacock struttings. His real name was Bernard Mueller. He was a traveling salesman with no means but the borrowed clothes on his back and, in Young's devastating phrase, the idea of happiness.

The arrival of the promised One did not seal the single-self project. It detonated it. The Count did not preach uniformity. He went through Economy person by person, learning each member's private history, and then he climbed into the pulpit and preached the exact opposite of everything Rapp had built. Every man, he said, was a world shut inside himself, onion skin within onion skin, mystery within mystery, which only God could peel. He asked the questions the individual asks when it reasserts itself against the organization that has been imposed: why were the graves nameless, where were the unborn children, who would carry on the family names, why had no one ever been shown the corporation's books. And he offered what Rapp had spent his life abolishing: marriage, the body, individual desire, restored not at the end of time but here and now.

A third of the community left with him. Of seven hundred members, two hundred fifty deserted, husband and wife retiring to separate camps, brother and sister taking opposite sides. It happened, Young writes, quietly, with no argument, only a division of the odd from the even, the fat from the lean. And in that division something is revealed that Rapp had spent decades hiding: the community was never one self. It was seven hundred plural people held under pressure, and the instant a figure arrived who named them as separate mysteries, a third of them came apart from the whole. The Count was, in Young's pun, a judgment on economy, on the town and on the entire economy of selfhood-suppression that built it. He was the return of everything Rapp had repressed, and he arrived, devastatingly, wearing the costume the system itself had taught everyone to wait for. The machine of uniformity contained the seed of its own shattering, because the raw material was never uniform to begin with.

Neither one works

Young does not turn the Count into a hero, which is the final proof of her honesty. The restoration of the flesh he offered was its own fiasco. He was a fraud and a bachelor and a gambler, interested in no one but himself and possibly his secretary. He blew through the settlement money in six months, his followers turned into a band of scarecrows squatting on bare ground, and when the Leonites tried to raid Economy for its hams they were driven off by the Rappite women with hot water and brooms and kicks. The Count absconded down the Red River and died of cholera. His community of honeymooners failed as completely as Rapp's community of angels.

That is the shape of Young's witness. She watches the machine that destroys the individual, and she watches the counter-figure who promises to liberate the individual, and she lets both of them fail without choosing a winner. She does not resolve Rapp into a villain or the Count into a savior. She keeps them both suspended, exactly as she keeps the angel suspended, because the truth is that neither the suppression of the plural self nor its cheap liberation actually delivered what it promised.

What Rapp's case leaves us with is the first and hardest lesson of the book. You cannot make many people into one self. You can demand it, enforce it, build a theology and an account book and a celibate order around it, press seven hundred people down toward a single angelic type for decades. And the plurality you suppress does not go away. It waits underneath, and it comes back, sometimes in the very form your own longing prepared for it, and when it comes back it takes a third of everything with it.

Chapter 8. Grief That Does Not Resolve

← Chapter 7 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 9 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 8

There are two ways to write about a thing that failed, and they feel completely different. One is tragedy. The other is elegy. Angel in the Forest is an elegy, and understanding the difference is the key to the emotional life of the book.

Tragedy resolves. It has a shape that completes itself: a rise, a fall, a moment of recognition, and then the strange peace that comes when the arc closes. Tragedy takes suffering and converts it into form, and the form is a consolation. You watch the hero go down, and something in you is purged and released, and you walk out having been through something and come out the other side. The doom means something. The ending settles.

Elegy does not resolve. It is mourning without the catharsis. The loss is not turned into meaning and handed back to you as a lesson. It is simply carried. An elegy does not end so much as it trails off, the way grief itself does not end but only thins and returns. There is no purge, no release, no redemption of the loss. You just go on missing the thing.

Young chose elegy, and she chose it for a hard reason. Tragedy needs the doom to be significant, needs the fall to matter cosmically, needs a flaw grand enough to ennoble the ruin. Young denies all of that. As this study has traced, the utopias were not brought down by a tragic flaw that dignifies them. They were doomed from the start by a plain structural error, a fixed account of human nature that could not hold the actual people. There is no catharsis available because there is nothing to purge; the failure was in the premise. And yet, here is the difficulty of the book, she mourns them anyway. She grieves, fully and without irony, something she also understands completely to have been impossible from the first day. That is the emotional structure of Angel in the Forest: grief that lives alongside total understanding of why the thing had to fail, and is not cancelled by that understanding.

The happiness she refuses to correct

The clearest instance is a small one, near the end. Young reports that years after the collapse, a few old citizens still confessed that the Owen period, for all its chaos and uncertainty, had been the happiest time of their lives. They were younger then, she writes, and filled to the brim with hopefulness. There had been, in her phrase, a morning hour upon all sublunary things.

Watch what she does not do. She does not correct this memory. She could. A different writer would step in and explain that the happiness was a delusion, that the community was already unraveling underneath them, that they had been deceived by a charismatic man and a doomed idea. Young lets the remembered happiness stand, whole and uncorrected, right next to the complete record of the failure. Both are true. The happiness was real. The failure was real. And crucially, the happiness is not made false by the failure. This is the elegiac move in its purest form. The sweetness of the lost thing is not diminished by the knowledge that it was doomed. If anything the doom is exactly what makes it elegy and not mere nostalgia. They were happiest during the one thing that could not last, and knowing it could not last does not make them fools for having been happy. It makes them human, and it makes the loss permanent.

A landscape that is grief itself

Young's 1940 town is the same grief written into a place. The ten-cent store cobwebbed and insubstantial. The abandoned Catholic church where swallows have nested in the belfry and flutter back and forth like bells. The maze of Hebrew and Greek letters that was put up hastily to symbolize the transience of man, itself already crumbling. The outhouses leaning with time. The water tower under its ivy.

It would be easy to read this as picturesque decay, the pleasant melancholy of an old ruin, and Young shuts that reading down. This is not scenery. It is grief made visible in a landscape. The town does not charm; it mourns. The decay is the physical form the loss takes, the way a grieving person carries the dead in their body, and Young names the reason directly: nothing lingers so like the memory of failure. She adds the turn that makes New Harmony heavier than any ordinary ruin, which is that this failure had reached for the extreme perfection. The ruins of an ordinary town are just ruins. The ruins of a town that tried to build heaven are grief, because the height of what was wanted is the exact measure of what was lost. New Harmony's grayness weighs more than another town's because the dream that failed there was so much larger.

The one dynasty that does not fail

In a book about grief, the single permanent institution is the undertaker. Young notes that his was the only unbroken dynasty in New Harmony, and she is not making a dark joke. She is stating what survives failure. Every utopia that came through this place promised, one way or another, to defeat death, and every one of them was buried, and the man who buried them stayed in business the whole time. Burial is the one human activity that never becomes obsolete, never runs short of work, never fails. The undertaker is the elegiac condition turned into a profession: the one whose living depends on the permanence of loss.

And Young draws him with real tenderness. He is, she says, the kindest man on earth, holding mortgages he will not foreclose, always on his way from the grave to the cradle. That tenderness is not incidental. The keeper of grief is not a ghoul. He is a gentle man, because grief handled honestly is an act of care, and the person who gives the dead dreams a decent burial is doing something closer to love than to profit.

A frame that will not close

The deepest expression of all this is the shape of the book. It opens with a chapter called "New Harmony Today," a glimpse of the ruined town in the summer of 1940. It closes, four hundred pages later, with "Farewell to New Harmony," set on a summer day in the same ruined town in the same year. The book ends where it began. Nothing has been resolved.

A tragic structure would close that frame. We would return to the opening scene transformed, carrying the understanding we had earned, the arc complete, the catharsis delivered. Young returns us to exactly the same place with exactly the same question still hanging in the air, the one she asked on the first page and never answered: what dream among dreams is reality? The frame is left open on purpose. This is formal grief, mourning built into the architecture. You do not come out the other side of this book. You come back to where you started, still grieving, except that now the whole weight of the history is beneath you, pressing up. The elegy's trailing-off has been turned into a structure. The book refuses to end because grief does not end, and Young will not lie about that even in the shape of her chapters.

The grief is not for a fixable thing

Here is the point that holds the book together, the grief in Angel in the Forest is not grief for the loss of a correct utopia. It is not "if only they had done it right, it would have worked." That would be a fixable grief, a grief with a cure, and a grief with a cure is not really this book's grief at all.

Young is mourning something that has no cure. She is grieving the permanent human condition of wanting something that cannot be made permanent. The Rappites and the Owenites are not wept over because their particular blueprints failed. They are wept over because they are the sharpest possible instance of the universal thing: the longing to build something that will not change and will not die, held by creatures who live in a world where nothing holds still and everything they love keeps changing. That longing is not an error to be corrected. It is simply what people are. And it will always be defeated, every single time, because the impermanence it runs up against is the one truly permanent fact. So the grief cannot resolve, because the condition it mourns cannot resolve. You do not get over grieving the impermanence of what you love. The impermanence is forever. New Harmony is only the place where this ordinary, universal, endless grief was made unusually visible, because the people there wanted permanence so nakedly, and lost it so completely, that you can see in their small failed town the shape of everyone's.

That is why the book had to be an elegy and not a tragedy. Tragedy would have let us off. It would have converted the failure into meaning and sent us home purged and released. Young will not let us off, because to resolve the grief would be to lie about the condition that produces it. So the frame stays open, and the town stays gray, and the question stays unanswered, and the grief stays exactly where it is. And there is something in that refusal that is not bleak at all. To carry a loss honestly, without converting it into a consolation you have not earned, is itself a form of faithfulness to the thing you lost. The elegy that does not resolve is the truest love the dead can be given.
