Chapter 11. The Figure on the Margin: Eccentrics, Fools, and the Hermaphrodite Angel

← Chapter 10 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 12 →

In the first pages of Angel in the Forest, before she has told you much of anything about history, Young gives you a list of the people who once walked the streets of New Harmony. It is one of the strangest sentences in the book. She lists, among others, an angel like a hermaphrodite butterfly, a Daniel Boone of the infinite, a finite Elijah, a herb doctor, a celibate breeder of horses, the Spirit of Nature, rational man, irrational men. She does not stop to explain any of them. She sets them down, one after another, and lets them stand, and then she tells you that the list does not begin to exhaust the possibilities. This is not a decorative flourish. It is a thesis about where truth is found. The people who do not fit are not the exceptions to New Harmony. They are the clearest description of it.

This is the seventh pillar of Radical Immanence, and Young builds a method on it. The idea is easy to state and hard to live by. Categories look natural from the inside. It is only at the edges, where someone fails to fit, that you can see the category was drawn by hand. A person who is neither fully male nor fully female shows you that the line between male and female was a decision. A person who is at once celibate and a breeder shows you that abstention and fecundity were only ever placed on opposite sides of a border someone invented. The eccentric is not a footnote to the system. The eccentric is the exposed seam, the place where the stitching shows.

The hermaphrodite butterfly angel

Look at the figures Young chose, because each one collapses a distinction the community depended on. The hermaphrodite butterfly angel folds together the angelic and the animal, the male and the female, the celestial and the earthly. A butterfly is an insect. An angel is a spirit. A hermaphrodite is neither one sex nor the other. Stack all three into a single figure and you have a being that cannot be filed under any of the community’s headings. It is heaven and dirt at once. Later Young turns the same figure against the Owenites, when Owen, speaking from Rapp’s old pulpit, declares the worship of “the hermaphrodite butterfly, exaggerated to the status of angel” happily finished. But you cannot legislate a figure like that out of existence. It survives precisely because it refuses the category. The thing both utopias wanted gone is the thing that reveals what both utopias were built to exclude.

The celibate breeder of horses

Rapp’s community practiced total celibacy and yet ran, in part, on the breeding of animals. The order that would not reproduce itself made a living reproducing horses. Hold that contradiction and you can see the shape of the Rappite economy in one impossible person: abstention for the people, fecundity for the livestock, the reproductive drive forbidden in humans and harnessed in the barn. The celibate breeder is not a joke. He is the Rappite economy walking around on two legs.

The Daniel Boone of the infinite

Young takes the great figure of American frontier expansion and aims him at metaphysics. Boone went looking for elbow room in the wilderness. The Daniel Boone of the infinite goes looking for elbow room in eternity, in the endless spiritual real estate of a New Jerusalem or a New Moral World. He collapses the frontier and the afterlife, the surveyor and the mystic. He shows you that the utopian and the pioneer are the same person facing two different directions, and that the promised land of the soul and the promised land of the map were always the same appetite.

The Fool of Nature

Young gives a chapter the title “The Fool of Nature,” and the fool keeps returning throughout the book, not as one man but as a recurring presence. He is the figure who, by refusing or failing to keep the social grammar, exposes how arbitrary that grammar is. When the fool speaks, the sensible people around him look, for a moment, no more sensible than he is. Near the end, Young lets the Fool rise like Triton from the waves and turn into an octopus with a golden book in every hand, and a different writing in every book. That is the fool’s function. He holds a different reading of the world in each hand and refuses to settle on one. The universe, from where he stands, is a series of illusions of grandeur, and he is right, and everyone treats him as mad. The community needs him to be mad. If he is sane, then its single official reading of the world is only one book among many.

Count Maximilian de Leon

And then there is the false messiah, who earns his own section because Young’s handling of him is a small masterpiece. Into Rapp’s community, which had waited decades for the second Coming of One, there arrives a letter announcing Count Maximilian de Leon, “the Great Ambassador and Anointed One of God,” descended from “the Stem of Judah and the Root of David,” child of Moses and Abraham and Solomon, the Lion of the Tribe of Judah. The Rappites line the streets. The band plays from the church tower. The herald blows his trumpet. And out of the curtained carriage steps a corpulent, blond gentleman in purple and green broadcloth, a golden book open in his green-gloved hands. It is very funny. But Young is doing more than comedy. De Leon is not simply a con man who fooled a gullible sect. He is the logical product of the sect’s own grammar. A community that organizes its entire existence around awaiting a single anointed figure has, in effect, issued an open invitation. When you build a world that requires a messiah, a messiah will arrive, and he will look exactly like this: fat, blond, green-gloved, and completely certain. The fraud is not a failure of the system. It is the system working as designed. The margin, once again, says the thing the center cannot say about itself.

What the self actually looks like

These figures share one more thing, and it points at the first pillar as much as the seventh. The hermaphrodite angel, the celibate breeder, the Daniel Boone of the infinite are all figures of plural, unstable selfhood. Each of them is two or three things at once that are supposed to be mutually exclusive. Each is exactly what a self looks like once you drop the demand that a person be one consistent thing. Both utopias ran on that demand. Rapp needed his people single-mindedly bound for heaven. Owen needed his uniformly rational. The eccentrics are the ones who would not collapse into a single identity, and Young loves them for it, because they are the most honest people in the book. They are not failing to be whole. They are showing you that a person was never one thing to begin with.

It is hard, in the end, not to see Young herself in the hermaphrodite butterfly angel. She is a writer who will not be filed. Angel in the Forest is history and poetry and fiction and philosophy, all at once, and it refuses to settle into any one of them. Readers have always struggled to say what kind of book it is, which is another way of saying that Young, like her own angel, crosses the categories the reader arrives with. The figure at the margin, impossible to classify, turns out to be a self-portrait. She stationed her own image at the edge of her own book, where, by her own theory, the truth is most legible.

Chapter 13. Angel in the Forest as Laboratory

← Chapter 12 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 14 →

There is a temptation, with a writer’s first book, to read it as a warm-up. Angel in the Forest came out in 1945. Twenty years later Young published Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, a novel of some twelve hundred pages that took eighteen years to write and that a certain kind of reader considers one of the great American books of the century. It is easy to file the first book as apprentice work for the second. That would be a mistake. Angel in the Forest is not a rough draft. It is a laboratory. In it, working with the real history of two failed utopias, Young develops the questions and the methods that Miss MacIntosh will later carry into the interior of a single mind. The history is where she learned how to do it. The novel is where she did it at scale. Nothing essential changes between the two books except the size of the experiment.

You can see this in a single question, because it is the same sentence in both books. In his introduction to Angel in the Forest, Mark Van Doren quotes a line and says it comes from the earlier book but could just as well be in the later one, and probably is: what is the nature of experience, “what dream among dreams is reality?” The sentence is there in Angel, in the opening pages, asked of New Harmony. In Angel the question is asked about history. Which of these visions was real, the Rappite heaven or the Owenite machine, and was either of them any more real than the mud they were built in? In Miss MacIntosh the identical question is asked about consciousness, about one woman’s memory and one woman’s search. The question does not deepen or develop between the books. It is already fully formed in the first one. What changes is only what Young points it at. First history, then a mind.

The catalog

The first method the laboratory produces is the catalog, and it is the most visible thing about Young’s prose. In Angel, the lists organize the historical material. She does not summarize the goods that came out of Rapp’s Harmony. She pours them: wheat, corn, oats, hides, furs, butter, wax, deerskins, hogskins, bearskins, on and on until the sheer quantity of the world defeats any attempt to add it up. This is not a stylistic tic. It is an argument in the shape of a sentence. What Young discovers, writing the histories, is that accumulation is more honest than synthesis. A summary tells you the world adds up to a single point. A list refuses to. The list says: here is more, and more, and more, and it does not resolve into a tidy total, because the world does not. When she comes to write Miss MacIntosh, the same method is waiting, and she turns it on the inside of a person. The catalog that once held deerskins now holds memories, sensations, the endless furniture of a consciousness, and it does the same work it did in the history. It keeps the interior from freezing into a single tidy self, exactly as it kept the history from freezing into a single tidy meaning.

The past beneath the present

The second thing the laboratory produces is a way of handling time. Angel in the Forest is built on the discovery that the past is not behind the present but beneath it, pressing up. The book opens in 1940, on a ferry, and the utopian centuries are not gone from that scene. They are underneath it, in the golden rain trees still growing, in the re-carved footprint, in the Indian graves one layer below the Rappite ones. Past and present are simultaneous, stacked, weighing on one another. This is the eighth pillar, and Angel is where Young learns to write it. Miss MacIntosh then applies the same structure to a single life. Vera Cartwheel, who narrates the novel, stands in the same relation to her own past that New Harmony in 1940 stands to its utopian history. Her memory is not a record of things that are over. It is a set of layers pressing up through the present moment, exactly as the two utopias press up through the filling-station town. Young worked the structure out on a place first, then moved it into a person.

The witness

The third thing, and the deepest, is an ethical position, and Radical Immanence calls it the witness. In Angel, Young trains herself to stay in the room with contradiction and not force it shut. The faith is real and the folly is real, and she will not let one cancel the other. Rapp was a tyrant who castrated his son and a genuine spiritual leader who built a place of real intensity, and both are true, and she holds them both. Owen was a generous visionary and a man whose rational program let children die in the mud, and both are true, and she holds them both. This is very hard to do, and Angel in the Forest is her learning to do it, refusing the historian’s usual move of settling the account. Miss MacIntosh is that stance extended to enormous length, more than a thousand pages of staying present with a single consciousness and its contradictions without once forcing them to resolve. The witness is not a natural talent. It is a discipline, and you can watch her acquire it in the first book so that she can sustain it through the second.

The philosophy she was building

Here is the thing worth saying, at the end of a study that has been circling it. What Young is doing across these two books is not describing a philosophy. She is building one. The eleven pillars this study has mapped onto Angel in the Forest are not a grid pressed down onto her from outside. They are the shape of the thing she constructed, first in the laboratory of the history book and then at full scale in the novel. The plural self. The constructed reality. The grief that accumulates. The witness. The building without foundations. The unfinished that is not failed. The margin that tells the truth. The past beneath rather than behind. The language that decides what is real. The sacred located here, in the ordinary. And the crossing point, the self as the place where everything that made it possible meets everything it will make possible. Radical Immanence is not a lens borrowed to read Young. It is, more nearly, the name for what Young spent her life making, and Angel in the Forest is where she made the first working model.

So the two books are one project at two scales. Angel in the Forest asks what dream among dreams is reality, and asks it of a place and its history. Miss MacIntosh asks the identical question of a mind. The catalog, the simultaneous past, the witness who will not resolve the contradiction, all of it is worked out in the history and then carried, intact, into the fiction. The laboratory was not a lesser thing than the experiment it prepared. It was the place where the experiment became possible. To read Angel in the Forest as a warm-up for Miss MacIntosh is to miss that the questions were already whole, the methods already sharp, the philosophy already standing. What the twenty years bought was not a better set of tools. It was room to use them on the largest possible subject, which for Young was always the same subject: a single dreaming mind, trying to learn which of its dreams is real, never quite arriving, and building anyway.
angel-post-02-the-catalog-as-philosophic:
Chapter 2. The Catalog as Philosophical Instrument

← Chapter 1 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 3 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 2

Marguerite Young makes lists where another writer would make an argument. Open Angel in the Forest to almost any page and you find them: long runs of nouns, joined by commas, pouring past faster than you can hold them. It is easy to read these as exuberance, a poet who fell in love with her material and could not stop naming things. Mark Van Doren more or less says as much, describing the objects that stream across the book like cosmic dust. But the lists are not an overflow. They are the main tool Young works with, and they are doing a specific and deliberate job: they are proving, over and over, that the categories we sort human life into cannot actually hold human life.

It helps to be plain about what a list is, structurally, because the whole argument of this chapter turns on it.

An argument subordinates. It has a main point and supporting points. It ranks things. It moves in a direction, toward a conclusion, and along the way it throws out whatever does not serve the conclusion. That is what makes an argument feel like knowledge: it cuts. A list does the opposite. It coordinates. Every item sits at the same level as every other item, strung along by commas and the word "and," and nothing is subordinate to anything else. Nothing is the main point. Nothing is the conclusion. Where an argument builds a hierarchy, a list lays everything flat and keeps it all.

Once you see that, you can see why Young reaches for the list at exactly the moments when another historian would reach for a thesis. She does not want to rank the people of New Harmony or reduce them to a type. She wants to keep all of them. And keeping all of them, refusing to cut, turns out to be an argument in its own right, made at the level of grammar.

The inhabitants who fit nowhere

Look at how she names the people who passed through the town. She calls the roll of an angel like a hermaphrodite butterfly, a butterfly catcher, a Daniel Boone of the infinite, a finite Elijah, a herb doctor, Lot's wife, and on through clouded dreamers, a celibate breeder of horses, poor Yahoos, the Spirit of Nature, rational man, irrational men, patriarchs, and undertakers.

Read that as an argument and it looks like nonsense. Read it as a catalog and it becomes precise. Nearly every figure on the list is a person who breaks a category by standing inside two at once. The angel is a hermaphrodite and a butterfly, crossing sex, species, and the line between earth and heaven in a single phrase. A Daniel Boone of the infinite yokes the most local of frontiersmen to the boundless. A finite Elijah does the reverse, pinning a prophet who ascended into the sky back down to a finite life. Lot's wife is the woman who looked back at what she was told to leave behind and paid for the looking. These are not random. They are, one after another, people the sorting machines cannot sort.

That matters because the two utopias were nothing but sorting machines. Father Rapp's schema turned people into future angels. Robert Owen's schema turned people into machines shaped by circumstance. Between them they claimed to have accounted for what a person is. Young's catalog answers by naming a town full of people who are neither angels nor machines, who spill out of both systems, and it makes the answer without a word of overt disagreement. She simply lists the ones who do not fit, and the list is longer than either schema can absorb.

This is the point the philosophy calls attending to the margins. The people at the edges of a category, the ones whose bodies or minds or lives cross the lines the system drew, are usually treated as exceptions, footnotes, problems to be explained away. The edge is exactly where you can see that the line was drawn by someone, that it was made and not found. When Young pours out her hermaphrodite angels and finite prophets, she is not decorating the history. She is showing the seams. The catalog holds difference without flattening it into a type, which is the one thing an argument, with its need to conclude, can never do.

The flesh that came back as commerce

Her most quietly devastating list is an inventory. When she describes what the Rappite community sold, she lists the goods: wheat, corn, oats, hides, furs, butter, wax, horses, cattle, hogs, and so on down the line, then a second cascade of every skin and animal product a frontier economy could render down, deerskins and bearskins and wolfskins, otter and muskrat and beaver and mink, honey and eggs and bristles and tallow and feathers.

On its face this is dull, the kind of trade record a normal historian summarizes in a sentence and moves past. Young does not summarize it. She lets it run, and letting it run is the point because of who these people were. The Rappites were celibate. They had renounced the flesh, renounced marriage and children, and believed all things fleeting but themselves. And here is the community they built, generating a torrent of flesh: fur, hide, fat, bone, feather, egg. The list is dense with animal bodies and animal increase, an overwhelming record of fecundity produced by people who had officially given up on the body. Young names the irony without arguing it. She calls the whole cascade the products of a marvelously fecund nature, operated by celibates. The list has already made the case. You cannot renounce the flesh. It comes back, if not as sons and daughters then as bearskins and honey, as commerce, as the sheer productive weight of the world reasserting itself through the very people who tried to step out of it. No sentence of analysis could carry that as plainly as the inventory carries it.

The utopia that contained everything it excluded

The third list is the widest. Describing what the two communities somehow held inside half a square mile of wilderness, Young writes a catalog that yokes the cosmic to the trivial with no transition at all: the burning of Rome, city planning, explosion of stars, a new calendar, anarchy, a New Jerusalem, moneyless Eden, a three-hour working day, exaltation of horses, infinite regress, the united nations of earth, and, a few beats later in a companion list, good dentistry and baby owls.

The juxtapositions are the argument. Set the explosion of stars beside good dentistry, or a New Jerusalem beside the falling of autumn leaves, and you get the point without being told it: any real attempt to reorganize human life ends up containing all of human life, the sublime and the petty and the contradictory all at once. A utopia sets out to exclude the mistaken parts of existence, to keep only the reasonable, the elevated, the sortable. And the more completely it tries, the more completely it fills back up with everything it meant to leave out. Young says this outright, in one of the few places she lets the catalog resolve into a claim: such perfectionist orders, which would have excluded much of mistaken life, seem mistaken life itself, with all its infinite variety. The list is how she earns the right to say it. She shows you the infinite variety first, item by item, and only then names what it means.

What accumulation knows that argument cannot

So the honest question is the formal one. What does a list know that an argument does not?

An argument buys its coherence by cutting. It gives you a clean line of reasoning and a conclusion you can carry away, and the price is everything that got left on the floor to make the line look neat and clean. A list refuses to pay that price. It keeps the contradictions in the same breath, on the same level, unranked and unresolved, and what it gives you in return is not a conclusion but a whole thing, contradictions included. That is a real kind of knowledge, and it is not the kind synthesis produces. Synthesis tells you what a thing means once the mess has been cleared away. The catalog tells you what the thing is while the mess is still in it, which is the only condition the thing ever actually exists in.

This is also why the list is the right grammar for what Young believes. Standard sentences assume a world of stable things that do stuff, a subject that governs and a verb that acts and an object that receives, a small machine for turning the world into causes and effects. Young does not think the world holds still like that. Her catalogs are almost all noun and almost no verb, and crucially they refuse to let any single noun become the governing one. There is no subject ruling the sentence, no main term the others serve. Everything is a coordinate, everything is kept, nothing is allowed to settle into the stable center that ordinary grammar demands. This is the same instinct the first chapter traced in her restless sentences, working now at a different scale. Where the standard vocabulary makes it hard to describe a world of process and contradiction, Young builds a grammar of accumulation that can hold exactly that.

The list, in other words, is not the poet losing control of the history. It is the philosopher choosing the only instrument honest enough for the job. To witness a place without rushing it toward a conclusion, to hold everything that was really there without deciding which parts were allowed to be real, you do not make an argument. You make a catalog, and you let it stay open.
angel-post-12-america-as-promised-land-t:
Chapter 12. America as Promised Land: The Utopian National Myth

← Chapter 11 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 13 →

The question at the center of the book is one Young mostly leaves for the reader to notice. Why here? Why did a German peasant and an English cotton lord, two men who agreed on almost nothing, both cross an ocean to build their perfect worlds on the same muddy bend of the Wabash in Indiana? They were not drawn by the soil, which bred malaria, or by the river, which was unnavigable half the year. They were drawn by an idea about the place, and the idea was older and larger than either of their utopias. America was the country where the past had been left behind, where the ground was clean, where a person or a people could start over from nothing. Young titles a chapter “America, the Promised Land,” and the book is, underneath its two failed communities, an examination of that phrase and what it costs.

The clean start is the American myth in its purest form, and it is exactly the lie that the eighth pillar of Radical Immanence exists to refuse. The past does not go away. It does not stay behind you. It accumulates beneath you, in the ground, in the arrangements of the present, in the bodies of the people the story stepped over. New Harmony looked, to Owen and to Rapp, like neutral ground, a blank slate on which a better human nature could be written. Young keeps showing you that the ground was never blank. Under the nameless graves of the Rappites, she notes, lay an Indian burial ground, its warriors and squaws and papooses and pottery and beads, one layer down. The Rappites in their gray gowns were only one layer above the people whose land it had been. The promised land was promised to the newcomers by erasing who had been promised it before. The clean start was a burial.

The two faces of one promise

The two utopias are the sacred and the secular versions of the same clean start. Rapp offered a scriptural redesign: leave the corrupt Old World, cross the water like the Israelites, and wait in the wilderness for the New Jerusalem. Owen offered a rational redesign: leave the superstitions of the past, apply the science of society, and manufacture a better human nature the way you would order a better cloth. Young quotes Owen turning to his son in the rose garden and proposing, “as casually as if he were ordering a fabric at the cotton mills,” that they should “manufacture a better human nature.” One promise wore Scripture and one wore science, but both promised the same thing, which is the thing America itself promised: that you could be made new by moving to a place where the past did not apply. Between them, the peasant and the cotton lord cover the whole of American faith.

Robert Dale Owen, from utopia to empire

The clearest single demonstration of where this promise leads is the life of Robert Dale Owen, and Young’s handling of it is one of the quietest, sharpest things in the book. He begins as a New Harmony radical, a young man who came to Indiana partly for utopia and partly for love of a mill girl named Jessie, and who believed in birth control, the unreality of God, liberation from the fear of death, and votes for women. Then the community fails, and he stays in America, and he goes into politics. He becomes an Indiana state senator, then a congressman. He lends his rhetoric to real and admirable causes, free public schools and the property rights of women. And then the same gift for the language of promise carries him somewhere else. He stands for the annexation of Texas. When the Mexican War comes, he takes the apologist’s line, that America had been invaded and the Mexicans deserved punishment for their crime. The rhetoric that once described a New Moral World now describes 918,000 square miles of “virgin territory” waiting to be taken.

Young does not call this a betrayal, and that restraint is the point. She treats it as the ordinary behavior of a plural person moving through time, a man who changed his mind, drew in his horns, and was, in her words, “merely human.” But she also lets you see, without underlining it, what has happened. The vocabulary of utopia and the vocabulary of empire turn out to be the same vocabulary. The “land of promise” becomes the “land of destination.” The dream of a clean start for everyone becomes the justification for taking the continent from the people already on it. Robert Dale did not abandon the promise. He followed it to its end.

The most consequential fiction

This is where the second pillar meets the eighth. Reality is built, and whoever gets to build the shared version of it holds enormous power. “The promised land” is not a description of North America. It is a construction, laid over the actual continent with its actual prior inhabitants, and it is arguably the most consequential constructed reality in the book, more consequential than either utopia, because it outlived them both and is with us still. Young sees this clearly. Right beside her question about experience she sets the answer: man is “the creator of those values by which he lives” and perhaps dies, and they are “not handed down from heaven, usually.” The promised land was created by people, here, and then treated as if it had been handed down. That treatment is the trick. A made thing gets presented as a given thing, and once it is a given, no one has to ask who built it or who paid for it.

The Devil is delighted

Young lets the deepest irony sit almost entirely without comment, in the form of a poem. When Owen’s community was starting, a piece of doggerel circulated in Philadelphia against it, and Young reprints it. In the poem, the Devil scrambles up out of a hole at the North Pole, hears that people are going to live on the Wabash with Mr. Owen, and rushes to be there. He is delighted. He has founded inquisitions and set sects to shedding blood and made kings swallow his lies, but he has never, in all his wandering, hit on a plan like this one, a community that believes men are held entirely by “power of circumstance” and owe no allegiance to heaven or to him. “This plan of free living beats all my schemes hollow,” the Devil says. “Here’s a plan beats the Devil.” Then he hurries home to enlarge his dominions.

What the poem is doing, and what it means is that Owen’s community was built, in part, on the rejection of irrational religion, on the refusal of Devil and Hell and holy lies. And here is the popular imagination of 1826 answering back: the community that rejects the Devil is the Devil’s masterpiece. To the pious American who wrote the poem, a world run purely on circumstance, with no God and no Devil, was not the absence of the Devil’s work. It was its perfection. Young does not tell you what to make of this. She lets the two readings stand in the same room, the utopia that thought it had banished the Devil and the Devil who welcomes it as his finest achievement, and lets you feel the vertigo of not being able to say which one is right.

New Harmony is America in miniature

That is why the book has not aged. The two utopias are gone, filling stations and dolls under glass where the angels and the machines used to be. But the promise that drew them, the promise of neutral ground and a clean start, is not gone. It is the national myth still, and the questions the book keeps alive are the ones worth carrying out of it. Who benefits from calling the ground neutral? Whose past has to be treated as over, as buried, as one layer down beneath the new graves, for the clean start to look clean? Young does not answer these questions for you, because answering them would be its own kind of clean resolution, and she does not believe in those. She only makes sure you cannot stop asking them. The promised land is still being promised. The Indian burial ground is still one layer down.

Chapter 7. The Witness and the Burning Glass

← Chapter 6 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 8 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 7

Every book has an ethics, whether it means to or not, some stance it takes toward the people and things it describes. Most histories take the stance of the judge. They gather the evidence, weigh it, and hand down a verdict: this leader was wise, that experiment was doomed, here is the lesson. Angel in the Forest refuses the bench. Its ethics is something harder and stranger, and Young never names it directly because she is too busy performing it on every page. The closest anyone has come to naming her instrument is Mark Van Doren, who described her gaze as a remorseless burning-glass. A burning glass gathers light to a single point until it scorches. That is exactly what Young does with her attention. She focuses it so hard it burns. And then, crucially, she never once uses the heat to reach a verdict. The stance is witnessing, and it is the most demanding thing the book asks of anyone, the author first and the reader after.

What witnessing is not

It is easy to mistake this for something weaker than it is, so it is worth saying what witnessing is not.

It is not neutrality. It is not the pose of the objective observer standing outside the scene with no stake in it. The very first pages of the book, as this study began by noting, are Young refusing that pose, arriving on the creaking ferry and planting herself inside the haunted present rather than above it. She has a position, and it is intensely felt. She loves this ruined town. She is appalled by Rapp's cruelty. She grieves the collapse of both dreams. Witnessing is not the absence of a position. It is the discipline of not letting your position foreclose the complexity of what you are looking at.

It is not both-sidesism either, that tired performance of having no view and calling the emptiness fairness. The both-sidesist has no position and pretends the vacancy is virtue. The witness has a strong position and refuses to let it blind her. Those are opposite things.

And it is not the same as sympathy, or as judgment, though it can look like either from a distance. Sympathy dissolves the thing you are looking at into your feeling about it. Judgment freezes the thing into your verdict on it. Witnessing does neither. It keeps the object fully itself, in all its contradiction, standing there in front of you, neither melted by your pity nor fixed by your sentence. This is why it is so hard. You have to hold the whole thing at once, and get nothing in return, no resolution, no relief.

Four things held without resolving

The book is a sequence of impossible objects that Young refuses to simplify, and it is worth walking through the hardest of them.

There is the Rapp problem. He was a genuine spiritual visionary and a man who ruled his community through sexual terror, and both of those are completely true at the same time. The reader wants Young to choose. Tell us whether to admire him or condemn him, whether he was a holy man or a monster, and let us close the book with a clean feeling. She will not. Van Doren caught the tone of it when he called Rapp a mountebank, perhaps, and certainly a tyrant, and in the same breath unforgettable, a man to be forgiven even for his monstrous ideas about sex. To resolve Rapp in either direction would be to look away from half of him, and looking away is the one thing the witness may not do.

There is the Owen problem, which is the same shape in a different man. Owen was a person of real moral seriousness who looked hard at the misery of the mill children and set out to end it, and he was a man whose certainty about human nature crushed the actual people placed in his care. Both true, held together, unresolved.

There is the Pears problem, and this is the subtlest and the most uncomfortable, because there is no grandeur in it to soften the difficulty. Thomas and Sarah Pears are witnesses to the collapse of a noble experiment, their letters the ground-level record of a dream failing. They are also small people complaining about mud, about the dancers arriving filthy at the balls, about the loss of comfortable Pittsburgh, fussing and homesick and a little snobbish. The temptation is overwhelming to pick one: to honor them as testimony or to dismiss them as petty. Young does neither. She does not excuse their smallness, the class fussiness, the endless looking backward. And she does not for one second dismiss their grief, which is real, Sarah worn out to the point where she felt like an animated mummy. Young lets them be small and grieving at the same time, because that is what people actually are, and this is where witnessing costs the most, because there is no nobility to take shelter in, only ordinary human pettiness and ordinary human pain held in the same hand without flinching and without condescending.

And there is the angel problem, which is the purest case of all. Rapp said an angel descended and left its footprint in stone. Was it real? Young never says. Van Doren noticed that she lets the question float and never brings it down, and that suspension is not evasion. It is the most precise possible statement of what a witness does: she stays in the room with a question she cannot answer, and she refuses to force it shut. She will not even grant herself the small comfort of debunking, the easy modern relief of "of course there was no angel," because that comfort would be a lie about the limit of what anyone can know, and it would flatten Rapp into a mere liar, foreclosing the possibility that he genuinely saw something. The angel hangs there, unresolved, for four hundred pages. It is the emblem of the Young’s method.

Attention as the only available sacredness

None of this is cold, and that is the part most easily missed. The burning glass is remorseless, but it is not indifferent. The heat is a kind of love.

Van Doren ended his introduction with a line that gives the Young’s engine away. He wrote that no one sees the world so well as the person who is afraid that nothing in it will turn out to be real. That fear is Young's fuel. Because she cannot count on any world beyond this one, because there is no guaranteed heaven to redeem the sandpipers and the ruined gardens and the failed dreamers, she attends to them with an intensity that amounts to reverence. She looks at the morning glories flourishing among the stinkweeds, at the yellowing lilies thriving in neglect, at a pair of baby shoes and an empty doll's cradle and a bracelet made of hair, and she does not use these things as signposts pointing upward to something better elsewhere. She rests her whole attention on them, here, and that resting is what makes them matter.

This is the sacred as this philosophy understands it, pointing not up toward heaven but down into the actual, ordinary, unredeemed world. Full attention to what is really here turns out to be the only sacredness a person can be sure of, and it turns out to be enough. Young's four hundred pages of relentless looking are the book's central argument about what holiness looks like once you stop expecting it to arrive from outside. To stay in the room with something, to refuse to reduce it to a verdict, to keep looking especially when the looking is uncomfortable, is what love is when it is being honest about the world. The witness and the lover, it turns out, do the same thing. They both refuse to look away.

Why the reader is the one being tested

The reason witnessing is the hardest thing the book asks is that the book asks it of the reader, not just the author. Young practiced this discipline writing it. She imposes the same discipline on anyone who reads it, through the form itself. Page after page withholds the relief you keep reaching for. You want to be told whether Rapp was good or evil, whether the angel was real, whether the Pearses deserve your sympathy or your scorn, whether the whole New Harmony experiment was noble or foolish, and the book never once hands you the verdict. You cannot finish it with a tidy opinion. If you have one, you were not paying attention, because paying attention is precisely what dissolves the tidy opinion.

So reading the book is itself the practice. The discipline Young performed in writing it is the discipline she requires of us in receiving it: hold the contradiction, stay in the room, love the thing enough to keep looking at it without needing it to resolve. She does not fix New Harmony and she does not judge it and she does not weep over it and walk away. She stays, and she looks, and she holds the whole impossible place in the burning light of an attention that will not quit and will not conclude. That staying is the book's ethics and its love at once, and it asks us, quietly and relentlessly, to learn to do the same.

Chapter 1. The Book That Is Not History

Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 2 →

Marguerite Young / Angel in the Forest, Chapter 1

Marguerite Young arrives in New Harmony, Indiana, in the summer of 1940, and the first thing she does is refuse to stand outside the thing she came to see.

She comes by a creaking ferry that has been running, according to the sign on the iron bell, for fifty years. The hills roll away on both banks. Sandpipers cross back and forth between the two shores, and she notices that they are primitive birds, that they build no nests but only holes in the mudbanks, so that the hills look coated in golden birds. There may be two blind mules riding with her, hauling pale logs of fallen birch. The ferryman never speaks a word. Then she climbs a path that seems to lead nowhere and reaches the town, which is a disappointment. Where there were two utopias, there is now a filling station. Where there was an angel, there is Mr. Babbitt, the ordinary striving American man.

This is how Angel in the Forest begins, and it is worth paying attention to, because nothing here is scene-setting in the usual sense. A conventional historian would clear her throat, place the town on a map, give us the dates, and only then let the past come forward. Young does the opposite. Before a single fact about the Rappites or the Owenites has been laid down, the place is already thick with what happened there. The present is haunted before the history starts. The ivy on the water tower, the swallows in the abandoned belfry, the two dolls under bell glass in a shop window labeled Father and Mother Rapp: all of it is soaked in a failure that has not finished happening. Young does not report on New Harmony from a clean distance. She wades in, and she wants us to understand that there is no clean distance to report from. There is no ferry that carries you to a vantage point above the wreck. There is only the wreck, and you standing in it, adding your own footprints to the ones already there.

That refusal is the entire method she used throughout her work, stated in the first pages. The book calls itself history, and by ordinary measures it is even good history. It has archives, letters, chronology, named and dated people. But it does not behave like history. It behaves like a long philosophical poem that has borrowed the furniture of the archive.

What Van Doren almost said

Mark Van Doren, introducing the book, put it this way: Young is a poet whose prose, the longer you look at it and listen to it, becomes poetry too. He is right, and the compliment is real, but the frame is a little too small. Calling her a poet who writes beautiful prose makes the poetry sound like a finish applied to the surface, a matter of gorgeous sentences laid over an otherwise normal work of local history.

The truth is stranger than that. Young is not decorating history with poetry. She is using the tools of history to do something history is not built to do. Archives, dates, real people: in her hands these are not there to settle what happened. They are there to stage a much larger question, which is how any version of reality gets built in the first place, and why the versions we build keep collapsing. The two communities at New Harmony are her material, but her subject is the construction of the real and its failure. That is not a poem sitting on top of a history. That is a history bent, from the first sentence, into the shape of a philosophical argument.

What she never does

The plainest way to see it is to notice what a normal history of New Harmony would do that Young refuses to do.

A normal history would adjudicate. It would weigh Father Rapp against Robert Owen and tell you which man was closer to right. It would measure outcomes: Rapp's celibate community ended, by its own logic, in heaven, and Owen's community fed, by a longer and stranger route, into the British labor movement. A normal history would assign causes. It would explain why the utopias failed, name the fatal flaw, close the case.

Young does none of this. She accumulates. She catalogs. Read the opening pages and you find her listing the inhabitants of the place across a century as if they were all present at once: an angel, a butterfly catcher, a herb doctor, a celibate breeder of horses, patriarchs, undertakers, the Spirit of Nature, rational man, irrational men. She lists what the two utopias managed to contain inside half a square mile of wilderness: city planning and anarchy, a new calendar and the burning of Rome, a three-hour working day and the exaltation of horses. The lists do not resolve into a thesis. They are not evidence marched toward a verdict. They are the thing itself, the whole teeming contradiction, held open and refused a conclusion.

She does the same with the men. Father Rapp said he saw an angel in Pennsylvania, in the old Harmony, and left the angel's big footprint pressed into a stone. Was the angel there? Was Rapp a madman? Young lets the question float and never lets it come down. Her Rapp is grotesque and, in his own way, great: a tyrant, a mountebank, a man with monstrous ideas about sex, and still someone she will not reduce to a diagnosis. She lets the faith and the folly stand in the same man at the same time, welded so tightly that you cannot pull them apart. That welding is deliberate. It is the argument.

Why the shape is the point

What is being laid out here connects to everything this fourteen-chapter study traces.

The first is the idea that the unfinished is the honest thing.

A history that adjudicates, measures, and assigns causes is telling you, by its very shape, that the matter can be closed, that a final account is available if you are rigorous enough. Young does not believe that, and so she does not let her book pretend it. No verdict is coming. No resolution is being withheld until the last chapter for effect. The book stays open because Young thinks reality stays open, and to seal it off in a tidy conclusion would be a lie about the thing described. The form is not a container for the argument. The form is the argument.

The second thread is that language shapes what can be thought at all.

Young's sentences do not settle. They keep moving, sliding from one image into the next, refusing to let a person or a place harden into a fixed and final noun. New Harmony is a filling station and an angel's footprint and a little planet whirling alone in space, and it is all of these in the space of a paragraph, because that is how the mind actually holds a haunted place. The prose enacts a conviction about reality: that it does not sit still to be named, that the moment you fix it in a stable word you have already lost most of it. This is not a style laid over the philosophy. It is the philosophy, working at the level of the sentence.

The question the book is built around

Early in that first chapter, in the middle of describing what it is like to spend time in the town, Young stops and asks it directly: what is the nature of experience, what dream among dreams is reality?

That is the sentence the entire book hangs from. It is not history's question. History asks what happened and why. Young's question goes underneath that, to whether we can trust the surface of anything at all, whether the past we reconstruct or the present we stand in is any more solid than the dreams the Rappites and the Owenites dreamed on this same ground and lost. She spends over four hundred pages not answering it, and the not-answering is not failure. It is the honest end of an honest method.

Radical Immanence

After reading Young for years I came upon what I believe she accomplished with her writing from her first poem at age 9 until her last work compiled and heavily edited after her death. I believe she developed over her lifetime a complete philosophical system. I call it Radical Immanence. I have written many books dedicated to explaining it, all free and gathered under Radical Immanence.

Here is a short version of it.

Not One Self.

A person is a crowd, not a single fixed identity. The many selves are not a malfunction to correct. They are the normal condition of being alive, and they make a person hard to sort into a clean box.

Reality Is Constructed.

Most of what feels like solid reality is built: money, borders, laws, status. These are agreements held in place by repetition, not facts dug out of the earth. Seeing the construction is the first step out from under its spell.

Grief Doesn't End.

Grief is not a stage to pass through on the way to recovery. It is permanent weather. Refusing to perform a tidy healing is a way of staying truthful about what was lost.

The Witness.

The hardest and most honest stance is to stay in the room with something painful and complicated without rushing to fix it or wrap it up.

Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary.

Since nothing is ever truly final, the honest move is to build anyway, provisionally, and keep revising. The frozen, finished blueprint is the thing to distrust.

Unfinished Is Honest.

The unfinished is not failure. It is honesty. Anyone who claims to hold the complete and final answer is usually selling something.

The Margins Reveal the Truth.

The people who do not fit the categories see the categories most clearly. The margins are where the seams show.

The Past Doesn't Go Away.

The past is not behind us. It is beneath us, pressed into the present like layers of rock. Calling any arrangement “inevitable” hides the people who actually built it.

Language Shapes What's Possible.

Grammar carries a worldview. Nouns freeze things into fixed identities; verbs keep them moving. And any voice that claims to speak “from nowhere,” in pure objectivity, is hiding where it really stands.

The Sacred Is Here.

Meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, not in a promised beyond. The appeal to a distant beyond, a golden age, a grand destiny, a final arrival, is the oldest tool of anyone who wants to justify sacrifice in the present.

The Crossing Point.

Each person stands where everyone who came before meets everyone who will come after. Every choice packs down the ground the next generations will stand on. Trading their future for a present advantage is the one unforgivable move.
angel-post-10-language-grammar-and-the-g:
Chapter 10. Language, Grammar, and the Grammar of Utopia

← Chapter 9 · Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters · Chapter 11 →

A utopia is a grammar before it is a place. Before anyone lays a brick, the founders decide which words are allowed. They settle on a set of nouns that will count as real, and a set of verbs that people will be permitted to do, and everything that falls outside that vocabulary becomes not just discouraged but unsayable. And a thing that cannot be said, inside a community organized around saying, might as well not exist. This is the ninth pillar of Radical Immanence in its sharpest form. Language is not a set of labels for a world that is already there. Language is where the world gets decided. Marguerite Young understood this better than most historians ever have, and Angel in the Forest is, among other things, a long demonstration that no single grammar is big enough to hold a living world. Both utopias on that bend of the Wabash had a grammar. Both grammars broke, in the same place, on the same rock. The world would not hold still long enough to be named.

The Rappite grammar

Father Rapp’s Harmony spoke Scripture. Its nouns came straight out of Revelation. Angel, paradise, the New Jerusalem, the golden rose of Micah, the second Coming of One. These were not decorations. They were the entire inventory of what the community agreed was real. The permitted verbs were few, and all of them pointed the same way: to wait, to ascend, to be lifted up into the society of imperishable angels. What the grammar had no verb for was the individual will. Rapp said if the community was to be preserved, “the individual must be destroyed.” A grammar of pure waiting has no room for a person who wants something now.

The trouble is that the grammar could not hold its own content. Harmony was, by any measure, a place of staggering material abundance. It poured out wheat and wool and whisky and shoes and silk, and its barges went down the Mississippi loaded with the produce of a fabulously fertile nature. And all of this was made by a community whose official theology held the material world to be a snare, a thing to be endured until the real world arrived from the sky. The nouns said heaven. The warehouses said earth. The grammar denied the exact thing the community was best at.

You can watch the contradiction most clearly in a single tender image. Father Rapp kept a compound of wild deer that he fed by hand, and Young describes them stepping toward him like dancers, “their eyes almost like the eyes of luminous angels.” The old man who had his own son castrated for the crime of loving his wife would push spoiled lettuce and roses through the bars to the deer. The grammar had a word for the light in a deer’s eye. It had no word at all for what passed between John Rapp and his wife in the dark. Angel it could say. Marriage it could not. The tenderness the community forbade its members leaked out toward the animals, because tenderness does not disappear when you strike it from the dictionary. It only goes looking for somewhere it is still allowed to land.

The Owenite grammar

Robert Owen spoke a language that looked like the opposite of Rapp’s and worked in exactly the same way. Where Rapp had Scripture, Owen had the machine. His nouns were the vocabulary of the new science of society: circumstance, environment, improvement, the rational man. Man, he taught, is “the best of all possible machineries,” delicate but still a machine, all of whose parts can be known. From this it followed, with the clean click of a syllogism, that “to change human character, it is necessary only to change the circumstance.” Man was “solely the creature of his circumstance.” The permitted verbs were the mechanic’s verbs: to improve, to educate, to adjust, to form. What the grammar had no verb for was everything that could not be tuned. Belief. Grief. Longing. The wish to go home to Pittsburgh. The wish, at the end of a long life in pain, to walk into a lightning storm and be done.

And here too the grammar could not hold what the community actually was. Owen’s rational language drew some of the most intellectually alive people in America to that muddy townsite. It placed education at the center of everything and left real marks on how the country would come to think about schooling. It gathered reformers like Frances Wright, who fought for the freeing of slaves and for the equality of women. There was genuine light in the place. And the same community, run on the confident grammar of improvement, could not reliably house or feed the people it had gathered. It could theorize the perfect formation of character while children died of whooping cough in the mud outside the lecture hall. The nouns said progress. The graves said otherwise.

A grammar of obstacles

The clearest specimen of the Owenite grammar is the document Owen thought more important than the Declaration of Independence. Standing in Father Rapp’s old pulpit on the Fourth of July, he issued his Declaration of Mental Independence, and named what he called “a trinity of the most monstrous evils” ever combined to injure the human race: private property, irrational religion, and marriage founded on property. He was so sure this was the hinge of history that he started a new calendar. The community’s Gazette began dating its issues from the first year of Mental Independence.

Look at what a grammar of obstacles does. By naming the three things that stand between man and happiness, the declaration makes instantly visible everything it left off the list. What is not among the great obstacles? The body. Grief. Malaria in the river bottoms. A woman going blind at her sewing. An old man’s readiness to die. The desire to go home. Owen’s list is a list of ideas and arrangements, all of them things a rational reformer could dismantle. It has no line for the stubborn animal facts that were actually defeating the community while he spoke. Young sets the whole thing down and then delivers the quietest, most devastating judgment in the book: “the word ‘ought’ is a different thing from the word ‘is.’” People of fifty summers could not remake themselves into bald infants because a declaration told them to. The grammar of ought could describe a world that should exist. It could not touch the one that did.

The people the grammar cannot hold

This is where the seventh pillar comes in. The people who do not fit the grammar are not exceptions to the utopia. They are the evidence. When someone cannot be said in the community’s language, the seams of that language show, and you can see for the first time that it was made, not found. John Rapp, whose marriage the Scripture had no word for, is the proof that the Scripture was a human invention. Mrs. Pears, whose homesickness and ruined eyes had no place in the science of improvement, is the proof that the science was incomplete. Greenwood in the storm, carrying a truth his community could not let him speak, is the clearest proof of all. The margins are not the footnotes to these utopias. They are the exposed edge, where you can see that a grammar was drawn around some experiences and not others, and that the drawing was a choice, and that the choice left people out.

Young’s own grammar

Against both of these closed systems, Young writes a third kind of language, and it is the real argument of the book. Her prose refuses to freeze. It moves in catalogs, in lists that pour objects across the page faster than any category can gather them up: deerskins, hogskins, bearskins, wolfskins, horsehides, and on and on, until the sheer surplus of the world overflows the sentence meant to contain it. Her sentences are full of verbs and reluctant to settle into nouns. She asks questions and leaves them open. She holds two contradictory things side by side and declines to let either one win. This is not looseness. It is a grammar built on purpose to do what the other two could not, which is to describe a world made of change without pretending the change has stopped.

The theology closest to her method is the one heresy the book treats with real tenderness. Frederick Rapp, the pantheist smuggled into the heart of the nature-denying celibates, believed that God was everything, and therefore that God was “a huge animal without eyes,” because there is nothing outside God for God to look at, “not even one small, wet violet.” A God with no outside has no vantage point, no fixed place to stand and name things from. A God that is everywhere cannot be located, and a God that cannot see itself cannot freeze itself into an object. That is also a fair description of Young’s prose. It has no outside. It stands nowhere in particular and everywhere at once. It is a grammar of verbs for a world of processes, and it does not try to see itself, because it knows that being seen from the outside, is exactly the thing a living world can never be.

The world that would not hold still

Both utopias believed their grammar was reality itself. Rapp believed the New Jerusalem was on its way and the material world a passing illusion. Owen believed the human machine could be perfectly tuned by adjusting its circumstances. Each was describing a world that does not exist, because each grammar required the world to be a set of stable things doing permitted actions, nouns performing approved verbs, holding still to be named. The world Young actually shows is nothing like that. It is mud and malaria and abundance and grief and wild deer and dying children, all of it moving, none of it staying inside the words built to contain it.

Her prose is the counterargument, and it is an argument you feel rather than one she states. The sentence that will not resolve is not a failure of grammar. It is the only honest grammar for a world that does not resolve. Rapp’s New Jerusalem never came. Owen’s twelve months came and went and the world was not remade. But the deerskins are still piling up in the warehouse, and the violet is still wet, and the sentence, in Young’s hands, is still going.
interview-parisreview-aof66:
"The Art of Fiction No. 66," Paris Review, Fall 1977 (interviewer Charles Ruas)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is the Paris Review's "The Art of Fiction No. 66," published in the Fall 1977 issue, conducted by Charles Ruas. It is the most widely cited of all Young's interviews and, for the project, its importance is partly a matter of status: it is the edited, author-approved print version of the same body of talk as the WBAI "career" recording that Ruas also made. Same interviewer, same anecdotes, largely the same wording, so the two are best treated as the raw and the finished forms of one interview, with this Paris Review text as the citation-grade version. Most of its content, the opium lady, the from-life method, the muralist and pluralist imagination after William James, the sea-walk, the deaf painter, the "prosaic sprite," Wilder's line about "revealing the unconscious," was analyzed already through the WBAI recording, so this reading concentrates on what the print version adds or fixes. The headnote supplies clean facts: the first poetry book "Prismatic Ground" in 1939, "Moderate Fable" and "Angel in the Forest" together in 1945, eighteen years on the novel to 1965, and a Riley biography abandoned in the late sixties for a "brief" life of Debs that grew into a large study of Utopian and anti-Utopian trends. The setting is the familiar red-walled Village apartment with a merry-go-round horse and a life-sized antique doll.

What the print version adds at the opening

The Paris Review opens on material the WBAI career analysis did not foreground. Young describes her grandmother's death from a series of strokes, when she and her sister were left to absorb the old woman's "wild hallucinatory statements" alone, a scene Young likens to "Lear on the heath," her grandmother "speaking and dancing at the edge of her grave," not mad but "between dream and reality." She recalls a childhood of "Angels in the House" and a game of whirling to catch Satan at the command "Get thee behind me Satan," and her first thought at the grandmother's death, that the old woman could now tell Anatole France in heaven that her granddaughter adored him. Prompted by Ruas that "Anais Nin tells the story of your attempting to commit suicide," Young deflects it, denying any real attempt and treating her adolescent thoughts as a literary pose, the conviction of every young poet that they will be "dead at 21, of old age," dressed up with Dorothy Parker and Cowper. Two craft anecdotes are sharper here than anywhere else: visiting Thornton Wilder's Chicago class, where he hid his cigarettes until the desk caught fire, she kept the one maxim "the patient loves his malady," which she says governed Miss MacIntosh; and she quotes a reviewer's image of her finishing the novel as Sidney flung down his "Arcadia," "There it is, it's finished."

What the print version fixes

Because it is edited text rather than a home recording, the Paris Review corrects details that the transcripts garble, which matters for anyone quoting the archive. The psychiatrist who confirmed the meaning of Miss MacIntosh's black gloves and of the detective who fears anything black is named here "Dr. Hammershlagd," where the WBAI transcript rendered the name as "Harberstock"; the print form is the more reliable one. The Virginia Woolf drowning is given as the River Ouse, which the transcript slurred. And the eighteen-year span is fixed twice, in the headnote and in Young's own remark that had she known the book would take eighteen years she "would have dropped in holy horror," which sits against the looser "seventeen years," "seventeen years and eight months," and "twenty years" that appear across the other sources. In general, where this text and the WBAI recording differ in wording, the Paris Review is the version to cite.

What it consolidates

For the rest, the interview is the authoritative statement of positions established elsewhere in the set. Indiana as legend to be raised into "a universal and cosmic statement" rather than regional local color; her use of birds and beasts "for their symbolic value, their value as icons" out of the bestiaries and her Euphues thesis; her coolness toward Cather and warmth toward Twain and Dreiser as "great thinkers, great dreamers"; the Midwest writer "dipped and dyed in education"; the "muralist imagination" and "the many as opposed to the one," which Ruas names as William James and Young accepts as "also my temperament"; characters taken "from the newspapers, and from biographies and medical histories," on the Browning principle that "the poet is a reporter," with the flat rule "I do not believe in inventing characters." The opium lady, unnamed here but given in full, remains the origin, and Wilder's "revealing the unconscious" the theme. This is the clean, quotable form of all of it.

Set against the other sources

The single most useful point for the compilation is the pairing itself: the WBAI "career" recording and this Paris Review interview are two forms of one interview event by Charles Ruas, one spoken and one edited for print, so they should be cross-referenced rather than counted as separate testimonies, and the Paris Review should be the quotation of record. It confirms the commission of Miss MacIntosh in 1944 on the strength of "Angel in the Forest" and "Moderate Fable," the opium-lady origin, the Toussaint L'Ouverture biography she set aside, and the Adlai Stevenson invisible-elephant letter, all in reliable form. Its corrections, above all "Dr. Hammershlagd" for the transcript's "Harberstock," should be carried into any master list. And its headnote gives the cleanest short account of the shape of her career, including the pivot in the late sixties from the abandoned Riley biography to the Debs project, which the Neville profile and the Dowling chapter document from the other end. Where the interviews disagree on the writing span, this text's "eighteen years," doubled in the headnote and in Young's own words, is the figure with the best authority.
interview-dowling-guru:
"The Guru," a chapter by David O. Dowling on her Iowa years

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is chapter five, "The Guru: Marguerite Young," of David O. Dowling's "A Delicate Aggression: Savagery and Survival in the Iowa Writers' Workshop" (Yale University Press, 2019), in the book's section on the Engle era. It is a documented scholarly account built from Young's letters to Paul Engle, from Bruce Kellner's recollections of studying with her, and from other students such as Peter Merchant. Its value for the project is that it covers the one long stretch of her life the interviews mostly skip, her career as a teacher and her navigation of the literary profession, and it supplies dated facts where the interviews give only memory. It covers three periods: her Chicago graduate apprenticeship of 1935 to 1936, her Iowa years as a doctoral student and lecturer from 1940 to 1943, and her return as Workshop faculty from 1955 to 1957. As a secondary source it should be weighed as biography rather than as Young's own testimony, though it quotes her letters directly.

The guru at Iowa

Dowling's portrait of Young as a teacher is the fullest anywhere. She arrived in a black woolen cape in ninety-degree heat, and students flocked to her over the other mentors, Ray West and Curtis Harnack, drawn by a novel-in-progress unlike anything since Melville or Proust. Her magnetism bred jealousy, above all from the professor Robert O. Bowen, whose own war novel was ignored and who once brandished a butcher knife at an Iowa City party, prompting Young's whispered "Bob is going to kill me." Against the harsh New Critical methods of the Workshop, and faculty like John Berryman, she gathered a devoted coterie. In class she would summon apparitions, pausing to greet Henry James at the door, and her two-room apartment overflowed with manuscript stacks and, in Kellner's phrase, a clutter of gimcracks and toys, with no discernible bedroom and no memory among friends of her cooking a meal. Dowling dates and firms the setting the interviews leave vague: she was about forty-five, on the faculty from 1955 to 1957, lured back by a Rockefeller fellowship Engle arranged.

Her pedagogy

The chapter gives Young a coherent teaching philosophy that the interviews only imply. She freed students from the tyranny of realism, singing out that "the subject matter doesn't matter," and she worked to defuse the savage criticism that passed for rigor, identifying with Virginia Woolf as a woman writer facing a male critical establishment. The clearest illustration is the student Peter Merchant, who dutifully cut a fantastical line as "nonsense" only to have Young write "As was" beside every deletion, telling him he had crossed out "the best parts" of his writing, since his rational mind had censored his deepest material. Where the workshop preached pruning, she preached restoration of the unconscious. She held that "style is thinking," refused the assumption that talent is innate, and took an Emersonian, democratic view that creative power is common because "most people dream." Asked why her students wrote, she cut through their answers to say they wrote "because you want to be loved." Her method produced results the skeptics did not expect, placing student work, and her own story "The Opium Lady," in Marguerite Caetani's Rome journal Botteghe Oscure.

Chicago, 1935 to 1936: Stein and the opium lady

Dowling documents and dates the two Chicago encounters the interviews return to. Young sat at Gertrude Stein's feet while taking a master's degree, drawing courage from Stein's radical individualism and carrying, like her, a handbag stuffed with food and manuscripts. The deeper figure was Minna K. Weissenbach, "the opium lady of Hyde Park," whom Young called the most remarkable person she ever knew and for whom she worked as reader and secretary after the university employment office sent her looking for money. Weissenbach was a patron who had housed Edna St. Vincent Millay, and Young slept in Millay's bed and sat among relics that later furnish Catherine Cartwheel's house, a silver cup said to be Keats's, a Persian letter set, a bird with a seashell. Instructed to keep reading aloud even when the old woman passed into an opium dream, Young realized she was providing "the verbal passport" to another world, the exact role she wanted as a novelist. Dowling names her "Minna K. Weissenbach," which is worth noting for the compilation, since the interviews call her "Minna" in the 1970s and 1980s and "Mette" in 1983.

Working the system: Young and Paul Engle

The most valuable new material is the record of Young as a shrewd professional, drawn from her letters to Paul Engle, which complicates the unworldly image of the other sources. "Angel in the Forest" began as sixty interrelated ballads in blank verse in 1940, when she was a doctoral candidate at Iowa and met Engle, who saw the commercial potential of her poetry. He arranged a fellowship and a lectureship that brought her back in 1942, and steered the Reynal and Hitchcock editor Frank Taylor to her, who signed the book. She never finished the doctorate, balking at a Greek and Latin requirement she resented as time stolen from writing. Moving to Bleecker Street, she became known in the Village as a "well of energy," unmarried and, in her phrase, with "neither chick nor child," and watched "Angel in the Forest" and the poetry book "Moderate Fable" appear together, "like being the mother of twins." She lobbied Engle openly to win her a Guggenheim, which came in 1948, told him plainly that he had started her "on the right road," and traded promotional reviews with him, once writing what she frankly called a "commercial review" of his book. She prized the money as much as the praise, boasting of a "huge advance" from Scribner's and her new standing as a "Scribner's author with Max Perkins as my editor." After years in New York, Naples, and Rome, where she cultivated the princess Marguerite Caetani and her journal, she returned to Iowa in 1954 to finish the novel. This is the Young the interviews never show, one who understood the fellowship-and-review machinery of American letters and worked it with skill.

Reception, the Debs book, and the end

The chapter also gathers reception and closes the arc. The critic Nona Balakian, a founder of the National Book Critics Circle, gave the keynote at a 1983 celebration of Young by the American Professors of Creative Writing, calling the novel American to its core and predicting that Young's recognition, like Proust's, would take fifty years. Nin called the book the voice of "nocturnal America," as Don Quixote was of Spain and Ulysses of Ireland, and a Nashville paper ranked it the most important American work since Moby-Dick. Dowling records the Algonquin encounter with Sinclair Lewis, grateful that she saw the Middle West on its own terms, and the poet Amy Clampitt's memory of Young as a lingering monument to a vanished world. On the Debs biography he notes what matters most for the record: the manuscript grew even larger than Miss MacIntosh and stood as a nonfictional substitute for a novel of ideas, and "Harp Song for a Radical" appeared posthumously under the editorial care of Charles Ruas, the same interviewer who conducted two of the recordings in this project. Young died in 1995 before completing the three-volume history.

Set against the other sources

This chapter mostly documents and dates what the interviews assert, and adds the professional life they omit. It confirms the from-life method, the Browning creed that "the poet is a reporter" and the refusal to invent characters, with Kellner's gloss that under every fantasy lay a hard truth, "nobody else's but hers." It confirms the excised-novellas regret, Young telling students the book would have sold far better published one volume at a time, and it confirms Maxwell Perkins as her editor and the large advance. It corrects or firms several things the interviews blur: "Angel in the Forest" was a Reynal and Hitchcock book brought about by Frank Taylor, the doctorate was never completed, and the Iowa faculty years were 1955 to 1957. Two links are worth carrying forward. The scholarship names the opium lady "Minna K. Weissenbach," a further data point in the Mette-versus-Minna question, and it shows that Charles Ruas, interviewer in two of these sources, edited her posthumous Debs biography, tying the archive together. Above all, this source supplies the one thing every interview leaves out, the picture of Young as a canny operator inside the literary marketplace, which belongs beside the dreamer she presents in her own voice.
interview-fuchs-liquescence:
"Liquescence as Form," a feminist-critical essay by Miriam Fuchs

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

See also: Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 6

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is not an interview or a profile but a work of literary criticism, "Marguerite Young's Miss MacIntosh, My Darling: Liquescence as Form," by Miriam Fuchs, from the anthology she co-edited with Ellen G. Friedman, "Breaking the Sequence: Women's Experimental Fiction" (Princeton University Press, 1989). It is the first theoretical treatment in the set, so it should be weighed as criticism, an argument about how the novel works, rather than as evidence about Young's life or intentions. Fuchs is also the scholar who interviewed Young, and lines from that interview appear in the Neville profile, so she reads the book with knowledge of its author. Her essay reads Miss MacIntosh through French feminist theory, chiefly Helene Cixous, to argue that the novel is a major example of what that school calls feminine writing. For the project its value is a rigorous vocabulary for the form Young describes only intuitively in the interviews, plus close-reading detail, page-anchored facts, and a candid account of the book's critical neglect.

Liquescence: the argument about form

Fuchs builds her title from Bernard Bergonzi's 1965 review, which reported the book at 3,449 typescript pages and about three and a quarter pounds, and she converts text to pages to pounds to gallons of water and oil to set up her governing image: the novel behaves like liquid. Vera Cartwheel narrates by mixing the recluses of her New England childhood with the eccentrics of her Midwestern bus trip, so that separate time frames diffuse, break into "particles" for close view, Miss MacIntosh's bald head and missing breast, Esther Longtree's swollen womb, Mr. Spitzer's double vision, then thicken and resurface. In Fuchs's reading the book's borders and partitions do not divide but collapse, and objects transform into other objects, a basket of grapes into a chair, a swan into a wash basin, a pear into a glove into a basket of peaches. Nothing is fixed; everything is "diffused, mixed, merged," seen only in analogous or related forms. To read the novel, she argues, is to yield to its "laws of baffling equivalences."

Against closure

Much of the essay is a close reading of how the novel refuses to end. Vera claims a traditional quest, to find her childhood nursemaid, yet Miss MacIntosh is almost certainly dead, having walked into the New England sea years before and left her corset and red wig on the shore, so the quest is illogical from the start, a search for her "where she was not." Fuchs tracks how plot resurfaces late only to be skewed further: with a sixth of the book left, instead of settling, the narrative starts over with Esther Longtree across some one hundred and sixty-five pages, then tilts again eight pages from the end with the stone-deaf man, whom Vera abruptly loves and marries in the final pages. When Young uses plot, Fuchs writes, she does so to negate its legitimacy. The two-line ending, Esther's misspelled sign that she is out to lunch and will be back, is a closure that promises reopening, and its conditional tense holds "the indefinite space between action and inaction," so that the novel ends without finishing, just as Esther is forever about to give birth without giving birth.

A feminine aesthetic
