Fuchs's central claim is that Miss MacIntosh joins the twentieth-century avant-garde, long treated as male, to twentieth-century women's fiction, long treated as traditional, and so stands as an innovative expression of a female aesthetic. She reads it as the feminine writing theorized by Cixous, prose that wrecks partitions and has no closure, that "starts twenty times, thirty times, over," and she supports this with Barthes on the morality of form and DuPlessis on a nonhierarchical writing that carries "a female signature." The encyclopedic lists, of butterflies, archaic languages, shipwrecks, battles, the dead and the living, become in her account a plenitude in which all things coexist and through which no linear path can be cut. She reads the book's world as matriarchal, "replete with mothers, mother-surrogates, would-be-mothers," while the fathers are absent or impotent: Esther calls herself the passive policeman's only daughter, Catherine's husband vanished under Alpine snow, and Esther cannot name the fathers of her dream children, "all like moths in a storm." Against the masculine question Cixous poses, where children come from, Fuchs sets Young's redefinition of paternity as the desire to nurture, embodied in Mr. Spitzer's devotion to Vera, and of maternity, in Esther, as "breathing and hoping," the equivalent of life itself. Mr. Spitzer becomes her figure for the reader, a man of common sense forced to adjust to a feminine space with no causality or chronology, where "on time" is the wrong time and a whole episode about a jewel thief builds from events that never happened, and who learns that sympathy, nurturing and patience "cross gender lines." Catherine's journey down the canal of her own inner ear, which opens into a vast continent of ballrooms and stone walls, is Fuchs's emblem of that interior feminine space, endless and never fully explored.

Reception and the record it documents

The essay is unusually useful on reception. Fuchs states plainly that despite laudatory reviews the novel has been overlooked by feminist and postmodern critics alike, earning only two MLA citations in the quarter century after publication, and she notes that the existing interviews, Newquist's of 1967 and Ruas's of 1985, offer "little more than basic information." She cites John Gardner's admiring review in The Southern Review, which called the book extraordinary for "breadth of mind and verbal genius," and her notes confirm that Gardner had been Young's pupil and wrote his first two novels in her class, corroborating the account in the complete Ruas interview. Her bibliography also fixes publication facts cleanly: "Prismatic Ground" (Macmillan, 1937), "Moderate Fable" (Reynal, 1944), "Angel in the Forest: A Fairy Tale of Two Utopias" (Reynal, 1945), and Miss MacIntosh (Scribner's, 1965), and a footnote records the familiar discrepancy that Bergonzi gives the writing span as seventeen years while Young says eighteen.

Set against the other sources

As the first critical rather than biographical source, this essay gives disciplined form to what Young only gestures at in conversation. Her talk of a "muralist imagination," of "the many as opposed to the one," of everything becoming everything else and of a prose that lets absolutely everything in, finds here a sustained account under the name of liquescence and feminine writing. It also corroborates and clarifies facts scattered through the interviews: the stone-deaf man marrying Vera in the final pages, the Spitzer and Peron doubling, Esther's dream pregnancy, and Miss MacIntosh's death in the sea. Two points are worth carrying into the compilation. Fuchs names the lawyer twin "Joachim Spitzer," which confirms that the "Joachim" in the 1983 recording is the character's real first name and not a transcription error, and she notes Miss MacIntosh's missing breast, a bodily detail the interviews omit in favor of the baldness but which the Neville profile also records. Above all, her remark that the interviews provide "little more than basic information" names precisely the gap this compilation is meant to close, since the value of the interviews, read together and against the criticism, is exactly the accumulation of detail and variation that no single one of them supplies. This essay should anchor the critical, as opposed to the biographical, side of the eventual portrait, and it pairs naturally with the reading Young herself gives, in the Fuchs interview, of a book about going on without certainty toward a utopia that may not exist.
interview-neville-profile:
"Where the Landscape Moved Like Waves," a late-life profile by Susan Neville

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is not a primary interview but a memoir-profile from the Indiana writer Susan Neville's collection "Sailing the Inland Sea." Neville, teaching at Butler, tracked Young down late in her life through her publisher, Dalkey Archive, and visited her over several months after Young returned to Indianapolis to recover from an illness, first in her niece's house and then in a nursing home, up to her death in 1995. The piece braids three kinds of material: Young's talk in her eighties, quotations from her published essays and from a Miriam Fuchs interview, and Neville's own narrative and criticism. For the project it should be weighed differently from the transcripts, since Young's late words come filtered through a devoted biographer and Young herself is frail, "going in and out of dream," as Neville puts it. What it uniquely provides is threefold: the record of the book's reception, a body of late-life biography the interviews never reach, and an account of her final years and death.

The reception it records

Neville documents the arrival of Miss MacIntosh in 1965 as an event, a Life magazine spread and a Fifth Avenue parade with rented buses and, she writes, angels handing out champagne. The praise she gathers is a useful compilation of the record: William Goyen's New York Times review calling the book a masterwork built by amassment like Joyce or Melville; Jerzy Kosinski's "novel of massive achievement"; Mark Van Doren's judgment that her eloquence "has no parallel among the novelists of our time"; Anna Balakian ranking her among the most innovative novelists of the age; Vonnegut calling her "unquestionably a genius"; and Truman Capote's "she was the one who taught us all," which Neville explains through a teaching line, Young taught Paul Griffith, who taught Flannery O'Connor, who called Young her "dearest grand mere." Anne Tyler's tribute frames the essay: she read Miss MacIntosh to recover her nerve while writing "The Accidental Tourist" and gave her hero a copy of it as a companion. Anais Nin's championship, calling the novel the greatest modern novel and Young "as valuable as an explorer of unknown planets," is the thread that first led Neville to Young. Against all this Neville sets the counter-fact the interviews only hint at, that Young was largely written out of her own state's literary memory, and notes the Dalkey reissues, the festschrift "Marguerite, Our Darling," and, importantly, that the Debs biography was published posthumously only in a condensed and heavily edited form, with her intended manuscript surviving in one or two copies.

New late-life biography

Several biographical facts appear here for the first time. The wig that becomes Miss MacIntosh's is tied to a real Indianapolis mentor, a Miss Alexander, who wore a spare wig to keep her head warm, told Young she had "the true gift," and taught her to crash the Art Museum's poetry evenings by acting as if she belonged, "and it worked." Young wrote her first book, the poetry collection "Prismatic Ground," while teaching at Shortridge High School and living at 16th and Penn. She recalls Booth Tarkington's sister, nicknamed "Hautey" for her talk of Terre Haute, who believed she was a resurrection of Cleopatra. She remembers Vonnegut in her Shortridge homeroom sitting with "a bottle of fireflies" for an experiment, later calling to ask whether he could tell Iowa he had studied with her, and she predicts he will be remembered as "a cult figure," a man who "wanted to be popular," which she did not. On marriage she is sharp: had she married she "would have married the worst man," since she sensed she had a large genius "that a man would always be jealous" of, and she says she should have written poems all along because they tell "with lightning swiftness" what she means. She reports lovers and, once, two proposals a day, and names as a crucial mentor a man she calls Freud's physician, who told her she was "a writer of the outside way" and to avoid "the middle way." On happiness she is flat: she "wouldn't give a nickel" for it, since life comes from "absorption in one's work." Her doctor, she says, sent her home to Indianapolis because staying in New York would kill her.

The sharpest statements of her creed

Because Neville draws on Young's essays and the Fuchs interview, the piece holds some of the most compact statements of Young's thought in the whole set. Genre dissolves: there is no real difference between fiction and nonfiction because "everything is fiction," even God, and in thirty or forty thousand years it will all be gone, not even a memory of Shakespeare. The central question of Miss MacIntosh, she says, is not whether you can love someone at first sight but "at second sight," once you know they are "other than you seem," which she calls a matter of illusion and "the depth of the psyche." Maturity is going on without certainty; all her writing concerns the recognition that there is no single reality, and yet one keeps "walking towards utopia," on "a bridge which might end before you reach the other side." She ties this directly to politics: knowing when a dream is real and when it is only a dream is the line "between being sane and being crazy," and whoever understands illusion "doesn't blindly follow any leader." Her Midwest is not provincial but cosmic, "a superficial, mediocre view of it" being the only shallow thing, and in her essay "The Midwest of Everywhere" she declares herself in love "with whatever is eccentric, devious, strange." Neville reads her as the recording angel of a Heraclitean flux nearer to modern physics than to most fiction, and Young grounds it in William James, whose stream of consciousness is "a stream and not a track," so that reason's straight pathways are themselves an illusion. On her method she is terse: "I'm a mirror," and in the realm of the surreal "the illogical is logic." She is cool, too, toward Nin and Henry Miller, whom she judges "ultimately cold" sensualists whose sensuality masked an innocence she avoided through a recognition of evil.

Late work and the end

Even bedridden in her eighties, Young was writing poetry at "a poem a day," a collection of dramatic monologues "modeled on Browning's monologues," beginning lines like "I, Elizabeth Hardwicke," which shows the Browning she names as her first master still governing her at the end. Neville records the astonishing Eartha Kitt poem, built on a story Young insists is true, that Kitt was born, tied off with silk and buried under leaves, and dug alive from the earth by a grandmother who heard her voice, an image that rhymes with the buried and dream children throughout Young's fiction. The old New Harmony material returns too: told that Jane Owen had the angel's stone footprint removed as unreal, Young objects that "the angel is real," since "angels are the dreams of men," and "as long as you're still dreaming, you're alive." Neville's closing scene is a July visit to the nursing home during a freak summer storm, Young talking on through the flooding and failing lights about Chicago in the thirties, about Jung and William James and Kay Boyle, about lovers male and female and a lover she gave to another poet on the condition he visit her on Tuesdays, while hail piled in the gutters until the July landscape looked like ice. She died soon after and was cremated, and Neville reports a funeral of eleven people, with two life-sized dolls seated in the front row, the size of the woman who had loved them.

Set against the interviews

As a secondary, retrospective source, this profile mostly confirms and frames what the transcripts establish, while adding three things they cannot. It supplies the reception and reputation record, the 1965 acclaim and the later neglect, which the interviews only gesture at from inside. It gives the late biography and the death, closing the arc the earlier sources leave open. And it sharpens several recurring threads into their clearest form: William James as "a stream and not a track," Browning's monologues governing her poetry from first to last, the real wig-wearing woman behind Miss MacIntosh now named as Miss Alexander, and above all the political point latent in every interview, that understanding illusion is what keeps a person from blindly following a leader. It also confirms the Anais Nin relationship that the Ruas career interview names from Young's side, here shown from Nin's. Two cautions for the compilation: Neville gives the writing span as twenty years, another figure to set beside the "17 years and 8 months" and "eighteen years" of the interviews, and she records that the published Debs biography is a condensed, heavily edited text rather than the book Young intended, which matters for anyone who would cite it as her work.
interview-ruas-angelintheforest:
The Ruas and Schwartz Interview on "Angel in the Forest," WBAI (undated)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

See also: Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The interview at a glance

This is a WBAI conversation recorded in New York, conducted by Charles Ruas, who taught at Columbia, and Joan Schwartz, a video artist. Unlike the other interviews, it is almost entirely about "Angel in the Forest," Young's nonfiction book on the two utopian communities at New Harmony, Indiana, and Miss MacIntosh barely enters. The transcript gives the date only as October 25 with no year. Young's reference to the 1961 plane crash that killed the champion skater Laurence Owen sets a floor, and Ruas conducted his WBAI author interviews in the late 1970s and early 1980s, which is the likely window. The talk is a long piece of oral storytelling, and its value for the project is twofold: it is the fullest record of how Young worked when the material was real history rather than invented lives, and it shows utopia, her declared lifelong theme, at its source.

How the book was made: no research, only living

Young is emphatic that "Angel in the Forest" grew from experience, not study. "I never did any research whatever on New Harmony," she says, and "the research took three days," spent checking a few dates. Her mother and a theater-owning stepfather had moved there and summoned her with a promise: "You'll love this new town. It's the scene of two lost utopias." She arrived around 1940 and "lived there for seven years, in and out," gathering the book from the old-timers, among them the town undertaker, Perry Schultz, who held the property deeds running back to both founders. The form came from her poetry. She began with "a series of 60 ballads in a Robert Browning manner," out of a Depression-era wish to travel the Ozarks and the Blue Ridge collecting American versions of Scottish ballads, and calls herself a "graveyard poetess" of that period, with Gray's "Elegy" and Edgar Lee Masters' "Spoon River Anthology" behind her rather than "Winesburg, Ohio," which she had not yet read. What she found at New Harmony was "a living folklore that is really unique," the only place with two utopias at once, one of married celibates and one of free thinkers.

The approach by water and the symbolic frame

Young reads the place symbolically from the first page. New Harmony sits "toward the toe of the boot" of Indiana on the Wabash, and she entered by water, crossing on a ferry summoned by a great iron bell that had stood "at the river's edge for 50 years," under a WPA bridge so costly that "nobody could afford to go over" it, so that everyone "laughed at Roosevelt's folly." Her governing image is the sandpiper, whose nest-holes in the surf are "older than man." The birds "built no nests," while "the two utopian communities attempted to build nests," and against the ancient shore the utopias "seem transient." She frames the water approach as "the lost Atlantean feeling," the notion that when Atlantis sank "it heaved up America." The utopias themselves she sets as opposites: Rapp's community expecting the world's end by fire and giving up "conjugal bliss," and Owen's built "upon the idea of an eternal future and nothing supernatural," though Owen still said "happiness is the instinct of the universe," which Young notes is itself "a supernatural thought."

Rapp's utopia: celibacy, surveillance, and the end of time

George Rapp came from Wurttemberg, founded a first "Harmony" near Pittsburgh, sold it, and moved inward because, in one explanation Young offers, "he apparently had to have the threat of nature in order to keep his community solidified." The Harmonists were celibate millennialists who believed "the true man was like the true angel," hermaphroditic, beyond the division of the sexes. Young reports the dark rumor, published decades later, that Rapp's son John "died during an act of castration," and notes the adopted Frederick Rapp, a liberal who became one of Indiana's first senators. Rapp solidified the community by claiming a vision of Gabriel, whose stone footprints an English traveler, Schoolcraft, identified in 1832 as those of a prehistoric Indian runner. When Young arrived, a WPA worker was re-chiseling "the footprints of the angel" at fifty cents an hour, explaining that he had "to buy the baby's shoes." Rapp kept order through an appearance of omniscience, "as many eyes as the eyes in the feathers of a peacock's tail," aided by an underground passage with peepholes, so that the daily confessions stayed trivial: "I have torn my coat. I have lost a button." Even the doorways were built so that "your back door would never face another person's back door," to prevent "back door gossip." White flags marked the property's edge, past which the Rappites never went, and they never learned English. A town crier sang each night, "Another Day Passes One Step Nearer the End." Whiskey was "the greatest of all their products." At the center of the maze, a symbol "of birth," sat a little golden book, which Young notes "came before Joseph Smith's discovery of the golden book of the angel Moroni." Byron gave the community a footnote in "Don Juan," calling it "an economy" he would not join because it faced "extinction at the end of the line." The one thing Rapp could not communize was the chicken yards. The Harmonists "would give up sex" and "individuality" but "would not give up their chickens," and Young delights in "father Rapp and the chickens that he could not control."

Owen's utopia: reason haunted by the irrational

Robert Owen bought the ready-made town after reading an advertisement, "fell in love with the description of the hattery, the cocoonery, the orchards," and set on that "Eviless and Adamless Eden" a community of free thinkers with "freedom of woman." A reformed mill owner from New Lanark, "an enlightened capitalist," he taught three states of mankind: the "capitalistic state of the past"; the present, a "rudderless ship" on "an unknown sea"; and a future of "cooperative socialism." He replaced the commandments with "twelve laws" and, as a young man, had debated Coleridge in Manchester against the existence of spirits. Yet the irrational, Young says, "is what appealed to me." When his communes failed and he went deaf, Owen "began to hear voices in the deep," among them "the voice of Coleridge, the voice of Thomas Jefferson, the voice of the Duke of Kent." The colony itself came apart in ordinary human ways. The intellectuals arrived on a keelboat Young calls "the boatload of knowledge," which froze in the ice; then "the mechanics and the intellectuals were having battles," and "social snobbery" reappeared among "the classes they had escaped." Women resented becoming "the mother of every child in the community." A glassblower, Bakewell, wondered "whether human nature could be blown into new forms." A goat ate the community bookkeeper's ledgers, and he "was fired for negligence." An old man, Greenwood, walked in a thunderstorm holding an iron bar, "praying to God to strike me dead." One resident summed up the disillusion: "you can keep your Utopias, but I do want my own shirts." Owen would not admit failure, sold the ground to a man named Walker who stripped the town and opened a saloon, leaving "a community of happy drunks still talking about happiness," and carried his crusade back to the British labor movement. He died at Newtown in Wales, lying down in the room where he was born to say, "relief has come." Along the way Young sets his great comic scene at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle, where he tried to hand the Tsar of Russia a scroll of the laws of human nature and was told, "I have no pockets," and later that "the spirits are very active tonight."

What drew her: the irrational and the city nowhere

The interview makes plain what Young was after. It was not the blueprint of utopia but "the whole inquest into the irrational things about utopias," the negative alongside the positive, and the founders' own descent into the supernatural, Rapp's Gabriel and Owen's voices. Her conclusion is that "the dream of utopia was never realized in its completion," that it was "a city outside every latitude and every longitude," "nowhere," which she likens to "Dickens' Castle Nowhere." Yet she credits both communities with lasting gifts, "beautiful workmanship in the Rappite community" and, from the Owenites, "the education of women" and the idea of housing with greenery, holding that "the whole thing is still a possibility for the future." Her final division is a good summary of the book's balance: "what we have of Rapp is physical," his brick houses and maze, while "what we have of Owen is spiritual," a continuing influence on "American political life and social consciousness."

New Harmony as living folklore

The last stretch describes the town Young knew as a place where the two utopias still quarreled. Sympathizers of Rapp and of Owen divided "like between Republicans and Democrats," so that a drink or a kiss drew the warning "father Rapp will get you," and the split was written even in the trees, the Owenites' golden rain trees against the Rappites' black locusts, with rain-tree shoots for sale "6 for 25 cents." She catalogs the Rappite dolls "under a glass bell," the farm women who chewed cloth to test whether the colors would run, and a newspaper editor who invented gossip until believing him left one "in a state of minor hysteria." The Rappite graveyard, still Rappite property, "has no tombstones," because Rapp wanted no one troubled with "rolling them away when Gabriel blew his horn" and wanted no "individuality" carried into death; its open graves were "filled with flowers," and the quail rustle in the grass "like dead souls," over an older Indian graveyard the Rappites never knew was beneath them. Young names the keepers and heirs: Jane Owen, Robert Owen's great-granddaughter-in-law, restoring the town and housing visiting poets and philosophers; the novelist Grace Zaring Stone, who wrote as Ethel Vance and hoarded Owen documents in Connecticut in fear of fire; and Frances Wright, whose harpsichord survived. The macabre threads keep coming: the self-styled Count Leon who lured a third of the later community into "Epicurean sex"; Frederick Rapp killed by a falling oak, "the foxes had eaten away his limbs," amid a rumor the tree had been "partially sawn"; and one man who lived "under celibacy and free love and polygamy in a single lifetime," moving from Rapp to the free lovers to the Mormons. The land was finally sold to Bethlehem Steel, "a fabulous fate for the old dream," and Young ends on the champion Owen skaters killed in the 1961 crash, "their silver skates strewn over the landscape for miles."

Set against the other interviews

For the compilation, this interview grounds several patterns the others state in the abstract. It shows utopia as her real subject, the "communal utopia" she names in 1983 as the first of her three, and it lets the graveyard sensibility she jokes about elsewhere ("I love dead people") be seen at work in a book born of a "graveyard poetess" among actual graves. The irrational that draws her to the opium lady in the Miss MacIntosh interviews is the same pull she names here toward Rapp's and Owen's visions, and the Gogol she credits in 1983 surfaces in the quail moving "like dead souls." Browning returns as well, now as the model for the ballads that became the book. The most useful cross-link is geographic: in 1983 Young says Vera arrives, in Miss MacIntosh, at the same New Harmony village on the Wabash "with all utopian references removed." This interview is the key to that erasure, since it holds the utopian history she stripped out to leave only the town. What this interview does not do is dwell on the making of the novel, so its drifts are few; its job in the set is to supply the lived Indiana ground beneath the whole body of work.
interview-wnyc:
The WNYC Interview (undated, the out-of-print years)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The interview at a glance

This is a WNYC radio conversation, labeled part one of three, and only part one has surfaced, so this reading covers what survives. The transcript carries no date, but Young says the novel "was published in 1965 by Scribners," went into paperback "the following year," and is now "out of print" with the reputation of "a great masterpiece," while a new edition is "always promised, always deferred like millennium." That places the talk well after 1965 and 1966, in the years the book was unavailable and awaiting a reissue. The recording degrades at the very end into unrelated audio, weather and a cat and a stray line about a "grandson of Eleanor Wiley," which is a bleed from another source and is set aside here. What remains is the densest of the three interviews on her childhood and her family, and it reworks the familiar Miss MacIntosh material through a new lens: the quarrel between Calvinism and Catholicism.

Indianapolis, the Athens of the Middle West

Young calls Indianapolis "the Athens of the Middle West" and jokes that it was a Greek city built on an Indian trading post. She adds a local legend, that the city's first banker, an ancestor of Kurt Vonnegut, kept settlers' money in a desk drawer so trustworthily that the drawer "grew to be the first bank." The point of the passage is her reversal of the usual story of a provincial leaving for the city. Moving to Greenwich Village was a "cultural shock" downward, she says, because the level "was so much higher in Indianapolis," where her childhood was spent among "brilliant older people, scholars, readers of books." In the Village, by contrast, "if you said you were a poet, you automatically were a poet."

The Bible as training, and a claimed lineage

The grandmother's program of reading is spelled out further here. Young says she was "a biblical scholar" at about eleven, taking weekly lessons in "the geography of the Holy Land," and that she read the Bible "for its literary style" because her grandmother thought she would be a writer and considered "the beautiful structures of the Bible" the best training there was, a view Young still holds. She then lays out an unusually specific family mythology, which is best read as her stated lineage rather than as verified fact. On her father's side she claims to be "a collateral descendant of Brigham Young," and on her mother's "a direct descendant of John Knox," whose line, she says, runs through James Boswell, Lord Byron, Herman Melville, and Robert Louis Stevenson. She also claims a French descent through the family of Madame de Sevigne, naming a sainted ancestor who "left her house and put on rags and lived with the beggars of Paris." She feels "very Scottish and also very French," has "a feeling of deja vu about Edinburgh," and reports that a woman in Scotland gives public readings of Miss MacIntosh, whose only complaint was that the novel, at "1135 pages," is "too short."

Calvin against Rome: the novel's two women

The genealogy is not idle, because Young uses it to open the interpretation that sets this interview apart. She reads Melville's "Moby Dick" as a struggle between "the Calvinism of his Scottish Presbyterian ancestors" and "his yearning for some faith like Catholicism," and calls that "my own conflict," since she is "very, very drawn to the Catholic Church" yet will "never go to any church." She then maps the conflict onto the two women at the center of Miss MacIntosh. Miss MacIntosh is the Calvinist Scottish nursemaid, "the stern voice of duty and the love of truth and common sense, none of which she had." The opium lady is "the irrational," the belief that "life itself is a play of illusions." Young's twist is that the opium lady is "more near to reality," because the nursemaid is "the one illusionist" in her faith that there is "a simple foundation of truth." Young also notes that Miss MacIntosh calls herself a descendant of John Knox in the novel, "so at least that much of it seems to be an autobiographical note," a small crack in her steady insistence that the book is not autobiographical.

Miss MacIntosh as the bald prince

The nursemaid's physical description is fuller here than anywhere else. She wears red curls, the mackintosh raincoat, sea boots and sea hat, and a black umbrella that "casts a shadow around her and forbids intimacy." Young calls her "an orphan angel," borrowing the phrase from Elinor Wylie's book about Shelley surviving and reaching America, and reveals a hidden ancestry inside the fiction: while writing, Young "discovered" that the MacIntoshes descend from "a bald prince, who was washed up on the shores of Scotland," presumed dead in France, who became a king. So Miss MacIntosh "is really a bald prince, disguised with a red wig and the woman's gear," able to appear "as a beautiful man when she takes off her wig," which makes her "the very crumbling of the illusion of reality." The sea-walk is described in detail: she carries the umbrella "until her bald head reaches sea level," then goes down "wearing nothing but a pair of black gloves," her wig left "on the back of a horseshoe crab," gone "back to the sea to get her hair." The baldness carries a homemade theology. God "took 6 days to create the earth and rested on the 7th," and she complains he "should have taken 7 days and rested on the 8th," because he left things unfinished, her hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows among them. Light burns her skin, so she carries the umbrella even on sunny days, and she is so compulsive that she sweeps seashells back into the waves. Young says she "had a great deal of fun" with "the one normal character" in a book where "none of the others even pretend to be normal." An editor loved the relief of her, then stopped short: "she committed suicide on page 6. If she was normal, why did she kill herself?" That question, Young says, is "the entire interest of this book," why the one supposedly normal person dies while "the mad lived and flourished like the green bay tree or the red, red rose." She frames the result as "an American existentialism" carried with joy and "a certain exuberance."

The child who woke up a poet

The interview is a trove of childhood writing. Young wrote a serial "about the adventures of a little yellow chicken" that kept her sister "in a state of nervous agitation for years," and a six-act play, six because a rival down the street was writing six and because she had heard plays had five and thought she had "better have six." The play, "The Black Box," turned on a switched-identity plot in which a nursemaid steals a rich baby from the cradle and leaves a poor one, so that a father unknowingly courts his own daughter. With five dollars of birthday money she joined the Authors League of America after an advertisement promising "instructions easy enough for a child of 12 to understand," and received "the most fabulous mail," including the counsel that "to write a story, you must find a germ," which she and her sister took literally, hunting motes in sunbeams and trying to catch them "like lightning bugs." At sixteen she went to sleep "a perfectly normal human being" and woke "with the absolute resolve that I would be a poet," then asked an older student how, and was shown iambs and stresses "that looked like basting stitches." Her first poem was about "preparing a layette for my unborn fatherless baby," an image she connects directly to Esther Longtree, who prepares layettes for "the children of her dreams," and which drew a scolding from an English teacher who said "a young girl should not have such thoughts."

Untermeyer, the opium lady's tutelage, and the Wylie circle

Louis Untermeyer came to town and Young served as his "girl guide," showing him everything of note, "including the mortuary establishment from which my family had been buried." He promised and delivered a good review of her first book, which Macmillan had "instantly accepted," an acceptance she took to be simply normal. Young says her second book, "Moderate Fable," was written "under the influence of a fabulous opium lady," the Chicago recluse she here names Minna Weissenbach, who urged her to read Darwin's journal of the voyage of the Beagle and filled her with bestiaries and books on birds, serpents, and butterflies, so as to bring the forms of nature "into the field of art." As the opium lady talked, "a beautiful golden cockerel" perched at the foot of her bed and issued "messages in the Greek language." Because Young was in and out of that house for years and "never once" accepted the opium she was offered, the lady called her "the prosaic sprite," and Young slept in a bed that "had once been occupied by Edna St. Vincent Millay," though she "did prefer Eleanor Wiley." The Wylie thread runs on: "Moderate Fable" won "the National Academy Award for the best book of the year," judged in part by William Rose Benet, Elinor Wylie's widower, with a citation "for preserving rarity in modern literature" that Benet linked to something reminiscent of Wylie. Young closes the circle with an anecdote about a socialist friend, Eleanor Robinson, who married Wylie's former husband and sent word that she was now "Eleanor Wiley," having inherited the poet's dresses and silver.

Set against the earlier interviews

This interview confirms the load-bearing story and adds a great deal that the other two do not carry. It repeats the opium lady as origin, the baldness and sea-walk, the suicide on page six, and the editor's puzzle over a normal woman who kills herself. What is new is substantial: the claimed descent from Knox, Byron, Melville, and Stevenson; the Bible as deliberate literary training; the Calvinist against Catholic reading that turns Miss MacIntosh and the opium lady into two halves of one religious conflict; the childhood writings; Louis Untermeyer and Macmillan; and the National Academy Award for "Moderate Fable." Several drifts are worth tracking. The opium lady is "Minna Weissenbach" here and "Mette Weissenbach" in 1983, and unnamed in 1965. The origin poem shifts again: in 1965 it is a bird-and-nest poem written at six that holds "all the themes"; here the formative first poem is the layette poem of her teens that seeds Esther Longtree. The page count she cites, "1135," is her own round figure. And the flat "not autobiographical" line of the earlier talks is qualified by her own admission that the Knox descent is "an autobiographical note." Across all three, Elinor Wylie keeps returning, as the "orphan angel" phrase, as Benet's citation, and, in 1983, as the model for the unheard deathbed confession behind Mr. Spitzer, which marks her as one of Young's steadiest touchstones.
interview-aapl-1983:
The American Audio Prose Library Interview, New York, May 1983

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The interview at a glance

The recording was made in New York City in May 1983 for the American Audio Prose Library. The interviewer is credited in the transcript as "Cabanetti," almost certainly a mis-hearing of Kay Bonetti, who founded that library and conducted its author interviews. The transcript is dense and roaming, and it garbles a fair number of proper names by ear. The corrections most useful for the record: the New School co-founder is Horace Kallen (given as "Callum"), the settlement house is Hull House (given as "Hall House"), the deathbed scene traces to the poet Elinor Wylie and her husband William Rose Benet (given as "Eleanor Wiley" and "William Rosemanet"), the Chicago thesis subject is John Lyly's "Euphues" (given as "Euphueus"), and the Carlyle book is "Sartor Resartus" (given as "Sartre, Ressartius"). With those fixed, the factual content is clear and consistent. The talk moves in two long stretches: her Midwestern formation and reading, then the years that made Miss MacIntosh and the Debs book she was writing at the time.

Formation: Indiana, books, and a grandmother who believed in metaphor

Young was born in Indianapolis and moved to New York in 1943. She corrects a common paraphrase of her own view: she did not say Midwesterners must become sophisticated, but that those who become literary are "more likely to be very sophisticated," because they grow up in isolation from other writers, "often a thousand miles away from another writer," and "only dream they're going to be writers." Thrown on books, they become "voracious readers of books from the beginning." She paints Indianapolis as a Victorian town proud of its literary life, with Browning and Holmes societies and people who had known Mark Twain or studied with William James. At about eighteen she read all of Browning under Catherine Merrill Graydon, who had known him in London, and worked through "The Ring and the Book."

The grandmother matters most. Young read Dickens, "Middlemarch," and Matthew Arnold by ten or twelve because this grandmother "encouraged the reading of serious books from the beginning" and, crucially, "never questioned the validity of anything in a poem." A talking frog spoke. "It was Bible truth as far as she was concerned." Young defends fairy tales on the same ground, calling "the fairy tale the psychology of its time," carrying moral and spiritual truth "in the realm of the talking bird, the talking beast." That single idea is a key to the nature imagery of Miss MacIntosh.

The University of Chicago years

At Chicago she wrote her thesis on "the birds and beasts" of Lyly's "Euphues, His England," the book she credits with carrying the bestiary tradition of Herodotus into English prose. Her major subject was Milton and "The Fall of Man," studied beside a comparative survey of epics, and she describes herself as a seventeenth-century and Baroque scholar. Two through-lines begin here. Milton's blindness seeded her lasting interest in "what happens when a sense is missing," which becomes the blind and deaf characters of the novel and their gifts of compensation. The epic catalog and the epic simile become her method of piling up people and correspondences. She worked her way through school in the depths of the Depression, a fact she returns to whenever money and time come up.

The opium lady: Mette Weissenbach

The single most important encounter in the interview is the "opium lady." Sent by the vocational guidance office to a room at Billings Hospital, Young was hired to read Shakespeare aloud to a bedridden woman who wanted "a vacation away from the modern world." She read to her for two years, through opium dreams and near-comas, "during the visitations of the elephant or balloon fish swimming over her bed." Already steeped in De Quincey and Coleridge, Young calls it "a marvelous education" and insists she was never tempted by the drug herself.

The woman was Mette Weissenbach of Chicago, a patron of Hull House and of Harriet Monroe's "Poetry," a friend of Thornton Wilder, a discoverer of Edna St. Vincent Millay, and part of the New School circle around Horace Kallen. She "had never shown the mark of time" while bedridden and aged overnight once she rose, the exact biography Young gives Catherine Cartwheel, Vera's mother in the novel. Weissenbach died in 1943, and part of what drew Young to New York was the hope of seeing her again; she arrived to find her recently dead. Young dedicated her poetry book "Moderate Fable" to her and calls the family connection "the most important connection of my entire life." When Young later told Wilder she had been writing about the opium lady, he answered at once, as she reports it, that it would be a novel "revealing the imagery of the unconscious."

What Young read and carried

Young is emphatic that she owes "nothing to any other fiction writer" for her characters, then names a long line of masters for method and vision. William James runs deepest: she studied his psychology "as if it were a Bible" and takes from him stream of consciousness (his coinage, first applied to his brother Henry's novels), false memory and substitution, the power of habit, and the many selves "under one roof or dome or hat." Two Jamesian phrases sit at the novel's moral center: "the person you did not become," which she pairs with Frost's "the road not taken."

Browning gives her the creed "the poet is the great reporter," which underwrites her rule that everything in the book is drawn from life. Gogol's "Dead Souls" and Dickens teach her to "give a being to any minor character" and to build a novel as a road of many meetings. Don Quixote stands behind the quest and the play of dream against reality. For temperament she places herself nearer Sterne and Joyce than Henry James, because she sees "a more chaotic world," and she reaches past James toward St. Augustine, Plutarch's "Lives," Carlyle's "Sartor Resartus," Melville's "Moby Dick," the Bible, and the "Lives of the Saints." She names Dylan Thomas as closer kin than James and calls herself, borrowing her own phrase for Allen Ginsberg, "a sad Walt Whitman." Visual and comic sources surface too: Chagall behind Esther, W.C. Fields behind the passive policeman and Esther's father, Ethel Barrymore behind Miss MacIntosh's walk, and Charlie Chaplin, who "has influenced every book I've ever written."

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling: the governing ideas

Young began the novel in 1943 and worked on it for about eighteen years. She set it in the 1930s on purpose, wanting the distance of memory rather than a current book; the bus driver who will not cut his hair "until Roosevelt gets out of the White House" fixes the period. On the first day she "listed all the strangest people I had ever known" and wrote out a page of questions: "Is it real? Or is it a dream? How much is real? How much is dream? What is man's fate on this planet?" Her aim was "a novel that would show what it was like to be alive in my period."

The book's recurring question is whether a thing is really there or rests on a false assumption, dramatized when Miss MacIntosh removes her wig and life delivers "a cold surprise." Around that turn several themes braid together: illusion against reality; how consciousness apprehends the world; loss and the compensations of a missing sense; multiplicity, the many selves and many people held in one design; and interdependence, the truth Vera reaches at the end. Young accepts the reading that the novel is political, "the exact theme of my Deb's book" and of "Angel in the Forest," and describes Miss MacIntosh herself as a Christian socialist who "can't wait for evolution" and "wants revolution." What she calls her "muralist imagination" is the formal expression of all this: she wants her characters "to flash back and forth," lighting one another so the past reads differently in the light of each new figure, in "reverberations, chords, and themes."

Miss MacIntosh: characters drawn from life

Young insists "there isn't a single character or event in that book that isn't based upon something which did happen somewhere." The interview supplies an unusually full key:

  • Catherine Cartwheel, the opium-dreaming mother, is Mette Weissenbach, down to the agelessness in bed and the sudden aging on rising. Mr. Spitzer's confession to a woman who has already died draws on the death of Elinor Wylie, who died at the table as her husband William Rose Benet spoke.

  • Vera Cartwheel, the narrator, is effectively motherless, since Catherine "denied her child's existence." Young says Miss MacIntosh becomes "the mother of us all," and the stone deaf man a kind of father.

  • Miss MacIntosh is a composite of Indianapolis spinsters, one of whom wore a wig and kept a spare. Her walk comes from Ethel Barrymore. She is the novel's labor advocate and Christian socialist.

  • Mr. Spitzer and his dead twin Peron carry the book's central uncertainty of identity. In the first draft Spitzer knew he was really Peron; Young rejected that as too neat, "almost like O'Henry," and rewrote it so he does not know. His silent, inward music mirrors her own.

  • Esther Longtree, who claims children she never bore, comes from a real Chicago case Young read in the paper: a man suing to prove he was not sterile, and a detective on the case. Her origin in a crude artificial insemination sets up her endless pregnancies as a search to replace a lost connection. Chagall and W.C. Fields feed her world.

  • The Christian hangman is based on a real hangman "who had no animals on his farm." Young read confessions and lives of hangmen as research, and every criminal case in the book rests on a real one. The lynched man who survives and pushes a baby carriage, later the father of Esther's first child, comes from a rope still hanging in a Southern town where she once lived.

  • Jackie, the tubercular homecoming queen, grew from a girl in New Harmony and a stranger's overheard line, "Poor Robert, he tried so hard to live long enough to see his sister graduate." Young now calls the roughly one hundred and forty page section "almost a book by itself" and thinks she might cut it.

  • Howard Mitchum, the stone deaf painter Vera marries, is a real friend who could "see music." His remembered refrain runs "little boydies don't have no tits... I'm glad I'm not a little boydy." Young calls it "a very loving portrait," made with his knowledge and blessing.

How the book was made

Young wrote slowly, "maybe a page or two a day," and revised for insight rather than to fix careless prose. When a passage "seemed to have gone dead, like a light bulb blowing out," she traced it to a character she had held to a "rigid preconception," then let the character "run away with the thing," which is why Spitzer's not-knowing cost her two or three years. She did not fear finishing; she was "hysterically anxious to finish it," pressed by the cost of the years and by teaching loads that put her on the subway seven hours a week. She refused to "part with anything until I've done the best I can," while insisting the result is not perfect but "just the best I could do." The ending was fixed early. She knew from near the start that Vera would marry Howard Mitchum, so "the end was in the beginning," a courtship she never expected to run eighteen years.

On writing, teaching, and the writer's life

Young does not intellectualize while composing. She listens "until I heard a kind of inner music," an inner voice she attributes partly to an ear injury at age three that, some musical friends told her, might otherwise have made her a composer. She rejects a purely regional idea of American literature, calling it "cosmic" and bound to millennial and religious dreams, while still telling students to "start where you are" and write "that which we know best." She believes firmly in "educated writers" and distrusts the unschooled, teaches poetry as reliably teachable, and is wary of fiction workshops because a teacher can "do great harm."

Money runs through all of it. She thinks "all writers should be rich," mourns the talents lost to rent and taxes and day jobs, and says only money kept her from becoming a criminologist, a comparative-religion scholar, or a labor reporter. She frames writing as protection, "like an island," where "no one can really hurt me," and as happiness rather than agony. Every book, she says, has been about utopia and about the fact that "we are a brother's keeper": "Angel in the Forest" a communal utopia, Miss MacIntosh "the search for perfection and happiness in the individual life," and the Debs book a "political and economic utopia."

The person in the room

The voice is erudite and associative, quick to reach for a dead writer's company. Young says she sees Poe at Sheridan Square "any rainy night," at least "his astral body," keeps portraits of dead writers in her apartment, loves graveyards, and jokes that she is a "necrophiliac... Dead writers," because "writers write because they want to be remembered 100 years from now." She dreamed nightly that Henry James looked over her shoulder and said "That's very good, Marguerite," yet insists she does not write "under the glass bell world that James had," since "42nd Street is my daily lot." She is warm and self-deprecating, claiming that with "naturally curly hair" she would have had more fun and never written, and that a fitting title for any memoir would be "Nothing Ever Happened to Me," since she is "not introspective" and would rather talk politics than dream about her inner life. The Kennedy anecdote gathers all of this at once: she wrote the president about the Pacific atoll tests entirely in the imagery of the ancient mariner and the albatross, asking how a mother could keep her baby from opening its eyes at the blast.

Threads to carry into the next interviews

Several claims here are load-bearing and worth tracking for consistency across the other interviews: the eighteen-year span and 1943 start of Miss MacIntosh; the flat assertion that every character and event is drawn from life; the primacy of William James and the missing-sense theme; the opium lady as the novel's origin and emotional root; the reading of the book as political and as one utopia among her three; and the self-portrait as a Midwestern, book-raised, deliberately unautobiographical writer who prizes education, reveres the dead, and works from inner music rather than theory. Where later interviews repeat these, the repetition will show which parts of the story Young had settled into a fixed telling; where they diverge will mark the places worth weighing.
interview-angelreissue-talk:
A Talk on "Angel in the Forest" (the mid-1960s reissue)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

See also: Angel in the Forest: A Reading in Fourteen Chapters

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The talk at a glance

This is a public talk, not an interview, and it was cut short when Young ran out of time, so it breaks off in the middle of Robert Owen's story with her apology, "I misunderstood the time." The occasion is the republication of "Angel in the Forest" "after two decades," which places the talk around the mid-1960s, roughly twenty years after the 1945 first edition and close to the 1965 appearance of Miss MacIntosh. An introducer, whom Young names as Mr. Daubier, frames the book through Thomas Carlyle and through Professor Charles Holt's essay in the Columbia University Forum on the nonfiction novel as, simply, "history," and praises "Angel in the Forest" as "history as a prose poem." The talk covers the same New Harmony material as the WBAI interview with Charles Ruas, so its worth lies less in the history it repeats than in the compressed statements Young makes when she has to say, quickly, what the book is about.

Facts from the introduction

The introduction is worth keeping for its hard numbers, which shift across the interviews. It gives Miss MacIntosh as "17 years and 8 months in the writing" and "1198 pages long," and notes that the manuscript was longer still, with "a complete novella within the novel" removed to be "published separately as The Lady and the Centaur." It also reports that Young was then "working on a biography of James Whitcomb Riley," the earlier Indiana poet. That detail helps with dating and with tracking her plans, since the later interviews find her at work on the very different Eugene Debs biography rather than Riley. The precise "17 years and 8 months" and "1198 pages" are the firmest figures in the whole set, against the looser "17 years," "eighteen years," and "1135 pages" she gives elsewhere.

Carlyle as master, and the two illusions

Young opens by seizing on Carlyle. She says the introducer "found out one of the great influences upon my literary life," then explains that "when I determined to write prose, after years of dedication to poetry, I took Carlyle as my master in the transfer of poetry to prose." That is the clearest account in any of these sources of how she thought about turning herself from a poet into a writer of prose. She follows it with the sharpest single line on how her two books rhyme: "as in Miss McIntosh, I pursue the themes of illusion begotten by opium, here I pursue those begotten by utopia in a political state." Rapp, "one of the greatest manufacturers of whiskey," was for her "manufacturing various kinds of illusion," which lets her fold the utopias into the same lifelong subject as the opium lady's dreams.

The same county as the novel

The talk makes the tie between the two books explicit in a way the others only gesture at. The bus journey in Miss MacIntosh, "said to be the longest in literary history," arrives in "Posey County, Indiana," the real county of New Harmony, and the figures met there, "a tattooed landlord" and "a hangman who tells of his excellent fruit orchards," appear in both books "because the dream county to which the bus comes is the same setting as Angel in the Forest." Young repeats her documentary claim, now for the nonfiction: "all that I have told in this story is absolutely true, down to the last butterfly or tree or flower." And she names the people who first drew her, "a kind of group of Steinbeck characters living in tents at the outskirts, wanderers from the Ozarks," the stragglers "who sat at the gates of both utopias and never joined either one," among them the old pioneer who said, "I studies it and I studies it."

Siding with Coleridge: the irrational as the reason she wrote

The center of the talk is Young declaring whose side she is on. She recounts Owen's Manchester debate with Coleridge, in which Owen argued that "man is a machine of which all the parts may be known" while Coleridge defended "angels and unearthly creatures, spirits without bodies, irrational beings." When the deaf, aging Owen began to "hear voices" and "debate with the dead Coleridge, with Thomas Jefferson, with the Duke of Kent, with Shelley," to the embarrassment of the labor movement, Young found her subject: "if he had not lost contact with reality, or gained it, whichever way you like to think, I'm sure I never would have written my book about him." She states the principle without hedging: "I fell in love with Robert Owen simply because he came over to the irrational in the end," and "I take Coleridge's point of view." This is the belief that runs under all her work, said here as plainly as she ever says it.

Women sacrificed in utopia

One interpretive thread is sharper here than anywhere else. Describing Jane Owen's restoration of the maze, Young notes that she "commissioned Frederick Kiesler, the sculptor," whose figure there is "the Madonna with her arms empty and no child." The two women were "delighted" to find "we had seen the same thing in Utopia," and Young draws the lesson: "in Utopias, no matter what they are, women are sacrificed," because "the fantastic, irrational, non-reasoning side of life must go in a perfect society." The Rappite women "may work in the fields, but they don't have babies." Set beside the WNYC interview, where Miss MacIntosh's missing hair stands for "the feminine in life" that "God did not give her," this shows Young binding the loss of the feminine to the loss of the irrational, and treating both as the price a perfected order exacts.

Set against the Ruas interview and the others

This talk is the compressed, performed twin of the WBAI interview, and reading the two together is useful in two ways. First, the drifts. Here Rapp advertises in "the London Times," while in the Ruas interview it is the New York Times; here Owen meets the Tsar "at Geneva," while there it is Aix-la-Chapelle; and Jane Owen is "great-great-granddaughter-in-law" here and "great-granddaughter-in-law" there. These are the small slippages of a story told many times from memory, and they mark the parts Young reconstructs rather than checks. Second, the gains. Because the talk is short, Young says outright what the interview leaves implicit: Carlyle as the master of her prose, the opium book and the utopia book as twin studies of illusion, her allegiance to Coleridge and the irrational, and the sacrifice of women in every utopia. For the compilation, this is the source to quote when the point is Young's own theory of her work, while the Ruas interview remains the source for the New Harmony history itself.
interview-ruas-complete:
The Complete Charles Ruas Interview, "Conversations with American Writers" (1985)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is the full published text of Charles Ruas's interview with Young, collected in his book "Conversations with American Writers." It is the most complete of the three forms of one interview: the Paris Review's "Art of Fiction No. 66" was a shorter excerpt of it, and the WBAI "career" recording was the raw session, so where all three exist this is the master version to cite. Because the opium lady, the from-life method, the muralist imagination after William James, the sea-walk, the deaf painter, and the "prosaic sprite" were already analyzed through those shorter forms, this reading concentrates on the very large body of material the complete text adds, which is where its value lies. The headnote is fuller too, laying out the novel's four parts and its circular, Elizabethan-derived style, and it introduces two small bibliographic drifts worth logging: it dates "Prismatic Ground" to 1937 (the Paris Review said 1939) and Young dates the commission of Miss MacIntosh to 1945 (she says 1944 elsewhere).

The grandmother, the dead cousin, and the mother

The complete grandmother section is far richer than the excerpt and supplies the single most illuminating new fact in the whole archive. Young's parents separated when she was three, leaving her with no memory of them, and the grandmother who raised her had lost a grandson two weeks before Young was born, a golden-haired boy named Harry who died of diphtheria. The grandmother believed "little Harry had been born again in me," and Young grew up as the reincarnation of a dead child, singing a folk song about Harry gone to heaven, a belief she compares to Dali taking the place of a dead brother and credits with feeding her sense of "the dualities of life and the depths of dreams." That childhood identity as a returned dead child stands behind the doubles and revenants that fill her fiction. She adds the Bible memorized daily in the King James version "under the aegis of one of my Stuart ancestors," the grandmother's line that "the stone that was rejected" would be "the foundation stone of the new creation," and a comparison of her own displacement to "What Maisie Knew." The mother, largely absent elsewhere, is drawn directly here: a rebel "who had to have many loves," beautiful "as the Gish sisters," who married Young's father "almost as a wager" and, saying "I do," was already thinking "I don't." This is the mother Young later admits is inside the opium lady.

The New York literary world

The full text expands the arrival in New York into a portrait of a whole milieu. It documents the reception of her first two books: the Reynal and Hitchcock scout Frank Taylor tracking "the poet in this neighborhood" through a snowstorm, Mark Van Doren reading "Angel in the Forest" aloud all night to his wife before accepting it, the two books appearing together, and William Rose Benet's award citation for "the preservation of rarity," which he confirmed was an echo of Elinor Wylie, Young's "ideal writer among women." Her closest early friend was George Davis, editor of Mademoiselle, who refused to believe the young woman before him had written "Angel in the Forest," insisting its author must be "an elderly woman who has spent her entire life writing one great book," which Young found prophetic of her own long labor. She describes the Brooklyn Heights "House of Genius" where Davis lived among Auden, McCullers, and Richard Wright, complete with an animal trainer's chimpanzee that wore a dress suit, played piano, and "pays the highest income tax" in the house, and she remembers meeting Kay Boyle there in a cowboy suit. Leo Lerman, first taken for a traveler back from Tibet, becomes a friend whose uptown parties roared "like some great baseball field."

Yaddo and the friends

An entirely new stretch recalls a summer at Yaddo that seeded the novel. Truman Capote occupied Katrina Trask's tower, where a harp played when the door opened, and Young says "I used that harp in my description of the Opium Lady," as the device by which the dreamer tells whether a visitor is living or dead. Capote was writing "Other Voices, Other Rooms" and ran through the rose garden at night howling that the guests were to "create, create under the trees." Most useful for the novel, the group played a murder game in which a person was accused if caught "under a black umbrella," which is the literal source of Miss MacIntosh's umbrella and its charge of guilt. Agnes Smedley threatened to "hang Truman from the trees," meaning the president, not the writer, who was offended not to matter enough to hang; and seeing an early television, Capote pronounced "this has no future." The section darkens into loss: Reeves McCullers's later suicide prompts Young's reflection that murder and suicide differ only in whether the gun turns outward or inward, and that Reeves was "just wrecked" from childhood. She recounts the friendship with Mari Sandoz, each first taking the other for a madwoman writing in a cafe, "the Sand Hills Kid" who told the Nebraska governor he had "no jurisdiction here, nor does God." And she deepens the Anais Nin relationship, Nin championing Miss MacIntosh across the country while dying of a cancer she called a "death warrant" delivered the very day her fame arrived.

John Gardner and the blood contract

The full text carries a major literary-history episode absent from the excerpt: Young taught John Gardner at Iowa, among students just out of the Korean War, when two ex-Marine instructors were pushing "bad imitations of Hemingway." Gardner, torn between that hard-boiled style and "the deeper resources of his cultivated mind," was told by Young that he was "too gifted to write in this bald way." To seal it they cut their fingers and signed a contract in blood in which Gardner promised to follow her advice and become a famous writer. He wrote his first two novels in her class, and the Beowulf novel Young dismissed as "kid stuff" became "Grendel." When Gardner died in a motorcycle crash, Young said she had kept him from becoming "a motorcycle writer" but not "a motorcycle rider." The passage is the clearest evidence in the set of her actual influence as a teacher, beside the students named in the Dowling chapter.

The rewrite, and the sacredness of the word

The complete interview settles the question of whether Young revised. Asked whether the novel was "written and rewritten in layers," she says she wrote it through once, then found "something was wrong," because Mr. Spitzer was pretending to be his dead twin while secretly knowing which he was. When she realized he must not be sure, she "went back and rewrote," and "that's where the book took on its cosmic magnitude," a change that cost "months and months." Before the rewrite, she says, it was "almost a de Maupassant joke." This confirms the same story she tells in the 1983 interview and shows that the flat claim of the 1965 interviews, that "not one word has been rewritten," describes her feeling about language, not the structural rewriting she plainly did. She frames the labor as moral: she could be clever but wants "to be real," "sincere and profound," and calls her comedy something "based upon a greater tragic sense." She offers her emblem of art's risk, a violinist who bowed without touching the strings for twenty years and was fired the day he made one true note, "you hit reality once and die," and insists there is "not one single invented moment" in the book. The Debs work, begun as a short protest against Vietnam and grown "like Topsy," extends the same creed into nonfiction "stranger than fiction," peopled by real figures like Victoria Woodhull and rooted in a "transcendental socialism" that "preceded Marx."

Set against the other sources

For the compilation this is the anchor text among the Ruas materials, and the three forms, this book, the Paris Review excerpt, and the WBAI recording, should be treated as one interview with this as the fullest and most reliable. It resolves a name the other versions garble: the psychiatrist who explained the black gloves is here "Dr. Ernst Hammerschlag, a friend who was a psychiatrist from Vienna," which should correct both the transcript's "Harberstock" and the Paris Review's "Hammershlagd." It names the deaf painter Howard Mitcham and gives the fullest form of the Henry James dream visitations, of the autobiography admission that the opium lady was "in a way" her mother, and of the Norman Mailer story and its "gentle Hercules in high heels." Its genuinely new contributions are large: the dead cousin Harry and the reincarnation belief, which reframes the doubles and revenants of the fiction as rooted in Young's own childhood identity; the full New York and Yaddo milieu, including the black-umbrella game that is the source of a central image; and the John Gardner blood contract. Two drifts to log: the commission date given here as 1945 against 1944 elsewhere, and "Prismatic Ground" dated 1937 against 1939 in the Paris Review headnote. Where the Ruas versions differ in wording, this complete text is the one to quote.
interview-ruas-career:
The Ruas Interview on Her Life and Miss MacIntosh, WBAI (undated)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The interview at a glance

This is a second WBAI conversation with Charles Ruas, a companion to his interview on "Angel in the Forest," and where that one stayed with New Harmony, this one is the career interview, moving from her Indiana childhood through her arrival in New York to the making of the novel. The introduction notes that Ruas was then staging "a multimedia performance of the text of Miss Macintosh, My Darling," and Young speaks of "the two biographies I'm now writing" covering "1870 to 1926," her Debs-era work, which places the talk in the late 1970s or early 1980s, the same period as the other Ruas session. As in the WNYC recording, a few asides to a pet interrupt the transcript and are set aside here. This is the richest single source in the set on her literary life, and it gives the fullest and most candid version of two things the other interviews only touch: the opium lady, and the question of whether the book is autobiographical.

The Hoosier-poet myth and the grandmothers

Young calls Indianapolis "the Athens of the West" and places herself after Booth Tarkington, Meredith Nicholson, and James Whitcomb Riley, "the old Hoosier group," raised to believe "that to be born in Indiana was to be born a poet," a belief she now calls "a myth." Both her grandmothers were artistic, and the maternal one she describes as "a genius personality" who "could have been a surgeon or a poet or almost anything," who predicted the child would be "a writer or the first woman president of the United States, or would become a lawyer who would work to restore the lost family fortunes," fortunes so storied that she and her sister feared kidnappers who wanted "our gold and crowns." The genealogy repeats the WNYC claims with additions: the family pride ran to the French Huguenot and Scottish lines rather than to the father's Brigham Young, and to the John Knox descent she now adds David Hume and Jane Welsh Carlyle beside Byron, Boswell, Melville, and Stevenson, "I claim them all as relatives." New here is her French formation: she was "translating professionally" a French book on Cinderella by fifteen, learned to "think and dream and feel in French," and loved Anatole France so much that at her grandmother's death she had "a rather horrible thought" that the old woman could now tell him in heaven that her granddaughter admired him.

Cosmic, not regional

Ruas presses the regional question, and Young resists it firmly. "It was my fate to be born in Indiana," she says, "I probably would have chosen Edinburgh," and her aim was to "transmute this legend into a universal or cosmic statement," not "to be strictly a regionalist." She is blunt that she is not a nature writer: "if you really ask me if I love nature, I couldn't say I do. I love the sea and the sand," and she uses birds and beasts only "for their symbolic value, their value as icons," the interest behind her Chicago thesis on the creatures of Lyly's "Euphues." She is cool toward Willa Cather ("I like her. I don't love her") and treats Twain, Dreiser, and Sinclair Lewis as "great thinkers, great dreamers" rather than favorites. Her clearest formulation of the Midwest writer comes here: Southern writers seem "born to sing" amid daily ballads, while the Midwest, "more prosperous" and "middle class," forces its writers to "become highly sophisticated, highly educated," so that "the Middle West begets bizarre and beautiful writers who have been dipped and died in education." What she wanted was not Paris but to go "by mulesback through the mountains of Tennessee, collecting ballads," after the folklorist Stith Thompson, a plan the Depression ended. And she insists, then and now, that she never watches other writers: "if I knew there was a vogue, I would avoid it."

Coming east: the wartime literary world

Young came to New York almost by chance, as a teacher at Iowa who won "a fellowship from the American Academy of Arts and Letters, \$1,500, which was a fortune," and left "within 48 hours." A letter from John Crowe Ransom, who had been publishing her poems in the Kenyon and Southern Reviews, was waiting when she arrived. Sally Benson, who with Ransom had urged the "Eastern experience," introduced her on her first day to Harold Ross and James Thurber, "half the literary world that day." She remembers the wartime city as a golden age when exiled Europeans filled the town and "every publisher was asking every man on the street, have you got a book," so that contracts came "like the leaves from the trees." The scene, she says, was "under the domination of the new critics," Ransom, Allen Tate, Mark Van Doren, Lionel Trilling, and Van Wyck Brooks, "people of great generosity," and she denies any split between a New Yorker set and a Greenwich Village set, calling it "the flowering of American culture at every level." One durable fact for the literary record: as fiction editor of the avant-garde magazine "the Tiger's Eye," under founder Ruth Stephan and poetry editor Horace Gregory, Young was "one of the first publishers of a chapter of Anais Nin's novels."

Psychology, not personality

Young knew Gertrude Stein, a visitor at Chicago with Thornton Wilder as host, and admired the person while feeling "not the slightest empathy with her as a writer." She does not do automatic writing, she says, but is "controlled by intellectual ideas" and "obsessions with certain pathologies, almost a medical imagination," and counts Sterne, Gogol, Dickens, and Twain as her kin. The distinction she draws is between psychology and personality. "I'm never much interested in individuals, even my closest friends," she says, preferring "the many as opposed to the one," a "muralist imagination" she calls "very much William James." Her characters come "from the newspapers and from biography and medical history," never from invention: "I believe with Browning that the poet is a reporter," and she points to "The Ring and the Book," built on "a real murder in Rome," as her model. "I don't believe in inventing character."

The opium lady, in fuller detail

The opium lady gets her most detailed portrait here. Young reads Shakespeare aloud to her to work through school; the woman had been "under opium for about 15 or 20 years," unable to walk for ten, and was "one of the original patronesses of Poetry" and of "Jane Addams Hall House." Young witnessed the dreams: "the golden bird, which was the spirit of Heraclitus," a "conversation with the head of John the Baptist," an imaginary elephant, balloon fish over the bed. Two new facts stand out. First, Young had meant to write "another biography," of "the Toussaint L'Ouverture of the Haitian Rebel," and it was her publisher who "wanted me to write a novel" instead. Second, she still keeps the objects the dying woman's daughter gave her, at her own bedside now: "a silver drinking cup which had belonged to John Keats," a "mosaic Persian letter set," and "a beautiful bird with a seashell." The woman called her "the prosaic sprite" because she refused the opium she was offered nightly, needing no drug "to dream." The Wilder anecdote appears again, and in the form it takes in 1983 rather than 1965: told she was writing a novel with the opium lady in it, Wilder said "as a way of revealing the unconscious." Young adds a working principle: "I start where it's easy. Start with something strange and beautiful," because, "I'm a Scot. I'm economical."

Verifying the imagination, and the making of the book

This interview is unusually specific about method. Young worried that her strangest inventions were mere fantasizing, "the one thing I believe I have never done," and checked them against a psychiatrist friend, Dr. Harberstock, who confirmed that Miss MacIntosh's black gloves carried the right meanings of "black" and "gloves" in relation to guilt, and that the detective who will not touch a case where "anything black appears, even a black rooster or the ace of spades," was "the classic case of schizophrenia," backed with case histories. She read medical literature throughout. Reality kept confirming her: after she wrote the sea-walk, "stark naked, except for wearing a pair of black gloves, which she had carefully darned the night before, as if she were going to her wedding," with the red wig left "on the back of a horseshoe crab" and an "Admiral Dewey corset" on the sand, she read of a boy on Long Island who "was stark naked except for black gloves, walked into the sea," which made her feel "psychologically correct." A real window-washer appeared at her window as she wrote the mystical one she cut from the book, one of the excised pieces she says were accepted as a separate volume of novellas. The bookkeeping details line up with the other accounts, with one variance: Scribner's "commissioned" the novel "in 1944," probably on the strength of "Angel in the Forest" and "Moderate Fable," after she submitted "about 15 pages." She expected "about 200 pages" and two years, but the characters kept deepening and she "worked from nine to five for 18 years," never bored, hearing "music when I'm writing," toward "a book of books, a song of songs." She calls a novel "a holy commitment," and names herself "a comic writer" who nonetheless sees "life as an absolute unredeemable tragedy," so that "what comes out is the other side, the comedy." She credits Scribner's for never interfering, running from her first editor Maxwell Perkins through John Hall Wheelock to Burroughs Mitchell: "Scribners never whistled in my ear."

The autobiography she admitted

The most significant passage complicates her steady claim that the book is not autobiographical. She describes her method as pursuit of "the archetype," projecting into a heightened character all it might become. Then she concedes the turn: "only toward the end of a book do I ever realize that after all, it is my own project, and that I am really writing an autobiographical novel." Pressed on whether the opium lady is her mother, she answers that she "didn't know that until almost the end of the book, since my mother was a kind of Titania-like dreamer, and irrational," and that "in a way, it was my mother," adding that had she known at the start "I would not have written the book." That is the frankest version in the whole set of a tension the WNYC talk only cracks open. The interview ends in lighter registers that suit her love of the strange: the Norman Mailer story, in which Mailer, learning her half-brother "was a champion of the ring," called her "a gentle Hercules" for "punching away for 18 years," and a cartoonist drew "Hercules in high heels"; and her collections, the thirteen "China-headed dolls" she calls "images of the soul" and names after friends "not after characters," and the seashells she says she "worships," including her relish for the true story of a collector ruined when a shell believed extinct reappeared and "the market was broken."

Set against the other interviews

For the compilation, this interview both confirms the settled story and sharpens it. It restates the opium-lady origin, the missing-sense theme, the muralist method, the Browning creed, and the 18-year span, and it firms up the Wilder anecdote in the "revealing the unconscious" form shared with 1983, against the "eliminating" version of 1965. A few new drifts appear: the commission is dated to 1944 here and the start to 1943 in 1983, and the abandoned projects multiply, a Toussaint L'Ouverture biography named here beside the James Whitcomb Riley biography of the mid-1960s talk and the Debs work of the later years. The interview's real contribution is threefold. It supplies the literary-world context the others lack, from the New Critics to the early publication of Anais Nin. It documents a concrete method, the checking of imagined pathologies against Dr. Harberstock and the medical literature, that grounds her claim that everything is drawn from life. And it gives the clearest admission that Miss MacIntosh is, at bottom and by her own late recognition, an autobiographical book with her mother inside the opium lady, which is the single most important line to weigh against the flat denials elsewhere in the set.
interview-moore-dalkey:
"Remembering Marguerite Young," a memoir by Steven Moore (Dalkey Days)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →
