See also: The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is a first-person recollection, "Remembering Marguerite Young," by the critic and editor Steven Moore, who worked at Dalkey Archive Press and its journal, the Review of Contemporary Fiction. He wrote it for Constance Eichenlaub's "Who Is Marguerite Young?" website in March 1999 and reprinted it in his memoir "Dalkey Days." It is the publisher's view of the 1990s revival of Young's work and of Moore's dealings with her in her last years, so it should be weighed as candid recollection rather than as Young's testimony. Its value for the project is a documented publishing history of the reissues, a frank late-life portrait from someone who negotiated with her, and confirmation, from the inside, of several threads that recur in the interviews: the excised novellas, the troubled Debs biography, and the archive's fate. Eichenlaub, who commissioned the piece, keeps the Young web archive, and the festschrift Moore mentions was edited by Miriam Fuchs, so this source ties the surrounding materials together.

How the revival happened

Moore came to Young in the early 1970s through Anais Nin's "The Novel of the Future," but did not read Miss MacIntosh until the late 1980s, when copyediting a Review of Contemporary Fiction issue on Acker, Brooke-Rose, and Young sent him to it. He fell for it at once, admiring what others dismiss as purple prose and writing that "no one's prose is purpler than Marguerite's," that she turned 1930s America into "Arabian Nights enchantment" and left her prose "roaring through my dreams." The reprint began with a phone call from a young editor at Oxford University Press who knew Young and had already floated Dalkey to her; John O'Brien, Dalkey's editor, trusted Moore's judgment even though Young "wasn't his type of author." Moore documents the chronology: Dalkey published Miss MacIntosh in two volumes in 1993, with before-and-after author photos on the covers, and in August 1994 followed with three more books, the essay-and-story collection "Inviting the Muses," a reprint of "Angel in the Forest," and Miriam Fuchs's festschrift. He also records the loose ends: contracts Young never signed, so the books appeared on her verbal permission alone, and a Young bibliography by Martha Sattler that O'Brien canceled. Moore left Dalkey in 1996.

Young's conditions and regrets

Two of Young's own wishes come through clearly. She insisted the reprint be in two volumes, over Moore's preference for a single book like the original, because the one-volume edition "intimidated people, scared them off," and she wanted something portable people could "read on the subway," so insistently that she threatened to withdraw the offer otherwise. And she voiced a real regret: she wished she had not waited until the whole novel was finished, but had published it in installments through the 1950s and early 1960s as British writers did, naming Powell, Durrell, and Lessing as models. She told Moore the final Esther Longtree section would have been titled "Mule," which matches the "mule woman" she describes in the interviews, and repeated that the book holds many novellas that might have made a different reputation had they appeared separately. She also mentioned having come across a few old novellas, perhaps sections cut from the novel, that she never sent, the same phantom collection that surfaces across the interviews.

The Debs book and Knopf

Moore gives the clearest publishing account of the Debs biography's troubles. In 1994 and 1995 Young doubted that Knopf truly meant to publish "Harp Song for a Radical," since the house said the long book would "have to be cut," and she asked whether Dalkey would bring out "the uncut book" instead. O'Brien saw the value in publishing so "legendary" a work and agreed, but when Young called Knopf to take it back, her editor there, Victoria Wilson, insisted the house wanted it, so it stayed. The negotiations were confused by her failing health, Moore recalling that she was "out of it most of the time" and increasingly worked through a friend or cousin as go-between, and then she died. This corroborates from the publisher's side what the Neville profile and the Dowling chapter report from elsewhere, that the Debs book was published posthumously and cut down rather than as Young intended, a caution for anyone who would cite it as her finished work.

The person a publisher met

Moore's portrait of Young in 1992 is affectionate but unsparing. They met in a West Village diner favored by transvestites, one of whom greeted her, and Moore notes that the novel was a favorite of the gay literary community. Asked for her Social Security number to sign a contract, she dug in her purse and produced what turned out to be her dentist's phone number. Invited to amend the novel's dedication in his copy, she crossed it out and then chose to leave it as it was, and she handed him a packet of old photographs that became the reissue covers and the festschrift inserts. Walking to her Bleecker Street apartment she held his hand and moved very slowly; inside were books, "boxes and boxes of manuscripts" she was readying for sale to Yale's Beinecke Library, and countless dolls. Moore could get little concrete from her, since every question drew "a flight of fancy" that was "entertaining but not always informative," the same storyteller the Neville profile describes. He is candid, too, about a vanity that the reverent sources soften: she made sure he knew of her descent from Brigham Young and relayed her "dear friend" Saul Bellow's praise, and she treated the Oxford go-between coldly, at times "like a lackey." It is the least idealized close-up of Young in the whole set, and a useful corrective.

Set against the other sources

As the publishing capstone, this memoir documents the machinery behind the revival that the Neville profile and the Dowling chapter only reference, and it confirms three recurring threads with new specificity. It fixes the fate of the archive, Young's papers to the Beinecke, where the Marguerite Young collection now sits. It corroborates the cut, posthumous Debs biography, adding the detail that the Knopf editor Victoria Wilson held onto it against Young's wish to reclaim it. And it extends the excised-novellas theme that runs from the 1965 interviews onward, giving the Esther section its intended title, "Mule," and recording Young's own regret that she did not serialize the book. Set beside Neville's tender deathbed portrait, Moore's franker account of a vain, declining, sometimes difficult woman in her final years rounds out the picture rather than contradicting it, and his framing of her neglect, as the result of critics' fixed notions of canon and genre that she "stands outside of," names the same problem the Fuchs essay diagnoses from the critical side. For the compilation this is the source to cite on the publishing history, the archive, and the honest texture of her last decade.
interview-observationpoint-1965:
The Duncan MacDonald Interview, "Observation Point," September 1965

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The interview at a glance

This is a radio conversation on a program called "Observation Point," hosted by Duncan MacDonald, recorded around the publication day of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling by Charles Scribner's Sons. The host dates it himself. He had just watched Arthur Ashe beat Roy Emerson at Forest Hills, and he cites William Goyen's Sunday Times review calling the novel "one of the most arresting literary achievements of the last 20 years in America." Those cues place the talk in September 1965, which makes this the earliest of the interviews and the one closest to the book's birth. Where the 1983 recording is a long retrospective, this one catches Young at the moment of release, still inside the Scribner's whirl, telling the story of the book before decades of retelling had smoothed it. It runs short, but the density is high, and several claims here are worth setting directly beside the later account.

The shape she meant and the shape it took

Young says she began with "rather humble feelings" and wanted the shortest novel she could publish. Told that the shortest was "about 200 pages," she aimed for that and "added a thousand." By the end of the second year she knew it would be long and was happy about it, because it kept growing "like Topsy, but under control." Two claims anchor her whole account of the book: "I always knew where it was going," and "I knew the last scene the day I started." She illustrates the second with the ending. About ten years before finishing, a painter friend suggested that Esther Longtree hang an "out to lunch" sign in her restaurant window, and Young did exactly that. The book closes on that sign, "out to lunch, be back in a while," with every word misspelled because "she could not spell either." Young insists she "had it in mind the day I started. Every major character and thing." The painter's prompt and the day-one claim sit slightly against each other, but her point holds: she worked toward an end she had fixed from the start.

The six-year-old poem and a self that does not change

The interviewer presses a natural question: over seventeen years a person changes, so how did the novel not change with her? Young answers that she "became more myself all the time," calls the writing "a wonderful experience in self-discovery," and argues that "we don't change any more than we change the color of our eyes about the deepest things of our lives." As proof she offers a poem she wrote at six, which she says "contains in it all the themes of my future work." She recites it: a bird sings of what it did when young, of its wife and baby birds, and the little birds fly away and the nest is "put into a museum... unless someone has taken it away." She reads it as memory, broken human relationships, and a vanished place preserved as a museum, and she traces the same figure forward. New Harmony in "Angel in the Forest" is literally a museum today, and the great domed house on the New England coast, swept away by the sea at the end of the novel, is another such place where dreams come to life. The poem is her evidence that the book was latent in her from childhood.

The grandmother's book

The grandmother, central in every telling, gets her fullest early portrait here. She was "very poetic and inspired," and from the time Young could hold a pencil she said "this child will be a writer," so that Young "became what she believed and dreamed." She died when Young was fifteen, and Young still feels her presence at the desk. Two anecdotes make the point. When a friend, Ella Tate, asked who looked over her shoulder as she wrote and guessed at T.S. Eliot and others, Young answered, "it's my grandmother." And Leon Edel, having read a third of the manuscript, asked who the influence of her life was; when she said her grandmother, he replied that he "just knew this was a grandmother's book," and Young links herself to Proust and his grandmother. She reflects that a grandmother near the end of life "has no competition with the child, only dreams of the child," so "the child becomes a vehicle for the grandmother."

The opium lady as searchlight

The opium lady appears here unnamed, "a friend of ours in Chicago." What stands out is how Young frames the drug. Opium in the book is "a way of lighting the mind, not of disassociating a person from reality, but of showing what reality is." It is "like a searchlight," and the dreamer is "a critic of reality," a professional dreamer who sits very close to the real. Young repeats that she has "never taken a drug in my life" and never would, because "I know I would stop dreaming instantly," adding that she is already "in a drug state when I'm undrug." She sets the dreamer beside Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Coleridge, and De Quincey. The Thornton Wilder anecdote recurs, though the wording differs from the later version. Told she was writing about the opium lady, Wilder here asks whether it is "a way of eliminating the unconscious," and Young agrees, pleased that he "knew instantly what the book would be."

One character at a time, and not a word rewritten

Asked how magazine excerpts could run in Mademoiselle and Harper's Bazaar before the book was done, Young explains the form. Miss MacIntosh is a psychological novel built on interior monologue, where "one character at a time dominates" and the book "isn't made of confrontation" but of each character taking over in turn. Any section can be lifted whole, as an episode of Proust or Joyce's "Ulysses" can, a trait she later found described as inherent to the psychological novel in "a very great book" on the subject. She makes a strong claim about method: she never rewrites, "never, never," and "not one word has been rewritten." She works so slowly that she has spent "as much as two weeks on a single sentence," not from any struggle with language, since her style is "as the air I breathe," but to keep faith with the personality of each character. Following Dickens and William James, who "said, man is body, soul, and clothing," she wanted to externalize the inner life and give every figure "flesh, blood, and clothing," even the walk-on. She refuses the mere butler who enters and leaves; a minor character must move "in an orbit of his own dream." She delights that a newspaper cartoonist drew the minor character Mrs. Hodgen with her birdseed and empty cage and "left the door of the birdcage open," doing, she jokes, "a little better than I have."

Miss MacIntosh: Boston, the nursemaid, and the sea

Young set the novel in Boston, though she had barely spent time in New England, "Boston three days" for an "Angel in the Forest" event. She chose it for transcendentalism and "my beloved Emerson," with Hawthorne and Henry James behind him. The city she knew intimately was Chicago, but as she puts it, "It had to be Boston." Working from a map, she made only one small street error, caught by a Boston-born Scribner's editor. Against the dreaming opium lady she set Miss MacIntosh as the seeming realist, a "flat-footed old nursemaid" from What Cheer, Iowa, in her mackintosh raincoat and black umbrella carried "indoors and out," "avidly normal." Young likens her to Dr. Johnson kicking a stone to refute Berkeley: "my foot feels this, it's not a dream." Yet by page six the nursemaid is revealed to have lived her own fantasy. "Her whole life is an impersonation," and "it's just her verbalism that makes her seem sensible." She commits suicide on page six, and the book still circles her. Born bald and buried bald, she reads through a biblical lens, and her missing hair becomes "the symbol of the dream and of the feminine in life" she was never given. She walks into the sea at dawn "when the moon and sun are both shining," wig off, wearing only black gloves, setting her umbrella at sea level before going down into the deep, "symbolic of eternity and the unconscious." John Hall Wheelock, reading the manuscript, kept insisting "she is normal... I don't care if she did commit suicide, she is normal." Young resists the Virginia Woolf comparison but admits she wrote the sea-walk with Woolf's drowning in mind, and was struck when an editor who had known Woolf told her Woolf "had left her walking stick at the tide's end," close to Miss MacIntosh and her umbrella.

Scribner's and the publication moment

A good deal of the interview is gratitude to Scribner's. Young stresses the risk they took on a very long first novel priced at \$10.95, "six novels almost," and calls their commitment the "most wonderful thing of all," "the greatest groundswell in their history before publication." They printed the "Hangman's Tale" section for the booksellers' convention in Washington. She names her editor Burroughs Mitchell and a Mr. White in charge of publicity, and admits she "hate[s] to see this book come out," not from reluctance to finish but because she will miss hearing from them every day. She and everyone around her, she says, always knew it would be finished.

Set against the 1983 interview

For the compilation, the two recordings agree on the load-bearing story and diverge in revealing ways. Both make the literary grandmother the origin, both root the book in the opium lady and repeat the Wilder anecdote, both insist she knew the last scene on day one, both hold that every character and event comes from life, and both describe the many-character, one-at-a-time method. The differences are worth marking. Here the opium lady is unnamed; in 1983 she is Mette Weissenbach. Here Wilder asks about "eliminating the unconscious"; in 1983 the same line becomes "revealing the imagery of the unconscious." Here Young says flatly that "not one word has been rewritten"; in 1983 she describes going back to rewrite Mr. Spitzer's uncertain identity over two or three years and letting characters "run away," which reads as rewriting of a structural kind even if not of language. The span drifts too, "17 years" here against "eighteen years" later. And this early telling carries material the retrospective drops or downplays: the six-year-old bird poem as the seed of everything, the suicide on page six, the Woolf walking-stick parallel, and the whole texture of the Scribner's publication. Read together, 1965 shows the story at its freshest and most formal, fixed on craft and the making of the book, while 1983 has folded in the political reading, the Debs work, and the named people behind the characters.
interview-sattler-chronology:
Martha J. Sattler's Chronology (Marguerite Young, Our Darling)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed

See also: Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 1

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is the "Chronology" compiled by Martha J. Sattler for the festschrift "Marguerite Young, Our Darling," edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). Sattler was the Young bibliographer whose separate bibliography Dalkey commissioned and then canceled, as Steven Moore recounts, so this timeline is the nearest thing the project has to an authoritative factual backbone. Unlike the interviews, it is dated, checked, and dry, and its chief value is that it converts most of the date drifts this set has tracked into settled facts, while leaving a few genuine open questions. It should be treated as the spine against which the looser memories of the interviews are measured.

The dates it settles

The chronology resolves nearly every contested point that has surfaced across the interviews:

  • Her parents separated in 1911, when she was three, and she and her sister went to live with the grandmother, whom Sattler names as Marguerite Herron Knight. Young was named for her.

  • "Prismatic Ground" was published in 1937, which settles the 1937-versus-1939 drift in favor of 1937.

  • She was at the University of Chicago from 1933, took the MA in 1936, and studied with Robert Morss Lovett, Ronald S. Crane, and T. V. Smith, the teachers she names in the Friedman and Fuchs interview. The opium lady is given as Minna Weissenbach, confirming "Minna" over the "Mette" of the 1983 recording.

  • "Angel in the Forest" began in 1940 as sixty ballads, then blank verse, and was turned into prose in 1942, exactly as she describes it.

  • The novel's working title was "The Worm in the Wheat," and Maxwell Perkins accepted forty pages of it in 1945, which fixes the commission at 1945 rather than the 1944 of the Paris Review, and confirms the working title Moore recalled.

  • Her Scribner's editors ran from Perkins, who died in 1947, to John Hall Wheelock, to Burroughs Mitchell.

  • She was on the Iowa faculty from 1955 to 1957 and taught John Gardner there, confirming the blood-contract account.

  • "Angel in the Forest" was reissued by Scribner's in 1966 with Van Doren's introduction, which dates the reissue talk to about 1966, and she began the Riley biography that year under the title "The Muse and the Little China Dog," setting it aside for Debs in 1967.

  • The WBAI program of dramatized readings was broadcast in 1974, which places the Ruas recordings in that period, and the American Professors of Creative Writing honored her in 1983, the year of the AAPL interview.

  • The first Debs volume, "Prelude in the Golden Key," was completed in 1991 and accepted by Knopf in 1992 for projected 1995 publication; Dalkey brought out the two-volume Miss MacIntosh in January 1993 and reprinted "Angel" with "Inviting the Muses" in 1994.

New facts it adds

Beyond settling old questions, the chronology supplies details no interview gives. Her first published poem was "Worship" in Indiana University's Crimson Quill in 1927, followed by "Jonathan's House" and a Butler literary prize; she took her BA from Butler in 1930 and first appeared in Poetry that year. In 1940 she was at Bread Loaf as assistant to Louis Untermeyer. Her first published fiction was "The Dead Woman" in American Prefaces in 1943, and her last lyric poem, "Proem to Reality," appeared in Partisan Review in 1945, the year she also took the National Institute of Arts and Letters Award. Albert Erskine, not only Van Doren, is named as her editor for the two 1945 books at Reynal and Hitchcock. She won the Guggenheim in 1948 and that year joined twenty-seven writers, led by Sinclair Lewis, backing Truman for president; a Newberry Library fellowship followed in 1951. In 1952 she sailed to Rome with the Stephans on the same ship as the McCullerses, stayed at the Hotel Inghilterra, and met Princess Caetani, who published "The Opium Lady" in Botteghe Oscure number ten. The teaching record is now complete: New School and Columbia from 1958, Fairleigh Dickinson from 1960 to 1962, Fordham from 1966 to 1977, Seton Hall from 1971 to 1977, and the New School again from 1977 to 1992. She and Nin met at Lawrence Maxwell's bookshop around 1959 and 1960, their close friendship dating from December 1960, and she recorded a "Poets for Peace" album against the Vietnam war in 1967.

Cautions

A few discrepancies remain rather than dissolve. The chronology itself lists Young as meeting Nin in 1943 and again at Maxwell's bookshop around 1959 and 1960, so the safest reading is an early acquaintance and a later close friendship. The number of pages Perkins accepted in 1945 is given here as forty, against the fifteen Young cites in the Ruas and Paris Review interviews. And the commission year, 1945 here, still sits against the 1944 of the Paris Review, though the weight of evidence, this chronology plus the complete Ruas interview, favors 1945. These are the points to flag in the compilation as settled where possible and openly noted where not.

How it anchors the compilation

This document is the timeline the rest of the archive can hang on. Where an interview offers a remembered date, the chronology usually supplies the checked one, and where they disagree, it marks the disagreement clearly rather than papering over it. For the compilation it does two jobs at once: it retires most of the "drifts" this project has been tracking, turning them into facts, and it preserves the handful of real uncertainties as uncertainties. Read beside the interviews, it also quietly confirms how consistent Young's memory actually was on the large shape of her life, even as she varied the small details and the origin stories from telling to telling.
interview-shaviro-exorbitance:
"Exorbitance and Death," a critical essay by Steven Shaviro

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

See also: Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 6

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is "Exorbitance and Death: Marguerite Young's Vision" by Steven Shaviro, first published in the Review of Contemporary Fiction in 1989 and reprinted in the festschrift "Marguerite Young, Our Darling" (ed. Miriam Fuchs, 1994), pages 122 to 128. It is the companion to Shaviro's Critique essay "Lost Chords and Interrupted Births," which is paywalled and now hard to find, and the two share an argument, so this piece effectively delivers that reading: the phrases "lost chords" and "interrupted births" appear here as themes even though they title the other essay. It is the second sustained critical treatment in the set after the Fuchs essay, and the most philosophically ambitious, reading the novel through a Nietzschean and Deleuzian frame of excess, immanence, and death. It should be weighed as criticism, an argument about the book, not as evidence about Young's life.

Exorbitance: the novel as excess

Shaviro begins where every reader begins, in disorientation. Entering the novel there are "no guideposts," and the "hypertrophy of its language," the page-long sentences and infinite variations, leaves the reader with nothing solid to hold, exactly as it leaves Vera Cartwheel. He calls the book "a delirious phantasmagoria of memories that cannot be recaptured," "an epic lament of loss and disappointment." His turn, and the heart of his reading, is that this space of absence is not empty but full: "a space of profusion and excess," "outrageously hyperbolic," "a universe of plural affirmations." The novel produces "a strange vertigo," a sensory and epistemological overload, because there is simply "too much to read," a surplus he insists is absolute rather than merely quantitative. Reiteration becomes a principle of variation, any point of origin is erased, and the book stages "the interchangeability of beginning and end." It resists fixed categories because it is "pleonastic to the point of excess," so that the empty space of repetition becomes an inexhaustible reservoir of meaning. This is the "ex-orbitance" of his title, a text that expends itself to infinity, "an inverted circle whose circumference is everywhere, and whose center is nowhere."

Against the academy, and against the feminist reading

Shaviro argues that the novel foregrounds exactly what interpretation usually brackets, the material thickness of the words, and so produces what he calls a "pre-interpretive hysteria" located "on the part of the reader" rather than, in a pointed aside, "as has been carelessly maintained in certain recent discussions of women's fiction," on the part of the woman writer. This is a direct counter to the feminine-writing reading that Fuchs applies, relocating the hysteria from author to reader. He holds that the book "does not sit well in the academy," since academic criticism is built for modernism's allusiveness and self-reflexivity, which Young deploys in abundance, but is "much less able to deal with passion," and that "the (usually male) academic reader's critical distance," his mastery, is what the book threatens. The novel is therefore "decidedly anti-formalist," not self-reflexive or metafictional but expending itself outward into "the chaos of unresolved passions." By virtue of this exorbitance it marks "a mutation in the history of English-language modernism," one that cannot spawn an academic industry like Joyce or Nabokov but instead creates "a community of readers" bound by a common experience rather than a fraternity of scholars, a prediction the book's later cult following bore out.

Mistaken life and a pluralistic ontology

Shaviro reads the novel as one that "affirms, and even glorifies, 'mistaken life'" instead of trying to set it right, and he traces this to "Angel in the Forest," where Young writes that perfectionist orders would have excluded the mistaken life that is life itself. The book is "strewn with suicides," and the one American myth absent from this very American book is "the myth of success," but failure here is the positive consequence of passion, its refusal to compromise. He aligns this with Young's admiration for William James while pushing past pragmatism toward a Nietzschean sense that truth is only a particularly stubborn error, and a "delirious aestheticism" that celebrates multiple errors for their own sake. He notes that there is "no conversation, no dialogue" in the book, "only multiple monologues," because dialogue would imply common ground, and the novel is too radically pluralistic for even Bakhtinian dialogism; Vera can only accept the impossibility of resolution, finding not harmony but "the beautiful malignancy of the ocean." In this ontology the fantastic and the real collapse into each other, "a delusion, a hallucination, is an actual event," and even lost or despised realities are granted their own positivity, which he calls the novel's most impressive achievement.

Exorbitance and death

The essay's second key term is death. The novel "swarms with an incredibly rich and various life," yet is "utterly obsessed with death," which Shaviro calls "the superabundant void" that no profusion can fill, "the excess which inhabits all multiplicities" and the condition of every obsession. Here the Critique title surfaces as argument: "the chord that would complete our harmonies is always already lost," the lost chord, and yet even death is not conclusive, so there is "no final cadence" and "no return to silence." He gathers the book's deprivations, birth and the failure to be born or to give birth, blindness and deafness, lost loves and deluded ambitions, as the "interrupted births" of the companion title, the moments of trauma and transition that define experience. His close is affirmative: loss is "the necessary condition of beauty and exuberance," and Young's "exorbitant vision is in no way transcendent or otherworldly," offering instead a celebration of something "available to us, at every moment, in ordinary life."

Set against the other sources

This essay is the second critical anchor of the compilation and the sharpest counterweight to the Fuchs reading. Where Fuchs reads Miss MacIntosh as feminine writing in Cixous's sense, Shaviro explicitly moves the "hysteria" from the woman writer to the reader and reads the book instead as a Nietzschean, immanent celebration of mistaken life and a mutation in modernism that is neither modernist nor postmodernist. Placed beside Young's own insistence, in the Friedman and Fuchs interview, that she is a traditionalist of the Grand Tradition, the three positions map the whole critical debate about her: feminine avant-garde, exorbitant singularity, and traditional epic. Shaviro's reading also tracks Young's own words more closely than Fuchs's does, since his "mistaken life" and failed utopias are exactly the "paradise lost" and lost utopias she names as her single theme, and his emphasis on William James, on death, and on the pluralistic real echoes her own. Because it carries the argument of the paywalled Critique essay, including the lost chord and the interrupted birth, this piece closes the one gap that remained in the archive, and it should be the source cited for the philosophical, as opposed to the feminist, account of the novel's form.
interview-terkel-1965:
The Studs Terkel Interview, 1965 (two-part radio program)

Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The interview at a glance

The host is not named in the transcript, but external records from the Marguerite Young archive confirm this is the 1965 Studs Terkel radio interview, recorded around the publication of Miss MacIntosh by Scribner's. It is the longest interview in the set and a distinctive one. Terkel runs it as a two-part musical program, weaving folk songs, hymns, and blues through the talk, and it plays almost as a duet: he keeps intuiting her "secret key images," the prospector, the bottomless pitcher, the roulette wheel, until she says he has named "three of the secret key images by which I wrote." Young performs the book, reading long passages aloud, so this is the source that best preserves her voice on the page. As in some of the other home recordings, a few stray asides to a pet intrude and are set aside here. Two framing points stand out. Young insists the book is "not a stream of consciousness novel" but "a very controlled, rather realistic treatment," and she explains that she chose a bus over a train because a bus "does not go on a rail" and can be "erratic," echoing William James, who preferred "the stream of consciousness" to "the train of memory." Read beside the 1965 Duncan MacDonald interview, this is the second publication-moment source, and the richest.

Where the book came from

This interview is unusually generous with origins, and revealingly it gives several. Young says she began writing about the rich for a plain reason: she was in "an apartment which did not have any heat," so "I'll write about very rich people so that I won't notice I was living in a cold apartment," and "wrote about the richest people I could think of." She then names a real court case as the true germ, "a famous court case" in which "a rich girl who declared publicly that she loved her nursemaid more than her mother," rejecting "the fabulous rich mother," so that, she says, "that is actually where the idea of the book came from." Later she names another seed entirely, a senile doctor she knew in Iowa City who kept delivering imaginary babies, "the idea of the senile doctor still carrying on his practice was one of the things which started me on the book." The multiplicity matters for the project: across the interviews Young offers the opium lady, a childhood poem, this court case, and this doctor as points of origin, and the Terkel interview alone holds three of them.

Reality checked, images filed, the book as experience

Young restates that "everything in the whole book came from observation of life, or from a reading of newspapers, or reading of biography," with "not a single invented episode or character," because "I distrusted pure imagination," a habit she traces to reading at "about 14" that Dickens studied shorthand to be a reporter, so "I instantly took shorthand." She checks her inventions against real people, as when she asked a hairdresser whether a bald woman ever came in and got the retort she gave a barber in the book, "I couldn't grow one hair on your head for a million dollars, and if I could, I wouldn't need a million dollars." Her aesthetic is stated plainly against the fashionable one. There are "putter-inners, as the Wolf said, and the taker-outers, as Scott Fitzgerald said," and Young defends putting in: "it takes terrible discipline in architectonics to put it in," managed by "a file-case mentality" in which every image is assigned its place for a psychological reason. The aim was not a "tight novel" but, in the words of the editor Margaret Cousins that Young embraced, "this book is not a book, it's an experience," "a searchlight upon experience." She read Jung "to give me courage along the way," and reports a University of Iowa researcher who measured brain waves telling her that her prose spent "as much energy in a morning as if you had heaved a ton of coal," which so horrified her that she "didn't write for at least three days."

The dragnet sentence

The clearest craft statement in any of these sources is Young's defense of the long sentence, delivered here as she reads the enormous catalog describing the pregnant girl on the bus. She uses long sentences, after Proust, Joyce, and Sterne, because a single sentence "gives an emotional unity to the description" and forces the writer to "catch every nuance of your own thought," where a short sentence catches "maybe a tenth of what you think." She calls it "the dragnet sentence," "like casting your seine upon the waters," and tells young writers that "if you can write a long sentence, you can write a short one." She invokes William James, that "we can never catch all our thoughts on the wing," and offers the long sentence as the nearest approach. She also loves the short sentence, "like ripples coming in after a storm," and believes finally in "variation of sentence length depending upon the emotional mood." She reports that Elizabeth Bowen, reading the manuscript, said "I knew on page two that it was a great book because of that sentence," and "burst into tears," thinking "here's a new voice."

Guilt and the albatross

When Terkel guesses that the opium lady's hidden birthmark is "the albatross on the neck of the mariner," Young answers, "you frighten me by being so absolutely right," and states a thesis she gives nowhere else so directly: "the secret heart of my novel is the albatross and guilt." Opium, through Coleridge, is "guilt and turning away," and the opium lady faces Coleridge's own final choice, to be "cured of opium and die or continue with opium and die," so that "like Coleridge, she comes back to reality as she dies," aging into "an old hag" at the end. The guilt theme runs through the book's Calvinism, which Young ties to Melville. "Moby Dick is my favorite of all American novels," she says, noting that she lives on Bleecker Street "in what is probably the exact site of his birthplace," and she accepts that her novel, like his, is "anti-Calvinist." The purest carrier of guilt is the Christian hangman, Mr. Weed, who married into a family in which "the Olivers always hang themselves," and who paused to put on his galoshes on the night his wife hanged herself, so that Young leaves open "was he a murderer because he put on his galoshes," "a man absolutely ruled by habit."

Doubles and the missing sense

Young gives her fullest account of Mr. Spitzer, the composer who has written no audible music since his gambler twin's suicide and who, at the end, tries to confess to the dying opium lady that he is really the gambler she loved, "like the Titchborne claimant," only for her to die "at the beginning of his confessions." The key was a discovery in the writing: "about the third draft" she realized this was "not just a case of twins, but the two parts of the same man," a "duality which might be in all of us, like left and right, shadow and sunlight, or illusion and reality," and that Spitzer becomes "the archetypal wandering Jew who cannot die." The missing-sense theme, which she treats as the book's "great obsession," is grounded in real research: to write the deaf painter Vera marries, Young wrote "a long article for a magazine called The World of Silence," interviewing "all the deaf leaders of New York," hearing "the Lord's Prayer in sign language" at St. Mark's, and meeting "the only deaf dentist in New York," who "couldn't hear the screams of the patients." She draws from it a social point that connects to her sense of the book as political: the deaf apologized to her for her being "in the minority" as a hearing person, and she links this to an affinity among people set apart, "the blind, the deaf, the crippled," and "the Negro," who help one another. Her one real invention here, she jokes, would seem to be the blind veteran touring Europe's galleries with a guide dog, except that she met exactly such a man "in the hotel lobby in Rome."

The women who dreamed

Two women carry the book's theme of the dreamed life, and both get fuller treatment here than elsewhere. Esther Longtree, the waitress "pregnant now for 21 months," embodies "dream pregnancies, which I wrote long before Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf," a coincidence that produced a warm exchange with Albee, who, hearing that the Herald Tribune had titled her review "Who's Afraid of Marcel Proust," said his next play "will be called Who's Afraid of Both of Them." Young calls Esther "the mule woman," inspired by Chaplin's "The Gold Rush," where a mule arrives for dinner and Chaplin plays the gracious host, and by a Chagall painting of a pregnant mule-faced bride Young saw only after writing, "a kind of folk dream" that is "universal." Beneath the comedy is a dark core: Esther, "a song of songs of schizophrenia" and yet "the mother of us all," has in fact killed "the only real child which was ever hers," a mixed-race baby left "in a drawer in a hotel room in the deep south," who returns as an eight-year-old conscience asking "mother, why did you kill me," a figure Young ties to the Child ballad of "the cruel mother." The other is the suffragette, Cousin Hannah, drawn from stories told by the NAACP founder Charles Studin about a "battle-axe" who fought men all her life, "one of the original bloomer girls," yet brought home sealed trunks for forty years that proved at her death to hold "a complete bridal trousseau" each, "she had a dream too." Young fuses her with a mountaineering story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at an Alpine summit and the younger, going back for hers, is lost, "the lady lost her life for a skirt," and with Margaret Fuller, "who drowned off Fire Island" within a step of a sandbar, perhaps by a suicidal wish, returning to America with a husband "to whom she was not really married."

Dreams need no passport

Terkel keeps steering toward the Cold War fear of annihilation, and Young answers with the book's largest claim. Her narrator projects herself into every stranger she meets until "she is all of them," which Young calls "a Walt Whitman theme, the one and the many," and, as in the later interviews, "a sad Walt Whitman." She grounds it in Dostoevsky's image of lifting the rooftops off Moscow at midnight to find that the sleepers, however divided by "reason, custom, social class," are "all dreaming the same dreams," so that "we all dream of mother, maze, child, water. Our dreams bind us, not our reasons." She adds the Fiji belief that the soul is a firefly and concludes that "the dream needs no passport." It is the political vision she names elsewhere as the book's hidden argument, here stated as brotherhood reached through dream rather than through "treaties and borderlines," against a present she and Terkel agree is threatened with being "blown to pieces."

Set against the other interviews

As the second 1965 source, this interview confirms the publication-moment story of the Duncan MacDonald talk, the roughly two-hundred-page intention, the last scene known from the start, Scribner's faith in a long novel, the sea-walk and the suicide on page six, while adding far more texture. It reinforces the "17 years and 8 months" figure, here with the detail that "the last five months were spent simply typing," and the Joyce anecdote in which Joyce's sister tells Young she "just missed my dear brother's record by four months." It repeats the Woolf walking-stick source, now attributed to Alan Pryce-Jones, and the black-gloves-as-guilt reading with the Long Island suicide that followed her writing. Two things are worth carrying forward in particular. First, Young's explicit rejection of the "stream of consciousness" label in favor of a "controlled, rather realistic" book, which cuts against the common description of her work. Second, the sheer number of origin stories she tells, the cold apartment, the poor-little-rich-girl court case, the senile doctor, alongside the opium lady and the childhood poems of other interviews, which suggests that Young thought of the book as having many seeds rather than one, and told whichever fit the moment. The interview also names early champions worth noting for the record, Elizabeth Bowen and Margaret Cousins, and her first Scribner's editor Maxwell Perkins, Thomas Wolfe's editor, which places her briefly in that lineage.
interview-friedmanfuchs-conversation:
"A Conversation with Marguerite Young," by Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs (Review of Contemporary Fiction)

← Previous · Young's Interviews Analyzed · Next →

See also: Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 7

A reading for the Miss MacIntosh project.

The source at a glance

This is a focused question-and-answer interview conducted by Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, the editors of the anthology "Breaking the Sequence," and credited here to the Review of Contemporary Fiction (Spring 2003, 23.1). It was held while Young was alive and at work on the Debs biography, which she describes as three volumes underway, so the conversation predates her 1995 death. Two things make it important for the project. It is the source the Neville profile quotes, including the closing image of walking toward a utopia across a bridge that may end first, and because the interviewers are the very critics who read Young as an experimental, feminist writer, it is the one place Young answers that framing directly, and largely rejects it. It is also among the richest of the primary interviews, giving the clearest statement of her single lifelong theme and a good deal of new detail on the book's losses, the excised novellas, her reception as a woman, and her own sense of her tradition.

One book: paradise lost

Asked whether her long, varied career marks changes of direction, Young gives the flattest denial in the set: "All the books I have written have been one book, from the beginning." Her first poem, written at five and about loss, held "the themes of everything I would ever write," and her single subject has always been "paradise lost, always the lost cause, the lost leader, the lost utopia." The poetry, "Angel in the Forest," Miss MacIntosh, and the Debs book are all, in her account, one search for lost utopia. She restates the novel's structure in her own words, Miss MacIntosh as "the center of the wheel, the hub," with the other characters as spokes and the whole "endlessly expanding like a universe," which confirms that the wheel image the Neville profile uses comes from Young herself. Miss MacIntosh she calls "the orphaned angel, the asexual angel, neither male nor female," who without her wig becomes the denuded figure any person would be stripped of illusions. She keeps one formal distinction: the Debs book is as poetic as the novel but "balladry rather than epic."

The political thesis

The interview is the most explicit of any on the novel's politics. "It isn't that Miss MacIntosh has a social conscience," Young says, "but the book does," and she ties this directly to the theme of illusion: understanding hallucination is what keeps a person from "blindly following a leader," since one must know whether a leader is "sane or insane, over the abyss." She holds that "there can be no poetic novel without political consciousness," and faults poetic writers who lapse into realism for lacking a philosophy to sustain them. She extends the claim to all her work, insisting that "Angel in the Forest is based upon social consciousness," as "every real book is," and that any big book must have "more than one undertow." She even reframes the origin of the utopia book around labor: it was a band of wandering Ozark coal miners, met near her mother's New Harmony, who made her want to write it.

Loss made flesh: the missing breast and the flaw

Here Young answers the bodily detail the interviews otherwise omit and the criticism notices. Miss MacIntosh is not only bald but missing a breast "because everything is lost," and Young adds that after the mastectomy the character went to work in a bowling alley, "a place where she could get herself killed," having lost "her hair, her love, her brother, her identity." The flaw is generative rather than merely tragic: Esther marries the most demented man and Vera the stone-deaf man because a perfect being is impossible, and "out of the flaw may come the universe," as with "the crystal flaw" in her poems, imperfect and therefore able to come into being. This idea has a private root she names for the first time, a real flour miller who tried and failed to pass his thumbprint to his son, whose son then killed himself; Young could never write the story but "put that flour miller and his thumb into everything," calling it "the thing I never could write, the idea of identity and passage of the soul." The recurring objects that turn into other objects, a coin into a drachma into a poker chip, she names as "transmutation and transmigration, metempsychosis," the same passage of the soul through matter.

The novellas she meant to free

This is the fullest catalog of the excised material that haunts the whole archive. Young says she hopes to bring out four or five novellas cut from or adjacent to the book, and describes two: one in which Mr. Spitzer, who "always gets it and never wants it," asks a shopkeeper for a town clock and is then burdened with whatever absurd thing he named; and one of Mr. Spitzer's quest to King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, to find an ageless pony that had belonged to Queen Victoria, "a quest for something that cannot be found." Her Scribner's editor, she says, wanted to publish the novellas, but she always wanted to revise them first. She repeats the regret that runs from 1965 onward, that the book would have sold far better published "one volume at a time," and Esther Longtree she again calls, borrowing from Stein, "the mother of us all," a "song of songs of schizophrenia" for whom every dead butterfly is a lost child.

On being a woman writer

This interview draws out Young's fullest statement on gender and reception, and it complicates her usual line. She says she felt no resentment at the time that experimental men drew attention while women were neglected, since she always rated women highly, Kay Boyle, Katherine Anne Porter, Christina Stead, Mansfield, Anna Kavan, Jane Bowles, and thought of herself as "neither a woman or a man" but a person "doomed to be a writer." Yet she then describes the reception of Miss MacIntosh as an ordeal of "brutal male reviewers" whose refrain was that "if she had gotten married she never would have done this," a tone she calls "sometimes hysterical" and different from the cruelty of women reviewers, and she names, without naming names, men who seemed to want to destroy her, while crediting William Goyen with beautiful reviews. "I think there is a rage against women," she concludes, "I've come to see that now although at the time I did not notice it." The passage is the one Fuchs's essay cites, and it shows Young arriving late at a feminist reading of her own neglect, alongside the punishing teaching-and-writing schedule she kept, teaching until four, sleeping an hour, writing until midnight.

Traditional, not experimental

The most valuable disagreement in the set occurs when the interviewers press the experimental label. Young resists it plainly: "I see myself as traditional even though I know you see my work as experimental." She places Sterne, Joyce, and Proust in a long line, "the Grand Tradition, clear back to Don Quixote," and calls realism the recent thing. She denies the usual comparisons, saying she was influenced not by Joyce or Eliot but by Saint Augustine's "City of God," "Tristram Shandy," Gogol's "Dead Souls," Dickens, and Poe, and even more by "the poetry of the Mormons." She rebuts the Eliot echoes directly, "there are no echoes of Eliot," only "echoes of the things that influenced him," pointing to her Chicago study of epic under Robert Morss Lovett and of structure under Ronald S. Crane, with whom she read "Tom Jones" thirteen times. When asked why the novel has no beginning, middle, or end, she answers, "because life has no beginning, middle or end." This head-on rejection of the avant-garde label is exactly the claim the Fuchs essay reads against, and the two together frame the central critical question about Young: whether she is a traditionalist working the Grand Tradition to an extreme or an experimentalist writing what that criticism calls feminine writing.

Set against the other sources

As the interview Neville mined and Fuchs argued against, this conversation is a hinge for the whole compilation. It gives, in Young's own voice, the unifying theme the other sources only imply, that every book is one book about lost utopia, and it confirms that the wheel-and-spokes structure is hers. It answers questions the other interviews leave open: the missing breast, and the lost brother, as part of Miss MacIntosh's total loss; and it clarifies the Riley puzzle from the Neville profile, since it is Riley and Debs, not Young and Riley, who were the drinking companions, with Young reporting "four books ready," the three-volume Debs and the nearly finished Riley. Its Debs origin, the champagne evening when Mark Van Doren cheered her choice of Riley, is new, as is the reading map of admired writers from James Merrill to Toni Morrison and Cynthia Ozick. Two tensions are worth carrying forward. Young's claim to be traditional stands directly against the experimental and feminist readings of Fuchs and Friedman, a disagreement best presented as a live question rather than resolved. And her late recognition of a "rage against women" complicates the "neither man nor woman" stance she takes elsewhere. It also adds one more origin poem, written at five and about loss, to the several ages she gives across the interviews for her first, theme-setting poem, a small but telling instance of the pattern this whole set has traced, of a writer who told the story of her own beginnings many ways.

Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion

Harp Song for a Radical · The Marguerite Young Society

How to use this companion

This companion identifies the people, events, and terms in pages 1 to 581 of Marguerite Young's Harp Song for a Radical (Knopf, 1999), in twenty-one units that follow the book's page order. Page numbers are those of the Knopf first edition.

Each unit has three tiers:

  • Major entries give what the subject was, why it matters in American history, how Young uses it, where her account differs from the historical record, and one book for going further.

  • Shorter entries give two or three sentences on secondary figures and period details.

  • Allusions give one line on literary, biblical, and classical references.
