harp-companion-unit-01-the-prelude-from-:
Unit 1, pp. 1-16: The prelude from prison

Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 2 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young opens at the end of Debs's life, with his wartime imprisonment, then circles through the summer of 1916, when a San Francisco bombing and the death of James Whitcomb Riley fell on the same day. The unit sets up the book's method: every figure is a doorway into a larger story.

Major entries

The Espionage Act (1917) and Sedition Act (1918) (pp. 4-5)

  • What it was: The Espionage Act, passed in June 1917 after the United States entered World War I, made it a crime to interfere with the draft or military operations. The 1918 amendments, known as the Sedition Act, went further and punished "disloyal" speech about the government, the flag, or the war.

  • Why it matters: Roughly two thousand people were prosecuted under these laws, most of them Socialists, anarchists, pacifists, and members of the Industrial Workers of the World. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions in 1919, including Debs's, in cases that shaped free speech law for decades.

  • Debs's case: Debs spoke against the war at Canton, Ohio, on June 16, 1918. He was sentenced to ten years, entered prison in April 1919, and was moved from Moundsville, West Virginia, to the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary that June.

  • How Young uses it: She treats Wilson's refusal to pardon conscientious objectors as "so black a page in American history" (p. 4). The prison becomes the book's frame, what she calls "the long leap to the Ultima Thule of prison" (p. 3).

  • Further reading: Geoffrey R. Stone, Perilous Times: Free Speech in Wartime (2004).

Debs's 1920 campaign from prison (p. 5)

  • What it was: The Socialist Party nominated Debs for president while he was prisoner number 9653. Campaign buttons read "For President, Convict No. 9653." He received about 914,000 votes.

  • Why it matters: It remains the only serious presidential campaign run from a prison cell. President Warren Harding commuted his sentence, and Debs walked out on Christmas Day 1921. His citizenship was not restored in his lifetime.

  • Where the record differs: The book's chronology gives the vote as 6 percent of the total. The standard figure is about 3.4 percent. His highest share came in 1912, at about 6 percent.

  • Further reading: Ernest Freeberg, Democracy's Prisoner: Eugene V. Debs, the Great War, and the Right to Dissent (2008).

Norman Thomas (pp. 4-5)

  • Who he was: A Presbyterian minister (1884-1968) who turned pacifist during World War I and joined the Socialist Party in 1918. After Debs's death he led the party and ran for president six times, from 1928 to 1948.

  • How Young uses him: Thomas is her witness to Debs's character, the man who "would preach Debs's funeral sermon from the front porch of his home at Terre Haute" (p. 4) and who called Debs one of the world's darlings in the Emersonian sense.

  • Further reading: W. A. Swanberg, Norman Thomas: The Last Idealist (1976).

Tom Mooney, Warren Billings, and the Preparedness Day bombing (pp. 8-11)

  • What happened: On July 22, 1916, a bomb exploded at a San Francisco parade held to promote military "preparedness" for war. Ten people died and about forty were injured. Labor organizers Tom Mooney and Warren Knox Billings were convicted on testimony later shown to be perjured.

  • Who Mooney was: Born in Chicago in 1882, he grew up in Holyoke, Massachusetts, where his widowed mother sorted rags in a paper mill. He became an iron molder, a Socialist, and a labor militant. He rode on Debs's campaign train, the Red Special, in 1908.

  • Why it matters: The case became an international cause, the most famous frame-up in American labor history before Sacco and Vanzetti. Wilson himself asked California to reconsider after protests reached Russia.

  • Where the record differs: Young writes that Mooney "was to spend more than two decades on death row" (p. 10). In fact his death sentence was commuted to life in 1918. He spent the next twenty years in San Quentin until Governor Culbert Olson pardoned him in January 1939. Billings was released later that year.

  • Further reading: Richard H. Frost, The Mooney Case (1968).

James Whitcomb Riley (pp. 11-16)

  • Who he was: Indiana's most beloved poet (1849-1916), born in Greenfield. He wrote in Hoosier dialect, first under the pen name "Benjamin F. Johnson of Boone" in the Indianapolis Journal. His best-known poems include "Little Orphant Annie" and "When the Frost Is on the Punkin."

  • Connection to Debs: They were close friends and drinking companions. Riley wrote a poem about Debs praising his generosity, though he never shared Debs's politics.

  • How Young uses him: Riley died at his Lockerbie Street home in Indianapolis on the same day as the Preparedness Day bombing, July 22, 1916. Young sets the two events side by side (p. 11), the gentle poet of childhood against the violence of a nation drifting into war. He was buried at Crown Hill Cemetery.

  • Further reading: Elizabeth J. Van Allen, James Whitcomb Riley: A Life (1999).

Debs's union path: the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen to the American Railway Union (p. 6)

  • What it was: Debs spent the 1880s building the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, a craft union of skilled railroad firemen. In 1893 he left it to found the American Railway Union, which took in every railroad worker regardless of craft.

  • Why it matters: This shift, from craft unions to one industrial union, is the main organizing argument in American labor history. The ARU grew to about 150,000 members in a year and was destroyed in the Pullman strike of 1894.

  • Where the record differs: Young places the firemen's brotherhood "under the aegis of the Knights of Labor" (p. 6). The two were separate organizations. The railroad brotherhoods kept their distance from the Knights.

  • Further reading: Nick Salvatore, Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist (1982).

Shorter entries

  • Horace Traubel (p. 6): Walt Whitman's secretary and literary executor, and a socialist editor. He was a friend of Debs and a living link between Debs and Whitman.

  • The Chinese exclusion question (p. 7): Congress barred Chinese laborers in 1882, the first federal law to exclude immigrants by nationality. Debs's answer, "The souls of Chinese children are yellow butterflies" (p. 7), is unverified.

  • Carl Sandburg (pp. 7-8): Before his fame as a poet he was a Socialist Party organizer in Wisconsin. He later wrote admiringly of Debs, and Young notes he went over to Wilson.

  • The Red Special (pp. 8, 10): The train the Socialist Party chartered for Debs's 1908 campaign against William Jennings Bryan and William Howard Taft.

  • The Lusitania (p. 8): The British liner sunk by a German submarine on May 7, 1915, killing 1,198 people, including 128 Americans. Young places the sinking in the North Sea, but it happened off the south coast of Ireland.

  • The International Socialist Congress at Stuttgart (p. 9): The 1907 gathering of the Second International, which debated how socialists should respond to a coming European war.

  • Colonel George Harvey and Newton D. Baker (p. 10): Harvey was a magazine editor who first promoted Wilson and then turned on him. Baker was Wilson's secretary of war, from 1916 to 1921.

  • The Haymarket affair (p. 10): The 1886 Chicago bombing after which four anarchists were hanged on weak evidence. Unit 18 covers it in full.

  • Elijah W. Halford (p. 14): Editor of the Republican Indianapolis Journal, which published Riley's early poems. He later served as private secretary to President Benjamin Harrison.

  • Benjamin Harrison (pp. 14, 16): Indiana Republican, president from 1889 to 1893. He reappears in Units 10 and 19.

  • "Pastels of Men" (pp. 12-13): Debs's late series of short memorial sketches. Young names Riley, Wendell Phillips, Robert Ingersoll, Eugene Field, and John Swinton among its subjects.

  • Eugene Field (p. 12): Chicago newspaper humorist whose column "Sharps and Flats" ran in the Chicago Morning News. He wrote the children's poem "Little Boy Blue."

  • John Swinton (pp. 12-13): New York labor journalist whose Striking for Life (1894) defended the Pullman strikers.

  • Wendell Phillips and Robert Ingersoll (p. 12): The abolitionist and the agnostic orator, both covered at length in Units 10 and 13.

  • The Dennison House (p. 16): A leading Indianapolis hotel, where Debs and Riley often met.

Allusions

  • Ultima Thule (p. 3): The ancient name for the farthest northern land, used for any remote extreme.

  • Abel and Cain (p. 3): Genesis 4. Young calls Debs the innocent Abel "branded Cain" by his accusers.

  • Little Nell and Tiny Tim (p. 7): Child characters from Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop and A Christmas Carol.

  • Emersonian, Transcendental (p. 4): The New England philosophy of Ralph Waldo Emerson, stressing individual conscience and the divine in nature.

  • Don Quixote (p. 16): Cervantes's idealist knight. Young uses the name for both Debs and Riley.

  • Croesus (p. 15): The proverbially rich king of ancient Lydia.
harp-companion-unit-06-the-rappites-and-:
Unit 6, pp. 105-120: The Rappites and the roots of Mormonism

← Unit 5 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 7 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Weitling travels up the Ohio River toward Pittsburgh and the Harmony Society at Economy, which gives Young the occasion to tell the Rappites' story from their first town to their third. She then turns to the young Joseph Smith, the treasure seeker of upstate New York, and the folk magic from which Mormonism grew.

Major entries

George Rapp and the Harmony Society (pp. 109-114)

  • Who he was: A vinedresser and lay preacher (1757-1847) from Iptingen in Württemberg, persecuted by the Lutheran church for separatism. He came to America in 1803 and was followed by several hundred families.

  • The three towns: The society built Harmony, in Butler County, Pennsylvania (1804-1814), then New Harmony on the Wabash in Indiana (1814-1824), then Economy, on the Ohio River below Pittsburgh (1824 onward), now Ambridge. They held all property in common and adopted celibacy in 1807, which Young calls a "community of married celibates" (p. 112).

  • Beliefs: They expected Christ's return within their lifetimes. They identified with the Sun Woman of Revelation 12, who flees into the wilderness, a figure Young returns to again and again (pp. 110-113). A limestone slab at New Harmony bearing two footprints was shown as the place where the angel Gabriel had stood (pp. 110-111).

  • Why it matters: The Harmonists were superb manufacturers and investors. Through Frederick Rapp, George's adopted son and business manager, they became major investors in Pennsylvania railroads and oil. The society dwindled with no children to succeed it and dissolved in 1905.

  • Further reading: Karl J. R. Arndt, George Rapp's Harmony Society, 1785-1847 (1965).

Frances Wright and Nashoba (pp. 111-112)

  • Who she was: A Scottish heiress (1795-1852), orphaned young, who toured America and wrote Views of Society and Manners in America (1821). She was a companion of Lafayette and a protégée of Jeremy Bentham.

  • What happened: In 1825 she bought land near Memphis and founded Nashoba, where enslaved people bought from their owners were to work off their purchase price and be educated for freedom. The experiment collapsed amid illness and scandal. In 1830 she took its thirty-one remaining residents to Haiti and freed them.

  • Why it matters: She became one of the first women in America to lecture publicly to mixed audiences. With Robert Dale Owen she edited the Free Enquirer in New York and backed the Working Men's Party of 1829, calling for free public schools. Opponents coined "Fanny Wrightism" as a slur for radicalism.

  • Where the record differs: Young places Nashoba on "the Fox River in Tennessee" and dates it to 1827 (p. 112). It was on the Wolf River and was founded in 1825. She also calls Wright "Bentham's ward," which is too strong.

  • Further reading: Celia Morris Eckhardt, Fanny Wright: Rebel in America (1984).

Joseph Smith, treasure seeking, and the golden plates (pp. 115-120)

  • Who he was: Born in Vermont in 1805, he grew up on a poor farm near Palmyra and Manchester, New York, in the "burned-over district," so called for its repeated religious revivals.

  • Treasure seeking: As a young man Smith was hired to find buried treasure with a seer stone. In 1826 he was brought before a justice of the peace as a "glass-looker." Local lore of the kind Young retells told of buried Spanish gold guarded by spirits, such as her "mysterious Spaniard" with his throat slashed (p. 119).

  • The plates: Smith said the angel Moroni led him in 1823 to golden plates buried in a hill near his home, later called Cumorah. He said he received them in 1827 with the Urim and Thummim, two seer stones for translating them. The Book of Mormon was published in 1830.

  • How Young uses it: For her, Smith's treasure digging and his scripture spring from the same American hunger for hidden gold, earthly and heavenly at once.

  • Further reading: Richard Lyman Bushman, Joseph Smith: Rough Stone Rolling (2005).

Emma Hale and Isaac Hale (pp. 117-118)

  • Who they were: Isaac Hale was a farmer and hunter in Harmony, Susquehanna County, Pennsylvania. Smith boarded in his house in 1825 while digging for a lost silver mine for Josiah Stowell (Young's "Stoal," p. 117).

  • What happened: Hale disapproved of Smith's trade and refused permission to marry. Smith and Emma eloped in January 1827. Emma became his scribe and, after his death, refused to follow Brigham Young west.

  • Where the record differs: Young places Hale's house "in Economy" (p. 117), the Rappite town. The Hales lived in a different Harmony, in northeastern Pennsylvania, unrelated to the Rappites. The shared name seems to have tangled the two.

  • Further reading: Linda King Newell and Valeen Tippetts Avery, Mormon Enigma: Emma Hale Smith (1984).

Shorter entries

  • Frederick Rapp (pp. 112-113): George Rapp's adopted son (1775-1834), architect and business head of the society. He negotiated the 1825 sale of New Harmony to Robert Owen for about \$150,000.

  • Abraham Ziegler (p. 114): The buyer of the original Harmony, Pennsylvania, in 1814, at a heavy loss to the society.

  • Robert Dale Owen (p. 112): Robert Owen's son (1801-1877). He was later an Indiana congressman who helped found the Smithsonian and pressed for emancipation during the Civil War.

  • Pontiac (p. 109): Ottawa leader of the 1763 uprising against the British in the Great Lakes country.

  • Anthony Wayne (p. 109): The general who defeated the Ohio Indian confederation at Fallen Timbers in 1794.

  • Red Pole (p. 109): A Shawnee chief who signed the Treaty of Greenville in 1795 and died in Pittsburgh that year.

  • Captain William Kidd (pp. 116, 119-120): Scottish privateer hanged at Execution Dock in London in 1701 for piracy. He really did bury treasure on Gardiners Island, New York, which fed a century of treasure legends.

  • The Gilded Age (p. 113): The title of Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner's 1873 satirical novel, which gave the postwar era its name. Young plays on it as the "Gelded Age" for the celibate Rappites.

Allusions

  • The Sun Woman (pp. 110-113): Revelation 12, the woman clothed with the sun who flees into the wilderness from the dragon.

  • The Golden Rose of Micah (p. 111): A Rappite emblem, drawn from Micah 4:8. It was carved over the door of their church.

  • Solomon's mines (p. 116): King Solomon's legendary gold mines of Ophir.

  • Atlantis (p. 119): Plato's lost island civilization.

  • El Dorado (p. 120): The Spanish legend of a golden kingdom in South America.

  • Antinous and Minerva (p. 112): The beautiful youth loved by the emperor Hadrian, and the Roman goddess of wisdom.
harp-companion-unit-19-indiana-in-1876-a:
Unit 19, pp. 513-544: Indiana in 1876 and 1877

← Unit 18 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 20 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young follows the Great Strike into Indiana, after a comic detour through the 1876 governor's race in which a farmer in blue jeans beat Benjamin Harrison. When the railroad men of Indianapolis struck in July 1877, Harrison helped organize armed citizens, and a federal judge jailed strikers for contempt. In Terre Haute, Debs's own lodge stayed on the job.

Major entries

The 1876 Indiana governor's race (pp. 517-528)

  • What happened: The Republican nominee, Godlove Orth, was tainted by scandal over claims he had pressed for Venezuelan bond interests (p. 517), and Judge Walter Q. Gresham said openly, "I don't believe that Orth is an honest man." Orth withdrew in August 1876. Benjamin Harrison, who had not sought the job, was drafted to replace him (p. 518).

  • "Blue Jeans" Williams: The Democrat, James D. Williams, was a six-foot-four farmer from Wheatland (p. 517) who campaigned in homespun blue jeans against "Kid Gloves" Harrison, mocked for his aristocratic manner. Williams won narrowly and served from 1877 until his death in 1880.

  • The Greenbackers: The Independent Greenback candidate, Anson Wolcott, withdrew at the last moment (p. 522). The Greenback movement wanted paper money to relieve debtors and farmers in the depression.

  • Further reading: Emma Lou Thornbrough, Indiana in the Civil War Era, 1850-1880 (1965).

The Hayes-Tilden election and the Compromise of 1877 (pp. 513, 525-526, 539)

  • What happened: In November 1876 Democrat Samuel Tilden won the popular vote, but returns from Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina were disputed. A special Electoral Commission gave every disputed vote to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes, who took office in March 1877. In the settlement, Hayes withdrew the last federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction.

  • The tax charge: Young notes the Republican charge that Tilden, a railroad lawyer, had underreported a ten-thousand-dollar fee from the Terre Haute, Alton and St. Louis Railroad on his 1862 income tax (p. 513).

  • Why it matters for labor: Within months, the troops pulled from the South were sent against striking railroad workers in the North.

  • Further reading: C. Vann Woodward, Reunion and Reaction (1951).

The 1877 strike in Indianapolis (pp. 523-538)

  • What happened: On July 23, 1877, railroad men in Indianapolis stopped freight trains, led by the fireman Warren Sayre (p. 530). Governor Williams and Mayor John Caven refused to use force (p. 526). Businessmen formed a Committee of Public Safety to arm citizens and a Committee of Mediation to negotiate (pp. 530-532). Harrison served on both and commanded a militia company.

  • Judge Gresham: Several railroads were in bankruptcy under federal receivers, so Judge Walter Q. Gresham treated interference with their trains as contempt of his court. Federal marshals and troops arrested Sayre and others, who were tried by the judge without a jury.

  • Why it matters: This use of court power over bankrupt railroads was a forerunner of the sweeping injunction used against Debs in 1894, when he was jailed for contempt without a jury trial. Harrison's role haunted him with labor voters for the rest of his career.

  • Further reading: Bruce, 1877: Year of Violence (1959).

The Vandalia strike in Terre Haute (pp. 539-543)

  • What happened: The Vandalia's president, Riley McKeen, was a local man with a reputation for treating employees decently (p. 539). When the strike reached Terre Haute, it was brief and peaceful. Debs's Vigo Lodge of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen did not support it.

  • Richard W. Thompson: A Terre Haute Republican and Hayes's secretary of the navy (1877-1880), who urged a hard line (p. 541).

  • Why it matters: Debs at twenty-one believed labor and capital could be partners. Watching Gresham's court, the troops, and the blacklists that followed, he began the long change of mind that ended in socialism.

Denis Kearney and the San Francisco riots (p. 514)

  • What happened: On July 23, 1877, a San Francisco meeting called in sympathy with the eastern strikers turned into three days of attacks on Chinese workers and businesses. Denis Kearney, an Irish-born drayman, then built the Workingmen's Party of California with speeches on the city's sandlots under the slogan "The Chinese must go!"

  • Why it matters: The anti-Chinese movement drove the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. Young notes the bitter irony that Irish and Chinese workers alike had died building the railroads.

  • Further reading: Beth Lew-Williams, The Chinese Must Go (2018).

Shorter entries

  • William H. Vanderbilt and the Albany strike (pp. 515-516): Vanderbilt's New York Central faced strikers at West Albany in 1877. The brakeman John Van Hoesen was arrested for saying workers would answer a diet of bullets with bullets.

  • Schuyler Colfax (p. 519): Indiana's Republican leader and Grant's first vice president, ruined by the Crédit Mobilier scandal.

  • Lew Wallace and Ingersoll (p. 529): Wallace said an 1876 train conversation with Ingersoll started him on the novel Ben-Hur (1880).

  • Petroleum V. Nasby (p. 529): The comic Copperhead preacher created by the Ohio journalist David Ross Locke, a favorite of Lincoln.

  • Albert G. Porter (pp. 529, 532): An Indianapolis lawyer who helped Harrison counsel the strikers and was later governor (1881-1885). Young calls him a general.

  • Coeur d'Alene and Homestead (pp. 536-537): Both struck in 1892, during Harrison's presidency. Federal troops occupied the Idaho mining district, and Pinkerton guards fought the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers at Carnegie's Homestead works.

  • Krupp (p. 544): The German arms maker. Debs's magazine reprinted an 1889 article on him.

  • "The only good Indian" (p. 544): A saying attributed to General Sheridan, which Young finds echoed in the press of the day.

Allusions

  • Regulus (p. 517): The Roman general who returned to torture in Carthage rather than break his word.

  • Vox populi, vox dei (p. 519): "The voice of the people is the voice of God."

  • Hamiltonian and Jeffersonian horses (p. 531): Rule by the propertied few against rule by the many.

  • "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God" (p. 513): Luther's hymn.

  • Bret Harte's "heathen Chinee" (p. 514): From his 1870 poem "Plain Language from Truthful James."

  • Byron's Childe Harold (p. 544): The wandering romantic hero.
harp-companion-unit-20-whistler-and-dost:
Unit 20, pp. 545-576: Whistler and Dostoyevsky

← Unit 19 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 21 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

In the book's strangest and most daring leap, Young moves from Debs's railroad magazine to St. Petersburg in the 1840s. An American engineer, Major George Washington Whistler, is building the czar's railroad with serf labor while a young writer, Fyodor Dostoyevsky, walks past the construction on his way to a socialist reading circle. Both roads end in Russia's iron order: Whistler dies there, and Dostoyevsky goes to Siberia. The episode prefigures Debs's own imprisonment.

Major entries

Major George Washington Whistler (pp. 546-554)

  • Who he was: A West Point graduate (1800-1849) who became one of America's first great railroad engineers. He worked on the Baltimore and Ohio and built locomotives at Lowell, Massachusetts.

  • In Russia: In 1842 Czar Nicholas I hired him to build the railway from St. Petersburg to Moscow, about four hundred miles, one of the great engineering works of the age. It was built largely by serfs under harsh conditions, and many died. Whistler died of cholera in St. Petersburg in April 1849, and the line opened in 1851.

  • The family: His wife, Anna McNeill Whistler, a devout North Carolinian (p. 547), is the woman in their son's painting Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871), known as Whistler's Mother (p. 546).

  • How Young uses him: An American technician serving an autocrat, Whistler links the railroads Debs fired on to the czar's empire. Young sets his serf crews beside the American workers his railroads later employed.

  • Further reading: Albert Parry, Whistler's Father (1939).

James McNeill Whistler (pp. 546-550)

  • Who he was: The painter (1834-1903), born in Lowell and raised partly in St. Petersburg.

  • West Point and after: He entered West Point in 1851, when Colonel Robert E. Lee was superintendent (p. 548), and was dismissed in 1854 for failing chemistry. He later joked, "If silicon had been a gas, I would have been a major general." He worked briefly at the Winans locomotive works in Baltimore and then as a draftsman for the U.S. Coast Survey in Washington, where he doodled faces in the margins of his maps (p. 549). In 1855 he left for Paris and never lived in America again.

  • Further reading: Daniel E. Sutherland, Whistler: A Life for Art's Sake (2014).

Vissarion Belinsky (pp. 555-561)

  • Who he was: The most influential Russian critic of his generation (1811-1848), called "Vissarion the Furious" (p. 555). He championed realism and social justice in literature and moved from Hegelian philosophy to socialism.

  • Dostoyevsky and Gogol: Belinsky hailed Dostoyevsky's first novel, Poor Folk (1846), as a work of genius, then cooled toward him. In 1847 he wrote a furious open letter to Nikolai Gogol, author of Dead Souls (1842) and "The Overcoat" (1842), attacking Gogol's turn to religious conservatism. The letter circulated in manuscript and was banned.

  • Why it matters: Belinsky died of tuberculosis in 1848, just before the police would have arrested him. His letter to Gogol became the crime that sent Dostoyevsky to Siberia.

  • Further reading: Isaiah Berlin, "Vissarion Belinsky," in Russian Thinkers (1978).

Dostoyevsky and the Petrashevsky Circle (pp. 555-572)

  • The circle: From 1845, Mikhail Butashevich-Petrashevsky, a Foreign Ministry official, hosted Friday gatherings in St. Petersburg where young men discussed Fourier, socialism, and censored books. Young calls him a "chatterer and mountebank" (p. 561). Dostoyevsky, a former student of the Main Engineering School, which was housed in the Mikhailovsky Castle where Paul I had been murdered (p. 563, see Unit 2), read Belinsky's letter aloud there.

  • Arrest and mock execution: After the European revolutions of 1848, Nicholas I cracked down. Dostoyevsky and others were arrested on April 23, 1849, and held in the Peter and Paul Fortress (pp. 565-566). On December 22, 1849, they were led to Semyonovsky Square, dressed in execution shirts, and tied to posts before a firing squad. At the last moment a messenger read the czar's commutation, which had been planned all along.

  • Siberia: Dostoyevsky served four years at hard labor in the prison at Omsk, in western Siberia (p. 569), followed by army service. He drew on it in Notes from the House of the Dead (1860-1862), a book Debs admired (Unit 21).

  • Later work: His novel The Possessed (Demons, 1871-1872) was based on the 1869 murder of a student at the Moscow Agricultural Academy by a revolutionary cell (p. 555), a savage portrait of the radicals he had once joined.

  • Where the record differs: Young places Omsk in a province she calls "Armolensk" (p. 569). Omsk lay in western Siberia, in Tobolsk province. "Armolensk" may be a garbling of Akmolinsk, a region to the south.

  • Further reading: Joseph Frank, Dostoevsky: The Seeds of Revolt, 1821-1849 (1976) and The Years of Ordeal, 1850-1859 (1983).

Shorter entries

  • Czar Nicholas I (pp. 559, 574): Emperor of Russia from 1825 to 1855. He came to the throne crushing the Decembrist revolt and ruled by censorship and secret police.

  • The Decembrists (pp. 567, 570): Officers who rose in December 1825 for a constitution. Five were hanged and more than a hundred exiled to Siberia, where their wives famously followed them.

  • The Nevsky Prospect (pp. 554, 564): St. Petersburg's main avenue, the setting of Gogol's 1835 story of the same name.

  • The Slavophiles (p. 553): Russian thinkers who rejected Western models and exalted Orthodox Christianity and the peasant commune.

  • The Russian commune and American Indians (pp. 569-570): Young compares the Russian peasant commune, the Mormon cooperative, and Native American common ownership as forms of communism older than Marx.

  • Thomas Hobbes and Malthus (p. 545): Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) argued for absolute state power. Thomas Malthus's essay on population (1798) held that the poor would always outrun the food supply, an argument used against relief.

Allusions

  • "The Fall of the House of Usher" (pp. 558-559): Poe's 1839 tale of a decaying family and house, for czarist Russia.

  • Byron's "The Prisoner of Chillon" (p. 565): The 1816 poem of a man chained for years in a Swiss dungeon.

  • Poe's "The Raven" (p. 565): The 1845 poem, with its refrain "Nevermore."

  • Liszt and Ole Bull (p. 566): The piano virtuoso and the Norwegian violinist. Ole Bull toured America and founded a short-lived colony in Pennsylvania in 1852.

  • Cromwell and Charles Stuart (p. 575): The English revolution that executed a king.

  • Prospero (p. 556): Shakespeare's magician, for St. Petersburg dissolving in mist.
harp-companion-unit-17-the-molly-maguire:
Unit 17, pp. 433-472: The Molly Maguires

← Unit 16 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 18 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

This unit tells the story of the Irish miners of Pennsylvania's anthracite country, the railroad president who set out to destroy their union, and the Pinkerton spy who lived among them for two and a half years. Twenty men were hanged. Young's sympathy is with the condemned, and she frames the trials as a model for later frame-ups from Haymarket to Sacco and Vanzetti (p. 466).

Major entries

Franklin B. Gowen (pp. 437, 445-447, 456, 465-472)

  • Who he was: A Philadelphia lawyer (1836-1889) and former district attorney of Schuylkill County who became president of the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad in 1869. He bought huge tracts of coal land through the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, so that one corporation carried, mined, and sold the coal.

  • What he did: In October 1873 he hired Pinkerton, through the agency's superintendent George Bangs (p. 437), to infiltrate the Irish miners. He then served as a special prosecutor at the Molly Maguire trials, delivering the closing arguments himself.

  • His end: On December 13, 1889, he was found shot dead in Wormley's Hotel in Washington, where he had come to argue a rate case against Standard Oil before the Interstate Commerce Commission (p. 471). It was ruled a suicide, though rumors of a Molly revenge circulated.

  • Further reading: Kevin Kenny, Making Sense of the Molly Maguires (1998).

James McParlan (pp. 441, 450-464)

  • Who he was: An Irish-born Pinkerton detective (1844-1919) from County Armagh. From October 1873 he lived in the coal towns as "James McKenna," a drifter and heavy drinker, moving through Swatara, Tremont, Rausch Creek, Donaldson, and other towns (p. 450). He joined the Ancient Order of Hibernians and rose to secretary of the Shenandoah lodge.

  • The trials: From May 1876 he testified for days, naming dozens of men. Defense lawyers argued that he had known of killings in advance and failed to stop them, even encouraged them (p. 464).

  • Later career: As head of the Pinkertons' Denver office, he took the 1906 confession of Harry Orchard, who blamed the leaders of the Western Federation of Miners, Big Bill Haywood, Charles Moyer, and George Pettibone, for the bombing murder of former Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg (p. 441). Debs wrote his fierce article "Arouse, Ye Slaves!" in their defense. Clarence Darrow won Haywood's acquittal in 1907.

  • Further reading: J. Anthony Lukas, Big Trouble (1997), on the Idaho case.

The Molly Maguires and the Ancient Order of Hibernians (pp. 437-460)

  • Who they were: The name came from Irish rural secret societies such as the Ribbonmen (p. 457), which used threats and violence against landlords and their agents. In Pennsylvania it was applied to Irish miners, many from Donegal (p. 452), accused of killing mine bosses and officials from the 1860s through 1875. Their meetings were said to happen within lodges of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, a legal Irish Catholic fraternal society.

  • The debate: Historians agree some killings happened and that some AOH members were involved. They dispute whether an organized conspiracy existed or whether Gowen used a few crimes to discredit the whole Irish working class and its union.

  • The church: Catholic bishops condemned the Mollies. Young tells of a priest, Father Koch, barring the burial of a suspected member (pp. 458-459).

The Workingmen's Benevolent Association and the Long Strike (pp. 446-447, 455-456)

  • What it was: The anthracite miners' union, founded in 1868 under John Siney (p. 455). In 1869 it accepted a sliding scale, which Young calls the "Gowen Compromise," tying wages to the price of coal (pp. 446-447).

  • The Long Strike: From January to June 1875 the miners struck against wage cuts. Gowen and the other operators starved them out, and the union collapsed. The murder trials that followed completed the destruction of organized labor in the anthracite fields for a generation.

  • Further reading: Harold D. Aurand, From the Molly Maguires to the United Mine Workers (1971).

The trials and hangings (pp. 463-470)

  • What happened: Juries excluded Irish Catholics. Young lists the men hanged (p. 463). On June 21, 1877, remembered as Black Thursday or the Day of the Rope, six were hanged at Pottsville and four at Mauch Chunk. Among those hanged at Pottsville were Thomas Munley, convicted of killing the mine boss Thomas Sanger on testimony such as that of Robert Heaton (p. 465), and several men convicted of killing the Tamaqua policeman Benjamin Yost (p. 470). Ten more were hanged by 1879, twenty in all.

  • Jack Kehoe: The Girardville tavern keeper of the Hibernian House and county delegate of the AOH (p. 453). He was hanged in December 1878 for the 1862 killing of the mine foreman Frank Langdon (p. 467). In 1979 Governor Milton Shapp granted him a posthumous pardon.

  • Alexander Campbell: Hanged at Mauch Chunk in 1877. Legend says he pressed his hand on his cell wall to leave a print as a sign of his innocence, and that it cannot be removed.

  • Further reading: Kenny, Making Sense of the Molly Maguires (1998).

Shorter entries

  • Muff Lawler and Pat Dormer (pp. 452-454): Michael "Muff" Lawler was the Shenandoah bodymaster, or lodge head. Pat Dormer kept a tavern where McParlan made his first contacts.

  • The Chain Gang and the Sheet Iron Gang (p. 453): Local gang names that appear in McParlan's reports, which Young suggests he folded under the single label of the Mollies.

  • The Centennial Exposition (p. 472): The 1876 world's fair in Philadelphia, where the giant Corliss steam engine powered the Machinery Hall. William Dean Howells described it in the Atlantic Monthly.

  • Mark Twain's "Revised Catechism" (p. 461): A satire in the New York Tribune of September 27, 1871, which answers the question of who is God with "Money is God."

  • Henry Adams's Democracy (p. 467): An anonymous 1880 novel of Washington corruption, whose heroine is Madeleine Lee.

  • The 1876 election (p. 468): Samuel Tilden won the popular vote, but Rutherford Hayes took the presidency after a disputed count (Unit 19).

  • Jesse James's death (p. 471): Bob Ford shot him in his home at St. Joseph, Missouri, on April 3, 1882.

  • Sacco and Vanzetti (p. 466): Italian anarchists executed in Massachusetts in 1927 after a trial widely seen as unjust.

  • Leo Tolstoy (p. 466): The Russian novelist, whose later Christian pacifism and anarchism Debs admired.

Allusions

  • Shylock (p. 433): Shakespeare's moneylender, for the railroad men.

  • David and Goliath (p. 466): The weak against the strong.

  • Cromwell (p. 451): Oliver Cromwell's brutal conquest of Ireland in 1649-1650, remembered by every Irish miner.

  • Bunyan's Pilgrim (p. 451): From The Pilgrim's Progress.

  • "Westward the Star of Empire Takes Its Way" (p. 447): From Bishop Berkeley's 1726 poem, a slogan of expansion.

  • The Great Pyramid (p. 467): Of Giza, for monuments built by labor.
harp-history-in-hsfar:
The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Harp Song for a Radical · The Marguerite Young Society · The History Companion

Harp Song for a Radical covers roughly the 1840s through the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, with flashes forward to Pullman, Haymarket, and Debs in prison. Young's method is to follow any thread that fed the world Debs was born into. So a chapter about Terre Haute can open onto a German tailor-communist in Iowa, a Mormon farmer mortgaging his land, or a Russian novelist facing a firing squad. What looks like digression is her argument: American radicalism came out of this tangle of utopian dreams, immigrant politics, war, and industrial violence. Below, the history is sorted into its main threads, with the context Young often assumes.

The utopian inheritance

Before there was a labor movement, there were communities that tried to live out a better world. Indiana was one of their main laboratories, which is partly why Young, a Hoosier herself, returns to them so often.

Father George Rapp led the Harmony Society, German Pietists who believed Christ's return was near. They practiced celibacy, held property in common, and were extremely productive farmers and manufacturers. They founded Harmony, Pennsylvania (1804), moved to New Harmony, Indiana (1814), then sold the whole town in 1825 and returned to Pennsylvania. The society lingered until 1905.

The buyer was Robert Owen, a Welsh mill owner who had run a model factory village at New Lanark, Scotland. His New Harmony (1825 to 1827) was secular and rationalist, meant to prove that people shaped by good conditions would cooperate. It collapsed within two years. But it drew scientists and educators by keelboat (the "Boatload of Knowledge," 1826), and Owen's son Robert Dale Owen later served Indiana in Congress. The younger Owen helped found the Smithsonian and pushed for married women's property rights in Indiana's 1850 constitution. Young wrote a whole earlier book, Angel in the Forest, on these two New Harmonys.

Frances Wright was a Scottish heiress, friend of Lafayette and a protégé of Jeremy Bentham. In 1825 she founded Nashoba, near Memphis, where enslaved people were to earn their freedom through labor and education. (Young places it on the Fox River and in 1827; most histories say the Wolf River and 1825.) The project failed, and in 1830 Wright took its enslaved residents to Haiti and freed them. She went on to become one of the first women in America to lecture publicly to mixed audiences, speaking for free thought, workers' rights, and birth control.

Étienne Cabet was a French communist whose novel Voyage to Icaria (1840) inspired a real emigration. His followers tried Texas in 1848, where fever wrecked the settlement. In 1849 they took over Nauvoo, Illinois, the town the Mormons had just abandoned. The group split in 1856, Cabet was expelled, and he died in St. Louis that year. Icarian offshoots survived in Iowa until 1898.

Zoar and Ebenezer, which Young mentions through Weitling's eyes, were German religious communes. Zoar, Ohio (1817 to 1898) was led by Joseph Bimeler. The Ebenezer community of New York moved to Iowa in 1855 and became the Amana Colonies, which stayed communal until 1932. The appliance company still carries the name.

Charles Fourier was a French theorist who planned society around cooperative units called phalanxes. His ideas swept America in the 1840s through Albert Brisbane and Horace Greeley's New York Tribune, and dozens of phalanxes were founded, including Brook Farm in its later years. The same ideas got Fyodor Dostoyevsky arrested in 1849 for belonging to a Fourierist discussion circle in St. Petersburg. He was marched out for execution, reprieved at the last moment, and sent to a Siberian prison camp, the basis for The House of the Dead. Young uses that scene to foreshadow Debs's own imprisonments, and she names The House of the Dead as one of the books Debs cared about.

The Mormons enter as another American millennial experiment. Martin Harris was the prosperous New York farmer who financed the first printing of the Book of Mormon in 1830 by mortgaging his farm. He also lost the first 116 manuscript pages after borrowing them to show his skeptical wife. He, Oliver Cowdery, and David Whitmer were the "Three Witnesses" to the golden plates. Brigham Young then led the migration to Utah, where the church experimented with cooperative economics. Young also brings in the Shakers (Ann Lee) and the Oneida Community (John Humphrey Noyes) as part of the same restless search.

The German radicals after 1848

When the European revolutions of 1848 failed, thousands of radicals fled to America. They became known as Forty-Eighters, and they brought socialism into American cities decades before most native-born workers heard the word.

Heinrich Heine, the German poet exiled in Paris and a friend of Marx, never came to America. Young uses him as the lyrical conscience of that European generation.

Wilhelm Weitling gets more pages than almost anyone except Debs. He was a German tailor, largely self-taught, and one of the first working-class communists. His books, especially The Gospel of a Poor Sinner, mixed communism with Christian feeling, and he clashed bitterly with Marx in 1846. In New York he edited Die Republik der Arbeiter (The Workers' Republic) from 1850 to 1855 and organized German workers' leagues. He also tied his hopes to Communia, a colony in Clayton County, Iowa, which collapsed in debt and lawsuits by the mid-1850s. He died in New York in 1871, largely forgotten. His story matters because it shows a socialism in America that was religious, utopian, and immigrant long before the Marxist version took hold.

August Willich was a Prussian officer who turned communist, fought in the 1849 Baden uprising, and broke with Marx in 1850. In America he became a Union general and commanded the 32nd Indiana, a German regiment. Joseph Weydemeyer, another Marx ally, also served as a Union officer. Friedrich Sorge, in Hoboken, ran the International Workingmen's Association after its headquarters moved to New York in 1872.

Indiana during the Civil War

This is some of the least-taught history in the book. Southern Indiana was deeply split, and the Ohio River connected more than it divided.

The Knights of the Golden Circle began as a pro-slavery society in the 1850s that dreamed of a slave empire around the Gulf of Mexico. During the war, it and related groups (the Order of American Knights, the Sons of Liberty) became networks of Northern Copperheads, Democrats opposed to the war, some plotting armed uprisings in the Midwest.

Lambdin P. Milligan was an Indiana lawyer and Copperhead who was arrested in 1864. A military commission, not a civilian court, sentenced him to hang. In Ex parte Milligan (1866), the Supreme Court ruled that civilians cannot be tried by military tribunals where civilian courts are functioning. It remains a landmark of civil liberties. Milligan later sued the officials involved and won five dollars in damages. The opposing lawyer was Benjamin Harrison, future president, which is the connection Young draws.

Oliver P. Morton, Indiana's wartime governor, faced a Democratic legislature that refused to pass a budget in 1863. He ran the state for two years on private loans and federal money, arguably outside the law. The press-smashing Young describes in Terre Haute belongs to this period.

Young also looks past the war's edges. At Sand Creek, Colorado, on November 29, 1864, militia under Colonel John Chivington attacked the peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho camp of Black Kettle and killed well over a hundred people, mostly women, children, and the elderly. Black Kettle survived, only to be killed by Custer's troops at the Washita in 1868. In Mexico, France installed Maximilian as emperor while the United States was busy with its own war. He was executed in 1867, and his wife Carlotta lived out her life in madness in Europe.

Railroads, money, and the Gilded Age

Major George Washington Whistler was an American railroad engineer who built the St. Petersburg to Moscow railway for the czar with serf labor, and who had earlier worked on the Baltimore & Ohio. He was the father of the painter James McNeill Whistler, and of course the husband of the woman in Whistler's Mother. Young uses him to link American railroads with Russian autocracy.

Tom Scott, president of the Pennsylvania Railroad, was one of the most powerful men in the country. He is widely credited, though the quote may be legend, with saying strikers should get "a rifle diet." His railroad interests are also tied by historians to the backroom deal that settled the 1876 election.

Amasa Stone was a Cleveland industrialist. The Ashtabula bridge he designed collapsed under a passenger train in December 1876, killing about 92 people, and he took his own life in 1883. His son-in-law John Hay, Lincoln's former secretary, later wrote The Bread-Winners (1883), an anti-union novel shaped partly by the 1877 strike.

The Panic of 1873, set off by the failure of Jay Cooke's bank, began a depression that lasted until 1879. It is the economic backdrop for nearly everything in the book's second half. Charley Ross, the four-year-old kidnapped from Germantown, Pennsylvania, in 1874, appears as period texture. His was the first widely publicized ransom kidnapping in America, and he was never found.

Labor's hard decade

The Tompkins Square Riot took place on January 13, 1874. Thousands of unemployed workers gathered in Manhattan to demand public works jobs. The police permit was revoked without proper notice, and mounted and foot police clubbed the crowd. A young cigar maker named Samuel Gompers escaped by jumping into a cellarway. He later said the day shaped his cautious approach to labor organizing, and he went on to lead the American Federation of Labor.

The Molly Maguires were Irish miners in the Pennsylvania anthracite region, allegedly a secret society that used violence against mine bosses. The central figure against them was Franklin B. Gowen, president of the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad and its coal company. He hired Allan Pinkerton's agency, whose detective James McParlan went undercover as "James McKenna" inside the Ancient Order of Hibernians from 1873 to 1875. At the trials, Gowen himself served as a special prosecutor, and the juries excluded Irish Catholics. Twenty men were hanged between 1877 and 1879, ten of them on June 21, 1877, remembered in the region as the Day of the Rope. Jack Kehoe, the tavern keeper Young mentions, was hanged in 1878 and granted a posthumous pardon by Pennsylvania in 1979. Historians still argue over how much of the conspiracy was real, but the destruction of the miners' union in the Long Strike of 1875 is not in dispute.

Allan Pinkerton was himself once a radical. He was a Scottish Chartist, a supporter of workers' voting rights, who fled Glasgow in 1842 and became a barrel maker in Dundee, Illinois. He ran an Underground Railroad station, helped John Brown, and guarded Lincoln on the way to his first inauguration. His agency's logo was an open eye with the motto "We Never Sleep," the source of both Young's refrain "The Eye That Never Sleeps" and the phrase "private eye." His turn from Chartist to strikebreaker is one of the book's great ironies.

The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 was the first national strike in American history. It began on July 16 at Martinsburg, West Virginia, after the B&O cut wages again, and spread along the rail lines within days. In Pittsburgh, militia fired into a crowd, killing around twenty. The crowd then burned the Pennsylvania Railroad's yards, destroying over a hundred locomotives and more than a thousand cars. St. Louis saw a brief general strike run by the Workingmen's Party, sometimes called the St. Louis Commune. President Hayes sent federal troops, the same troops just withdrawn from the South under the Compromise of 1877 that ended Reconstruction. Roughly a hundred people died nationwide. In Terre Haute, Debs, then a young officer of the firemen's union, did not back the strike, a stance he would later outgrow. Federal Judge Walter Q. Gresham in Indianapolis used his authority over bankrupt railroads to jail strikers for contempt, an early version of the injunction later used against Debs in 1894.

Indiana politics in 1876 also get Young's comic treatment. The Republican candidate for governor, Godlove Orth, withdrew under scandal. The Democrat, James "Blue Jeans" Williams, was a six-foot-four farmer who campaigned in homespun and won.

Debs's Terre Haute circle

The Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was founded in 1873 at Port Jervis, New York, originally more as an insurance and temperance society than a fighting union. Debs was a charter member of its Terre Haute lodge in 1875 and became editor of its magazine in 1880.

The Occidental Literary Club was where Debs gave early speeches and used his connections to bring national figures to town. They included Robert Ingersoll, the "Great Agnostic" and the most famous orator of the age; Wendell Phillips, the abolitionist who turned to labor reform after the war; and Susan B. Anthony, whom Debs hosted when much of Terre Haute shunned her.

Ida Husted Harper was Debs's school friend and ran the women's department of the firemen's magazine. She later became Susan B. Anthony's authorized biographer and co-wrote the last volumes of the History of Woman Suffrage. James Whitcomb Riley, the Hoosier poet of "Little Orphant Annie," and the humorist Bill Nye were close friends of Debs. The Reverend Myron Reed was a former Grand Banks fisherman turned Denver minister who became one of Debs's closest allies. Herman Hulman was a German-born Terre Haute grocer. His family's Clabber Girl baking powder fortune later bought the Indianapolis Motor Speedway.

Glimpses forward

Young repeatedly foreshadows events past 1877. In the Haymarket affair of 1886, a bomb at a Chicago labor rally led to the conviction of eight anarchists on thin evidence and four hangings. After the Preparedness Day bombing in San Francisco in 1916, labor organizer Tom Mooney was convicted on perjured testimony and spent over two decades in prison before his pardon in 1939. Coxey's Army was the 1894 march of the unemployed on Washington. The Pullman strike of 1894 put Debs in jail and was the chapter Young was writing when she fell ill.

Why this history feels hidden

Most of these stories fall between the categories schools use. Utopian communities get filed under religion or curiosities, Copperheads under Civil War footnotes, and the Molly Maguires and 1877 under "labor unrest," if they appear at all. Young's point is that they belong together: the same country produced New Harmony and the Pittsburgh roundhouse fire, and Debs was shaped by both the dream and the violence.

For reading in the same spirit as Zinn, several books go further on these threads. Jeremy Brecher's Strike! tells labor history from below. Robert V. Bruce's 1877: Year of Violence is still the fullest account of the Great Strike. Kevin Kenny's Making Sense of the Molly Maguires untangles myth from record. Carl Wittke's The Utopian Communist is the standard life of Weitling. Frank Morn's history of the Pinkertons borrows Young's own phrase for its title, The Eye That Never Sleeps. Frank Klement's Dark Lanterns examines the Copperhead secret societies. Nick Salvatore's Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist is the best conventional biography to set beside Young's lyrical one.

The book has no titled chapters. It runs in two parts (Part One, "Prelude in a Golden Key," and Part Two, "Harp Song for a Radical," beginning on page 179) made of roughly 170 short numbered sections, many only a few pages long. In the uploaded scan, many section numbers are too garbled to track reliably. So this plan groups the sections into 21 units by page range (using the 1999 Knopf first edition pagination), each built around a subject Young stays with for a stretch.

Unit 1, pp. 1-16: The prelude from prison

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 1

Young opens at the end of Debs's life, then circles back.

  • The Espionage Act (1917) and its 1918 amendments, known as the Sedition Act, criminalized speech against the war. Debs was convicted under them for his June 1918 antiwar speech in Canton, Ohio.

  • Woodrow Wilson refused to pardon Debs. Norman Thomas was a Presbyterian minister and six-time Socialist presidential candidate, who later preached Debs's funeral sermon. Carl Sandburg was a Socialist Party organizer in Wisconsin before his fame as a poet.

  • Tom Mooney and the Preparedness Day bombing: a bomb at a pro-war parade in San Francisco on July 22, 1916 killed ten people. Mooney, a labor organizer, was convicted on perjured testimony and pardoned in 1939.

  • The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was the first federal law to bar immigration by nationality.

  • James Whitcomb Riley, the Hoosier poet and Debs's friend, appears here and throughout.

Unit 2, pp. 17-32: Colmar, and the dream of reason

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 2

  • Daniel Debs and Marguerite Marie Bettrich ("Daisy") were Alsatians from Colmar. Daniel arrived in 1849 and they settled in Terre Haute in 1855.

  • Eugène Sue was a French novelist of the Paris poor, and Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables. Debs was named for both.

  • Napoleon and Czar Alexander I stand for the Europe of empire and the post-1815 Holy Alliance of monarchs against revolution.

  • Jeremy Bentham, the English philosopher of utility, and Thomas Jefferson at Monticello stand for Enlightenment reason.

  • Robert Owen and Charles Fourier are the two great utopian planners, and Walt Whitman is the American poet of democracy. Young introduces all three as the book's intellectual ancestors.

Unit 3, pp. 33-48: Weitling's youth and Heine

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 3

  • Wilhelm Weitling was born in Magdeburg in 1808. He was a journeyman tailor who became the leading voice of the League of the Just, the secret German workers' society that later became Marx's Communist League. He was arrested in Zurich in 1843, and the prison poems Young quotes date from that time.

  • Heinrich Heine was a German-Jewish poet in exile in Paris. His Germany: A Winter's Tale (1844) satirized Prussia.

  • Mathilde was Heine's French wife. Uncle Salomon was his wealthy Hamburg banker uncle, who supported him grudgingly.

Unit 4, pp. 49-80: Paris, Brussels, Marx

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 4

  • Ludwig Börne was a radical German journalist in Paris and Heine's rival.

  • Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels: Marx came from Trier, and Engels managed his family's cotton mill in Manchester. Eleanor Marx, Marx's daughter, later toured America as a labor speaker (1886).

  • The 1846 Brussels confrontation: Marx attacked Weitling's moral, prophetic communism as unscientific, a split between two kinds of socialism that runs through the whole book.

  • Joseph Weydemeyer was Marx's ally who emigrated to New York and first published Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire there in 1852.

  • John Jacob Astor, the richest man in America, appears as the New York money power Weitling found on arrival.

Unit 5, pp. 81-104: Weitling in America, and the communes

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 5

  • The Arbeiterbund (Workers' League) and Die Republik der Arbeiter were Weitling's New York organization and newspaper, 1850 to 1855. German workers' networks in Cincinnati, Milwaukee, Sandusky, and Dubuque were its base.

  • Communia was a communal colony in Clayton County, Iowa. Weitling tied his hopes to it, and it failed in debt and lawsuits by the mid-1850s.

  • The Oneida Community (1848 to 1881) was John Humphrey Noyes's perfectionist commune in New York.

  • Étienne Cabet and the Icarians: a disastrous Texas settlement in 1848, then Nauvoo, Illinois, from 1849.

  • Zoar, Ohio was a German Separatist commune (1817 to 1898) under Joseph Bimeler. Ebenezer became the Amana Colonies of Iowa.

Unit 6, pp. 105-120: The Rappites and the roots of Mormonism

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 6

  • George Rapp's Harmony Society moved from Harmony, Pennsylvania, to New Harmony, Indiana (1814), then to Economy, Pennsylvania (1824).

  • Joseph Smith's early life as a treasure seeker in upstate New York included folk magic, seer stones, and tales of Captain Kidd's buried gold. Young links this to the angel Moroni and the Urim and Thummim, the seeing instruments Smith said came with the golden plates.

Unit 7, pp. 121-152: The Book of Mormon to Salt Lake

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 7

  • Martin Harris was the Palmyra farmer who mortgaged his farm to pay for the 1830 printing and lost the first 116 manuscript pages.

  • Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Peter Whitmer: the church was formally organized in 1830 in Fayette, Seneca County, New York, at the Whitmer farm.

  • Brigham Young led the exodus to Utah (1846 to 1847). The Lion House was his Salt Lake residence for his plural family.

  • Mark Twain's Roughing It (1872) recounts his 1861 trip west with his brother Orion Clemens, secretary of Nevada Territory, including a visit to Salt Lake. William Dean Howells, editor of the Atlantic Monthly, praised it.

Unit 8, pp. 153-176: Weitling's later years

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 8

  • Wilhelm Keil was a German tailor turned revivalist who founded communal colonies at Bethel, Missouri (1844) and Aurora, Oregon (1856).

  • August Willich was a Prussian officer and communist who broke with Marx and later became a Union general commanding the 32nd Indiana.

  • Weitling's inventions: in later life he earned patents on sewing machine improvements, set against Elias Howe and Isaac Singer's sewing machine patent wars.

  • Caroline Tödt was Weitling's wife. Friedrich Sorge in Hoboken led the American branch of the International Workingmen's Association.

  • Castle Garden was New York's immigrant landing station, 1855 to 1890, before Ellis Island.

Unit 9, pp. 177-200: Terre Haute and the coming war

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 9

  • The Wabash and Erie Canal and the Vandalia Railroad were the transport lines that made Terre Haute. Daniel Debs's first job was laying ties.

  • Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not bar slavery in the territories.

  • Richard Gatling of Indianapolis patented the Gatling gun in 1862.

  • Oliver P. Morton was Indiana's war governor, who ran the state without a legislative budget from 1863 to 1865.

  • The Knights of the Golden Circle were a pro-slavery secret society that became a Copperhead network in southern Indiana.

Unit 10, pp. 201-224: Treason trials and abolition

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 10

  • John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry was in 1859.

  • Lambdin P. Milligan was a Copperhead lawyer sentenced to death by a military commission in 1864. Ex parte Milligan (1866) barred military trials of civilians where courts are open. Benjamin Harrison opposed him in his later damages suit.

  • Wendell Phillips was a Boston abolitionist who became a labor reformer after the war. Henry Ward Beecher was the celebrity Brooklyn preacher.

  • George Pullman's early career: he raised Chicago buildings out of the mud in the 1850s and launched his luxury sleeping car, the Pioneer, in 1865. The legend attached to it is that it carried Lincoln's body home.

Unit 11, pp. 225-256: Assassination, Reconstruction, Mrs. Lincoln

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 11

  • John Wilkes Booth assassinated Lincoln in April 1865.

  • Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868 and acquitted by one vote in the Senate. Reconstruction policy is the backdrop.

  • Black Kettle and Sand Creek (1864): Custer killed Black Kettle at the Washita in 1868.

  • Mary Todd Lincoln was committed to a private asylum in Batavia, Illinois, in 1875 at her son Robert's instigation. Tad Lincoln died in 1871.

  • Susan B. Anthony was arrested for voting in 1872. Victoria Woodhull was the first woman to run for president (1872). She was a stockbroker, spiritualist, and radical, and she exposed the Beecher adultery scandal.

Unit 12, pp. 257-272: Europe, Mexico, St. Louis

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 12

  • Mary Lincoln lived in Pau, France, from 1876 to 1880. On her voyage home, Sarah Bernhardt caught her from a fall on the stairs. She died in 1882 at the Springfield home of her sister, wife of Ninian Edwards.

  • Maximilian was the Austrian archduke France installed as emperor of Mexico. He was executed in 1867, and his wife Carlotta went mad.

  • Joseph Pulitzer began his career in St. Louis.

  • Herbert Spencer coined "survival of the fittest" and was the philosopher of Social Darwinism, hugely popular with American industrialists.

  • Debs's own start: he left school at fourteen in 1870 to scrape paint in the Vandalia shops, then worked as a fireman.

Unit 13, pp. 273-304: The Brotherhood and the lecture circuit

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 13

  • The Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was founded in 1873 at Port Jervis, New York. Its grand master Joshua Leach signed Debs up in Terre Haute in 1875. It began as mutual insurance, since insurers would not cover railroad men.

  • Herman Hulman was a German-born Terre Haute wholesale grocer. Debs worked for his firm as a clerk after the Panic of 1873 cost him his railroad job.

  • Robert Ingersoll, the "Great Agnostic," was the most famous orator of the day. The Redpath Lecture Bureau booked speakers like him, Twain, and Phillips.

  • Elijah Lovejoy was an abolitionist editor killed by a mob in Alton, Illinois, in 1837. Phillips's career began with a speech about him.

  • Debs was elected Terre Haute city clerk as a Democrat in 1879. James Garfield was elected president in 1880 and assassinated in 1881. Cornelius Vanderbilt was the New York Central rail king.

Unit 14, pp. 305-352: Home life and the wider 1880s

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 14

  • Charley Ross was kidnapped in 1874, the first famous ransom kidnapping.

  • The Beecher-Tilton scandal ended in an 1875 adultery trial with a hung jury.

  • Ida Husted Harper was a Terre Haute journalist who wrote the women's column in the Firemen's Magazine, later Anthony's biographer and a historian of suffrage.

  • Kate Metzel married Debs in 1885. Theodore Debs was Eugene's brother and lifelong aide.

  • The Statue of Liberty was designed by Bartholdi. Pulitzer's newspaper campaign funded its pedestal in 1885.

  • Oscar Wilde toured America in 1882. Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus stories appeared in 1880.

  • Charles Stewart Parnell was the Irish nationalist leader ruined in 1890 by his affair with Kitty O'Shea. "Boycott" comes from Captain Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent shunned by tenants in 1880.

  • The lodge names Young lists (Nauvoo, Marais des Cygnes at Osawatomie) connect the union to older American dreams.

Unit 15, pp. 353-392: Rail kings and Hoosier politics

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 15

  • Jay Gould was the most hated financier of the age. The Knights of Labor beat him in the 1885 Wabash strike and lost to him in the 1886 Great Southwest Strike.

  • The Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers was founded in 1863. Young follows Debs's resistance to the engineers' sense of superiority over firemen, which foreshadows his later push for one union for all rail workers.

  • Chauncey Depew was Vanderbilt's lawyer, later a senator.

  • John Perego was a fireman whose 1887 act of heroism saved President Cleveland's train.

  • Labor Day began with a New York parade in 1882 and became a federal holiday in 1894, days after Pullman.

  • Riley and Bill Nye toured together in joint readings.

  • Daniel Voorhees was Terre Haute's Democratic senator, the "Tall Sycamore of the Wabash." "Waving the bloody shirt" was the Republican habit of invoking the war against Democrats. Edward Hannegan was an expansionist Indiana senator who stabbed his brother-in-law to death while drunk in 1852.

Unit 16, pp. 393-432: Allan Pinkerton

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 16

  • The Chartists were the British workers' movement for the vote. George Julian Harney, their fiery orator and a friend of Engels, later lived in Boston. Pinkerton was a Glasgow Chartist cooper who fled in 1842.

  • In Dundee, Illinois, on the Fox River, Pinkerton exposed counterfeiters. He became Chicago's first detective in 1849 and founded his agency in 1850.

  • The Illinois Central Railroad was an early client, where George McClellan was an officer and Lincoln a lawyer. Pinkerton also foiled the Baltimore plot against Lincoln in 1861.

  • The Reno brothers of Seymour, Indiana, carried out the first peacetime American train robbery in 1866. Three were lynched by vigilantes in New Albany in 1868.

  • Zerelda Samuel was Jesse James's mother. In 1875 a Pinkerton raid threw a device into her Missouri home that took her arm and killed her eight-year-old son Archie.

  • The Larches was Pinkerton's estate at Onarga, Illinois. William and Robert Pinkerton were his sons and successors.

Unit 17, pp. 433-472: The Molly Maguires

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 17

  • The name came from Irish agrarian resistance. Many anthracite miners came from Donegal.

  • Franklin B. Gowen ran the Reading Railroad and its coal company and personally prosecuted the accused.

  • The Ancient Order of Hibernians was an Irish fraternal society, and James McParlan was the Pinkerton spy inside it.

  • Pat Dormer, Muff Lawler, and Jack Kehoe were a Pottsville tavern keeper, a Shenandoah lodge leader, and a Girardville tavern keeper. Kehoe was hanged in 1878 for the 1862 killing of mine foreman Frank Langdon and pardoned posthumously in 1979.

  • Thomas Duffy was among the executed.

  • Twenty men were hanged in total. Schuylkill County and Pottsville were the center.

Unit 18, pp. 473-512: Tompkins Square to the Great Strike

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 18

  • The Tompkins Square Riot was in 1874. Samuel Gompers was there.

  • The Knights of Labor was a secret order from 1869 until 1881. Terence Powderly led it from 1879.

  • John Swinton was a New York labor journalist whose Striking for Life (1894) defended the Pullman strikers.

  • George Blair was a Knights of Labor box maker Young ties to the Tompkins Square organizing; confirm his role in a labor history, since Young's account is thin.

  • The Martinsburg walkout on the B&O began the strike on July 16, 1877. John W. Garrett was the B&O's president.

  • Pittsburgh and Tom Scott: the militia shooting and the burning of the Pennsylvania Railroad yards.

  • Amasa Stone and John Hay: see Unit 13 context. Hay's novel The Bread-Winners (1883) came out of this era.

  • General Philip Sheridan brought federal troops into Chicago in 1877.

  • Mr. Dooley and Hennessy were Finley Peter Dunne's fictional Chicago Irish bartender and his listener, the sharpest political satire of the 1890s.

Unit 19, pp. 513-544: Indiana in 1876 and 1877

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 19

  • James "Blue Jeans" Williams won the 1876 governor's race after Republican Godlove Orth withdrew under scandal. Benjamin Harrison, mocked by Democrats as "Kid Gloves," replaced Orth and lost.

  • The Hayes-Tilden election was settled by the Compromise of 1877, which ended Reconstruction. The Greenbackers were the party of paper money and debtor relief.

  • Judge Walter Q. Gresham used federal receivership power against strikers. The Indianapolis Committee of Public Safety was a businessmen's body that organized armed citizens, with Harrison commanding a company.

  • The Vandalia strike in Terre Haute went ahead without the backing of Debs's Brotherhood.

Unit 20, pp. 545-576: Whistler and Dostoyevsky

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 20

  • George Washington Whistler was a West Point engineer who worked on the B&O, then built the St. Petersburg to Moscow railway for Nicholas I. He died in Russia in 1849. His son James worked for the U.S. Coast Survey before becoming a painter.

  • Vissarion Belinsky was a radical critic. Dostoyevsky was arrested in part for reading Belinsky's banned letter to Gogol, author of Dead Souls, aloud.

  • The Petrashevsky Circle was a Fourierist discussion group. Its members were held in the Peter and Paul Fortress, subjected to a mock execution in December 1849, and sent to prison in Omsk.

Unit 21, pp. 577-580: Afterword

Entries for this unit: History Companion, Unit 21

  • Debs's essays "Unionism and Socialism," "Socialism," and "The American Movement" were his own account of the forgotten early organizers. They make a good closing reading to test the whole project against his memory of the period.

Unit 4, pp. 49-80: Paris, Brussels, Marx

← Unit 3 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 5 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

This unit carries the German exiles from Heine's deathbed in Paris to Marx's confrontation with Weitling in Brussels in 1846, then brings Weitling across the Atlantic to New York. The central event is the split between Weitling's prophetic, Christian communism and Marx's "scientific" version, a quarrel that shaped American socialism for fifty years.

Major entries

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (pp. 52-69, 78-79)

  • Who they were: Marx (1818-1883) was born in Trier, studied philosophy in Berlin, and married Jenny von Westphalen. Expelled from Paris in 1845, he moved to Brussels, then settled in London after 1849. Engels (1820-1895) was the son of a textile manufacturer and managed his family's mill in Manchester, which let him support Marx for decades.

  • Why it matters: Together they wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848). Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) drew on Manchester. Marx wrote for Horace Greeley's New York Tribune from 1852 to 1862, his largest audience in his lifetime, which Young touches on at p. 61.

  • The family: Young follows the Marx household in poverty and grief. Three children died young: Heinrich Guido in 1850, Franziska in 1852, and Edgar in 1855 (p. 59). Daughters Laura and Eleanor survived and became socialists.

  • Further reading: Jonathan Sperber, Karl Marx: A Nineteenth-Century Life (2013).

The Brussels confrontation of March 1846 (pp. 67-69)

  • What happened: On March 30, 1846, Marx, Engels, Weitling, and others met in Brussels in the Communist Correspondence Committee. Marx demanded to know what doctrine Weitling was preaching. When Weitling defended stirring workers with moral appeals, Marx struck the table and shouted that ignorance had never helped anyone.

  • The witness: The Russian traveler Pavel Annenkov recorded the scene. Young draws on him for the goblets jumping on the table (p. 69).

  • Why it matters: It marked the break between the older, religious, conspiratorial communism of the artisans and Marx's theory of class struggle rooted in economics. Weitling lost, and within two years the League of the Just had become Marx's Communist League. In America the two strands kept competing, and Debs's own socialism, moral and Christian in tone, sits closer to Weitling than Young's reader might expect.

  • Further reading: Wittke, The Utopian Communist (1950), chapter 8.

The League of the Just and the Communist League (pp. 66-67)

  • What it was: A secret society of German artisans founded in Paris in 1836, with branches in London and Switzerland. Weitling was its leading theorist in the early 1840s.

  • What happened: In June 1847, in London, it reorganized as the Communist League and commissioned Marx and Engels to write its program, which became the Manifesto.

  • Where the record differs: Young mentions the International Workingmen's Association in this setting (p. 67). That body, the First International, was founded later, in London in 1864.

Weitling's first American journey, Kriege, and the League of Deliverance (pp. 72-78)

  • What happened: Hermann Kriege, a German radical in New York, invited Weitling in 1846 to help edit his paper, the Volks-Tribun. By the time Weitling arrived the paper had folded (p. 73). Weitling founded the Befreiungsbund, or League of Deliverance, in 1847 and began traveling among German workers in Philadelphia, Cincinnati, St. Louis, and elsewhere.

  • Kriege: Hermann Kriege (1820-1850) linked German radicals to the American land reform movement of George Henry Evans, which demanded free homesteads from public land. Marx and Engels issued a circular condemning him in 1846.

  • Why it matters: This is the first organized socialist politics among German-American workers, a generation before the Socialist Labor Party. The benefit societies Young describes (burial insurance, a building and loan, a singing society, p. 76) were the actual fabric of immigrant working-class life.

  • Further reading: Bruce Levine, The Spirit of 1848: German Immigrants, Labor Conflict, and the Coming of the Civil War (1992).

John Jacob Astor (pp. 79-80)

  • Who he was: Born in Walldorf, Germany, in 1763, he came to America in 1784. Family legend says he arrived with seven flutes to sell. He worked for a fur dealer, built the American Fur Company, and then bought Manhattan real estate.

  • Why it matters: At his death in 1848 he was the richest man in the United States, worth roughly twenty million dollars. His Astor House hotel (1836) was New York's grandest. For Young he is the German immigrant who succeeded by the opposite path from Weitling, and the symbol of the "money king" (p. 80).

  • Further reading: Axel Madsen, John Jacob Astor: America's First Multimillionaire (2001).

Shorter entries

  • Ludwig Börne (pp. 51-62): German-Jewish radical journalist in Paris (1786-1837), author of Letters from Paris. Heine's 1840 book on him offended Börne's companion Jeannette Wohl, and her husband Salomon Strauss fought a duel with Heine in 1841.

  • Heine and the Marx family (p. 52): Heine is credited with saving the Marxes' baby daughter Jenny during convulsions. Young places the visit in Brussels, but the episode belongs to Paris in 1844, and Heine did not visit the Marxes in Brussels.

  • George Eliot and Matthew Arnold on Heine (pp. 55-57): Eliot's essay "German Wit: Heinrich Heine" (1856) and Arnold's essay "Heinrich Heine" (1863) and poem "Heine's Grave" introduced him to English readers.

  • Alfred Meissner (pp. 64-65): Austrian poet who visited the dying Heine and wrote a memoir of him.

  • Red Sefchen (p. 55): The executioner's niece in Düsseldorf, Heine's youthful love, as he told it in his memoirs.

  • Proudhon's System of Economic Contradictions (p. 62): Proudhon's 1846 book, which Marx attacked in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847).

  • Karl Grün (p. 62): A "true socialist" whose sentimental socialism Marx and Engels mocked.

  • Ludwig Simon of Trier and Wilhelm Löwe (pp. 61-62): Members of the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848-1849 who went into exile. Löwe presided over its last session in Stuttgart. Simon attacked the dead Heine in a New York German paper, which Marx resented.

  • Joseph Weydemeyer (pp. 68, 78): Marx's ally who emigrated to New York in 1851. He published Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire there in 1852 and later served as a Union officer.

  • Robert Owen in Paris, 1848 (pp. 76-77): Owen went to revolutionary Paris and posted addresses, including a "Dialogue Between France, the World, and Robert Owen" (p. 77).

  • Weitling's Guarantees of Harmony and Freedom (p. 77): His main work (1842), a plan for a communist society run by elected councils of experts.

  • Charles Dickens (pp. 71-72): His American Notes (1842) and Martin Chuzzlewit (1843-1844) satirized American boasting and greed.

  • John Humphrey Noyes and Oneida (p. 80): Noyes founded his community in Putney, Vermont, fled adultery charges in 1847, and resettled at Oneida, New York, in 1848 (Unit 5).

  • Horace Greeley (pp. 61, 74): Editor of the New York Tribune and patron of Fourierism, known for his white hat.

Allusions

  • Diderot and Sterne (p. 49): The French encyclopedist and the English author of Tristram Shandy, both digressive writers Young admired.

  • The Tower of Babel (pp. 70-71): Genesis 11, for the confusion of tongues among the exiles.

  • Acheron (p. 64): A river of the Greek underworld.

  • Lazarus and the Kaddish (p. 64): The dying poet's poems of Lazarus, and the Jewish prayer for the dead.

  • Gulliver and the Lilliputians (p. 54): From Swift's satire.

  • Hamlet, Ophelia, Yorick (p. 79): The Marx family's love of Shakespeare.

  • Mephistopheles (p. 54): The devil in Goethe's Faust.
harp-companion-unit-08-weitlings-later-y:
Unit 8, pp. 153-176: Weitling's later years

← Unit 7 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 9 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

After Communia fails, Weitling becomes a New York family man, an immigration clerk, an amateur astronomer, and an inventor cheated of his sewing machine patents. He dies in January 1871, the night after a festival of the new International. Young makes his decline a parable: the prophet of the wageless society ends as a worker beaten by the patent wars of the machine age.

Major entries

Weitling's family and inventions (pp. 161-173)

  • What happened: In 1854 Weitling married Caroline Tödt, a young seamstress whose family had come from Mecklenburg-Schwerin and farmed near Utica, New York (pp. 161-162). They had six children. He worked as a tailor and devised improvements for sewing machines, including an automatic buttonhole attachment. Young records that he applied for patents in October 1861 on nine improvements, and five were granted (p. 168).

  • Why it matters: The sewing machine was one of the first mass-produced household machines, and its makers fought the "Sewing Machine War" of patent lawsuits until they pooled their patents in 1856. Weitling complained to his friend August Schilling that he was being cheated by Singer and the others, and that "whoever was without funds in this country had no chance against those who had funds" (p. 171).

  • His son's name: Weitling named his first son William Wangansky, after a Chinese reformer he admired (p. 166). This was probably Wang Anshi, the eleventh-century Song dynasty minister whose state loans to farmers some European socialists admired. The family shortened it to Wangan.

  • Further reading: Wittke, The Utopian Communist (1950), final chapters.

Weitling's death and burial (pp. 174-176)

  • What happened: On January 24, 1871, Weitling attended a festival of the German, French, Czech, and English sections of the International Workingmen's Association in New York (p. 174). He died the next day. He was buried in a poor section of Greenwood Cemetery in Brooklyn.
