  • Why it matters: He died two months before the Paris Commune, when the International he had helped foreshadow reached its height of fame. His obituary in the New York Times remembered him chiefly as an inventor (p. 176).

  • How Young uses it: His lapsed dues to the Journeyman Tailors' Protective and Benevolent Union (p. 174) and his pauper's plot make him one of the "nameless" pioneers Debs wanted remembered.

August Willich (pp. 155, 157)

  • Who he was: A Prussian army officer (1810-1878) who turned communist and fought in the Baden uprising of 1849, with Engels as his aide. In London in 1850 his faction split from Marx's in the Communist League. Marx mocked him in letters to Weydemeyer.

  • In America: He presided at the Shakespeare Hotel banquet where Weitling spoke (p. 155) and edited a German paper in Cincinnati. In the Civil War he rose to brigadier general, commanding the 32nd Indiana, an all-German regiment, and later a brigade.

  • Further reading: David T. Dixon, Radical Warrior: August Willich's Journey from German Revolutionary to Union General (2020).

Wilhelm Keil and the Bethel and Aurora colonies (p. 156)

  • Who he was: A German tailor (1812-1877) who emigrated in 1836, became a mystic healer and Methodist preacher, and broke away to lead his own communal flock. Young says Weitling first met him in Kentucky and found his hellfire preaching distasteful.

  • What happened: Keil founded Bethel, Missouri, in 1844, a prosperous communal town. In 1855 he led a wagon train to Oregon, carrying the body of his son Willie in an alcohol-filled coffin, and founded Aurora, south of Portland, in 1856. Both colonies dissolved after his death.

  • Where the record differs: Young calls Keil a tailor "from Darmstadt" (p. 156). He was born in Prussian Saxony, at Bleicherode.

  • Further reading: Robert J. Hendricks, Bethel and Aurora (1933).

Friedrich Adolph Sorge (pp. 174-175)

  • Who he was: A veteran of the Baden revolution (1828-1906) who came to America in 1852, taught music in Hoboken, New Jersey, and became Marx's and Engels's chief American correspondent.

  • Why it matters: When the International moved its headquarters to New York in 1872, Sorge served as its general secretary. He is often called the father of Marxian socialism in America, the organizational link between the 1848 exiles and the Socialist Labor Party of the 1870s.

  • Further reading: Philip S. Foner and Brewster Chamberlin, eds., Friedrich A. Sorge's Labor Movement in the United States (1977).

Castle Garden (p. 169)

  • What it was: A former fort and concert hall at the Battery in lower Manhattan that served as New York State's immigrant landing depot from 1855 to 1890, before Ellis Island. About eight million immigrants passed through it.

  • Connection: Weitling worked there briefly as a registrar of immigrants. Young notes his pay was a tenth of a superior who left him all the work (p. 169).

Shorter entries

  • Governor Thomas Ford and Governor Lilburn Boggs (p. 154): Ford governed Illinois when Joseph Smith was murdered in the Carthage jail in 1844. Boggs, governor of Missouri, issued the 1838 "Extermination Order" driving the Mormons from the state.

  • Joseph Weydemeyer (pp. 155, 157-159): Marx's ally in America, a rival to Weitling among German workers. He joined the Union army in Missouri.

  • Charles A. Dana (p. 171): Former Brook Farm member and managing editor of the New York Tribune. He edited the Chicago Republican briefly after the war, which fits Young's "a Republican then living in the city of Chicago." He was later Lincoln's assistant secretary of war.

  • Elias Howe and Isaac Singer (pp. 168-173): Howe patented the lockstitch sewing machine in 1846. Singer built a practical machine in 1851 and the Singer company came to dominate the world market.

  • Richard Gatling (pp. 168, 171): Inventor of the Gatling gun (Unit 9), whom Young sets beside Weitling as an inventor who prospered.

  • The Fenians (p. 172): The Fenian Brotherhood, founded in 1858, organized Irish Americans for Irish independence. Its members raided Canada between 1866 and 1871.

  • William Dean Howells (p. 153): Editor of the Atlantic Monthly and Twain's friend, who praised Roughing It.

  • Hans Christian Andersen (p. 164): The Danish writer of fairy tales. Young pictures Weitling's crowded household of cats, birds, and babies as an Andersen fairy-tale world.

Allusions

  • Prometheus (p. 156): The Titan who stole fire for humanity and was chained to a rock.

  • Golgotha (p. 156): The hill of the crucifixion.

  • Newton's dog Diamond (p. 163): The legend that Isaac Newton's dog knocked over a candle and burned years of his papers.

  • Copernicus, Ptolemy, Tycho Brahe (pp. 163-171): The astronomers Weitling studied in his hobby of reforming astronomy.

  • Pegasus (p. 167): The winged horse of Greek myth.

  • Hannibal and Carthage (p. 160): The general of Carthage, and a play on Carthage, Illinois, where Smith died.
harp-companion-unit-10-treason-trials-an:
Unit 10, pp. 201-224: Treason trials and abolition

← Unit 9 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 11 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

The Civil War years in Indiana run through John Brown, the Copperhead treason trials, Lincoln's assassination, and the funeral train that passed through Indianapolis and Chicago. Young ends with the boy Debs at school in Terre Haute, learning from McGuffey's Readers. The unit shows how close the war came to the Debs doorstep and how its heroes became his models.

Major entries

John Brown (pp. 202-205)

  • Who he was: An abolitionist (1800-1859) who fought proslavery settlers in "Bleeding Kansas." In May 1856 his band killed five proslavery men at Pottawatomie Creek. That August his son Frederick was killed in the fight at Osawatomie (p. 203).

  • Harpers Ferry: On October 16, 1859, Brown and twenty-one men seized the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to arm enslaved people for a rising. Marines under Robert E. Lee captured him. He was hanged at Charles Town on December 2, 1859.

  • Why it matters: Northern writers made him a martyr. Victor Hugo pleaded publicly for his life, which Young connects to Debs's namesake (p. 204). Louisa May Alcott and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow mourned him (p. 203). The South saw proof of Northern aggression, and secession followed within a year.

  • How Young uses him: Brown is the ancestor of Debs's moral absolutism. Debs was later called "the second John Brown" (p. 210).

  • Further reading: David S. Reynolds, John Brown, Abolitionist (2005).

Lambdin P. Milligan and *Ex parte Milligan (pp. 207-211)

  • What happened: Milligan, a lawyer and Copperhead Democrat of Huntington, Indiana, was arrested in October 1864 with William A. Bowles, Stephen Horsey, and others. They were accused of plotting an uprising for August 16, 1864, to free Confederate prisoners and kidnap Governor Morton (p. 208). A military commission in Indianapolis sentenced Milligan to hang on May 19, 1865 (p. 209). President Andrew Johnson commuted the sentence to life.

  • The ruling: In Ex parte Milligan (1866) the Supreme Court held that civilians cannot be tried by military tribunals where civilian courts are open. Milligan was freed. He then sued the officials who had arrested him. Benjamin Harrison defended them, and in 1871 a jury awarded Milligan five dollars.

  • Why it matters: It remains a landmark of civil liberties, cited in debates over military trials to this day. Young draws an implied line from Milligan's military trial to the federal injunctions and wartime prosecutions later used against Debs.

  • Where the record differs: Young calls Milligan "Irish-born" (p. 207). He was born in Belmont County, Ohio, in 1812, and was admitted to the Ohio bar with Edwin Stanton, as she notes.

  • Further reading: Frank L. Klement, Dark Lanterns (1984), and Mark E. Neely Jr., The Fate of Liberty: Abraham Lincoln and Civil Liberties (1991).

Lincoln's assassination and funeral train (pp. 205-219)

  • What happened: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on Good Friday, April 14, 1865 (p. 206). The funeral train retraced his inaugural route west. His body lay in state at the Indiana State House on April 30, a Greek temple with a dome designed by the architect Ithiel Town (p. 217). It reached Chicago on May 1 and Springfield on May 3.

  • Pullman's Pioneer: George Pullman's first luxury sleeping car, the Pioneer, is traditionally said to have joined the funeral train from Chicago to Springfield, which made his name. Young writes that the widow suggested the car "for her passage and that of her surviving sons" (p. 217). Mary Lincoln was too prostrate to travel and stayed in Washington. Historians also question how much of the Pioneer legend is true.

  • Booth and the Knights: Young links Booth to the Knights of the Golden Circle (p. 205). The claim circulated widely at the time but has never been proved.

  • Further reading: Michael W. Kauffman, American Brutus (2004).

Robert Todd Lincoln and the Pullman connection (pp. 217-219)

  • Who he was: Lincoln's eldest son (1843-1926), a lawyer, secretary of war (1881-1885), and minister to Britain.

  • Why it matters: In 1875 he had his mother committed to an asylum, which Young compares to driving nails into her heart, calling him the "future Prince of Nails" (p. 217). He served as Pullman's lawyer and became president of the Pullman Company after George Pullman's death in 1897. So the Great Emancipator's son ended up running the company whose 1894 strike sent Debs to jail, the irony Young is setting up (p. 219).

  • Further reading: Jason Emerson, Giant in the Shadows: The Life of Robert T. Lincoln (2012).

Wendell Phillips (pp. 214-216)

  • Who he was: A Boston patrician (1811-1884) who became the most eloquent abolitionist orator. His career began with a speech in 1837 denouncing the murder of Elijah Lovejoy.

  • The Disunion speech: On January 20, 1861, at the Boston Music Hall, he argued for letting the South go. He praised democracy as a force "crumbling classes into men" and said, "For this, Leggett labored and Lovejoy died" (pp. 214-215). He was often a harsh critic of Lincoln, though he delivered a eulogy for him at Tremont Temple.

  • Why it matters: After the war Phillips turned to labor reform, the eight-hour day, and the Greenback cause, bridging abolition and the labor movement. Debs counted him among the master spirits of his life (Unit 1).

  • Further reading: James Brewer Stewart, Wendell Phillips: Liberty's Hero (1986).

McGuffey's Readers (pp. 221-223)

  • What they were: Schoolbooks compiled by William Holmes McGuffey (1800-1873), born in Washington County, Pennsylvania, and later a professor and college president (pp. 221-222). The first appeared in 1836. They sold an estimated 120 million copies and taught most American children to read for the rest of the century.

  • Why it matters: They mixed moral lessons, patriotic speeches, and literary selections. Recitations from them on Friday afternoons (p. 223) gave Debs's generation its oratorical style. Young notes Debs was later called "the Terre Haute Rienzi" (p. 223), after the fourteenth-century Roman tribune Cola di Rienzo, whose rousing address from a popular play was a schoolroom favorite.

  • Debs's schooling: Terre Haute could not yet fund public schools well, so Debs attended the Old Seminary School (p. 224). He left school at fourteen for the railroad shops.

  • Further reading: John H. Westerhoff III, McGuffey and His Readers (1978).

Shorter entries

  • Dred Scott's last years (pp. 201-202): After his freedom he worked as a porter at Barnum's Hotel in St. Louis. He died of tuberculosis in September 1858 and was buried in Calvary Cemetery.

  • Henry Ward Beecher and "Beecher's Bibles" (pp. 206, 213-214): The Brooklyn preacher said a Sharps rifle would do more good in Kansas than a Bible. His Plymouth Church paid for twenty-five rifles for a Kansas colony, whose congregation became the Beecher Bible and Rifle Church at Wabaunsee. Young calls it "the Church of the Holy Rifles" (p. 206).

  • Harriet Beecher Stowe (pp. 204, 206): Beecher's sister, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852).

  • Copperheads (p. 206): Northern Democrats who opposed the war, named by their enemies after the venomous snake.

  • William A. Bowles and French Lick (pp. 207, 210): A Mexican War officer and doctor who owned the French Lick springs hotel. He was sentenced to death with Milligan, then commuted. The springs later sold "Pluto Water" nationwide.

  • Stephen Horsey (p. 207): A farmer of Shoals, Indiana, tried and sentenced with Milligan.

  • Camp Morton and Burnside Barracks (p. 209): Indianapolis military posts. Camp Morton held Confederate prisoners.

  • Daniel Voorhees (p. 210): Terre Haute's Democratic congressman and later senator (1877-1897), "the Tall Sycamore of the Wabash." In 1859 he defended one of John Brown's raiders. Covered further in Unit 15.

  • "Waving the bloody shirt" (pp. 210-211): The Republican tactic of reminding voters that Democrats had led the rebellion.

  • Lincoln's Indiana boyhood (p. 213): The Lincolns lived on Little Pigeon Creek in Spencer County from 1816 to 1830. He took a flatboat to New Orleans in 1828.

  • The Quaker model farm (p. 207): Quaker missionaries set up a farm among the Miami on the upper Wabash around 1804, associated with the chief Little Turtle. Young describes Harrison's troops burning it in the War of 1812.

  • The plot to steal Lincoln's body (p. 218): In 1876 counterfeiters planned to take Lincoln's body from its Springfield tomb and hide it in the Indiana dunes for ransom. Young credits Pinkerton's detectives with foiling it. Standard accounts credit the Secret Service.

  • Robert Ingersoll (p. 220): The agnostic orator, whose ideas Daniel Debs shared. Covered in Unit 13.

Allusions

  • Brutus and Caesar, Sic semper tyrannis (p. 205): Booth cast himself as Brutus and shouted Virginia's motto, "Thus always to tyrants."

  • Macbeth and Duncan (p. 213): Shakespeare's murdered king, one of Lincoln's favorite plays.

  • Canaan (p. 212): The biblical promised land that Moses saw but did not enter, a common image for Lincoln.

  • Perrault, Grimm, Aesop, Pilgrim's Progress (p. 221): The fairy tales, fables, and Christian allegory of a nineteenth-century child's reading.

  • Pluto and Prospero (p. 207): The Roman god of the underworld and Shakespeare's magician, names of the French Lick springs.

  • Little Nell (pp. 206, 223): Dickens's dying child heroine, a staple of McGuffey-era recitation.
harp-companion-unit-16-allan-pinkerton:
Unit 16, pp. 393-432: Allan Pinkerton

← Unit 15 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 17 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young gives a full portrait of Allan Pinkerton, the Glasgow Chartist who became America's most famous detective and the scourge of organized labor. His career runs from counterfeiters on a Fox River island to Lincoln's secret passage through Baltimore, the Reno gang, and the botched raid on Jesse James's mother. By the end, Debs's magazine is calling his agents carrion crows.

Major entries

Allan Pinkerton's Chartist youth (pp. 399-406)

  • Who he was: Born in the Gorbals of Glasgow on August 25, 1819, the son of a police sergeant. He became a cooper, a barrel maker, and joined the Chartists, the workers' movement demanding the vote for all men, a secret ballot, and pay for members of Parliament.

  • The Newport Rising: On November 4, 1839, several thousand Welsh Chartists led by John Frost marched on Newport to free the imprisoned Chartist Henry Vincent. Soldiers fired from the windows of the Westgate Hotel, killing about twenty-two (p. 404). Frost was transported to Australia.

  • Where the record differs: Young places Pinkerton in Frost's march with "his cooper's hammer on his back" (p. 404). There is no good evidence he was in Wales. He belonged to the militant "physical force" Chartists of Glasgow, and his arrest warrant there in 1842 is why he fled.

  • George Julian Harney (pp. 404-405): A fiery Chartist orator and friend of Marx and Engels, who first published the Communist Manifesto in English, in his paper, in 1850.

  • Further reading: James Mackay, Allan Pinkerton: The First Private Eye (1996).

From Dundee to Chicago (pp. 407-413)

  • What happened: Pinkerton married Joan Carfrae and sailed for America in 1842. They were shipwrecked off Nova Scotia and robbed before reaching Chicago. He set up a cooperage in Dundee, Illinois, on the Fox River. In 1847 he tracked a gang of counterfeiters to an island in the river later called Bogus Island (p. 410), which launched his career.

  • The agency: He became a deputy sheriff and Chicago's first police detective in 1849. In 1850 he founded what became the Pinkerton National Detective Agency, working mainly for railroads, among them the Illinois Central, the Michigan Southern, and the Rock Island (p. 411). Its logo was an open eye with the motto "We Never Sleep," which Young turns into "The Eye That Never Sleeps."

  • The abolitionist: His Chicago house was a station on the Underground Railroad. In March 1859 he helped John Brown move eleven freed slaves toward Canada (pp. 411-412), and he was expelled from his Baptist church at Dundee for his views and his drinking (p. 412).

  • The Baltimore Plot: In February 1861 Pinkerton reported a plot to kill Lincoln in Baltimore, centered on a barber named Cipriano Ferrandini (Young's "Fernandina," p. 412). Lincoln passed through the city secretly at night. During the war Pinkerton ran intelligence for General George McClellan and famously overestimated Confederate strength.

  • Further reading: Frank Morn, "The Eye That Never Sleeps": A History of the Pinkerton National Detective Agency (1982).

The Reno gang (pp. 414-419)

  • What happened: On October 6, 1866, John and Simeon Reno and Franklin Sparks robbed an Ohio and Mississippi train leaving Seymour, Indiana (p. 415). It is usually counted as the first peacetime train robbery in the United States. The gang's later robberies ranged as far as Council Bluffs, Iowa (p. 416).

  • The lynchings: Pinkerton's men captured most of the gang, but vigilantes did the rest. In July 1868 a mob hanged three members near Seymour. On the night of December 11, 1868, masked men stormed the jail at New Albany, Indiana, and hanged Frank, William, and Simeon Reno and Charlie Anderson (p. 417).

  • Why it matters: The Renos made train robbery a national fear and made the Pinkertons the railroads' private police, the role they later played against strikers.

  • Further reading: Frank Morn's history of the agency, cited above, covers the Reno pursuit.

The raid on the Samuel farm (pp. 420-427)

  • What happened: After Jesse and Frank James and the Younger brothers killed several Pinkerton operatives in 1874, agents surrounded the Missouri farm of the Jameses' mother, Zerelda Samuel, in Clay County, on the night of January 25-26, 1875. They threw a device into the house that exploded. Her right arm was mangled and had to be amputated, and her eight-year-old son Archie Samuel was killed (pp. 425-426).

  • Why it matters: The raid turned public sympathy toward the James brothers and nearly won them an amnesty from the Missouri legislature (p. 427). It fixed the Pinkertons' reputation for violence.

  • Further reading: T. J. Stiles, Jesse James: Last Rebel of the Civil War (2002).

Pinkerton's decline and legacy (pp. 419-432)

  • What happened: A stroke in 1869 partly paralyzed him. Young describes his cure at a mineral spring on the Pine River at St. Louis, Michigan (p. 419), a town later known for manufacturing DDT. The Chicago fire of October 1871 destroyed his office and records (p. 420). His sons William and Robert took over the business, and he retired to his estate, the Larches, at Onarga, Illinois (p. 428). He died in 1884.

  • Against labor: Under his sons the agency supplied armed guards and spies to break strikes. At Homestead, Pennsylvania, on July 6, 1892, about three hundred Pinkerton guards arriving by barge fought striking steelworkers, and several men on each side were killed (pp. 396, 404). The public outcry led Congress in 1893 to bar the federal government from hiring the agency.

  • Debs's view: The Locomotive Firemen's Magazine wrote that Pinkertons "come as carrion crows come to a carcass" (p. 431).

  • Further reading: Paul Krause, The Battle for Homestead, 1880-1892 (1992).

Shorter entries

  • Terence Powderly (p. 394): A machinist from Pennsylvania who led the Knights of Labor as grand master workman from 1879 to 1893 and was mayor of Scranton. The Knights kept their name secret until 1881, reached perhaps 700,000 members in 1886, and then declined quickly.

  • Charles O. Morton (p. 393): The grave robber who stole the body of Benjamin Harrison's father in 1878, helped by his wife, dressed as a man.

  • The 1892 election (p. 396): Harrison lost to Cleveland. Many blamed the Homestead violence for turning labor votes against the Republicans.

  • John Whistler (pp. 407-408): An Irish soldier captured with General John Burgoyne's army at Saratoga in 1777. He switched to the American side and built the first Fort Dearborn at Chicago in 1803. He was the grandfather of the painter James McNeill Whistler (Unit 20).

  • Mrs. O'Leary's cow (p. 420): The legend that her cow kicked over a lantern and started the Chicago fire was invented by a reporter, Michael Ahern, who admitted it in 1893.

  • The American Miners' Association (p. 430): Founded near St. Louis in January 1861, the first national union of coal miners.

  • Pinkerton's books (pp. 426-432): Ghostwritten volumes under his name included The Molly Maguires and the Detectives (1877) and Strikers, Communists, Tramps and Detectives (1878).

  • Morgan's Raiders (p. 419): John Hunt Morgan's Confederate cavalry, which raided Indiana and Ohio in July 1863. Young says the Renos rode with them. They are better known as bounty-jumpers who enlisted and deserted repeatedly.

Allusions

  • King Log (p. 397): Aesop's fable of the frogs who asked for a king and got a log, for a do-nothing ruler.

  • Romeo and Juliet, Macbeth (p. 400): Shakespeare, for Chicago's feuds.

  • Robert Burns, "Address to the Unco Guid" (p. 409): Burns's poem against the self-righteous, a favorite of both Scots and Debs.

  • Robin Hood (p. 421): The outlaw hero the James brothers were made into.

  • Salus populi (pp. 416-417): "The welfare of the people," the vigilantes' justification.
harp-companion-unit-03-weitlings-youth-a:
Unit 3, pp. 33-48: Weitling's youth and Heine

← Unit 2 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 4 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young sets two German exiles side by side: Wilhelm Weitling, the tailor jailed in Switzerland for preaching communism, and Heinrich Heine, the poet exiled in Paris. Around them she gathers the religious visionaries, from Ann Lee to the Saint-Simonians, who shared their hunger for a new world.

Major entries

Weitling's imprisonment and prison poems (pp. 33-40)

  • What happened: Swiss police arrested Weitling in Zurich in June 1843 as he prepared to publish The Gospel of a Poor Sinner, which presented Jesus as a communist. He was convicted of blasphemy and incitement, served about ten months, and was deported to Prussia in 1844.

  • The poems: He wrote a cycle published as Kerkerpoesien (Prison Poems, 1844). Young lists titles such as "Conscience," "The Betrayer," "To My Judge and to My Prosecutor," and "Forty-eight Hours in the Dark" (p. 35). "The Monster" is the detective staring through the peephole of his cell.

  • Why it matters: His arrest made him famous across the radical underground. The London Communist Chronicle named him with Babeuf and Joshua Jacob as the three "illustrious communist martyrs" since the French Revolution (p. 33).

  • How Young uses it: The cell, the peephole, and the sense of being buried alive all prefigure Debs in Atlanta. Weitling becomes Debs's ancestor in suffering.

  • Further reading: Carl Wittke, The Utopian Communist (1950).

Heinrich Heine (pp. 40-48)

  • Who he was: German-Jewish poet (1797-1856), born in Düsseldorf. He studied in Berlin, where he heard Hegel lecture, and converted to Protestantism in 1825, calling baptism his "ticket of admission" to European culture. He moved to Paris in 1831 and never lived in Germany again.

  • Why it matters: His Book of Songs made him the most popular German lyric poet of the century. His satire Germany: A Winter's Tale (1844) mocked Prussian censorship and was banned. He knew Marx in Paris in 1843 and 1844.

  • Family: His rich uncle Salomon Heine, a Hamburg banker, paid him an allowance and resented his writing. Heine's unrequited love for his cousin Amalie, Salomon's daughter, fed his early verse. His wife Mathilde was a Paris shop girl he married in 1841. From 1848 he was paralyzed and bedridden in what he called his "mattress grave." He is buried at Montmartre.

  • Where the record differs: Young calls Heine's weavers' poem popular with "old Hamburgers" and ties it to power-loom competition (p. 42). The poem, "The Silesian Weavers" (1844), was written about the uprising of hand-loom weavers in Silesia that June, which the Prussian army crushed.

  • Further reading: Jeffrey L. Sammons, Heinrich Heine: A Modern Biography (1979).

Ann Lee and the Shakers (p. 37)

  • Who she was: A Manchester mill worker (1736-1784) whose followers believed her to be the second appearance of Christ, in female form. She led a small group to New York in 1774. Young describes her supporting the group by laundering near City Hall.

  • Why it matters: The Shakers (the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing) practiced celibacy, equality of the sexes, and common property. At their peak in the 1840s they had some six thousand members in about twenty villages. The central community at New Lebanon (later Mount Lebanon), New York, was organized after her death.

  • Further reading: Stephen J. Stein, The Shaker Experience in America (1992).

Andreas Dietsch and New Helvetia (p. 35)

  • Who he was: A Swiss brush maker and follower of Weitling who wrote a utopian tract, The Thousand-Year Kingdom (1842). In 1844 he led a band of Swiss emigrants to found a communal colony, New Helvetia, in Missouri.

  • What happened: The colony dissolved almost at once. Young writes that its founder died "alone in St. Louis of a broken heart" (p. 35). Weitling was offered free passage to join it and declined.

  • Why it matters: It is one of dozens of small German communal colonies of the 1840s that left almost no trace. Young rescues it from oblivion in exactly the way Debs wanted forgotten pioneers remembered.

Saint-Simon and the Saint-Simonians (pp. 45-46)

  • Who they were: Henri de Saint-Simon (1760-1825) was a French aristocrat who argued that society should be run by producers, industrialists, scientists, and workers, rather than idle nobles. After his death, Barthélemy Prosper Enfantin turned his followers into a quasi-religious sect that preached the "rehabilitation of the flesh" and sought a female messiah.

  • Why it matters: The Saint-Simonians shaped French banking, railroads, and the Suez Canal, which Enfantin promoted. Heine admired them and dedicated a book to Enfantin.

  • Where the record differs: Young places Enfantin's followers in a community "near the forest of Rambouillet" on Fourier's pattern (p. 45). The Saint-Simonian retreat of 1832 was at Ménilmontant, outside Paris. The phalanstery near Rambouillet, at Condé-sur-Vesgre (1832), was a Fourierist project. Saint-Simon did propose a Panama canal to Spanish officials in his youth.

  • Further reading: Frank E. Manuel, The New World of Henri Saint-Simon (1956).

Shorter entries

  • Gracchus Babeuf (p. 33): French revolutionary executed in 1797 for the "Conspiracy of Equals," an attempt to abolish private property. He is often called the first modern communist.

  • Joshua Jacob (p. 33): An Irish Quaker who founded the "White Quakers" in Dublin and was jailed for contempt of court. The Communist Chronicle counted him a martyr.

  • The Communist Chronicle (p. 33): A London paper edited by Goodwyn Barmby, an early English communist, in the 1840s.

  • Father George Rapp (p. 37): Leader of the Harmony Society, who came from Württemberg. He is covered in Unit 6.

  • The Mormons in Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois (p. 36): The church moved from Kirtland, Ohio, to Missouri, where it was expelled in 1838, then to Nauvoo, Illinois. Unit 7 covers them.

  • Moses Moser (p. 42): Heine's close friend in Berlin and a founder of the Society for the Culture and Science of the Jews.

  • Julius Campe (p. 43): Heine's Hamburg publisher, who kept his books in print despite censorship.

  • Charles Fourier (p. 45): See Unit 2. Young calls him "the cloth merchant," which was his trade.

Allusions

  • Swedenborgian (p. 33): Followers of Emanuel Swedenborg, the Swedish mystic who taught that the spiritual world surrounds and penetrates this one.

  • Samson (p. 41): The Hebrew strongman who pulled down the Philistine temple. Heine used the image of himself.

  • Aristophanes, The Birds (p. 46): The Greek comedy in which birds build an ideal city in the sky, Cloudcuckooland.

  • Dante's Divine Comedy (p. 44): Heine compared his own exile to Dante's.

  • Beelzebub (p. 38): A name for the devil.

  • Zion (p. 48): The biblical holy mountain, used for any promised land.
harp-companion-unit-02-colmar-and-the-dr:
Unit 2, pp. 17-32: Colmar and the dream of reason

← Unit 1 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 3 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young follows Debs's parents from Alsace to New York in 1849, then widens to the Europe they left: a czar who flirted with reform, philosophers drafting constitutions, and utopians promising a "New Moral World" (p. 20). The unit introduces the planners whose communities fill Units 5 and 6.

Major entries

Daniel Debs and Marguerite Marie Bettrich ("Daisy") (pp. 17-20)

  • Who they were: Daniel Debs (1820-1906) was the son of a prosperous textile mill owner in Colmar, Alsace. Marguerite Bettrich worked in his father's mill. His family opposed the match across class lines.

  • What happened: Daniel emigrated in 1849, and Marguerite followed. They married in New York that year and settled in Terre Haute, Indiana, in the early 1850s, where they ran a small grocery from the front room of their house. Eugene was born there on November 5, 1855.

  • How Young uses them: She admits the childhood record is thin. She notes that Henry Schnittkind's 1929 biography supplied "an idyllic and symbolic way" of imagining it, "for which there was no documentation" (p. 17). Daniel's love of French literature explains Eugene's names.

  • Further reading: Nick Salvatore, Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist (1982), chapter 1.

Robert Owen and *A New View of Society (pp. 20-21, 25, 30)

  • Who he was: Welsh-born mill owner (1771-1858) who turned the cotton mills at New Lanark, Scotland, into a model community with schools, shorter hours, and no child labor under ten. His essays A New View of Society (1813-1816) argued that character is formed by circumstances, so a better environment makes better people.

  • Why it matters: Owen is a founder of both the cooperative movement and British socialism. In 1825 he bought the town of Harmony, Indiana, for his experiment at New Harmony, which fell apart by 1827.

  • How Young uses him: Owen lobbied kings as readily as workers. Young describes him approaching Czar Alexander I "at a convention of kings in Frankfurt" (p. 25).

  • Where the record differs: Owen presented his proposals to the allied sovereigns at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818, not at Frankfurt. He had earlier shown the future Czar Nicholas I around New Lanark in 1816.

  • Further reading: Arthur Bestor, Backwoods Utopias (1950).

Charles Fourier and Albert Brisbane (pp. 20-21, 25, 30)

  • Who they were: Fourier (1772-1837) was a French clerk and theorist who designed communities called phalanxes, about 1,600 people each, where work would be arranged around natural passions. Albert Brisbane (1809-1890) was an American who studied with Fourier and brought his ideas home.

  • Why it matters: Brisbane's book Social Destiny of Man (1840) and his column in Horace Greeley's New York Tribune set off an American craze. More than two dozen phalanxes were founded in the 1840s, including the North American Phalanx in New Jersey and Brook Farm near Boston. Young's "Brisbaneites" (p. 20) are these followers.

  • Further reading: Carl J. Guarneri, The Utopian Alternative: Fourierism in Nineteenth-Century America (1991).

Czar Alexander I (pp. 23-27)

  • Who he was: Emperor of Russia from 1801 to 1825. He came to the throne after conspirators murdered his father, Paul I, in the Mikhailovsky Castle in St. Petersburg, a plot he had allowed to go forward believing Paul would only be forced to abdicate.

  • Why it matters: Alexander began as a reformer who corresponded with Jefferson and courted Bentham and Owen. After defeating Napoleon he turned mystical and reactionary and founded the Holy Alliance of monarchs against revolution. That shift set the political climate the 1848 radicals rose against.

  • How Young uses him: Weitling's French father died in Napoleon's 1812 Russian campaign, so Alexander's Russia swallowed the father Weitling never knew. Young notes Alexander "had apparently died" (p. 27) at Taganrog in 1825. The word "apparently" nods to the Russian legend that he faked his death and lived on as the hermit Fyodor Kuzmich.

  • Further reading: Janet M. Hartley, Alexander I (1994).

Wilhelm Weitling's origins (pp. 22-23, 28-32)

  • Who he was: Born in Magdeburg, Prussia, in 1808, the illegitimate son of a housemaid and a French artillery officer in Napoleon's occupying army. The officer died in the 1812 Russian campaign. Weitling became a journeyman tailor who wandered Europe for work.

  • Why it matters: He was the first German communist to come from the working class itself. His Guarantees of Harmony and Freedom (1842) was praised by Marx before the two fell out.

  • How Young uses him: Weitling is the book's second hero, a mirror to Debs. Young describes his proposal that coins bear emblems of labor, "the hammer and the anvil and the chisel and the saw" (p. 32), in place of kings. His Swiss imprisonment of 1843 anticipates Debs's own. Unit 3 continues his story.

  • Further reading: Carl Wittke, The Utopian Communist: A Biography of Wilhelm Weitling (1950).

The Mormon mission to England and the Chartists (pp. 29, 31)

  • What it was: From 1840 to 1841 Brigham Young and other Mormon apostles preached in Lancashire and around Manchester. They founded the Millennial Star newspaper there and sent thousands of converts to America, advancing passage money to the poorest.

  • Why it matters: The mission ran at the height of Chartism, the British working-class movement for the vote, and both drew on the same distressed mill towns. Young's point is that religious and political hopes competed for the same people.

  • Further reading: James B. Allen, Ronald K. Esplin, and David J. Whittaker, Men with a Mission: The Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in the British Isles, 1837-1841 (1992).

Shorter entries

  • Henry Schnittkind (p. 17): Author of The Story of Eugene Debs (1929), an early, admiring biography. Young calls him "Uncle Henry Schnitkind."

  • The Shakespeare Hotel (pp. 20, 22): A New York hotel at Duane and William Streets frequented by German and French exiles. It returns in Unit 8 as the site of a banquet for Weitling.

  • The World's Convention at Clinton Hall (p. 20): Robert Owen organized a gathering of reformers in New York in October 1845. Young places the young Walt Whitman there as a reporter for the Brooklyn Eagle. Whitman joined the Eagle in 1846, so this detail is unverified.

  • The Perfectionists (p. 20): Followers of John Humphrey Noyes, who believed people could live without sin in this life. They founded the Oneida Community in 1848 (Unit 5).

  • Étienne Cabet and the Icarians (pp. 20, 30): Cabet's 1840 novel Voyage en Icarie inspired a communist emigration to Texas in 1848 and to Nauvoo, Illinois, in 1849. Unit 5 covers them.

  • Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (p. 22): French anarchist (1809-1865), author of What Is Property? (1840), with its answer "Property is theft."

  • Jeremy Bentham (p. 25): English philosopher of utilitarianism (1748-1832). Alexander I sent him a diamond ring, which Bentham returned with the seal unbroken, as Young reports. He lived at Forde Abbey in Somerset from 1814 to 1818.

  • Aaron Burr and Francisco de Miranda (p. 25): Burr, the former vice president, schemed to seize territory in the Southwest and Mexico and was tried for treason in 1807. Miranda was a Venezuelan revolutionary. Both sought Bentham's help.

  • Jefferson's last letter (p. 27): Written June 24, 1826, ten days before his death, to Roger Weightman, then mayor of Washington, declining an invitation to the Fourth of July jubilee. It holds his famous line that mankind was not born "with saddles on their backs." Young calls Weightman "librarian of the Patent Office."

  • The Barbary War and Tripoli (p. 24): The frigate USS Philadelphia ran aground off Tripoli in 1803 and its crew was held captive. Young credits Alexander with helping, and Jefferson thanked him, but the extent of Russian help is uncertain.

  • Félicité de Lamennais (p. 30): French priest (1782-1854) whose Words of a Believer (1834) joined Christianity to democracy. The pope condemned it, and Lamennais left the church.

  • Joseph Smith's death at Carthage (p. 30): The Mormon prophet and his brother Hyrum were killed by a mob at the Carthage, Illinois, jail on June 27, 1844 (Unit 7).

  • The Mexican War (p. 20): The 1846-1848 war that took California and the Southwest. Its gold rush drew many of the immigrants Young describes.

Allusions

  • "When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd" (p. 21): Whitman's 1865 elegy for Lincoln.

  • Icarus (p. 30): The Greek youth whose wax wings melted when he flew too near the sun. Cabet's Icaria takes its name from him.

  • The Rubicon (p. 30): The river Caesar crossed in 49 BC, meaning a point of no return.

  • Sphinx of the North (p. 23): A period nickname for Alexander I, for his inscrutable character.

  • City of God (p. 30): Saint Augustine's heavenly city, used for Nauvoo.
harp-companion-unit-21-afterword-and-edi:
Unit 21, pp. 577-581: Afterword and Editorial Note

← Unit 20 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

The book stops short of the Pullman strike, the chapter Young was writing when she fell ill. The Afterword instead lets Debs speak for himself, through his essays remembering the nameless pioneers of labor, and closes with Victor Hugo and Norman Thomas. The Editorial Note sketches what the book leaves out: the strike of 1894 and Debs's first term in jail, where his socialism began.

Major entries

Debs's essays on the labor movement (pp. 577-579)

  • What they are: Young quotes three pieces. "Unionism and Socialism: A Plea for Both" (1904) remembers the "untitled agitators of the earlier day" who organized their trades and often "filled an unknown grave" (p. 577). "Socialism" contrasts idle capitalists "choosing judges, buying editors, hiring preachers" with workers who "sweat and groan and bleed and die" (pp. 578-579). "The American Movement" surveys the century and concludes that "the few have ruled, the many have served, the parasite has worn the purple of power" (p. 579).

  • Why it matters: These essays are Debs's own account of the history this book reconstructs. His claim that "No strike has ever been lost" (p. 578) expresses his belief that every defeat, from the anthracite fields to Pullman, built the movement.

  • Further reading: Tim Davenport and David Walters, eds., The Selected Works of Eugene V. Debs (2019 onward), which collects his writings by year.

Victor Hugo's words on socialism (pp. 579-580)

  • What it is: Debs drew strength from a passage Hugo wrote in exile in 1864, in the book William Shakespeare: "The transformation of the crowd into the people—profound task! It is to this labor that the men called Socialists have devoted themselves during the last forty years" (p. 580).

  • Why it matters: Hugo was exiled to the Channel Islands from 1851 to 1870 for opposing Napoleon III. His socialism was moral, humane, and national, the tradition Debs belonged to, closer to Weitling and Phillips than to Marx's economics.

The Pullman strike and boycott of 1894 (p. 581)

  • What happened: In the depression of 1893 George Pullman cut wages at his car works by about a quarter without lowering rents in his company town. His workers struck in May 1894. In June the American Railway Union, Debs's industrial union of all railroad workers, voted to stop handling Pullman cars. Traffic halted across much of the country west of Chicago.

  • The government's response: The railroads' General Managers' Association had the U.S. attorney general, Richard Olney, a former railroad lawyer, obtain a sweeping federal injunction forbidding the union's leaders to direct the strike. President Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago over Governor Altgeld's protest. Some thirty people were killed. Debs was arrested for contempt of the injunction.

  • Where the record differs: The Editorial Note names the union the "American Railroad Workers Union" (p. 581). It was the American Railway Union.

  • Further reading: Richard Schneirov, Shelton Stromquist, and Nick Salvatore, eds., The Pullman Strike and the Crisis of the 1890s (1999).

Debs in Woodstock jail and *In re Debs (p. 581)

  • What happened: In December 1894 Judge Peter Grosscup's court sentenced Debs to six months for contempt, without a jury. In In re Debs (1895) the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the injunction as a use of federal power over interstate commerce and the mails. Debs served his term in the county jail at Woodstock, Illinois, in 1895. The American Railway Union never recovered.

  • Becoming a socialist: In his essay "How I Became a Socialist" (1902), Debs wrote that visitors, among them the Milwaukee socialist Victor Berger, brought him books in jail, including Marx's Capital. He came out saying the injunction had taught him what the government served. He backed the Populist William Jennings Bryan in 1896 and declared himself a socialist in 1897.

  • Thoreau: The Editorial Note compares Debs to Henry David Thoreau, jailed for a night in 1846 for refusing to pay a poll tax that supported the Mexican War and slavery. Thoreau's essay "Civil Disobedience" (1849) came from it.

  • Further reading: Salvatore, Eugene V. Debs (1982), chapters 5 and 6.

Shorter entries

  • The House of the Dead (pp. 577, 581): Dostoyevsky's prison memoir (Unit 20). The Editorial Note says Debs felt "a shock of recognition" reading it.

  • Plato and Sir Thomas More (p. 577): The Republic and Utopia (1516), the founding books of the utopian tradition that fills Part One.

  • Norman Thomas's portrait (p. 580): Young ends with Thomas's image of Debs walking the earth in his gray suit among the stars (Unit 1).

Allusions

  • "Scrip in his purse" (p. 577): From Christ's instructions to the apostles to travel without provisions, Luke 10.

  • "Screw courage to the sticking point" (p. 577): Lady Macbeth's words in Macbeth, Act 1.

  • "By its fruits we know the tree" (p. 579): Matthew 7 and 12.

  • Les Misérables (p. 579): Hugo's poor, whom Debs saw in every factory town.
harp-companion-unit-14-home-life-and-the:
Unit 14, pp. 305-352: Home life and the wider 1880s

← Unit 13 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 15 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Debs marries Kate Metzel in 1885 and honeymoons in the East as the Statue of Liberty arrives in New York harbor. Around the marriage Young sets the decade's scandals and struggles: a kidnapped child, a preacher's adultery trial, a president's assassin, and an Irish word, "boycott," crossing the Atlantic. The unit ends with the Burlington strike of 1888, which taught Debs that craft unions fighting alone would lose.

Major entries

Debs's marriage and household (pp. 311-321, 333-350)

  • What happened: On June 9, 1885, Debs married Katherine Metzel at St. Stephen's Episcopal Church in Terre Haute (p. 315). She came from a German family of Louisville, and her stepfather, John Baur, kept a Terre Haute drugstore. They had no children. In 1890 they built the house on North Eighth Street (p. 340) that is now the Debs Home museum.

  • The family circle: His sister Emilie married the electrical engineer C. Odilon Mailloux in 1883 (p. 311). His sister Marie married the florist John G. Heinl, who designed the floral locomotive for a brotherhood celebration (p. 310). His brother Theodore became his lifelong secretary and partner in the work (pp. 318-320).

  • How Young uses it: Kate has been cast by many biographers as cold to Debs's causes. Young treats the marriage with more sympathy, through their letters signed with railroad pen names such as "Signal" and "Headlight" (p. 336).

  • Further reading: Salvatore, Eugene V. Debs (1982), chapter 3.

The Statue of Liberty and Pulitzer's campaign (pp. 323-326)

  • What it was: France's gift, designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an iron frame by Gustave Eiffel. It arrived in pieces off Sandy Hook on June 17, 1885, and was met by General Charles P. Stone, the engineer in charge of its assembly (p. 326).

  • The pedestal: Congress and wealthy New Yorkers failed to fund the base. In 1885 Joseph Pulitzer's New York World printed the names of every donor, and more than 120,000 people, most of them giving under a dollar, raised over \$100,000 (p. 325). Emma Lazarus's poem "The New Colossus" (1883), with its line "Give me your tired, your poor," was written to raise money for the pedestal.

  • The dedication: President Grover Cleveland dedicated the statue on October 28, 1886. Chauncey Depew, the New York Central Railroad's lawyer, gave the main oration (p. 326). It came less than six months after the Haymarket bombing, when immigrants were being blamed for radicalism.

  • Further reading: Edward Berenson, The Statue of Liberty: A Transatlantic Story (2012).

The Burlington strike of 1888 (p. 349)

  • What happened: In February 1888 the engineers and firemen of the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad struck for better pay and an end to wage classifications. The railroad hired replacements, some from the Knights of Labor, which had its own grudges against the brotherhoods, and brought in Pinkerton guards. The strike was lost by the end of the year.

  • Why it matters: Debs saw the lesson plainly: rail workers divided by craft could each be beaten one by one. In his January 1888 essay "The Vitality of Labor Organizations" (p. 349) and after, he pressed for federation. That path led to the Supreme Council of the United Orders of Railway Employees (1889) and then to the American Railway Union (1893).

  • Further reading: Shelton Stromquist, A Generation of Boomers: The Pattern of Railroad Labor Conflict in Nineteenth-Century America (1987).

The boycott and the Irish Land War (pp. 351-352)

  • What it was: In 1880 tenants in County Mayo, organized by the Irish National Land League, refused all dealings with Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent who evicted them. His name became the word for collective shunning. Young quotes Debs's account of it (p. 352).

  • Why it matters: American unions, especially the Knights of Labor, adopted the boycott widely in the 1880s. Courts soon ruled many boycotts illegal conspiracies, a key weapon in the later use of injunctions against labor, including against Debs in 1894.

  • Where the record differs: Young quotes Debs calling Boycott "an Englishman, owner of landed estates" (p. 352). He was the agent for an absentee landlord, Lord Erne, not the owner.

  • Parnell: Charles Stewart Parnell, the Irish nationalist leader, was ruined in 1890 when he was named in the divorce of Katharine ("Kitty") O'Shea. Debs wrote on it in the magazine in January 1891 (p. 351).

  • Further reading: Joyce Marlow, Captain Boycott and the Irish (1973).

David M. Parry and the manufacturers' crusade (pp. 306-307)

  • Who he was: An Indianapolis carriage and buggy manufacturer (1852-1915) who became president of the National Association of Manufacturers from 1902 to 1906. He led its open-shop campaign against unions and wrote The Scarlet Empire (1906), a novel imagining socialism as a tyranny beneath the sea.

  • Where the record differs: Young calls him "George A. Parry" and his group the "American Association of Manufacturers" (p. 306). She uses the phrase "the Scarlet Empire" for the poor districts of Indianapolis (p. 307), a sly borrowing from his book.

Shorter entries

  • Charley Ross (p. 306): A four-year-old kidnapped from Germantown, Philadelphia, on July 1, 1874. The first American kidnapping for ransom to become a national sensation, it was never solved.

  • Charles H. Black (p. 305): An Indianapolis carriage maker credited locally with one of the first gasoline automobiles, around 1891.

  • The Beecher-Tilton scandal (pp. 312-313): Theodore Tilton sued Henry Ward Beecher in 1874 for adultery with his wife, Elizabeth. The 1875 trial ended in a hung jury. Victoria Woodhull had first published the charge.

  • The Franco-Prussian War (p. 310): Prussia and its German allies defeated France in 1870-1871 and annexed Alsace, including the Debs family's Colmar. Daniel Debs sided passionately with France.

  • The Brooklyn Bridge (p. 323): Opened in 1883. The editor Frank Harris claimed to have worked in its caissons as a young man. As editor of Pearson's Magazine he later published Debs's writing.

  • Garfield and Guiteau (pp. 330): Garfield was shot on July 2, 1881, and died on September 19 at Elberon, New Jersey. Guiteau had lived at the Oneida Community in the 1860s. Horatio Alger rushed out a Garfield biography, From Canal Boy to President (1881).

  • Maud Gonne and William Butler Yeats (p. 352): Gonne, an Irish nationalist, campaigned against evictions. Yeats loved her for decades without success.

  • Colonel J. B. Maynard (p. 350): A Civil War veteran and friend of the brotherhoods.

  • Joel Chandler Harris (p. 342): The Atlanta author of the Uncle Remus tales (1880). His home was called the Wren's Nest.

  • Riley's poems (pp. 346-348): "The Old-Fashioned Roses" and "An Old Sweetheart of Mine" were among the favorites Young mentions. Admirers called Riley "the Hoosier Theocritus."

  • Popular songs (p. 334): "Katie Lee and Willie Grey" and "The Old Oaken Bucket" (1817), which Young says an elocutionist recited for the newlyweds.

Allusions

  • Venus de Milo (pp. 324, 327): The ancient statue in the Louvre, set beside Lady Liberty.

  • Esmeralda, Cosette, The Man Who Laughs (p. 324): Characters and a novel of Victor Hugo.

  • Camelot and Elaine (p. 343): Tennyson's Arthurian idylls.

  • Rodin's The Thinker (p. 349): The sculpture of 1880-1904.

  • The Bridge of Sighs (p. 351): The Venetian bridge prisoners crossed to their cells.

  • Eros and Dan Cupid (pp. 311, 339): The gods of love.

  • Hawthorne's The House of the Seven Gables (p. 342): The 1851 novel of an inherited curse.
harp-companion-unit-09-terre-haute-and-t:
Unit 9, pp. 177-200: Terre Haute and the coming war

← Unit 8 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 10 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Part Two opens with the Debs family's journey from New York to Cincinnati to Terre Haute, where Eugene was born on November 5, 1855. Young sketches the town's frontier founding, then the tensions of the 1850s: the Dred Scott decision, a southern Indiana full of Confederate sympathizers, and an Indianapolis doctor inventing the Gatling gun.

Major entries

The Debs family's arrival and Eugene's naming (pp. 181-186)

  • What happened: Daniel and Marguerite first lived in Williamsburg, then a separate town, now part of Brooklyn, where their first baby died at birth (p. 181). They tried Cincinnati, then settled in Terre Haute. Daniel worked in a slaughterhouse and laid railroad ties (p. 183) before the family opened a grocery.

  • The names: Eugene Victor was named for two French novelists of the poor: Eugène Sue, whose The Wandering Jew (1844-1845) attacked the Jesuits, and Victor Hugo (p. 186).

  • A note on dates: Young mentions Les Misérables in this passage (p. 186). That novel appeared in 1862, seven years after Eugene's birth. Daniel's admiration for Hugo rested on earlier work such as Notre-Dame de Paris (1831).

  • Further reading: Salvatore, Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist (1982), chapter 1.

The founding of Terre Haute and Fort Harrison (pp. 187-190)

  • What it was: Terre Haute ("high land" in French) sits on a bluff over the Wabash. William Henry Harrison built Fort Harrison nearby in 1811 during his campaign against the Indian confederacy. Abraham Markle and Joseph Richardson scouted the site in 1815 (p. 187), and the town was platted in 1816 in Vigo County, named for the fur trader Francis Vigo.

  • Abraham Markle: Born in Ulster County, New York, he moved to Upper Canada. During the War of 1812 he switched sides and served as a major in the Canadian Volunteers, a unit of Canadians fighting for the United States. Losing his Canadian property, he was compensated with western land and helped found Terre Haute.

  • Growth: The Wabash and Erie Canal reached the town in 1849, and railroads from Indianapolis arrived in 1852. The line later known as the Vandalia gave Daniel Debs work and Eugene his first job.

  • Further reading: Mike McCormick, Terre Haute: Queen City of the Wabash (2005).

Tecumseh, the Prophet, and Tippecanoe (p. 187)

  • What happened: The Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa, called the Prophet, built a pan-Indian confederacy to stop the sale of Native land. On November 7, 1811, while Tecumseh was away in the South, the Prophet's warriors attacked Harrison's army camped near their town, Prophetstown, at Tippecanoe Creek. Harrison held the field and burned the town.

  • Why it matters: The battle made Harrison a national hero and later president ("Tippecanoe and Tyler Too," 1840). He died a month after taking office in 1841. Tecumseh allied with Britain and was killed in 1813.

  • Where the record differs: Young describes "the cowardly attack upon the utopian philosopher Tecumseh and his sleeping red men when they had already surrendered" (p. 187). In fact Tecumseh was absent, and the Indians attacked Harrison's camp before dawn. Her sympathy for Native Americans runs through the book, but here the facts are reversed.

  • Further reading: Peter Cozzens, Tecumseh and the Prophet (2020).

The Dred Scott decision (pp. 198-200)

  • What it was: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, sued for freedom because his owner had taken him to live in a free state and a free territory. On March 6, 1857, the Supreme Court under Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens and that Congress had no power to bar slavery from the territories.

  • Why it matters: The ruling voided the Missouri Compromise, outraged the North, and pushed the country toward war. It was overturned by the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868.

  • Connections Young draws: Scott and his family were freed in May 1857 by Taylor Blow, a son of Scott's original owner (p. 200). Roswell Martin Field, the St. Louis lawyer who took Scott's case into federal court, was the father of the poet Eugene Field, later Debs's friend (p. 200).

  • Where the record differs: Young places the decision on "the very day after" Buchanan's inauguration (p. 198). It came two days after, on March 6.

  • Further reading: Don E. Fehrenbacher, The Dred Scott Case (1978).

Richard Gatling and the Gatling gun (pp. 193-197)

  • Who he was: A North Carolina-born physician and inventor (1818-1903) living in Indianapolis. He patented his hand-cranked, multi-barrel rapid-fire gun in November 1862. The Army adopted it in 1866.

  • The Union Repeating Gun: Before Gatling, the salesman J. D. Mills promoted the "coffee mill" Union Repeating Gun as "an army in six square feet" (p. 194). Lincoln watched a demonstration and ordered ten in October 1861.

  • Why it matters: After the war, Gatling guns were deployed against strikers and miners. Young lists the Pullman strike of 1894 and the mining wars at Coeur d'Alene, Idaho (1892, 1899), Cripple Creek, Colorado (1894, 1903-1904), and Goldfield, Nevada (1907) (p. 197).

  • Further reading: Julia Keller, Mr. Gatling's Terrible Marvel (2008).

Oliver P. Morton and the Knights of the Golden Circle (pp. 194-196)

  • Morton: Indiana's Republican war governor (1861-1867), later a senator. When Democrats won the legislature in 1862 and refused to pass a budget, he ran the state for two years on federal money and private loans, outside the law.

  • The Knights: Founded by George Bickley in Lexington, Kentucky, on July 4, 1854 (p. 195), the Knights of the Golden Circle first aimed at a slave empire around the Gulf of Mexico. During the war the name was attached to Copperhead networks in the Midwest, the Order of American Knights (1863) and the Sons of Liberty (1864). Young says the Hoosier council began in Terre Haute in 1863 and spread to sixty counties (p. 195), a detail that is unverified.

  • Why it matters: Southern Indiana was settled largely from the upland South. Many residents opposed the war and emancipation. Morton used the secret societies, real and exaggerated, to justify arrests and military trials (Unit 10).

  • Further reading: Frank L. Klement, Dark Lanterns: Secret Political Societies, Conspiracies, and Treason Trials in the Civil War (1984).

Shorter entries

  • Franklin Pierce (pp. 184-185): Democratic president from 1853 to 1857. His only surviving son, Benjamin, was killed in a train wreck two months before the inauguration. He signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which repealed the Missouri Compromise.

  • The Missouri Compromise (p. 185): The 1820 law admitting Missouri as a slave state and barring slavery north of 36°30' in the Louisiana Purchase.

  • Butternuts (p. 192): A nickname for settlers of southern origin in the lower Midwest, from clothing dyed brown with butternut hulls. It came to mean Confederate sympathizers.

  • The Terre Haute State Bank (p. 189): The Greek Revival branch of the State Bank of Indiana on Ohio Street, built in the 1830s. It still stands.

  • Bill Nye (pp. 189-190): Edgar Wilson Nye (1850-1896), a humorist and Riley's touring partner. Young says he and Debs, both tall and bald, were taken for twins.

  • Vigo County Court House (p. 190): Where Debs later served as city clerk (1879-1883).

  • Helen Keller (p. 198): The deaf and blind author was a Socialist and a supporter of Debs, and wrote to him in prison.

  • Karl Marx and the Pullman strike (p. 197): Newspapers in 1894 blamed the strike on foreign radicalism. Young notes that few Americans had heard of Marx.

Allusions

  • St. Bartholomew's Day (p. 181): The 1572 massacre of French Protestants in Paris, used for New York's mass killings of stray dogs.

  • Mammon (p. 181): Wealth as a false god, from the Gospels.

  • Infant Hercules and River Queen (p. 182): Nicknames for Cincinnati, the fast-growing river city.

  • Hades (p. 184): The Greek underworld.

  • The Mason-Dixon Line (p. 191): The boundary surveyed in the 1760s, taken as the line between North and South.

  • Methuselah (p. 200): The oldest man in the Bible.
harp-companion-unit-07-the-book-of-mormo:
Unit 7, pp. 121-152: The Book of Mormon to Salt Lake

← Unit 6 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 8 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young tells how the Book of Mormon was financed, translated, lost in part, and printed, largely through the story of its patron Martin Harris. She then leaps to Salt Lake City in 1861 through the eyes of Mark Twain and his brother Orion. The thread connecting them is the American dream of a kingdom built from nothing, and what it cost.

Major entries

Martin Harris (pp. 123-138)

  • Who he was: A prosperous farmer of Palmyra, New York (1783-1875), and one of Joseph Smith's first believers. His religious restlessness led him through several churches before Mormonism, as Young lists (p. 124).

  • The lost 116 pages: In 1828, while acting as Smith's scribe, Harris begged to show the manuscript to his skeptical wife. Smith allowed him to show it only to her, his brother Preserved Harris, and a few others (p. 128). The 116 pages vanished and were never recovered. Many suspect his wife destroyed them.

  • The mortgage: In August 1829 Harris mortgaged his farm to the printer Egbert B. Grandin for three thousand dollars to pay for five thousand copies. The Book of Mormon appeared in March 1830, and Harris later sold land to cover the debt.

  • Later life: He left the church in the 1830s but never denied his testimony. He went to Utah at eighty-seven, rejoined, and died there in 1875.

  • Further reading: Susan Easton Black and Larry C. Porter, Martin Harris: Uncompromising Witness of the Book of Mormon (2018).

The Three and Eight Witnesses (pp. 131-139)

  • What they were: Printed in every copy of the Book of Mormon are two statements. Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris swore an angel had shown them the plates. Eight other men, among them Joseph Smith, Sr., his sons Hyrum and Samuel H. Smith, several Whitmers, and Hiram Page, swore they had handled them.

  • The translation: Much of the work was done in 1829 at the farmhouse of Peter Whitmer in Fayette, Seneca County, New York (p. 131), where the church was formally organized on April 6, 1830.

  • David Whitmer's later testimony: Whitmer broke with Smith in 1838 and settled in Richmond, Missouri. He gave newspaper interviews into old age, including one Young cites from the Chicago Tribune of December 15, 1885 (p. 132) and another from the Kingston, Missouri, Times of December 27, 1887 (p. 135). He died in 1888 affirming the book, as the Richmond Democrat reported (p. 139).

  • How Young uses it: She dates Whitmer's recollections against the eight-hour strikes and the Haymarket executions of November 1887. The same newspapers carried a dying prophet's witness and the hanging of the anarchists.

  • Further reading: Richard Lloyd Anderson, Investigating the Book of Mormon Witnesses (1981).

Brigham Young (pp. 136-152)

  • Who he was: A Vermont-born carpenter and painter (1801-1877) who joined the church in 1832. After Smith's murder he led the majority of the Saints from Nauvoo to the Great Salt Lake valley in 1846-1847. Young calls him "the Golden Lion of the Tribe of Zion" (p. 139), a play on his nickname, the Lion of the Lord.

  • Why it matters: He built one of the most successful colonizing efforts in American history, planting hundreds of settlements across the Great Basin. He was territorial governor of Utah from 1850 until the Utah War of 1857-1858, when federal troops were sent to assert control. He practiced plural marriage on a large scale, and his family lived in the Lion House and the Beehive House in Salt Lake City (pp. 142-143).

  • The beehive: The beehive was the Mormon emblem of cooperative industry. Twain described the crest as "a Golden Bee Hive, with the bees all at work" (p. 142). It remains Utah's state emblem.

  • Further reading: John G. Turner, Brigham Young: Pioneer Prophet (2012).

Mark Twain, Orion Clemens, and *Roughing It (pp. 139-152)

  • What happened: In 1861 President Lincoln appointed Orion Clemens secretary of the new Nevada Territory. His younger brother Samuel, whose career as a Mississippi River pilot had been ended by the war, paid both fares and went along. They crossed the plains by stagecoach and spent two days in Salt Lake City in August 1861.

  • The book: Twain turned the trip into Roughing It (1872). Its chapters on the Mormons mock Brigham Young's many wives and call the Book of Mormon "chloroform in print."

  • Where the record differs: Young dates the stagecoach trip to 1862 (p. 139). It was the summer of 1861.

  • How Young uses it: Twain is her guide through the Gilded Age. Here he is still Sam Clemens, a young man going west for silver, the gold rush dream in its Nevada form.

  • Further reading: Ron Powers, Mark Twain: A Life (2005), chapters on Nevada.

Shorter entries

  • Oliver Cowdery (pp. 131-138): A schoolteacher who became Smith's main scribe. He was excommunicated in 1838, practiced law, and returned to the church in 1848, two years before his death.

  • Kirtland, Ohio (pp. 136-138): The Mormon headquarters from 1831 to 1838. Its temple was dedicated in 1836, when Smith and Cowdery reported visions of Moses, Elias, and Elijah (pp. 137-138).

  • Nephites and Lamanites (pp. 133, 139): Peoples of the Book of Mormon, descendants of Israelites who sailed to America. The Lamanites were taught to be ancestors of the American Indians, which shaped Mormon missions to Native peoples.

  • The Salt Lake House (pp. 141-142): The city's main hotel in 1861, where the Clemens brothers stayed.

  • The Tithing House (pp. 142, 150): The church storehouse where members paid their tenth in goods, the core of the Mormon cooperative economy.

  • Anson Call (p. 144): A Mormon pioneer and colonizer. Young retells a family legend of Brigham Young by his fireside.

  • Polygamy (pp. 134, 143-152): The church publicly acknowledged plural marriage in 1852. Federal pressure, including the Edmunds Act of 1882, forced its official end in 1890, and Utah became a state in 1896.

Allusions

  • The Golden Calf (pp. 126-127): Exodus 32, the idol Aaron made while Moses was on the mountain.

  • Mot and Anat (p. 127): Canaanite gods of death and war, from the Ugaritic myths.

  • Klopstock's The Messiah (p. 126): The German religious epic of 1748-1773.

  • Golconda (p. 127): An Indian city famous for diamonds, meaning any source of great wealth.

  • Aladdin (p. 122): From The Thousand and One Nights, the boy with the magic lamp.

  • Haman (p. 152): The villain of the Book of Esther.
harp-parallels-from-debs-to-the-present:
Parallels from Debs to the Present

Harp Song for a Radical · The Marguerite Young Society

Passages from the book, with page numbers, sorted by the complaint they share with the present.

Money and corporations run the government

  • p. 261: The government "conspired with the regnant financial powers of Wall Street."

  • p. 364: Cleveland's government was "in thralldom to iron and steel and gold and silver and copper and lead."

  • p. 482: Railroad presidents "had the government in their back pockets."

  • p. 509: The "industrial lords to whom the government had prostituted itself."

  • p. 527: "The railroads owned the government."

  • p. 535: Companies "whose ambassadors were not only in Washington but in the Congress and the Senate, no matter what administration was in power." This is the lobbyist complaint.

  • p. 578: In Debs's essay "Socialism," capitalists spend their time "choosing judges, buying editors, hiring preachers, corrupting politics."

Lawmakers who are slow, self-serving, or bought

  • p. 305: Lawmakers "all too slow for him in the righting of wrongs and were very good in the passage of half-baked bills."

  • p. 314: Debs left the legislature because of "pettifogging political hucksters who delayed progressive decisions for years and acted in behalf of the vested interests."

  • p. 389: Senators tried to kill the Sherman Antitrust Act by loading it with amendments. Senator Ingalls: "The purification of politics is an iridescent dream."

  • p. 414: In the Crédit Mobilier scandal, stock was paid off "to high officials in the government."

  • p. 513: President Hayes left income and assets off his tax reports.

The two parties are really the same

  • p. 170: Weitling thought "both major parties were iridescent bugbears very much like each other."

  • p. 231: Debs's father came to see that Republicans and Democrats were "governed by the same powers."

  • p. 352: The "differences between the two major parties were mainly delusional."

  • p. 517: A warning of "corruption at no distant day if the people continue to ignore the duties of citizenship in the blind adherence to party leaders."

Voting doesn't change anything, and elections get stolen

  • p. 195: "Their ballots had been chewed up by water rats."

  • p. 363: "They had the ballots, but the laws were so framed that their interests and rights were ignored."

  • p. 397: Henry Adams: voters "could not be sure where King Banker lurked behind."

  • pp. 468, 486, 525: The disputed 1876 election, when Tilden won but Hayes took office.

One justice system for the rich, another for the poor

  • p. 27: "Those who stole a country's treasures from the poor were not punished by corrupt governments," and "if they were fined, the penalties were less than the rewards."

  • p. 51: The rich "raised up a barricade of laws by which to protect themselves from the starving poor."

  • p. 198: The Supreme Court was "following elections as the hearse follows the horse."

  • p. 328: The courts "tilted the scales of justice in favor of the rich."

  • p. 366: The Supreme Court ruled that a railroad owed nothing to the widow of a brakeman killed on the job.

  • p. 449: "The law did not pertain for the rich man who stole a continent" but came down hard on a poor man who stole an ear of corn.

  • pp. 197, 506: Court injunctions used as a corporate weapon against strikers.

  • p. 236: Debs was jailed without a jury trial.

Government force used for corporations, against workers

  • p. 197: Federal troops were sent in against the 1877 strikers.

  • p. 469: "The state and federal governments protected corporation heads."

  • p. 487: Putting down the strike cost more than meeting "the far from immoderate demands of the workers" would have.

  • p. 489: Troops were sent to protect "the poor, starving, abused, beaten, battered imperial corporations."

  • p. 491: The city police force was cut in half to save money, while Pinkerton security men were brought in against strikers.

  • p. 536: Harrison sent federal troops to Coeur d'Alene. Strikers were held in barbed-wire bullpens.

Profiteering and public money going to the well connected

  • p. 234: The federal government "ignored as many malfeasances as it could" by corporate land grabbers "while poor war widows and their children living in hog huts in that same North starved."

  • p. 237: "The profiteering war vultures" of Wall Street.

  • p. 413: Money for rebuilding Chicago after the fire went to the merchants and railroad men, who were "channeling the golden sluices to themselves."

  • p. 448: The Civil War "enriched the war profiteers by not taxing them but by passing the burden on to the poor."

  • p. 498: The rich could buy their way out of the war.

Inequality, and democracy for the few

  • p. 75: A "hypocritical democracy which gave protection to the few rich but not to the many poor."

  • p. 191: The nation's real split was between rich and poor, not North and South.

  • p. 258: A "dollars and cents democracy" with "dollars for some and cents for others."

  • p. 490: The Constitution seemed "to favor business interests and property owners and those of privilege."

  • p. 491: The middle class was "not rising but were sinking."

  • p. 511: "The true threat to this democracy came from the rich corrupter and not from the masses of the poor."

  • p. 525: A democracy "where everything was measured by the cost, the cost to the rich and not to the poor."

  • p. 531: Workers wanted a government "more concerned with life and liberty and less with property and property rights."

Monopolies

  • p. 197: Industrial empires whose heads had "more power than was given to the czar of Russia."

  • p. 448: A "monarchical monolith such as had no business in a democracy."

  • p. 526: The Farmers' Declaration of Independence called the railway monopoly "a history of repeated injuries and oppressions."

Contempt for the poor and unemployed, and no safety net

  • p. 138: The "powers in Washington" left the poor to drift.

  • p. 197: The Chicago Tribune "advocated a little strychnine or arsenic as the cure" for the unemployed tramps.

  • p. 263: Higher education was open only to those who could afford it.

  • p. 472: Banks foreclosed on farms, and machines put people out of work.

  • p. 479: President Arthur refused to enforce the eight-hour law. Petitioners asked for public works for the starving.

  • p. 483: Homeless people took turns sleeping on police station floors.

  • p. 504: Tom Scott's view: "the duty of the Government merely to protect the people while they are taking care of themselves."

Worker safety and corporate responsibility

  • p. 185: After a train wreck, the railroad blamed God, and the president-elect had the railroad defended in court.

  • p. 307: Debs's bill to make railroads compensate injured workers.

  • p. 434: "Let the laws be so framed that soul-less corporations cannot starve it to death."

  • p. 450: Company negligence killed 566 miners and maimed 1,665 in seven years, all "called those accidents which were inevitable."

The press

  • p. 349: "The subsidized press employed to dwarf the importance of labor."

  • p. 502: Newspapers called striking workers "alien" communists.

Civil liberties

  • pp. 3–5: Wilson and the Espionage Act, which jailed conscientious objectors.

  • pp. 215, 230, 448: The suspension of habeas corpus.

Partisan fighting and bad management

  • p. 234: The Johnson impeachment as a partisan show trial.

  • p. 248: Congress's mud-slinging over Mary Lincoln's pension.

  • p. 339: Kate Debs "could have given a lesson to the United States government in how to make both ends meet on a limited budget."
harp-companion-unit-15-rail-kings-and-ho:
Unit 15, pp. 353-392: Rail kings and Hoosier politics

← Unit 14 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 16 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

In the late 1880s Debs's magazine turns sharper. He quarrels with the engineers' brotherhood, attacks George Pullman and Jay Gould, and records wreck after wreck. Young then turns to Indiana's political theater: Riley and Nye on tour, Senator Daniel Voorhees, and the Harrison family, whose rising son would become president.

Major entries

Engineers versus firemen: Peter M. Arthur (pp. 353-358)

  • Who he was: Peter M. Arthur (1831-1903), Scottish-born, was grand chief engineer of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers from 1874 until his death. He ran the richest and most conservative of the railroad brotherhoods.

  • The conflict: The engineers considered themselves an elite and refused to support strikes by lower-paid crafts. Young notes Arthur's position that engineers could keep working if the "lower class" of firemen struck (p. 353). Debs resented this caste line between men who died in the same wrecks.

  • Why it matters: The engineers' refusal to back other crafts was a main reason Debs left the brotherhood system in 1893 to found an industrial union for all railroad workers.

  • Further reading: Paul Michel Taillon, Good, Reliable, White Men: Railroad Brotherhoods, 1877-1917 (2009).

George Pullman and the town of Pullman (pp. 359-361)

  • Who he was: George Mortimer Pullman (1831-1897) made his fortune building and operating luxury sleeping cars. Between 1880 and 1884 he built the company town of Pullman south of Chicago, with brick housing, a library, and a church, all owned by the company.

  • Debs's early critique: Years before the 1894 strike, Debs attacked Pullman in the magazine: "Pullman means purple and fine linen, sumptuous living" for the owner, and for his workers "no independence" (p. 359). He listed the grievances of Pullman car employees: "spotters" watching them, fines cutting pay, and blame for errors in berth diagrams (p. 360).

  • Why it matters: The model town became a symbol of paternalism. When Pullman cut wages in 1893-1894 without cutting rents, his workers struck, and Debs's American Railway Union refused to handle Pullman cars nationwide.

  • Further reading: Almont Lindsey, The Pullman Strike (1942).

Jay Gould (pp. 354-355, 361, 364)

  • Who he was: The most hated financier of the Gilded Age (1836-1892). He looted the Erie Railroad with Jim Fisk, tried to corner gold in 1869, which caused the "Black Friday" panic, and built a western railroad empire around the Missouri Pacific and the Wabash.

  • His war with labor: The Knights of Labor won a strike against his Wabash line in 1885, and the Knights' membership soared. In 1886 Gould crushed the Knights in the Great Southwest Strike. He is credited with boasting, "I can hire one-half of the working class to kill the other half." Young mentions a proposed "Knights of Capital" to fight the unions (p. 361).

  • Further reading: Maury Klein, The Life and Legend of Jay Gould (1986).

Daniel W. Voorhees and Edward Hannegan (pp. 385-391)

  • Voorhees: Terre Haute's Democratic leader (1827-1897), called "the Tall Sycamore of the Wabash." He defended John Brown's raider John E. Cook in 1859 and was a leading Copperhead in Congress during the war. As a senator from 1877 to 1897 he championed cheap money and the building of the Library of Congress. His Senate clashes with John J. Ingalls of Kansas were famous for their insults (pp. 388-389).

  • Hannegan: Voorhees grew up in Fountain County, where he knew Edward Hannegan (1807-1859), a senator known for the expansionist cry over Oregon, "Fifty-four forty or fight!" In 1852 at Covington, drunk, Hannegan stabbed his brother-in-law, who died. Lew Wallace, the county prosecutor and later author of Ben-Hur, declined to prosecute (p. 387). Hannegan died of an overdose of morphine and whiskey in 1859.

  • Further reading: Leonard S. Kenworthy, The Tall Sycamore of the Wabash: Daniel Wolsey Voorhees (1936).

Benjamin Harrison (pp. 388-392)

  • Who he was: Grandson of President William Henry Harrison, an Indianapolis lawyer, Union general, senator (1881-1887), and president (1889-1893).

  • Connections: He defended the officials in Milligan's damages suit (Unit 10), commanded a militia company against the 1877 strikers (Unit 19), and signed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890 (p. 389). That law, aimed at monopolies, was first used heavily against unions, including Debs's in 1894.

  • The stolen body: In 1878 the body of Harrison's father, John Scott Harrison, was stolen from its grave at North Bend, Ohio. Searchers found it hanging in a chute at the Medical College of Ohio in Cincinnati (pp. 391-392), a scandal that exposed the trade in corpses for anatomy classes.

  • Further reading: Charles W. Calhoun, Benjamin Harrison (2005).

The Chatsworth wreck (pp. 364-365)

  • What happened: On August 10, 1887, an excursion train of the Toledo, Peoria and Western bound for Niagara Falls crossed a burning wooden trestle near Chatsworth, Illinois (p. 364). The bridge collapsed and more than eighty people died.
