  • Why it matters: It was among the deadliest wrecks of the century. The coroner's jury blamed a section boss rather than the railroad (p. 365), which was typical. Debs used such cases to argue that the companies, not the workers, should answer for safety.

Shorter entries

  • John Perego (p. 364): A fireman who crawled through scalding steam to stop the engine of President Cleveland's special train after the engineer was killed, as the magazine reported in October 1887.

  • Charles A. Dana and the New York Sun (p. 363): Dana's Sun was one of the most hostile papers to labor in the 1880s.

  • Chauncey Depew (p. 363): The New York Central's lawyer and president, a famous after-dinner speaker, later a senator.

  • Elliott F. Shepard (p. 369): Son-in-law of William H. Vanderbilt and a crusading Presbyterian publisher. Young calls him a brother-in-law.

  • Austin Corbin (p. 372): President of the Reading Railroad in the late 1880s. Debs wrote that men like him had "Russianized the anthracite coal regions of Pennsylvania."

  • Labor Day (p. 370): First celebrated with a New York parade in 1882 and made a federal holiday by a law signed on June 28, 1894, in the midst of the Pullman crisis.

  • The American Federation of Labor (p. 371): Founded in 1886 under Samuel Gompers, a federation of craft unions.

  • Myron Reed in Denver (pp. 370-371): As pastor in Denver, Reed preached for organized labor and against the Pinkertons.

  • Debs's organizing trips (pp. 373-374): Debs later recalled being put off trains as an "agitator" and dropped in a snowbank at Elmira, New York.

  • Art Young (p. 365): The socialist cartoonist (1866-1943) of The Masses, who was tried under the Espionage Act in 1918.

  • Riley and Nye's tours (pp. 375-381): The poet and the humorist toured together from 1886 to 1890 and published Nye and Riley's Railway Guide (1888). Riley's poem "Regardin' Terry Hut" (pp. 383-385) was one of his Hoosier dialect pieces.

  • Major Charles Holstein (p. 379): Riley boarded with the Holstein family on Lockerbie Street in Indianapolis from 1893 until his death.

  • Maria Halpin (p. 390): In the 1884 campaign, Grover Cleveland admitted he might be the father of her son. Opponents chanted "Ma, Ma, where's my Pa?" and Cleveland told his managers, "Tell the truth."

Allusions

  • The Gate of Tears (p. 366): Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the mouth of the Red Sea, from Thomas Moore's poetry.

  • Phidias, Raphael, Michelangelo (p. 357): Masters of sculpture and painting.

  • Judas Iscariot (p. 365): The betrayer of Christ, for union traitors.

  • Morpheus (p. 360): The god of dreams, for sleeping cars.

  • Cardinal Wolsey (p. 385): Henry VIII's minister, and Voorhees's middle name.

  • Hogarthian (p. 389): Like William Hogarth's satirical prints of London's poor.
harp-companion-unit-12-europe-mexico-st-:
Unit 12, pp. 257-272: Europe, Mexico, St. Louis, and Debs's first job

← Unit 11 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 13 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Young closes Mary Lincoln's story with her return from France and death in Springfield in 1882, then turns to the fourteen-year-old Debs going to work in the Vandalia railroad shops. The unit follows him onto the footboard as a locomotive fireman and to St. Louis during the depression of 1873, where he met Gilded Age poverty up close.

Major entries

Debs goes to work on the railroad (pp. 261-268)

  • What happened: In 1870, at fourteen, Debs left school for the paint shop of the Terre Haute and Indianapolis Railroad, the line later called the Vandalia, scraping grease and paint from locomotives for fifty cents a day. Young credits the introduction to a family friend, the French car painter Pierre Solomon, and names the shop boss "Old Man Pebbles" (p. 264), details that are unverified.

  • The fireman: By sixteen he was a locomotive fireman, shoveling coal into the firebox. Young describes the winter runs, snow driving into his eyes so that he seemed "to see two moons at once" (p. 265). Firemen died often: Young notes a young man named Stewart killed near Terre Haute, whose death Debs kept from his mother (p. 268).

  • Why it matters: Railroading was among the deadliest work in America. In the 1880s thousands of railroad workers were killed each year, and brakemen and firemen could not buy insurance. That danger is why the railroad brotherhoods began as insurance societies (Unit 13).

  • Further reading: Walter Licht, Working for the Railroad (1983).

St. Louis and the depression of 1873 (pp. 267-272)

  • What happened: When the Panic of 1873 struck, the Vandalia laid Debs off. He went to St. Louis looking for railroad work and wrote home about bedbugs and the misery around him (p. 268). He returned to Terre Haute in 1874 to clerk for the Hulman grocery firm.

  • Why it matters: The depression that began in 1873 lasted until 1879, the longest in American history until the 1930s. Unemployment, wage cuts, and tramping men on the roads set the stage for Tompkins Square (Unit 18) and the Great Strike of 1877.

  • The city: St. Louis was a railroad and river hub and home to many German Forty-Eighters. Its smoke and fogs over the "River Queen" (p. 270) come from the coal economy Debs fed as a fireman.

  • Further reading: Scott Reynolds Nelson, A Nation of Deadbeats: An Uncommon History of America's Financial Disasters (2012).

Joseph Pulitzer in St. Louis (pp. 270-271)

  • Who he was: Born in Hungary in 1847, he came to America in 1864 as a recruit for the Union cavalry. In St. Louis he became a reporter for the Westliche Post, the German paper co-owned by Carl Schurz, and a Missouri legislator.

  • Why it matters: He campaigned with Schurz's Liberal Republicans against the corruption of the Grant administration (p. 270). In 1878 he founded the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, and in 1883 he bought the New York World, pioneering the crusading popular press. His prizes for journalism began in 1917.

  • Further reading: James McGrath Morris, Pulitzer: A Life in Politics, Print, and Power (2010).

Herbert Spencer and Social Darwinism (p. 266)

  • Who he was: English philosopher (1820-1903) who coined the phrase "survival of the fittest" in 1864. He applied evolution to society and argued that the state should not interfere with competition.

  • Why it matters: Spencer was hugely popular with American industrialists. Andrew Carnegie called himself a disciple, and Spencer was feted on his 1882 American tour. His The Man Versus the State (1884) attacked socialism and reform legislation as doomed to fail, the view Young sets against Debs's faith in human perfectibility (p. 266).

  • Further reading: Richard Hofstadter, Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944).

Mary Lincoln's last years (pp. 259-261)

  • What happened: After her release she lived in exile at Pau, in southern France, from 1876 to 1880. Sailing home on the Amérique, she nearly fell down a stairway and was caught by Sarah Bernhardt, who told the story in her memoirs (p. 259). She died on July 16, 1882, in the Springfield house of her sister Elizabeth and brother-in-law Ninian Edwards, the house where she had married Lincoln. She was buried beside him at Oak Ridge Cemetery.

  • How Young uses it: Young ties the year of her death to Twain's The Prince and the Pauper, a tale of rags and riches. That book appeared in 1881, the year before she died.

Shorter entries

  • Manifest Destiny (p. 257): The belief, named in 1845, that the United States was destined to spread across the continent. It justified the Mexican War.

  • Seward and Mexico (p. 257): Secretary of State William Seward pressed Napoleon III to withdraw French troops from Mexico after the Civil War, which doomed Maximilian.

  • The Reverend James A. Reed (p. 260): The Springfield Presbyterian minister who preached Mary Lincoln's funeral sermon.

  • Daniel Debs, "Dandy Lion" (pp. 262-268): Young's nickname for Debs's father, who read French and German classics aloud to his children. Hugo's Les Misérables and its hero Jean Valjean shaped the boy (pp. 266-267).

  • The heroes of liberty (p. 262): Young lists the figures the young Debs admired: the abolitionists William Lloyd Garrison, Wendell Phillips, and William Wilberforce; the Hungarian patriot Louis Kossuth, who toured America in 1851-1852; and the Italian republican Giuseppe Mazzini.

  • The Southern Illinois railroad and Belleville (p. 267): Lines Debs knew around St. Louis. Belleville was a center of German radicalism in Illinois.

Allusions

  • Quetzalcoatl and Montezuma (p. 257): The Aztec feathered-serpent god and the emperor defeated by Cortés.

  • The True Cross (p. 257): The relic of Christ's cross, here a symbol of imperial piety.

  • Charles Martel (p. 262): The Frankish leader who stopped the Muslim advance at Tours in 732.

  • John Chrysostom (p. 262): The fourth-century bishop called "golden-mouthed" for his preaching.

  • Plato's Republic (p. 262): The first great utopia.

  • Lazarus (p. 263): The beggar at the rich man's gate in Luke 16.

  • Nimrod (p. 266): The mighty hunter of Genesis, for Daniel Debs.

  • Gog and Magog (p. 269): The hostile powers of biblical prophecy.
harp-companion-unit-05-weitling-in-ameri:
Unit 5, pp. 81-104: Weitling in America and the communes

← Unit 4 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 6 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Weitling tours the German towns of the Great Lakes and the Mississippi, then pins his hopes on Communia, a small colony in Iowa. Along the way Young surveys the rival communities that dotted the Midwest around 1850: Oneida, Nauvoo, Icaria, Zoar, and Ebenezer. It is a map of American utopia at its peak.

Major entries

Communia, Iowa (pp. 81, 85-90, 102)

  • What it was: A communal colony founded in 1847 near Elkader in Clayton County, Iowa, by the Volga River, a tributary of the Turkey River. Its founder, Heinrich Koch, was a German radical who had come to America after the revolution of 1830 and edited a freethinking paper in St. Louis.

  • What happened: Koch left the presidency accused of taking colony money for his family (p. 86). Weitling's workers' league in New York invested in the colony around 1851, and Weitling arrived, as he reported in his paper, "on Good Friday" (p. 88). Quarrels over money and control followed, the league's funds were lost, and lawsuits dragged on until the colony dissolved in the mid-1850s.

  • Why it matters: Communia was the one place where Weitling's ideas met real soil. Its failure ended his public career. It is typical of dozens of small immigrant communes that vanished with almost no record.

  • Further reading: Wittke, The Utopian Communist (1950), chapters 13 and 14.

Die Republik der Arbeiter* and the Arbeiterbund (pp. 82-88)

  • What it was: Weitling's monthly, later weekly, newspaper, The Workers' Republic, published in New York from 1850 to 1855. It served the Arbeiterbund, a league of German workers' associations in cities such as Cleveland, Sandusky, Toledo, Detroit, Chicago, and Milwaukee.

  • Why it matters: The league promoted a "labor exchange bank" and cooperative workshops, an early attempt at a workers' economy inside capitalism. Young notes a cooperative tailor shop in Cleveland where the women did the sewing "when the men had failed" (p. 82).

  • Further reading: Bruce Levine, The Spirit of 1848 (1992).

Nauvoo, Illinois (pp. 93-96, 99, 102-103)

  • What it was: The Mormon city on the Mississippi. The site began as a village called Venus, then Commerce (p. 95). Joseph Smith bought land there after the Mormons were driven from Missouri in 1838-1839 and renamed it Nauvoo, from a Hebrew word for "beautiful."

  • Why it matters: By 1844 Nauvoo had perhaps twelve thousand people, rivaling Chicago. After Smith's murder that June, Brigham Young led the Saints west in 1846, and the Icarians bought part of the emptied town in 1849. One site thus held two utopias in succession, the religious and the secular.

  • Further reading: Glen M. Leonard, Nauvoo: A Place of Peace, a People of Promise (2002).

Étienne Cabet and the Icarians (pp. 96-102)

  • Who he was: A French lawyer and deputy (1788-1856) exiled to England in 1834 for his radical journalism. There he absorbed Owen's ideas. His novel first appeared in 1840 as the "travels and adventures of Lord William Carisdall in Icaria," presented as a translation from an English author, Francis Adams (p. 99). It described a communist republic run by elected committees.

  • What happened: On Owen's advice Cabet bought Texas land sight unseen (p. 97). The first party of sixty-nine men sailed from Le Havre in February 1848, landed at New Orleans, and found scattered parcels, fever, and failure. Cabet brought the survivors to Nauvoo in March 1849. The community split in 1856, Cabet was expelled, and he died in St. Louis that November. Successor colonies lasted in Iowa until 1898.

  • Why it matters: Icaria was the longest-lived secular commune in American history. Its members were mostly French artisans, the counterparts of Weitling's German tailors.

  • Further reading: Robert P. Sutton, Les Icariens: The Utopian Dream in Europe and America (1994).

Zoar, Ohio, and Ebenezer (pp. 103-104)

  • What they were: Zoar was founded in 1817 by German Separatists from Württemberg under Joseph Bimeler, in the Tuscarawas valley of Ohio. They went communal in 1819 to pay for their land and earned much of their capital by building a section of the Ohio and Erie Canal. They practiced celibacy for part of the 1820s and dissolved in 1898. Ebenezer was the settlement near Buffalo, New York, of the Community of True Inspiration, which moved to Iowa in 1855 and became the Amana Colonies.

  • Why it matters: These pietist communes were the most durable of all. Weitling admired that their women worked in the fields alongside the men (p. 103), which he saw as the key to their harvests.

  • Further reading: Kathleen M. Fernandez, Zoar: The Story of an Intentional Community (2019).

Coxey's Army (p. 104)

  • What it was: In 1894, during the worst depression the country had yet known, Jacob S. Coxey, a businessman from Massillon, Ohio, led a march of unemployed men to Washington. With his partner Carl Browne he called it the "Commonweal of Christ" (Young's "Army of Christ"). They demanded federal road building to create jobs, paid for with paper money.

  • What happened: About five hundred marchers reached the Capitol on May 1, 1894. Coxey was arrested for walking on the grass.

  • Why it matters: It was the first protest march on Washington and the seed of public works programs of the 1930s. It unfolded the same spring as the Pullman strike.

  • Further reading: Carlos A. Schwantes, Coxey's Army: An American Odyssey (1985).

John Peter Altgeld (p. 83)

  • Who he was: Born in Germany in 1847 and raised on an Ohio farm, he became a Chicago judge and governor of Illinois (1893-1897).

  • Why it matters: In 1893 he pardoned the three surviving Haymarket defendants, declaring the trial unjust, which ended his political career. In 1894 he protested President Cleveland's sending of federal troops against the Pullman strikers. Vachel Lindsay's poem "The Eagle That Is Forgotten" mourns him.

  • How Young uses him: She pictures him as a sorrowful German boy and calls his path "a transcendental and yet secular socialism" (p. 83), a bridge from the 1848 exiles to Debs.

  • Further reading: Harry Barnard, Eagle Forgotten: The Life of John Peter Altgeld (1938).

Shorter entries

  • John Humphrey Noyes and the Oneida Community (pp. 80-81): Noyes's Perfectionists practiced "complex marriage," in which all adults were considered married to one another, and group criticism. The community prospered making traps and silverware and gave up communal life in 1881.

  • The Millerites (p. 81): Followers of William Miller, who predicted Christ's return in 1843-1844. The failure of October 22, 1844, is called the Great Disappointment. The Seventh-day Adventists grew from it.

  • Cyrus Hall McCormick (p. 83): Inventor of the mechanical reaper, who moved his factory to Chicago in 1847. His works later saw the 1886 strike that led to Haymarket.

  • John Hay (p. 82): Lincoln's private secretary, later a Cleveland resident by marriage (Unit 18).

  • George Miller (p. 94): A Mormon bishop who refused to follow Brigham Young after Smith's death.

  • Massillon, Ohio (p. 104): Named, as Young says, by the wife of founder James Duncan after the French bishop Jean-Baptiste Massillon. He opened his funeral oration for Louis XIV with "Dieu seul est grand," God alone is great.

Allusions

  • Midas (p. 91): The king whose touch turned everything to gold.

  • Noah's Ark (p. 93): Joseph Smith taught that the ark had sailed from America.

  • Herod (p. 97): The biblical tyrant, used for Cabet's persecutors.

  • Lot and Zoar (p. 103): In Genesis, Zoar is the small city where Lot took refuge from the destruction of Sodom. The Ohio commune took its name from it.

  • Stygian (p. 102): Of the river Styx, dark and gloomy.

  • Father of Waters (p. 86): The Mississippi River.
harp-companion-unit-13-the-brotherhood-a:
Unit 13, pp. 273-304: The Brotherhood and the lecture circuit

← Unit 12 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 14 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

Debs clerks for a German grocer, joins the firemen's brotherhood, and begins filling its magazine with notices of men crushed under wheels. At the same time he brings the great orators of the age to Terre Haute: Robert Ingersoll, Wendell Phillips, and Susan B. Anthony. By 1884 he has been city clerk twice and is running for the state legislature.

Major entries

The Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen (pp. 277-283)

  • What it was: A union founded on December 1, 1873, at Port Jervis, New York, by Joshua Leach and ten other firemen of the Erie Railroad. Young tells how Leach, born near Nenagh in Tipperary, founded it after watching a fellow fireman die and helped the man's widow (pp. 277-278). It began as a mutual benefit society, paying death and disability benefits no insurer would offer.

  • Debs's role: Leach organized Vigo Lodge No. 16 in Terre Haute in February 1875, with Debs as a charter member and its secretary. Debs became associate editor of the Locomotive Firemen's Magazine in 1878 and in 1880 its editor and the brotherhood's grand secretary and treasurer.

  • The magazine: Young quotes its lodge notices of brothers killed, such as Grant Hall of the Seymour lodge, who fell between platform and train at Shoals (p. 279), and its reports of track sinking into coal mines (p. 283). These obituaries are among the best records of how dangerous railroad work was.

  • Where the record differs: Young dates the organization to 1863 (p. 278). That is the founding year of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. The firemen organized in 1873.

  • Further reading: Salvatore, Eugene V. Debs (1982), chapters 2 and 3.

Robert Green Ingersoll (pp. 284-289)

  • Who he was: The son of a Congregational minister (1833-1899), a Union cavalry colonel, and attorney general of Illinois (1867-1869). He became the most famous orator in America and the "Great Agnostic," drawing huge paying crowds to hear him attack the Bible.

  • Why it matters: His lecture "Some Mistakes of Moses" (1879), which Young notes some magazine readers took for "The Mistakes of Mosaics" (p. 284), made freethought popular entertainment. He was also a Republican power, famous for his 1876 speech nominating James G. Blaine as "the Plumed Knight." Debs brought him to Terre Haute and they became friends despite Ingersoll's defense of the gold standard (p. 289).

  • Where the record differs: Young calls Ingersoll a "Republican Speaker of the House" (p. 287). He never served in Congress. He was a Republican stump speaker.

  • Further reading: Susan Jacoby, The Great Agnostic: Robert Ingersoll and American Freethought (2013).

Wendell Phillips in Terre Haute (pp. 290-292)

  • What happened: Debs brought Phillips to speak to the Occidental Literary Club, and the old abolitionist became a lasting influence. Phillips's heroes, Elijah Lovejoy, John Brown, and Toussaint Louverture (p. 292), became Debs's heroes.

  • Why it matters: After the war Phillips argued that wage labor was the next slavery to abolish. He ran for governor of Massachusetts in 1870 on a Labor Reform ticket. He is the clearest bridge between abolition and the labor movement, and Debs crossed it.

  • Faneuil Hall, 1837: Phillips's career began with an unplanned speech at Boston's Faneuil Hall on December 8, 1837, answering a speaker who had defended the mob that killed Lovejoy in Alton, Illinois.

Susan B. Anthony in Terre Haute (pp. 293-299)

  • Who she was: Born a Quaker in Adams, Massachusetts, in 1820, raised in Battenville, New York, and based in Rochester (p. 297). With Elizabeth Cady Stanton she led the National Woman Suffrage Association from 1869.

  • What happened: When she came to lecture in Terre Haute, many townspeople shunned her. Debs welcomed her publicly and escorted her. Newspapers mocked her everywhere, and Young quotes the scorn of Ambrose Bierce in the San Francisco News Letter (p. 295).

  • Why it matters: Debs supported woman suffrage from the start, well before most labor leaders. His magazine gave a woman editor her own department.

  • Further reading: Ann D. Gordon, ed., The Selected Papers of Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony (1997-2013).

Debs in local politics (pp. 300-304)

  • What happened: Debs was elected Terre Haute city clerk as a Democrat in 1879 and reelected in 1881. In 1884 he won a seat in the Indiana legislature (p. 303), where he served one term and pushed railroad safety and employer liability bills with little success.

  • Why it matters: His disappointment in the statehouse, where railroad lobbies ruled, turned him away from ordinary party politics.

  • The wider scene: Young notes that 1879 was the year of Henry George's Progress and Poverty (p. 300). George argued that land speculation caused poverty and proposed a single tax on land values. It sold millions of copies and inspired reformers worldwide. She also recalls the assassination of President James Garfield in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a former member of the Oneida Community (p. 300).

  • Further reading: Edward T. O'Donnell, Henry George and the Crisis of Inequality (2015).

Shorter entries

  • Herman Hulman (p. 273): A German-born Terre Haute wholesale grocer. His firm, with partner Robert S. Cox, employed Debs as a clerk from 1874. It later made Clabber Girl baking powder, and his descendant Tony Hulman bought the Indianapolis Motor Speedway in 1945.

  • Debs's reading (pp. 274-275): Young lists the books of his youth: Hugo, Sue, Dickens, Stowe, Gogol, Poe, Burns, Shelley, and Appleton's Encyclopedia, which he bought on installments.

  • The Occidental Literary Club (pp. 283-294): The Terre Haute debating club where Debs gave his early speeches and booked lecturers.

  • The Redpath Lecture Bureau (pp. 286-287): Founded in Boston in 1868 by James Redpath, a Scottish-born abolitionist journalist and biographer of John Brown. It booked Ingersoll, Twain, Phillips, and others.

  • Daniel Voorhees and the Opera House (p. 288): Terre Haute's senator introduced Ingersoll at the local Opera House.

  • Gold bugs and silver bugs (p. 289): The long quarrel over money. Gold bugs backed a gold standard. Silver bugs wanted free coinage of silver to expand the money supply and help debtors, the cause Bryan carried in 1896.

  • Myron Reed (pp. 290-291): A minister (1836-1899) in Indianapolis and later Denver, and a Christian socialist who became Debs's close friend. Young's claim that he was once a Grand Banks cod fisherman is unverified.

  • "Go West, young man" (p. 291): Young credits the slogan to John B. L. Soule in the Terre Haute Express in 1851. The story is a popular legend. No one has found the line in that paper, and it is usually linked to Horace Greeley.

  • Ida Husted Harper (pp. 293-294): Terre Haute journalist (1851-1931) who wrote the Woman's Department of the firemen's magazine. She later became Susan B. Anthony's authorized biographer.

  • Taylorsville (p. 301): Terre Haute's red-light district, which Young calls its "Tenderloin" and "Babylon."

  • "Jim Goff" (p. 302): The Irish work song "Drill, Ye Tarriers, Drill," in which a blasted driller is docked pay "for the time you were up in the sky."

Allusions

  • Oliver Wendell Holmes, "The Chambered Nautilus" (p. 275): The 1858 poem on the soul's growth, a favorite of Debs.

  • The Styx (p. 277): The river of the dead in Greek myth.

  • Pickwickian (p. 281): From Dickens's Pickwick Papers, genial and comic.

  • Galahad and the Holy Grail (p. 291): The pure knight of Arthurian legend.

  • The Mermaid Tavern (p. 290): The London tavern of Shakespeare and Ben Jonson, for a company of great talkers.

  • Vesuvius and Pompeii (p. 304): The volcano and the buried city.
harp-companion-unit-11-assassination-rec:
Unit 11, pp. 225-256: Assassination, Reconstruction, Mrs. Lincoln

← Unit 10 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 12 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

While the schoolboy Debs wins a Bible for spelling, Young sweeps through the nation's postwar crises: Andrew Johnson's impeachment, Sand Creek and the Washita, and the long unraveling of Mary Todd Lincoln. The unit ends with Maximilian's execution in Mexico. Its theme is what the war's victors did with the peace.

Major entries

Andrew Johnson and his impeachment (pp. 229-236)

  • Who he was: Born poor in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 1808, he was apprenticed as a tailor and settled in Greeneville, Tennessee (pp. 231-232). He was the only senator from a seceding state to stay loyal to the Union, which made him Lincoln's running mate in 1864.

  • What happened: As president he pardoned former Confederates wholesale and vetoed civil rights measures, clashing with the Radical Republicans in Congress. When he fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act, the House impeached him in February 1868.

  • The trial: Chief Justice Salmon P. Chase presided in the Senate. The vote to convict was 35 to 19, one short of two-thirds (p. 234). Seven Republicans voted to acquit, among them William Pitt Fessenden of Maine, James Grimes of Iowa, and Lyman Trumbull of Illinois (p. 235). Senator Ben Wade of Ohio, next in line, had been so sure of conviction he had begun choosing a cabinet.

  • How Young uses it: Johnson, the former tailor, is a dark mirror of Weitling, the tailor who stayed poor. She treats the Reconstruction South as a feast for the "Lords of Grab and Graft" (p. 233).

  • Further reading: Eric Foner, Reconstruction: America's Unfinished Revolution, 1863-1877 (1988).

Marx's letter to Lincoln (p. 237)

  • What it was: After Lincoln's reelection in November 1864, the International Workingmen's Association in London sent him an address of congratulations, drafted by Marx. It hailed the war as a fight against slavery that mattered to workers everywhere. The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, sent a courteous reply.

  • Why it matters: It is a little-known meeting between the founder of modern socialism and the Great Emancipator. Young adds that it drew protest from the Communist Club of New York (p. 237).

  • Further reading: Robin Blackburn, An Unfinished Revolution: Karl Marx and Abraham Lincoln (2011).

Sand Creek, the Washita, and the Indian wars (pp. 238-240)

  • What happened: On November 29, 1864, Colorado volunteers under Colonel John Chivington attacked the peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho camp of Black Kettle at Sand Creek, Colorado. Most of the dead were women, children, and the elderly, and many bodies were mutilated. Four years later, on November 27, 1868, George Armstrong Custer's cavalry attacked Black Kettle's village on the Washita River in present-day Oklahoma, killing him and his wife.

  • Why it matters: Congressional inquiries condemned Sand Creek, but no one was punished. Chivington resigned his commission before he could be court-martialed. Young links it to the Ludlow Massacre of April 20, 1914, when Colorado militia burned a tent colony of striking coal miners and about twenty people died, among them eleven children (p. 239).

  • Where the record differs: Young gives "approximately four hundred and fifty" dead at Sand Creek (p. 239). Most modern estimates run from about 150 to 230. Her story of Custer's son "Yellow Swallow" (p. 240), by the Cheyenne captive Monahsetah, is Cheyenne oral tradition that historians dispute.

  • General Nelson A. Miles: The Indian fighter who later commanded the federal troops sent to Chicago in the Pullman strike of 1894 (p. 240). Young quotes Mr. Dooley's line that Miles had faced "death and promotion in every form."

  • Further reading: Ari Kelman, A Misplaced Massacre: Struggling over the Memory of Sand Creek (2013).

Mary Todd Lincoln after the war (pp. 241-256)

  • Grief and debt: She lost three of her four sons: Eddie in 1850, Willie in 1862, and Tad in 1871. She ran up heavy debts and in 1867 tried to sell her old clothes in New York, a public humiliation.

  • Herndon and Ann Rutledge: In 1866 Lincoln's former law partner William Herndon lectured that Lincoln's only true love had been Ann Rutledge of New Salem, who died in 1835 (p. 246). The claim wounded her deeply.

  • Europe and the pension: She sailed with Tad for Bremen on the City of Baltimore on October 1, 1868 (p. 247). In July 1870 Congress granted her a pension of three thousand dollars a year after bitter debate.

  • The insanity trial: In May 1875 her son Robert had her tried for insanity in Chicago. Merchants testified about her compulsive buying (p. 253). The jury, which included Lyman Gage, later McKinley's treasury secretary, found her insane, and she was sent to a private sanitarium at Batavia, Illinois. She was released that September and declared sane in 1876. Robert hired Pinkerton operatives to watch her (p. 252).

  • Further reading: Jean H. Baker, Mary Todd Lincoln: A Biography (1987).

Maximilian and Carlotta (p. 256)

  • What happened: While the United States was absorbed in civil war, Napoleon III installed the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor of Mexico in 1864. After the war, Secretary of State William Seward pressed France to withdraw its troops. Mexican republicans under Benito Juárez captured Maximilian, and he was shot on the Cerro de las Campanas, the Hill of the Bells, near Querétaro, on June 19, 1867.

  • Carlotta: His wife, Charlotte of Belgium, went to Europe in 1866 to plead for help and broke down mentally. She lived in seclusion until 1927.

  • Further reading: M. M. McAllen, Maximilian and Carlota: Europe's Last Empire in Mexico (2014).

Shorter entries

  • William Starke Rosecrans and the St. Louis printers (p. 237): The Union general, who won at Corinth and Stones River and lost at Chickamauga, commanded in Missouri in 1864. He used soldiers to replace striking St. Louis printers and machinists, an early use of troops against labor.

  • The Ku Klux Klan (p. 233): Founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865-1866. It waged terror against freedpeople and their allies during Reconstruction.

  • Carl Schurz (p. 242): A German Forty-Eighter, Union general, and later senator. He toured the South for Johnson in 1865 and reported harshly on the treatment of freedpeople. Young calls him "a spokesman for the Deep South," but he was one of its sharpest critics.

  • Frederick Douglass (p. 244): The abolitionist leader. Mary Lincoln sent him one of the president's walking sticks as a keepsake.

  • Victoria Woodhull (p. 249): A spiritualist, stockbroker, and radical who ran for president in 1872 on the Equal Rights Party ticket. Young's claim that she was once a "tramp clairvoyant" in Indianapolis is unverified.

  • Susan B. Anthony and the vote (p. 249): Anthony broke with former allies when the Fifteenth Amendment (1870) enfranchised Black men but not women. She was arrested for voting in 1872.

  • Jay Cooke and Crédit Mobilier (p. 255): Cooke's bank failed in September 1873 over Northern Pacific Railroad bonds, setting off the Panic of 1873. Crédit Mobilier was the Union Pacific construction company whose bribes to congressmen became the Grant era's great scandal.

  • Quincy Adams Ward's Indian Hunter (p. 239): The sculptor's bronze in Central Park, one of the first by an American sculptor placed there.

  • Miss Abbie Flagg (p. 225): The Terre Haute teacher who gave the boy Debs a Bible as a spelling prize.

  • Diamond Dick (p. 226): Hero of dime novels. His stories began in the late 1870s, after Debs's school years.

Allusions

  • Benedict Arnold and Aaron Burr (p. 231): America's archetypal traitors.

  • Brutus, Othello, Iago (p. 234): Shakespeare's figures of betrayal, applied to Stanton and Johnson.

  • Dolley Madison and the Blue Room (p. 242): The first lady famous for her White House hospitality, and its oval reception room.

  • Saint Bernard (p. 245): The rescue dog of the Alps.

  • Dante, the Pitti Palace, Ghiberti (p. 248): Florence, where Mary Lincoln wandered in her exile.
harp-companion-unit-18-tompkins-square-t:
Unit 18, pp. 473-512: Tompkins Square to the Great Strike of 1877

← Unit 17 · Harp Song for a Radical: A History Companion · Unit 19 →

Background for this unit: The History in Harp Song for a Radical

The unit opens with the 1874 police riot against the unemployed in New York and builds to July 1877, when a wage cut on the Baltimore and Ohio set off the first national strike in American history. Young follows it from Martinsburg to Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Reading, Chicago, and St. Louis. Along the way she looks ahead to Haymarket, whose martyr Albert Parsons first spoke to strikers in 1877.

Major entries

The Tompkins Square Riot (pp. 476-483)

  • What happened: On January 13, 1874, in the depth of the depression, thousands of unemployed workers gathered in Tompkins Square on the Lower East Side (p. 478) to demand public works jobs and relief. Police had revoked the meeting's permit at the last minute without telling the crowd. Mounted and foot police charged and clubbed men, women, and children.

  • Samuel Gompers: The young cigar maker escaped a police club by leaping into a cellarway. In his autobiography, Seventy Years of Life and Labor (1925), he said the day taught him that radical rhetoric invited repression (p. 481). The lesson shaped the cautious, craft-based American Federation of Labor he later led.

  • Why it matters: The riot made clear that the authorities would treat the unemployed as a threat to order, not a responsibility.

  • Further reading: Herbert G. Gutman, "The Tompkins Square 'Riot' in New York City on January 13, 1874," Labor History (1965).

The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 (pp. 482-512)

  • Martinsburg: On July 16, 1877, firemen and brakemen of the Baltimore and Ohio at Martinsburg, West Virginia, stopped trains after a second ten percent pay cut. The B&O's president, John W. Garrett, was staying at New York's Brevoort House (p. 482). West Virginia's governor, Henry M. Mathews, found his militia sympathetic to the strikers (p. 485), and President Rutherford Hayes sent federal troops.

  • Baltimore and Pittsburgh: In Baltimore on July 20, militia fired on a crowd and killed about ten people. In Pittsburgh on July 21, militia brought from Philadelphia fired into a crowd and killed about twenty. The crowd then burned the Pennsylvania Railroad's yards, destroying more than a hundred locomotives and over a thousand cars (pp. 489-493).

  • Reading and Chicago: At Reading, Gowen's town, militia killed about ten more (p. 503). In Chicago, police and troops fought crowds at the Halsted Street viaduct on July 25-26, and some thirty people died (p. 508). General Philip Sheridan brought regulars back from the Sioux campaigns (p. 503).

  • St. Louis: The Workingmen's Party led a general strike that briefly ran the city, sometimes called the St. Louis Commune.

  • Why it matters: About a hundred people died nationwide. Federal troops broke a strike on a national scale for the first time, and states built armories and expanded the National Guard for the next one. Pennsylvania Railroad president Tom Scott called in the North American Review for federal troops to be used without waiting for governors to ask (p. 504).

  • Debs's position: Debs, then a young officer of the firemen, did not support the strike. He told the firemen's 1877 convention that strikes hurt workers, a view he reversed completely by 1894.

  • Further reading: Robert V. Bruce, 1877: Year of Violence (1959).

Albert Parsons and Haymarket (pp. 476, 500, 509-510)

  • Who he was: Albert R. Parsons (1848-1887), a Confederate veteran from Texas who became a Radical Republican, married Lucy Gonzalez, a woman of Black, Mexican, and Native ancestry, and moved to Chicago. In 1877 he addressed the strikers, lost his printing job, and was warned by Mayor Monroe Heath to leave town (p. 509).

  • Haymarket: On May 4, 1886, during the national eight-hour movement, anarchists held a rally at Chicago's Haymarket Square. As police moved to break it up, someone threw a bomb. Seven police and at least four civilians died, many from police fire. Eight anarchists were convicted with no evidence tying them to the bomb. Parsons, August Spies, Adolph Fischer, and George Engel were hanged on November 11, 1887. Louis Lingg killed himself in his cell.

  • Where the record differs: Young calls him "Alfred Parsons" (p. 509).

  • Further reading: James Green, Death in the Haymarket (2006).

John Hay, Amasa Stone, and *The Bread-Winners (pp. 495-500)

  • Who they were: Hay, Lincoln's former private secretary and later secretary of state, married the daughter of the Cleveland industrialist Amasa Stone. During the 1877 strike Hay managed Stone's business in Cleveland (p. 495) and wrote frightened letters about the mobs.

  • The novel: Hay published The Bread-Winners anonymously in 1883, an anti-union novel in which a strike leader is a scheming villain. Young sets it beside his earlier folk poems, Pike County Ballads (1871), with "Jim Bludso" and "Little Breeches" (pp. 498-499).

  • Amasa Stone: Stone designed the Ashtabula River bridge in Ohio, which collapsed under a passenger train in December 1876, killing about ninety-two people. He died by suicide in 1883.

  • Further reading: John Taliaferro, All the Great Prizes: The Life of John Hay (2013).

Shorter entries

  • The eight-hour movement of 1872 (p. 477): About a hundred thousand New York workers struck for the eight-hour day in the spring of 1872. Employers organized to defeat them.

  • Peter J. McGuire (p. 479): Founder of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners in 1881 and often called the father of Labor Day. Young ties him to "the first Labor Day, May 1, 1886," but the first Labor Day parade was held in New York in September 1882. May 1, 1886, was the national eight-hour strike.

  • Lucien Sanial (p. 479): A French-born leader of the Socialist Labor Party and an editor of its paper, The People.

  • Henry George in San Francisco (p. 482): George wrote Progress and Poverty in San Francisco in 1877-1879.

  • James Ford Rhodes (p. 483): The historian, son of an Ohio coal operator, who recalled the strike as "a thunderbolt out of a clear sky."

  • The Brotherhood of Railroad Brakemen (p. 488): Founded in 1883, later the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. Debs helped organize it.

  • Louise Michel (p. 499): A heroine of the 1871 Paris Commune. Hay mentions her in a letter about an 1883 Paris bread riot.

  • Frederick Dent Grant (p. 503): President Grant's son, an army officer who helped restore order in Chicago.

  • Mr. Dooley (p. 509): Finley Peter Dunne's fictional Irish saloonkeeper on Chicago's Archey Road, whose comic monologues in the Chicago Evening Post from 1893 skewered the powerful.

  • The Chicago Board of Trade (pp. 510-511): The grain exchange whose members, with Pullman and Marshall Field, backed armed citizen patrols in 1877.

  • The Louisville strike (p. 502): Black sewer workers in Louisville struck in 1877 for \$1.50 a day. Young's report of a leader called "Buffalo Bill" is unverified.

  • Herman Melville's Clarel (p. 512): His long 1876 poem of a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, which Young quotes on the injustices of the decade.

Allusions

  • Vesuvius (p. 479): Tompkins Square as a volcano about to erupt.

  • Gethsemane (p. 490): The garden of Christ's agony before his arrest.

  • Shays's Rebellion (p. 510): The 1786-1787 uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers.

  • The Paris Commune (p. 492): The workers' government of Paris in 1871, crushed with some twenty thousand killed, the specter behind every American strike of the 1870s.

  • Mark Twain's "Jumping Frog" (p. 483): His 1865 tall tale of Calaveras County.

  • Moby-Dick (p. 499): Melville's 1851 novel, for obsession.
poetry-04-01-the-same-ideas-across-the-f:
The Same Ideas Across The Four Books

← The Vision At Its Most Concentrated · Exploring Young's Poetry · Conclusion →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Not One Self

The poems open the single self in "Like Secret Roots" and "Ventriloquist: The Coffee Hour." Its longest home is Miss MacIntosh, where one consciousness pours through Vera, her opium-dreaming mother Catherine, the bald nursemaid, and Mr. Spitzer until they can no longer be told cleanly apart. In Harp Song the plural self turns public: Eugene Debs is at once the private man from Terre Haute and the symbol of a whole movement made of him.

Reality Is Constructed

The poems capture the built world in "Dubious Ground" and "Bishop Berkeley of Cloyne." Its longest home is Angel in the Forest, whose subject is two utopias invented from nothing on one patch of Indiana ground: Father George Rapp's "Scriptural communism" and the rationalist colony of Robert Owen, "an English cotton lord, who believed all men to be machines." Each rebuilt money, work, marriage, and worship by decree, and each came apart. Harp Song carries the same recognition into economics, showing the wage system Debs fought as an arrangement people made and could unmake, not a law of nature.

Grief Doesn't End

Stated most nakedly in the poems of Movement IV. In Miss MacIntosh it is Mr. Spitzer's endless mourning and Esther Longtree's stillbirths, grief that never converts itself into recovery. In Angel it is the sorrow left in the grass after paradise fails. In Harp Song it is Debs outliving the defeat of nearly everything he built.

Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Not a subject but a stance, and the same stance in all four books. It is how Young writes Angel, standing in the ruins of New Harmony without tidying them into a lesson. It is Vera's whole task as narrator of the novel. It is the refusal, in Harp Song, to shrink Debs into either a saint or a cautionary tale. The readings in this book have tried to keep the same discipline.

Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The poems hold the unfinished open in "Daniel" and "A Crystal Principle." Its fullest work is in Angel in the Forest, whose two failed utopias are not mocked but honored as experiments, since "in imperfection itself there might be many values," and "nothing so beautiful as trial and error, this side of paradise."

Unfinished Is Honest

The moral edge of the same idea, and again the method of all four books more than a topic in any one. Angel refuses to call either utopia simply a failure. The novel refuses a final account of what was dream and what was real. Harp Song refuses to close Debs's case with a verdict. This volume refuses to be the last word on the poems.

The Margins Reveal the Truth

The poems give it the misfit and the condemned in "Silken Hair," "Lot's Wife," and "Milton's Wife." Its longest home is split three ways. Angel recovers the forgotten communitarians and celibates at the margin of the official record. The novel is built almost entirely of figures the world cannot file. And Harp Song is the life of a man who saw the country most clearly from a prison cell, and who counted himself unfree as long as a single soul remained in one.

The Past Doesn't Go Away

The poems press the past up under the present in "Legend in Grass" and "Currin Valley." Angel is the extended demonstration: two utopias layered in one ground, the whole book an argument that no arrangement was inevitable and every one had builders. Harp Song keeps the same watch over labor's buried history, refusing the story in which the present order simply arrived on its own.

Language Shapes What's Possible

Distributed across all four, because it is finally a fact about Young's own sentences. The poems name it in "Experience in Song." But the baroque, self-aware prose of the three longer books, and Angel's decision to call a documented history a fairy tale, keep the maker's hand permanently in view. No book in the set pretends to speak from nowhere.

The Sacred Is Here

The center of the vision, held at its purest in the poems by "Sky of Grasses." Its longest home is Angel in the Forest, which measures a promised heaven against "a city as measured by the jimson weed" and watches paradise come to rest in common soil. The novel finds the same holiness in the smallest domestic and natural detail, and Harp Song locates it in ordinary working people rather than in any promised future state.

The Crossing Point

The poems state it in the war poems of Movement VI, and it is the moral hinge of Harp Song for a Radical, whose whole subject is what a cause may ask one generation to spend for the next. Debs's answer, refusing to trade the future for a wartime advantage, going to prison rather than sign his name to that spending, and then running for president from a cell, is the Crossing Point lived out to the end of a single life.

Eleven ideas, one vision, four books. The poems have shown it whole and small. The history, the novel, and the life are where it opens out. A reader holding these terms can walk into any of the three and find the ground already familiar, which is the only kind of arrival Young ever trusted: not a destination reached at last, but the same ground, underfoot, opening further.
poetry-04-the-vision-at-its-most-concent:
The Vision At Its Most Concentrated

← The Thesis Tested · Exploring Young's Poetry · The Same Ideas Across The Four Books →

This book began with a small question and ended with a large claim. The question was whether Marguerite Young's poems carry the themes of her novel Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. The claim is that all four of her books carry one vision, and that the poems carry it in the smallest space.

That smallness is the poems' particular gift to the series. A conviction that takes Angel in the Forest a whole history of ruined utopia to demonstrate, and Miss MacIntosh, My Darling over a thousand pages of dream to enact, and Harp Song for a Radical an entire biography to test against a real life, a poem can set down in a handful of lines. "Sky of Grasses" is the proof. A reader who has moved through these movements has seen the whole of Radical Immanence at close range and at speed, every one of its eleven ideas stated clearly and briefly enough to hold in the mind at once.

That is what the poems are for, inside the set. They are the map drawn small, the key handed over before the doors. Whoever goes on from here to the longer books will not meet a new writer or a new set of concerns. They will meet the same eleven ideas living at length, given room to move, tested against history in Angel, against consciousness in Miss MacIntosh, and against one working life in Harp Song. The poems are where the vision is densest. The other three are where it is most fully worked out.

To make that passage between the books easy, what follows names each of the eleven ideas once more and points to where it does its longest work in the other three volumes. The vocabulary is the same in all four books on purpose, so that a single set of terms carries from the poems into the history, the novel, and the life, and finds the same vision waiting under each.

In this part
