poetry-01-07-movement-v-the-many-selves-:
Movement V. The Many Selves: The Self That Will Not Stay One

← Movement IV. Grief That Stays: The Weather That Does Not Lif · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement VI. The Crossing Point: What One Generation Spends →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

A person, in Young, is never only one person, and this movement watches the idea travel the whole length of her life, changing temperature as it goes. It begins gently, in the early "Song of Two," where a beloved's words "Dip softly, softly through my days," the other already lodged inside the self. In the early "Transition" a dropped mirror breaks and "one bluebird" becomes "a thousand bluebirds," the single view shattered into multiplicity. Prismatic Ground gives the warm version, "Like Secret Roots," whose speaker yields until "I must be both sky and field," and "Minnows and a Monster," where the fisher becomes his catch. The Middle Years push it cosmic in "Who is limited?", the lovers "absorbed by leaves." And the late "Of Deed, Love, Death" turns it to dread, the soul "dividing like an annelid" into an endless regress of selves. The point is not that these people are broken. It is that a single fixed identity was always the fiction, and the crowd inside a person is the ordinary truth of being alive. The novel runs on this current, a consciousness that pours through every character until they can no longer be told cleanly apart.

"Song of Two"

"Like wings which dip into a cloud ... Dip softly, softly through my days / The words which you have spoken." The beloved's words move through the speaker's days like something living inside them, the other person lodged in the self. It is the small early cousin of "Like Secret Roots," the boundary of the self already porous to what it loves.

"Transition"

A dropped looking glass breaks and "all things multiply": "one bluebird drifts above / A thousand pools of glass" until "I watch / A thousand bluebirds pass." The single view shatters into multiplicity and the speaker is "lost forever" in the "breaking silver light." The one becomes many, Not One Self arriving early through a broken mirror, with the unfixable real of Dubious Ground close behind it.

"Like Secret Roots."

The beloved works "under my brow" like roots beneath a field until the speaker yields and "must be both sky and field." The self stops being one thing and becomes the whole landscape it loves. Not One Self here is not disintegration but expansion, identity opening past its own edge.

"Minnows and a Monster."

The one who casts "delicate meshes" to catch songs ends up merged with the "eerie being" hauled from the water, fisher and catch changing places. The self dissolves into what it went out to seize. To grasp the other is to become it.

"The White Rat."

The "white rat" is both the self and a trapped thing in "a theatre of emptiness," body and soul split and set against each other. The poem makes the divided self its whole stage. Not One Self, here, is a captivity as much as a truth.

"Ventriloquist: The Coffee Hour."

A speaker throws his voice into a wooden boy who is "impassive" and heartless yet carries the speaker's life, self and dummy talking across a single throat. The poem literalizes the crowd inside a person. In the novel the same divided selves live in Mr. Spitzer and Miss MacIntosh, and in Vera's struggle to tell dream from waking.

"Night Watches."

"Meteors falling, broken from dolorous stars" scatter the self into "prisoned valleys," fragments cast down and confined. The poem sets the divided self against itself in cosmic dark. Exile and transformation are two names for the same plural condition.

"Who is limited?"

Two lovers imagine "none between us and the most hypothetical / Stars," until "We are absorbed by leaves," their "wedding ring ... mirrored entire on space." The self expands past every limit into the universe it touches, the boundary erased upward and outward. It is "Like Secret Roots" grown cosmic, Not One Self reaching the stars and the leaves at once.

"Of Deed, Love, Death"

"The soul dividing like an annelid ... one soul all souls ... dividing," "everything twice and all souls repeated," "Infinities of bodies swinging from infinities of trees in regress." Not One Self reaches its darkest, most vertiginous form, the self splitting without end into a terror of repetition. What "Like Secret Roots" felt as expansion the late poem feels as endless division, the same principle turned to dread.
poetry-01-06-movement-iv-grief-that-stay:
Movement IV. Grief That Stays: The Weather That Does Not Lift

← Movement III. The Ones Who Do Not Fit: The Margins Reveal th · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement V. The Many Selves: The Self That Will Not Stay One →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer

Grief in these poems is not an illness to recover from. It is a climate the living go on living inside, and it was there from the beginning. Two of the earliest poems are already pure elegy: "Little Fawn," told that its mother's "tracks are lost in the snow," and "Mothers," which forbids a child the comfort of recovering a parent dead too young. The grief never lets up and never tidies. "The Visit" states the whole weather in a breath, "Here grief is delicate and light, / Falling like leaves on sightless sight," while "Elegy for the Body" and "The Funeral" stay in the room with a death and refuse to hurry it toward a lesson. The Middle Years add the ashen "Phoenix," a resurrection bird that will not rise. A second group treats every parting as a voyage out with no promised arrival, from the early "Door-Way," where death is an ordinary threshold near where children play, to "The Departure" and "Farewell at the Station." None of these poems performs the tidy healing that grief is usually asked to perform. Their refusal is the point. To keep the loss unresolved, to let it fall and go on falling, is the truthful thing, and truth is worth more here than comfort.

"Little Fawn"

"Can't you stay by yourself, little fawn? ... You must not always be looking for / Your mother's tracks in the snow," and then the hard line, "Her tracks are lost in the snow." The mother is gone and will not be found, and the poem offers the fawn no comfort, only the fact. Grief Doesn't End is already here in its plainest form, a loss the poem refuses to soften.

"Mothers"

"Child with the withered mouth ... Dream not that now / By fierce remembrance you should recover / The light sweet frame of her ... She was younger than you are / When she died." A child cannot recover a mother lost too young, and the poem forbids the consolation of memory doing that work. It is the same refusal "Two Angels" makes years later, made early and made bare.

"Jonathan's House"

A couple planned a dream house with a hidden escape panel; Jonathan died; she married Thomas, who built a stone version, but "No panel gave. The wide, unyielding stone was there." Grief is the discovery that the lost thing cannot be rebuilt, that the second house is a lifeless replica of the first. The dead dream will not be reoccupied, and the poem sits with that stone fact, the failed replica edging it toward the constructed unreal of Movement II.

"Song of Moving Away"

Moving house, the speaker takes "These old, old days and my old friends / And all that I cannot forsake," and "Old sunlight and old rain." The past is not left at the old address; it is carried, unforsaken, into the new street. The grief of leaving is answered by refusing to leave the past behind, which is also The Past Doesn't Go Away in its gentlest, earliest form.

"Door-Way"

"I think that Death is like an old door-way / Half hidden on a little street of elms ... Not far from where the rosy children play, / Yet quiet with a peace that overwhelms." Death is domesticated here, an ordinary threshold in a familiar neighborhood rather than a cosmic gate. The passage out is set down among the elms and the playing children, grief made neighborly.

"Lover."

The poem carries "the burdens of existence" and the pull between spirit and flesh toward an enduring essence beyond physical decay. Its grief does not resolve into consolation; it holds the weight and the decay together. Grief Doesn't End means refusing to trade the body's loss for a tidy promise about the soul.

"Elegy for the Body."

It asks what "bird or flower" could revive a heart that has stopped, and lets the question stand unanswered. The poem wants resurrection and knows better than to grant itself one. That withheld comfort is the honesty the movement is built on.

"The Tree."

The dead go on shading and accompanying the living, their thoughts persisting like branches over the path. Grief here is not recovery but ongoing company, the lost kept present rather than released. The weather does not lift; it keeps the shape of who is gone.

"Death in Lilliput."

A fragile, dreamlike world of fireflies and "under-meadows" shrinks death to a small, flickering scale. The poem grieves at miniature size, which ties it to the diminished heaven of Movement I even as it stays elegy. Loss is no less total for being tiny.

"Heart Who Stays."

The "dark Omnivorous and eyeless Head" swallows everything and sees nothing, death as a blind appetite the heart must go on facing. The poem stares at the thing that takes the dead and refuses to look away. To stay with that Head is Grief Doesn't End at its hardest.

"The Visit."

"Here grief is delicate and light, / Falling like leaves on sightless sight," sorrow so pervasive it becomes the air. The poem states the movement's whole climate in two lines. It does not push toward healing; it lets the leaves keep falling.

"Two Angels."

The poem admits it "cannot collect the melody" of the "rose-soft lady," that memory fails to hold the one it loved. Grief here is the failure of recall itself, the beloved slipping past every attempt to keep her. What cannot be reassembled is mourned as it dissolves.

"Recurring."

Sorrows are folded "in a pretty box" and locked under "two quaint locks," grief made private and guarded from "rats" and "moths." The poem shows mourning as something kept rather than cured. Grief Doesn't End includes the instinct to protect the wound from tidy exposure.

"Tree of Blood."

The body is a tree losing its vitality, a "light bloom" flaring under "a shrunken sun." The poem watches life ebb without softening the decline. Its grief is for the ordinary fact of a body giving out.

"Death by Rarity."

The nighthawk, the roseate spoonbill, the trumpeter swan: rarity itself becomes the omen of extinction, beauty vanishing because there is too little of it. The poem grieves the disappearing at the level of a species. In the novel Mr. Spitzer's mourning for Martha, the last passenger pigeon, is the same elegy for the last of a kind.

"White Lethe."

A robin redbreast dies "with no savior," dissolving like stars in rain, abandonment without rescue. Lethe, the river of forgetting, names a grief that ends in erasure rather than peace. The poem refuses even the comfort of being remembered.

"Moderate Fable."

The poem opens in uncertainty and disbelief in love, a spiritual desolation with no resolution offered. Its grief is quiet and total, the flat weather after feeling fails. The title, a modest and unfinished story, also belongs to the open construction of Movement II, and that doubleness is worth keeping in view rather than settling.

"The Funeral."

A coming "cold rain" and whitening willow leaves mark an approaching end, the natural world dressing for mourning. The poem stays with the ritual and the decay without hurrying past them. Grief is given its full slow weather.

"The Pattern."

A "still-born heir" and generations growing "colder than its star" make loss into an inherited condition, mortality handed down. The poem grieves and also looks toward the Crossing Point, the cold passed from one generation to the next. In the novel this is Esther Longtree's repeated stillbirths, the mental sorrow of all ending made flesh.

"The Whales."

A southern whale turns toward home because "a memory maketh the whale to turn," the vast creature carrying grief and longing across the sea. The poem holds loss and the pull of homecoming together, and it also touches the Crossing Point, since a hunted species is what a people spends. Its mourning reaches past the single death toward the vanishing kind.

"Leaves, Leaves."

The speaker stands "in the long avenue of the arid vistas," a barren place "without clock," time and guidance both stripped away. Grief here is desolation, an emptiness beyond even the measures that usually hold a life. The falling leaves of the title are the only motion left.

"The Raven."

The raven takes "a single wife for life," an "imperishable" bond marked all the while by time's passage. The poem holds enduring love and inevitable loss in one image, devotion that outlasts and still grieves. What is faithful is also what will be bereaved.

"Drowning Song."

The drowning is a surrender to a vast, enveloping water as familiar as "father's clover meadows," death met as inheritance rather than terror. The poem illustrates going under a return to lineage and origin. Its grief is calm, which is its own kind of honesty.

"The Departure."

"Glow worms" and "seraphic darkness" light the border between life and death, a leaving that is luminous and dark at once. The poem treats departure as passage, neither denied nor consoled. It stands at the threshold and names it.

"Departing Song."

A love "faint," "tremulous," "softly blown to the ground" is also the "brightest" and "saddest" the speaker holds. The poem lets tenderness and loss occupy the same breath. Grief Doesn't End keeps the brightness inside the sorrow instead of choosing between them.

"The Journey."

A "glass-walled chamber wheeling / under the low sky's snow ceiling" carries the traveler through a cold, enclosed Christmas Eve. The passage is fragile and solemn, life moving toward an unnamed end. The poem grieves the journey even as it takes it.

"Farewell at the Station."

"Every farewell" is a departure of a voyager, the Pullman "death and voyage simultaneously." The poem makes each ordinary parting rehearse the final one. To say goodbye at all is to practice the kind of leaving that has no return ticket.

"Phoenix"

The bird of resurrection is shown "ashen," "crying like the lost sheep's crying," its "wings folded in monstrous quiet," a phoenix that does not rise. The poem takes the one myth that guarantees return and refuses it, leaving the bird dead. Grief Doesn't End works by declining exactly the consolation the phoenix is supposed to provide.

"Love Mourned"

A fractured elegy for love: "Tower of mourning, my lost bloom," lovers who "kiss souls" and "breathe in other ways, / together," a mourning that dissolves the line between the two even as it grieves. Grief Doesn't End here is inseparable from the merging of selves, the loss and the union spoken in one broken voice, which is why it also touches Not One Self.

"Death Bed of Beauty"

"The early death of Beauty," whose lover then "has taken her sister to sleep," so that "The children of that old sister are Beauty's, her children, / Her unburied eyes." Beauty dies and continues sidelong, through the substitute and her children, grief and persistence folded together. The dead keep a foothold in the living, as they do in "The Tree."

"The Dead Moon"

"The dead moon whose moonlight does not cease," the dead persisting as light, and at the end "all my nights were a discrepancy / Between the event and its knowledge in me." The lost go on shining like a moon already dead, present and gone at once. Grief here is the gap between what happened and what the mind can hold of it, mourning that never closes.
poetry-05-conclusion:
Conclusion

← The Same Ideas Across The Four Books · Exploring Young's Poetry

A girl in 1920s Indiana, writing her first poem at nine, was already reaching for the idea that would organize everything she made. Not a mood, not a set of images, but a philosophy: the conviction that meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, and nowhere else. She spent the next six decades working it out in whatever form was in front of her. She put it in poems, first the early ones and then the two collections. She put it in history, in the account of two failed utopias sunk into the ground at New Harmony. She put it in biography, in the life of Eugene Debs and the price a cause charges one generation for the next. And she put it in the novel, the 1,198 page prose poem that most people know her name from and almost no one finishes.

The astonishing part is not that the vision is present in all four. It is that it is the same vision, held with the same eleven ideas, from the child's poem to the last work. Most writers spend a life circling a subject and finding it. Young seems to have started with hers and never let it go, and the poems are the proof, because they carry the whole philosophy in miniature before the longer books stretch it out.

Kurt Vonnegut, who studied with her, called her a genius, and the word does not feel loose here. It is the right size for a woman who built a complete and coherent system of thought and then dissolved it into poetry, history, and prose so dense and strange that the system almost disappears into the beauty of the thing she made. That she did it largely unread, and kept doing it anyway, provisional and unfinished and saying that it was enjoyable to do so, is not a footnote to the accomplishment. It is the accomplishment. The ground her work rests on was there from the beginning, and it held.
poetry-01-08-movement-vi-the-crossing-po:
Movement VI. The Crossing Point: What One Generation Spends

← Movement V. The Many Selves: The Self That Will Not Stay One · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement VII. Naming: The Made Word →

Pillar: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point · Across every book

Every person stands at a seam in time where the dead hand the world forward to the unborn, and every choice packs the ground the next ones will walk on. Like the Dubious Ground philosophy, this principle is a later arrival, and it takes the war years to bring it fully out. The war poems name the crime without flinching, "Didactic Poem Against War" reporting that "this century has willed / Men like walrus herds shall all be killed," "The Clinic" turning to the state killing its own, "The Responsibility of Parentage" to what is handed down to a child. Beside them stands the Middle Years' "Guide to New Harmony, Indiana," a walk through a real ruined utopia where "Only the dearly dead remain / To populate a little town," The Past Doesn't Go Away made local and literal. In this vision the one unforgivable move is to trade the future for a present advantage, to cash in the next generation's ground for this generation's gain. This is the movement that reaches hardest toward Harp Song for a Radical, where the same accounting is kept across the whole of one working life, and toward Angel in the Forest, whose whole subject is the New Harmony that "Guide" tours in miniature.

"Archer in a World."

The landscape is terminal, "bare and cold," with "falling hawks" and "withered corn," an earth that has already had its end. The poem stands at the far edge of the Crossing Point, showing the future once it has been spent. This is the ground left for no one, the warning the whole movement turns on.

"Currin Valley."

In "rock-bitten lands" people labor "year after year" for "empty hands," endurance pressed into a merciless valley. The Past Doesn't Go Away is literal here: generations packed into hard ground that gives nothing back. The poem holds the long cost the land keeps of the people who work it.

"The Responsibility of Parentage."

"Being being," and a "mattress-striped whore" name existence at its most exposed, the poem weighing what one life hands to the next. The Crossing Point is in the title: parentage is the moment the world gets passed forward, for better or for ruin. What we bequeath is the whole question.

"Didactic Poem Against War."

"In pathos of distance, this century has willed / Men like walrus herds shall all be killed," the killing was named without euphemism. War is read as a built arrangement that spends the next generation for a present advantage, the one unforgivable move. This is the poem that reaches hardest toward Harp Song for a Radical, where Eugene Debs went to prison rather than sign his name to that spending.

"The Clinic."

A six-year-old prisoner faces death in "an airless room" behind glass, watched by cold observers, the state killing the most defenceless in its care. The poem indicts the arrangement that calls this justice. The Crossing Point condemns any order that balances its books with a child's life.

"The Long War."

The sweet pea "does not close its fragile heart again," and "invader space" is a city besieged, small and delicate, bearing the weight of history's violence. The poem measures war by what it does to the vulnerable rather than the powerful. The Past Doesn't Go Away keeps the record of who paid.

"The Trains."

"Glassy sparrows" wheel in "polar winds" over a "steel season," a chilling machinery of transit and disappearance. In the war years these trains carry more than the poem says aloud, the movement of the doomed through history's cold. It sits between grief and the Crossing Point, the loss and the machine that causes it in one image.

"Summer Day."

A "star wanderer" strikes the sun, and the earth forms and takes its orbit, the white heron moving along a pattern set in deep time. The poem reaches back to the world's making, The Past Doesn't Go Away at cosmic scale. It also touches the sacred ground of Movement I, creation held as both ancient and holy.

"Legend in Grass: Of Innocence and Evil."

A "drunken general" leers "vastly underground / As if he were unburied still," the war-dead refusing to stay buried under the field. The Past Doesn't Go Away made ghostly: the past is not behind the present but beneath it, pressing up. History's violence keeps surfacing in the grass that grows over it.

"Guide to New Harmony, Indiana"

A tour of the ruined utopia: the ferry over the Wabash, "a Rappite door," "Gabriel's footprint in blue chalk," the arch-angel "Father / Rapp saw sudden, terrible and bright," the Owenite and the Duke of Saxe-Weimar, and then "Only the dearly dead remain / To populate a little town." This is The Past Doesn't Go Away made local and literal, a built paradise sunk into Indiana ground until only the dead hold the town, and no arrangement that once seemed destined survived. It is the single poem that reaches most directly into Angel in the Forest, whose entire subject is this same New Harmony, the two utopias tried and lost on one patch of earth.
poetry-02-poems-that-bridge-pillars:
Poems That Bridge Pillars

← Movement VII. Naming: The Made Word · Exploring Young's Poetry · The Thesis Tested →

A handful of these poems refuse to sit still in one movement, which is not a flaw in the sorting, and it is not a flaw in the poems. The eleven ideas were never separate boxes. They are facets of a single vision, and a vision that holds together will naturally show more than one facet at once. When a poem carries two pillars at the same time, it is doing exactly what the whole argument of this book says Young's work does. The overlap is the proof, not the problem. A seam is where two pieces are joined, not where one is coming apart.

Each of the poems below has a center of gravity, which is why it lands in the movement it lands in. But each also opens onto a second pillar, and reading it with both in view is richer than forcing it to choose.

"Moderate Fable" sits in grief for its desolation, though its title, the modest and unfinished story, belongs just as truly to the open construction of II.

"Noah's Ark" and "Summer Day" hold creation and deep time at once, pulling between the sacred ground of I and the long history of VI.

"The Trains" and "The Whales" carry loss and also the machinery of what a people destroys, bridging IV and VI.

"The Home-Coming" and "Voyager Man" turn on belonging and the passage out, joining III and IV.

"That Cloud" wavers between perception and a dissolving self, holding II and V together.

"Ballad-Loving Woman" is filed under song but is also a portrait of a singular woman, bridging VII and III.

"Death in Lilliput" and "Strange Prophecy" shrink death to the small scale of I while grieving like IV.

"Guide to New Harmony, Indiana" holds The Past Doesn't Go Away, the invented utopia of Reality Is Constructed, and the brown-grass Sacred Ordinary all at once, bridging VI, II, and I.

"The Contravalid" and "Proem to Reality" are late summas that fuse the constructed real of II with Unfinished Is Honest, and "The Contravalid" pulls hard on The Margins Reveal the Truth besides.

"Elegy" closes the whole Collected on The Sacred Is Here while carrying Grief Doesn't End and the memory of The Past Doesn't Go Away.

"Transition" and "Jonathan's House" show the Dubious Ground of II already latent in the early work, one through a broken mirror and one through a dead stone replica.

"Love Mourned" grieves and dissolves the self in the same breath, bridging IV and V.

None of these needs to be resolved. The movement a poem sits in names where its weight falls, not the only thing it is about. Left to carry two or more pillars at once, these poems become small demonstrations of the book's central claim, that the vision is one and its ideas run into each other the way the parts of any living thing do.
poetry-01-09-movement-vii-naming-the-mad:
Movement VII. Naming: The Made Word

← Movement VI. The Crossing Point: What One Generation Spends · Exploring Young's Poetry · Poems That Bridge Pillars →

The last movement turns and looks at its own instrument. If grammar carries a worldview, if a noun freezes what a verb would keep alive, then the poem is not a clear window onto the world but a made thing with a maker's hand on it. Young knew this from the start. The early "Song's Dissemination" calls the poem an "edifice" she "welded together / And airily hammered," and then predicts it "will not stand." The Prismatic Ground poems keep the awareness alive. "Experience in Song" watches meaning condense out of sound into "pollen of a syllable," "Song's Preface" and "Anthology Piece" ask what a song is and what it can hold, and "Ballad-Loving Woman" measures a life by the songs it loved. To name a thing is already to shape it, and these poems keep that shaping in view instead of hiding it. The voice that pretends to have no hand at all, the one that claims to speak from nowhere, is the only voice this movement does not trust.

"Song's Dissemination"

The poem calls itself an "edifice" that the speaker "welded together / And airily hammered," and then admits it "Will crumble apart," a "Structural being" that "will not stand." Language Shapes What's Possible is enacted at the outset of her career: the poem names itself a made thing and forecasts its own collapse. It is the earliest proof that Young saw the word as built rather than given, and it doubles as Unfinished Is Honest, a made thing content not to last.

"Experience in Song."

A falling star survives only as "pollen of a syllable" and "the frosts of sound," its whole aftermath condensed into language. The poem watches meaning get made out of noise, the word as both veil and revelation. Language Shapes What's Possible is enacted rather than stated: the event exists now only as the words that hold it.

"Anthology Piece."

"Moon-struck syllables" carry a speech pulled by irrational, lunar force, expression shaped before sense arrives. The poem shows language as a made and moody thing, not a clear window. What gets said is built by the pull on the one who says it.

"Ballad-Loving Woman."

A woman who "lived until she died" is framed by the ballads she loved, a life measured in the songs that held it. The poem knows a life becomes a made thing when it is sung, and it also draws a portrait of a singular woman, which ties it to The Margins Reveal the Truth. It sits between Movement VII and Movement III, and reads richer for both.

"Song's Preface."

A song is "fleeting or ephemeral like the cherry blossom," blooming and gone, and the poem asks what this made thing can hold. Turning to speak about the song itself, it keeps the maker's hand in view. To preface a song with its own impermanence is Language Shapes What's Possible admitting what it is.
poetry-01-02-the-poems-in-movements:
The Poems in Movements

← Radical Immanence Explained · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement I. Diminished Heaven: The Sacred in the Small →

A note on how this is arranged. It is based on The Collected Poems of Marguerite Young which can be purchased at Chatwin Books and I encourage you to do so.

Seven movements gather the one hundred and twenty-eight poems by the idea each one presses hardest on, not by the collection it came from. Within every movement the poems run across the same five periods in The Collected Poems book: Early Poems (1927 to 1934), Prismatic Ground (1937), Middle Years (1938 to 1943), Moderate Fable (1944), and Late Poems (1945).

Two of the eleven ideas, the Witness and Unfinished Is Honest, are not sorted here at all. They are the book’s method, the stance the readings keep and the openness the book admits about itself, and they run through every movement rather than owning one. A short list of the poems that sit on a seam between two movements closes the movements.
poetry-03-the-thesis-tested:
The Thesis Tested

← Poems That Bridge Pillars · Exploring Young's Poetry · The Vision At Its Most Concentrated →

The early poems were the honest test, and the result holds with a real and useful qualification. The felt principles are there from the start. The Sacred Is Here, Grief Doesn't End, The Margins Reveal the Truth, Not One Self, and Language Shapes What's Possible all appear in the 1927 to 1934 work, including "I Heard a Bird," written at nine, and "Worship," a teenager's creed that finds God "In stars and flowers and shining eyes" and nowhere near a church. That a nine-year-old and a teenager were already doing this is the strongest possible evidence for Young's claim that her preoccupations were fixed by the age of nine.

What is not there early is just as telling. The Dubious Ground philosophy, the metaphysics of perception and the constructed real, barely registers in the early poems and then floods the Middle Years, where "Snow in the Mountains," "And even the wild goat of Ephesus," and "But where come the innuendos" think the problem out loud for the first time. The Crossing Point, the political and war principle, arrives with the war years. By analyzing Young’s poems the emotional core was innate and the intellectual and political apparatus grew onto it. The vision is one, but it was felt before it was argued.
poetry-01-04-movement-ii-dubious-ground-:
Movement II. Dubious Ground: The Constructed and Uncertain Real

← Movement I. Diminished Heaven: The Sacred in the Small · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement III. The Ones Who Do Not Fit: The Margins Reveal th →

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

What feels most solid turns out to be the least trustworthy, and this is the one movement whose principle Young had to grow into rather than carry from the start. The early poems barely touch it. It arrives in force in the Middle Years, when the poems begin to think their doubt out loud. "Snow in the Mountains" sets Plato's ideal snow against the actual snow and cannot say which is the more real, "And even the wild goat of Ephesus" cannot pry the knower from the known, and "But where come the innuendos" finds a pattern only in the accidental. By Moderate Fable the doubt is a full method. "Dubious Ground" walks a sleepwalker across a field that is not firm, "A High Subjectivity" states it flatly, "The idea of the universe is inconclusive," and "Bishop Berkeley of Cloyne" hands the movement its patron, the philosopher who held that a thing exists only in being perceived. The late "Proem to Reality" closes the line: "There is no whole." The honest response to a built and shifting world is not to pretend it is bedrock but to keep questioning and keep revising. This is the country the novel lives in, a thousand-plus pages where waking and dreaming trade places without warning.

"Sequence."

A woman stands between "waves of the meadow" and "the sea's crying," two worlds that will not resolve into one, and the closing question goes unanswered on purpose. The poem lives in the Invention, treating the solid categories of land and sea, past and present, as fluid and provisional. The novel's dream-and-waking country begins here.

"Dubious Ground."

A sleepwalker crosses "the dubious texture of the ground," aware even in sleep that the field is not firm. The poem is the movement's namesake because it makes uncertainty a form of perception rather than a failure of it. To feel the ground's dubiousness is to have woken up to the Invention.

"Whorl."

"Waxen leaves" and a "clear-cut bloom" look preserved, artificial, a little too perfect, a made surface passing for a natural one. The poem catches the built quality of what claims to be given. Seeing the wax is the first step out from under the spell.

"Daniel."

The speaker accepts that regret is unavoidable and keeps questioning anyway, refusing both false certainty and despair. This is Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary as a temperament: build a life provisionally, revise it, distrust the finished answer. The seeking is the faith.

"Heroics."

"Wind and foam" dominate a turbulent, shifting world where nothing human holds against the elements. The poem sets the self inside forces it cannot fix or found itself on. Solid ground is exposed as the illusion it always was.

"A Crystal Principle."

Crystal stands for a fragile, evolving purity that nature reaches toward and never secures, undone by "accident unknown / And least departure." Perfection is provisional, always one small deviation from breaking. The poem holds the ideal open rather than closing it.

"A High Subjectivity."

The poem states the movement's thesis outright: "The idea of the universe is inconclusive." Reality cannot be finished or fully known, only entertained. This is Reality Is Constructed pushed to the scale of the cosmos, the whole of things left unsettled on principle.

"That Chance."

Existence itself is founded on chance, and yet chance can "propose a system like a sphere," order arising from the accidental. The poem refuses both pure chaos and fixed design, holding the built world as contingent all the way down. Nothing here had to be, which is why nothing here is inevitable.

"Null Class."

The unicorn and the "non-existent" hover on the line between real and imagined, entities that defy proof yet insist on presence. The poem makes the boundary between fact and fiction porous, which is the Invention's home ground. What we agree to imagine has its own kind of being.

"Bishop Berkeley of Cloyne."

The poem hands the movement its patron, the idealist who held that "to be is to be perceived," and pairs him with the severed head of John the Baptist, thought and martyrdom together. If a thing exists only in being perceived, then perception builds the world, and the builder is answerable for it. The novel, a thousand pages of consciousness making and unmaking reality, is Berkeley's principle turned into a book.

"Failing Perspective."

The bright earth turns and drags along colored elements, a child and a balloon and a plover pulled through ceaseless change. Nothing in the frame stays fixed long enough to be certain of. The poem treats perspective itself as unstable, a view always failing and reforming.

"The Time Is Not Now."

"Thin blood needling in the brain" and a flight of "ashen swallows" scramble past and present until time will not stay put. The poem lives in the seam where the clock loses authority. When now is not now, the ordered timeline is revealed as one more arrangement.

"Speculative Evening."

"If there were no past now, but specious present only" opens a world where time is disjointed and possibly illusory, made by a "heavenly geometer" no one can see. The poem questions whether a design means anything if no mind can grasp it. It keeps the construction open by refusing to trust the blueprint.

"Slow Motion."

The heart becomes "a camera of slow motion" and "a stellar eye," an organ that does not simply beat but perceives, holding time at a deliberate delay. The poem relocates perception into the body and makes it strange. What we call seeing is a built and lagging thing.

"That Apple Was Mental."

The apple is "mental, a constellation of ideas," and the poem asks whether the real can be invisible, whether sound can be inaudible and still exist. The line between physical fact and mental construct dissolves. This is Berkeley's question again, put to a single piece of fruit.

"That Cloud."

Love, identity, and perception all turn out to be mutable here, selfhood interchangeable and dissolving under a passing cloud. The poem wavers between the unreliability of perception and the unreliability of the self, which is why it also belongs to the Many Selves. Two pillars meet in one cloud, and neither cancels the other.

"The Process."

The poem imagines clock hands running backward as easily as forward, questioning whether time has any fixed direction at all. Causality is treated as a convention rather than a law. Once time is up for revision, so is everything built on it.

"Figures of Space."

Nature declares "a pact of unaltered peace" and lets sleep enter softly, a surrender to a process no one controls. Sleep stands in for death, the ultimate uncontrollable, met not with terror but with acceptance. The poem keeps the construction open right to the edge of oblivion.

"At the Cinema."

Time unwinds as "mechanic timelessness" on "the waste expanse of canvas," a dead lover held as a spectral frame of film. The poem makes time itself a projected illusion, a reel that can be paused and rerun. Reality flickers, and the flicker is the truth of it.

"Snow in the Mountains"

Plato arrives: "Plato's snow more real than the shadow of snow," the mountains "expanding with the theme / Of absolute," the travelers "twin souls / Of real and unreal." The poem sets the actual snow against its ideal and cannot say which is more real, which is Reality Is Constructed lifted into open metaphysics. This is where the Dubious Ground of the later work first thinks out loud.

"But where come the innuendos"

"The causeless winds, the illogical tear," accidents "Happening so, because it has happened so," until "how dark, / Dark is its responsibility." The poem turns chance and causelessness over the way "That Chance" will, finding a pattern only in the anomaly. Reality is contingent all the way down, and the mind that notices carries the weight of it.

"And even the wild goat of Ephesus"

"We are both subject thinking and object / thought of," and "we cannot know how much of us is involved in the act / of knowledge," with "all things are process." The poem pushes perception to its limit, unable to pry the knower from the known. It is Dubious Ground as pure epistemology, the same question "That Apple Was Mental" asks of a single fruit.

"Flea Circus on Times Square"

A prose letter to a child: from a skyscraper's height people are "just dolls or spiders," yet "to themselves each is very different from the other," and the circus fleas are people to themselves too. The poem turns the scale over until every vantage is provisional, the giant's view and the flea's equally partial. The bald showman "with a face just as round as the moon's" is the Miss MacIntosh of the flea world, and the novel's play of scale and perception is here in a nursery voice.

"The Priesthood of Motion"

A sea gull wheels over cotton fields where an old Black field worker looks up in tears, and everything becomes "a process wayfaring in stellar space," "No goal ... but a tide." The poem dissolves a fixed scene into pure motion without destination, the flux that "Process" will name outright. Its grieving laborer keeps a foot in the world the Crossing Point watches, but the poem's argument is that nothing arrives.

"Proem to Reality"

"Polaris will not be always the north North Star," "There is no reference but to shifting fixity," "There is no whole," reality "perceived partially / By particles," "the putting together of names." The poem is a late summa of Dubious Ground, the built and shifting real stated without a hedge, and it folds in the naming of Language Shapes What's Possible and the immanent present of The Sacred Is Here. Its closing admission, that "god was the only project admitting of completion," is Unfinished Is Honest signed at the bottom.
poetry-01-05-movement-iii-the-ones-who-d:
Movement III. The Ones Who Do Not Fit: The Margins Reveal the Truth

← Movement II. Dubious Ground: The Constructed and Uncertain R · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement IV. Grief That Stays: The Weather That Does Not Lif →

Pillar: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth · Across every book

Characters: Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh

The people who cannot be filed are the ones who see the filing system, and Young returns to that figure from her earliest work to her last. In "The Seeker" a farmer dreams his whole life over postcards of places he will never reach, and in "Flame" a landlocked woman sails a peddler's wagon "through waves of wheat" and takes it out one last time as she is dying, both of them shaped to lives that had no room for them. The Prismatic Ground poems sharpen the figure into the outright victim: "Silken Hair," destroyed for nothing but "the fact of ambiguous hair," and "The Return," where the land itself rises "like whips" against the stranger. "Lot's Wife," "Plea for Sodom," and "Milton's Wife" speak for the condemned and the unheard. And in the late "The Contravalid" the whole stance hardens into a philosophy, "the crippled dancer is the dance, at last, / The only truth." Seen from the center, these figures are failures or footnotes. Seen from where they stand, they are the only ones with a clear view, because the margin is the one place the seams of the arrangement actually show.

"The Seeker"

A farmer spends his life dreaming over "faded ancient picture postal cards" of places he saved to visit and never reached, sending his son to Paris in his place while he still plows "beneath a hot white sun." He is the dreamer stranded in a life with no room for him, kin to "Biography" and "Lesser Magellan." The Margins Reveal the Truth falls on the man whose longing points always at an elsewhere the plow will never let him reach.

"Flame"

A woman "reared inland" who longed for the sea gets "a wagon / To steer through waves of wheat," a restless peddler with "wide sailor's eyes" who on her last morning, dying, takes the wagon out anyway. She is the singular woman who makes her own voyage on land and will not be held, even by death. The Margins Reveal the Truth honors the one who never fit the settled life the village kept for her.

"The Return."

"Buffalo weed," "wild onion flower," and "blue crab grass" rise like whips to bar the one who tries to come back, the land itself refusing the stranger. The Margins Reveal the Truth is literal here: the returning outsider is the one who feels the country's hostility, because belonging was never extended. The margin is a place a person is put, not a place they choose.

"Lesser Magellan."

An "intrepid explorer" is lost "in the politest wilderness," his grand quest shrunk to a wandering with no discovery at its end. The poem watches the heroic frame fail the man inside it. Seen from the edge, the great voyage is just a person who does not fit the map he was given.

"Biography."

"Young Harry" plays chess with Lucifer and loses everything while barely present, a soul out of step with the game the world set for him. The Margins Reveal the Truth falls on the dreamer the system reads as a failure. His inability to play by the rules is also the clearest sight of what the rules cost.

"Woodlands Far Removed."

The hunter sets out gallantly each morning and returns each night defeated, "he whom nothing small eludes" and who still catches nothing. The poem sits with fruitless pursuit and the neighbors' quiet judgment of it. To keep going out and coming back empty is the outsider's whole biography.

"Gulliver."

Young's Gulliver is the giant among the small and the small among the giants, never the right size for the world he lands in. His displacement becomes a way of seeing what the natives cannot, the arbitrariness of their scale. The one who does not fit measures the room.

"Silken Hair."

A woman's entire "tragic fault" is "the fact of ambiguous hair," an ambiguity the town cannot place and therefore cannot forgive. The Margins Reveal the Truth is stated at its barest: she is destroyed by nothing she did, only by being unclassifiable. In the novel this is Miss MacIntosh's essence, the figure whose strangeness the world can neither hold nor pardon.

"The Dark Wood."

Ellen is trapped in a maze, "too far from the sun," watched by "armies of frogs" whose eyes stream like a miner's lamp. The poem is pure surveillance and entrapment, the outsider hemmed in and stared at. The edge here is a cell with a hundred watching eyes.

"Marriage in Heaven."

The "cozened spouse" was "taught no trade / But to grace the lorn beautiful," a woman's whole life narrowed to appearance and submission. The poem speaks from inside a constraint the social order calls normal, which is exactly where The Margins Reveal the Truth sees most, and its ironic title marks a heaven that is really a cage. In the novel the same walls close on Madge Capehorn, submissive to a "spectral kiss."

"Voyager Man."

The "voyager man" hangs "between the upper and the under air," a liminal figure belonging to neither element he crosses. Isolation is his medium; he is defined by the realms he falls between. The poem also leans toward the passages of Movement IV, since to voyage endlessly is a way of departing without arriving.

"The Home-Coming."

A gate and a pasture mark a threshold reached in "the mind's eye," a return that is spiritual before it is physical. The poem turns on belonging, the outsider's oldest ache, and on whether coming home is ever quite possible. It touches Movement IV as well, because a homecoming imagined this hard is close to a leave-taking.

"The Giraffe."

The creature is "born out of error or misalignment," a flawed thing that names human imperfection through its own odd shape. The Margins Reveal the Truth falls on the being that creation seems to have gotten wrong. Its wrongness is a mirror.

"The Parachutist."

The poem rejects "neutrality and public facades" for the uniqueness of one person's inner view, dropping in alone and apart. To refuse the shared surface is to stand at the edge on purpose. The individual perception it insists on is also a quiet version of Language Shapes What's Possible's warning against the voice from nowhere.

"Lot's Wife."

Young's treatment is tender, "Poor dear! Her fault," siding with the woman punished for the human need to look back. The poem takes the condemned figure's part against the verdict handed down on her. The Margins Reveal the Truth here is a defense attorney's.

"Plea for Sodom."

The poem argues for the small doomed city itself, refusing to accept its destruction as deserved. It speaks up for the place everyone else was content to see burn. To plead for Sodom is to insist the condemned had a life worth the name.

"Milton's Wife."

The poem gives voice to the woman written out of the great man's story, the wife whose account was never allowed to count. The Margins Reveal the Truth recovers the silenced witness at the margin of a famous life. Her side of it was there the whole time, unheard.

"The Contravalid"

"More beautiful ... is the contravalid, the mouse-sized insect ... the crippled dancer is the dance, at last, / The only truth, the double-headed dwarf of paradox." The poem raises the marginal and the deformed above the valid and the logically true, making the broken figure the bearer of the real. The Margins Reveal the Truth becomes an explicit metaphysic here: the seams show clearest at the edges, so the edges are where the truth is. It carries Unfinished Is Honest with it, since "the circumnavigators of being always err."
poetry-01-01-radical-immanence-explained:
Radical Immanence Explained

← The Ground Underfoot · Exploring Young's Poetry · The Poems in Movements →

Immanence is the plainer half. It means that whatever matters is here, in the actual world, and not stored somewhere above it or beyond it. The opposite belief, that the true meaning of things waits in a heaven, a hereafter, a golden age, a final arrival, is the old and familiar one. Immanence refuses the wait. It holds that meaning is in the dirt and the weather and the body, or it is nowhere at all. Radical names the reach of that refusal. At its root the word means “of the root,” thoroughgoing, carried all the way down. Radical Immanence is the conviction that everything worth having is already here, in the world underfoot, all the way down, with nothing kept back in a beyond.

From that one conviction the rest follows because the same words run through all of her work.

Start with the self and the world it moves in. A person, in Young, is a crowd and not a single fixed identity. The many selves are the normal condition of being alive and not a fault to be corrected. This is Not One Self. The world those selves move through is, for the most part, built. Money, borders, laws, rank and class: these feel like bedrock, but they are agreements held in place by repetition, not facts dug out of the earth. Reality Is Constructed is the recognition of that, and seeing the construction is the first step out from under its spell. Even grammar is part of the building. Nouns freeze things into fixed identities and verbs keep them moving, and any voice that claims to speak from nowhere, in pure objectivity, is quietly hiding where it actually stands. That is Language Shapes What's Possible.

If the world is built, then time is not a clean line leaving the past behind. The past is beneath the present, pressed into it like layers of rock, and calling any arrangement inevitable is a way of hiding the people who actually laid it down. This is The Past Doesn't Go Away. It gives every person a particular place to stand where everyone who came before meets everyone who will come after, and where every choice packs down the ground the next generation will stand on. This is the Crossing Point. Trading that future for a present advantage is, in this vision, the one unforgivable move. And the people best placed to see all of this are the ones who do not fit the categories, since the margins are where the seams show. That is The Margins Reveal the Truth.

The vision also asks for a way to stand inside a built and grieving world without lying about it. Grief, here, is not a stage to be passed through on the way to recovery. It is permanent weather, and refusing to perform a tidy healing is a way of staying truthful about what was lost. That is Grief Doesn't End, and its companion is the Witness, the hard discipline of staying in the room with something painful and unresolved without rushing to fix it or wrap it up. Because nothing is ever truly finished, the honest move is to build anyway, provisionally, and keep revising, distrusting the frozen blueprint. That is Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary, and its ethical form is Unfinished Is Honest: the unfinished is not failure but honesty, and anyone who claims to hold the complete and final answer is usually selling something.

At the center of all of it is The Sacred Is Here, which is immanence felt rather than argued. Meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, and not in the promised beyond. The appeal to a distant beyond, a golden age, a grand destiny, a final arrival, is the oldest tool of anyone who wants to justify a sacrifice in the present. To hold the ordinary as sacred is to take that tool out of their hands.

Eleven ideas, one conviction. They are not a checklist Young worked from. They are the shape that shows up when her work is set side by side, and setting them side by side is what this series does. There are four.

Angel in the Forest is history. It is her account of New Harmony, Indiana, the patch of ground that tried twice to become a paradise and twice came back down to earth. Its very chapters carry the vision in their titles, one of them simply “Paradise Was Lost.” Young measures its heaven against the plainest possible yardstick, calling the promised city “a city as measured by the jimson weed,” a paradise sized against a common roadside plant.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is the novel, a 1,198 page descent through consciousness, dream, and the porous line between the living and the dead.

Harp Song for a Radical is the biography, the life of Eugene Debs and the labor movement he gave himself to, a book that asks in a real life what a cause is allowed to ask one generation to spend for the next.

And then there are the poems which run from 1927-1945.

Each of the four holds the same vision, but the poems hold it most compressed. What the novel takes a thousand-plus pages to enact, a poem can say in six lines. “Sky of Grasses” watches a person die and reports, without comfort, that “Heaven has shrunk to the dim size / Comprehended by insects’ eyes,” until it is “smaller than the faint far sound / Of a seed pod shaking the grey ground.” That is The Sacred Is Here stated outright and whole. The same idea that Angel walks through the ruins of New Harmony to reach, and that the novel dissolves into over a thousand pages of dream, the poem sets down in the space of a breath. This is the particular work of the poetry volume in the series. It is the vision at its most concentrated, the place where the whole shape can be seen at once before it is watched being worked out at length in the longer books.

Two of the eleven ideas do not appear in this book as a subject. They appear as its method. The Witness is the stance the readings try to keep, staying in the room with each poem, following what is difficult in it without smoothing the difficulty away. Unfinished Is Honest is the book’s own honesty about itself. These readings are offered as provisional, since I am admitting here that I am not an expert at analyzing anything, much less poetry. This is one pass through the poems and not the last word on them, built to be argued with and revised. To read Young any other way, to close the case and hand down a finished verdict, would be to betray the very vision the poems carry. Young herself found the finished thing suspect and the trying beautiful, and put it better than any framing can: “nothing so beautiful as trial and error, this side of paradise.”

Because the vision, and the vocabulary for it, are set out fully here, the series has no required order. A reader can begin with the utopias, the novel, the life of Debs, or the poems, and meet the same eleven ideas under the same names in each. This volume begins with the earliest of her poems, one written at nine, which is the very age Young named as to when her lifelong preoccupations began.

What follows reads them in movements, each movement gathering the poems that press hardest on one or two of these ideas, and reaching, where a passage truly deepens a poem, into the other three books where the same idea is living a longer life. The place to start is the ground underfoot, which is where Young always said the ground her work rested on.

poetry-01-the-ground-underfoot:
The Ground Underfoot

Exploring Young's Poetry · Radical Immanence Explained →

The question that started this book was a small one. A reader at Involutions of the Seashell, on Substack, asked whether Marguerite Young’s poetry carried any of the themes of her novel, Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. The honest first answer was uncertainty. The poems had been read, but not with confidence, and poetry is a harder country to feel sure of than prose and there was little certainty back then to feel sure about even that. So the book began as an attempt to answer one reader’s fair question: do the poems connect to the novel?

They do. That answer held, poem after poem, and it was worth making. But in the making, the question turned out to be too small for what the poems were doing. Young said as much herself. She held that all her writing came from a single set of preoccupations, ones she had been turning over since she was nine years old. If that is so, then the poems do not connect to Miss MacIntosh, My Darling the way a stream connects to a river, running into it and vanishing. They connect the way four windows connect. Each opens on to the same room from a different wall.

This second edition follows that correction. It stops treating the poems as a doorway into one novel and starts treating them as one full statement, among four, of a single vision that runs under everything Young wrote. The vision needs a name, and the name this series uses is Radical Immanence. Both of its words are the kind that can hide more than they show, so both are worth going in depth with.

poetry-01-03-movement-i-diminished-heave:
Movement I. Diminished Heaven: The Sacred in the Small

← The Poems in Movements · Exploring Young's Poetry · Movement II. Dubious Ground: The Constructed and Uncertain R →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer

The oldest promise is that the meaning of a life waits somewhere above the life, in a heaven, a hereafter, a reward for the patient. These poems refuse that promise and put the sacred back where the body actually stands, in the grass and the weather and the smallest living things. This is the movement that shows the vision was native to Young rather than arrived at, since the refusal is already complete in the earliest work. "Worship," written young, will not bow in "church" or "chapel" and finds the divine only "In stars and flowers and shining eyes," and "I Heard a Bird," written at nine, gives its whole heart to one small creature and its nest. From there the principle holds for the next forty years. "Sky of Grasses" shrinks heaven to the sound of a seed pod, "Fall of Man" lets the angels down into a field of clover, "Wild Orchard" names the human being "the errant vegetable," and her very last poem, "Elegy," gives the vision the closing word: "our God is not the God of Weight / But ourselves." The grief in these poems is real, since bringing heaven down to earth means giving up the consolation of a beyond. What is gained is the world itself, held as holy. This is the ground Angel in the Forest, watching a promised paradise sink back into Indiana soil.

"Worship"

The poem refuses God in "church" and "chapel" and finds the divine instead "In stars and flowers and shining eyes, / In dewdrops and in pearls." This is The Sacred Is Here stated as a young person's creed, immanence chosen over the institution before Young could have named it that. It belongs at the head of the movement as proof that she located the holy in the actual world from the beginning.

"Twilight"

The mind's "intrepid eagle" would soar "Toward the sun's red streaming" against oblivion, but "the eagle turns, he veers" and "This lesser dark descends." The upward reach toward transcendence fails and the poem settles back into the actual dark. The refused ascent is The Sacred Is Here's discipline, keeping the self on the ground the eagle could not leave.

"I Heard a Bird"

Written at nine, and already the vision is here in miniature: a bird sings of its own small life, and "the nest was put into a museum," kept but perhaps already taken. The poem gives its whole attention to one ordinary creature and what remains of it, which is The Sacred Is Here before Young had any theory for it. That a child reached for exactly this subject is the first evidence that the ground under her work was there from the start.

"Street Fires"

Old women sweep and burn autumn leaves so "That Beauty may die, they light their fires," an ordinary chore made a small rite of loss. The Sacred Is Here here is the ceremony hidden inside a domestic task, beauty consumed and consecrated in one motion. Meaning is in the raking and the smoke, not above them.

"Sonnet"

A woman buys "thin painted china when she needed bread," prizing the beautiful and useless though the world "laughed at loving this so old." The poem holds that such things are worth more than the practical, which is The Sacred Is Here as a way of valuing, and it edges toward The Margins Reveal the Truth in the mockery she draws for it.

"Brave Youth"

A vain young fowl is plucked and eaten, "reduced to food / For hunger," youth served up as ordinary meat. The humbling is the reverence, as in "Wild Orchard": the strutting human is one more mortal creature, and the poem plucks his feathers "with apology."

"Eclipse"

When darkness falls on the sun, "The lizard and my spotted soul / Kept their counsel well, / Remembering the sun." The speaker's soul is kin to the lizard, the ordinary creature, both keeping faith with the plain light rather than any beyond. Immanence is a loyalty to the sun that is actually there.

"Proud Lady"

"She was vain / Of curious things, / Not her bright hair / Nor ruby rings. / Of orioles / And sky and cloud / Of such she was / Absurdly proud." It is the seed of "Proudest Lady" from Prismatic Ground, the same pride in the unownable, reworked years later. Set side by side, the two show The Sacred Is Here as a lifelong habit rather than a late idea, and pairing them makes the point without a word of commentary.

"Sky of Grasses."

A body passes as lightly as dew, and heaven shrinks until it is no bigger than a seed pod's sound. This is The Sacred Is Here at its purest: the holy is not overhead but underfoot, in the grass and the glow-worms that see the dying woman off. It is the exact move Angel in the Forest makes across 435 pages, watching a promised heaven come to rest in ordinary Indiana ground.

"Fall of Man."

The angels do not crash. They come down softly as sparrows that dropped from frozen nests, the celestial folding quietly into the earthly. The Sacred Is Here works here as a descent that is also a homecoming, the divine consenting to be ground-level, and what theology calls a catastrophe the poem makes a settling.

"All Saints' Day."

After death the human essence does not rise. It returns, the "fibrous hearts" unspun into leaves on a wild cherry branch. Sainthood, in this poem, is what the body becomes when it rejoins the orchard. The sacred is the compost, not the cloud.

"Wild Orchard."

Calling a man "the errant vegetable" strips the species of its claim to stand above the growing world. The humbling is the reverence: The Sacred Is Here insists that a human is one more temporary green thing, mortal and rooted, and that this is not a demotion but the truth.

"Wild Deer."

A garden pulls the wild deer away from "the village streets and laughter," making a small cultivated plot into a meeting place between the tame and the untamed. The sacred gathers at the edge of an ordinary garden and needs no altar. Meaning is local, and it grazes.

"Strange Prophecy."

Only bees keep company with "the portals of the dead," small workers tending a threshold the living avoid. Whatever survives death is located not in a heaven but in the hum of insects at the grave. It is the seed-pod scale of "Sky of Grasses" turned toward what lingers.

"Rosary in Discord."

The poem opens in prayer and then lets the sacred tone break against discord, refusing the clean devotional resolution. What is holy here has to be said inside noise and disorder, not above them. The Sacred Is Here keeps its reverence and gives up its calm.

"Paradise Is Still Lost."

Angels are "obscured in gaslight faces," the divine dimmed and cheapened by the Club Ha-Ha and the Dime. Paradise stays lost because it was always sought in the wrong direction, upward and elsewhere, when the only ground available is here. The title rhymes on purpose with Angel in the Forest's chapter "Paradise Was Lost," where two real utopias sink back into the soil that outlasts them.

"The Angels."

The poem hunts for where angels might still live, finds only remote atolls and the names of vanishing birds, and concludes that "death is the flight of angel and golden plover." The sacred has retreated into the last wild habitats and the fact of extinction. Heaven is a bird sanctuary, and it is going.

"Noah's Ark."

The ark becomes body and soul at once, "a prison of purple wood" riding a drowned world, carrying life across catastrophe toward a ground it cannot yet see. The poem holds The Sacred Is Here and the long reach of the Crossing Point together, creation as a cargo handed forward through the flood. It is one of the poems that will not sit in a single movement, and that doubling is the point rather than a flaw.

"Winter Scene."

The earth leans "toward the one invisible, the prince of space," and the poem lets that pull be "disproved," keeping belief and the plain cold world in tension. The mystical is entertained and then set back down in the snow. Reverence survives here only by staying honest about what cannot be confirmed.

"Awakening."

After crying and "the mark of many whips," the sufferer is covered by "the spider's web of summer," a shroud that heals instead of traps. Nature does the work a heaven is supposed to do, taking the pain into itself. The Sacred Is Here is the world's own capacity to close over a wound.

"Spring."

Birth, growth, and the pressure of death share one season, life arriving already carrying its end. The poem finds the sacred in the ordinary turning of the year rather than in any promise beyond it. In the novel this same current runs through Esther Longtree, forever pregnant and forever losing, the season that cannot complete itself.

"Proudest Lady."

Her vanity is not in "jewelled rings" but in "bright orioles" and "April's opalescent cloud," pride taken in things no one can own. Attention to the small and the passing becomes a kind of devotion. To treasure the overlooked is The Sacred Is Here practiced as character.

"Advertisement."

Refusing "shillings in purses of silk," the poem prizes a rabbit's paw and a crow's call instead, wealth reckoned in charged, useless, living things. Value is pulled back down from the market to the field. What matters was never for sale.

"Country Scene."

An "innocent cow" stands in "bitter salt" and "fields but of ice," the ordinary animal set against a hard, barren world. The poem refuses to prettify the earth and still holds it as the only place meaning lives. The Sacred Is Here includes the cold.

"Lenten Feast."

The "subtle spiritual nourishment" here is made of "pigeon shadows" and song sparrows, a communion taken from the passing natural world. The sacrament is birds. In the novel Mr. Spitzer mourns Martha, the last passenger pigeon, and the poem's feast is lit by the same grief, the holy and the vanishing bound together.

"A Girl's Song."

April stands for renewal and for how quickly renewal passes, youth and beauty already leaving as they arrive. The poem keeps its reverence for the fleeting without wishing it permanent. To love the transient as transient is The Sacred Is Here's discipline.

"To the Strangest Lady."

The gift is a catalog of the discarded: "a freckled rock," "mouse's fur," "snake skins drying in the grass." The poem hands the marginal and the imperfect to its strange addressee as if they were treasures, which under The Sacred Is Here they are. Nothing is too small or too spoiled to be holy.

"Experiment in Azure."

A "feathered breast" and a "moon-washed sea" hold warmth and cold together, life nurtured inside a shifting, fragile element. The poem finds tenderness in the ordinary precariousness of a living thing. Care is sacred precisely because it is uncertain.

"Song."

Body and soul keep returning into each other in a cycle with no exit and no final rest, existence renewing and spending itself. The reverence is for the turning itself, not for any escape from it. Meaning is the loop, held here rather than beyond.

"Elegy"

Her last published poem gathers the vision and gives it the closing word: "our God is not the God of Weight / But ourselves," reality "wild and on the wing," and the final line, "An apple toward the sky is always falling." God is relocated into the self and the world, weight and apple and all, with nothing kept in a beyond. The Sacred Is Here has the last word in the last poem, and the title and its "reproach of distance" keep Grief Doesn't End folded inside it.

Angel in the Forest: A Fairy Tale of Two Utopias

← Miss MacIntosh, My Darling · The Marguerite Young Society · Harp Song for a Radical →

Published: first published in 1945; reissued by Scribner in 1966 and now available from Dalkey Archive Press.

In the late 1930s Young visited New Harmony, Indiana, a small town that had been the site of two nineteenth-century attempts to build a perfect society. She moved there and stayed for years, and this book came out of that time.

The first utopia was founded in 1814 by Father George Rapp, a German mystic whose followers practiced a Scriptural communism while they waited for the New Jerusalem. The second began in 1825, when Robert Owen, one of the founders of British socialism, bought the settlement and tried to build a perfect community on rational lines. Both failed.

Young braids history and imagination into a study of people who tried to build heaven on earth and how their dreams came apart in their hands. The book won her a Guggenheim Fellowship, and its subject stayed with her for the rest of her life.

radical-immanence-the-philosophy-of-marg:
Radical Immanence: The Philosophy of Marguerite Young

The Marguerite Young Society

Marguerite Young never gave her philosophy a name. She did not write a treatise or lay out a system. Yet the same convictions run through everything she made, from the early poems of Prismatic Ground and Moderate Fable, through Angel in the Forest and its two lost utopias on the banks of the Wabash, into the eighteen years she spent on Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, and on to Harp Song for a Radical, the life of Eugene Debs she was still writing when she died.

The same ideas surface in her stories, essays, and reviews, and again in the interviews she gave across her long career. A self is never only one person. Reality is something people build out of dreams and memory. Grief does not end. The sacred does not live somewhere beyond this world. It lives here, in the ordinary and the overlooked, among the people at the edges.

Coral Russell calls this philosophy Radical Immanence. The name is new. The thinking is Young's, worked out over a lifetime of writing and talking, and gathered here into eleven pillars that show how it holds together.

The Eleven Pillars

Pillar 1 Not One Self

"You are not one person. The self is multiple, simultaneous, and irresolvable. This is not a problem to fix. It is what you are."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"Reality is not what we find; it is what we make. The line between illusion and reality is itself a construction. There is no sunlit world outside the cave, only a larger cave more carefully lit."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"Grief does not move through stages and arrive at resolution. It accumulates. It is the climate of a world where everything you love is always already changing. The honest life stops pretending otherwise."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

"The central ethical stance is not to fix or conclude, but to stay in the room. To see fully, without flinching, without rushing toward resolution. Attention is the practice. Refusal to simplify is the act."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"You build anyway, knowing the building is provisional. You return to the beginning with what you learned. The building is never finished. That is not failure. That is how it works."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

"The unfinished is not failure. It is honesty. The demand for completion is its own violence against experience. Integrity looks like the ongoing sentence, not the concluded one."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

"The edges of categories are where the constructed nature of reality becomes most visible. The marginal person is not the exception. They are the evidence."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

"The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath us, layer on layer. What was lost is not behind us. It is beneath us, still pressing up through the ground we stand on."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

"Language is not a neutral vehicle for truth. It shapes what can be seen, who can exist, what counts as real. Honest language names its own location. Language that pretends to speak from nowhere speaks from somewhere in particular."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

"The sacred is here, inside the ordinary world, pointing deeper into the immanent rather than outward to a beyond. The grey bus, the permanent grief, the plural self in all its unresolved reality: this is where the sacred lives."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"You are not a self moving through time. You are where time crosses itself. You are constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, and you are constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on. This obligation is not chosen. It is structural. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues."

Chapter by chapter: the pillar in all 82 chapters · Across every book: the crosswalk

Where it began

"The system did not arrive with the novel. It grew first in her poetry, where its terms can be watched taking shape before they were ever asked to carry a narrative. The poems test the idea that a self is many rather than one, that the solid world is a thing built and held in place by repetition, that grief is weather rather than a wound that closes, that meaning lives in the ground underfoot and not in any promised beyond."

How Each Lesson Is Built

Every lesson follows the same frame so readers learn to trust the rhythm.
