muses-part-6:
Inviting the Muses, Part 6

← Part 5 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 7 →

Part 6 finishes "The Artist as Wanderer," covers the two previously unpublished academic essays on Edward Young and Coventry Patmore, and ends partway into the "Memorial Speech in Honor of Mark Van Doren."

"The Artist as Wanderer" (untraced, ca. 1965–66)

The phrases "the work reproduced here" and "all the artists here" show that this essay was written to accompany a set of art images: the twelfth-century sculptor Gislebertus, Bernini, Rouault, Chagall, and Ben Shahn. Its argument is that the artist is the Wandering Jew, a figure who "never sleeps the sleep of death" and carries all of history in "an eternal now." The artist is "like every other dreamer except that he is more conscious of his dreams."

Young's handling of the legend is the heart of the piece. In the usual telling, a man mocks Christ on the way to the cross and is cursed to wander until the Second Coming. Young asks whether the words "you will be here when I return" might have been "a benediction" instead. She notes that the mocker only became a Jew in later versions, "a crime projected upon the Jew as scapegoat, a crime committed by all men who would kill the dreamer and the dream." By that reading the supposed punishment becomes a form of the eternal life Christ promised. It links directly back to "My Grandmother's Foot," where Jewish suffering and scattering become the source of "the great sanity of vision."

Her reasons for why the figure matters now are grounded in the century: "so many people displaced, so many flights, exoduses, barriers, walls, concentration camps," and "desert lands created by atomic tests to illustrate the feasibility of mass murder." The atomic tests have now appeared in three essays. Shahn's painting of a Jewish father fleeing the Nazis with a shrouded baby is read as the Wandering Jew and the Christ child fused into one image. She folds in Joyce's Bloom, Ishmael, Ahab, the Ancient Mariner, Don Quixote, and Huck Finn as versions of the same wanderer.

The ending is a creed. Art "by its very nature is an act of faith, of affirmation," and "cannot die as long as man endures." She takes Pasternak's claim that he was "the eyeball of a horse" as proof of a vision no state can wall in, and closes: "Better that it should crumble into man's creative dreams than into nothingness."

"The Theistic Mysticism of Young's Night Thoughts" (previously unpublished)

This essay and the next read like graduate-school work: denser, more formal, heavy on quotation, with little of her usual play. Their dates are unknown, which is why Moore placed them late in the section. They still matter, because they show where her convictions came from.

She places Edward Young's poem (1742–44) against the Augustan age of Pope and Addison, when poetry was treated as "machinery, like the Cartesian universe" and there was deep "distrust of any dark, irrational" knowledge. Young's courage, in her view, was to write a mystical poem inside a Newtonian cosmos that no longer offered Dante's or Milton's stage, so "the drama had to be interior." Lorenzo, the worldly young man the poem addresses, stands for "the prodigal philosophy," the realist position the poet argues against.

Two of her own sentences stand out in a crowded argument. One is "Sanity may consist only in sharing the hallucinations of our neighbors," which could stand as an epigraph for Miss MacIntosh. The other is her closing note that William Law called "the fund or bottom of the soul" eternity, a term taken from Boehme. The mystic's eternity and the modern unconscious turn out to be the same place, which is exactly the ground "The Artist as Wanderer" stands on.

"Coventry Patmore's Theory of Knowledge" (previously unpublished)

This is the more interesting of the two, because Young argues against the obvious reading. Patmore is known as a Catholic convert and religious poet, but she contends that in his work "God as God, if subtracted from that cosmos, would hardly be missed," since the poems would still be full of psychological detail and "the minutiae of quiet domesticities." The sexual imagery outweighs the religious meaning, and she notes, with some dryness, that "Freudian addicts" would find proof of their thesis throughout his odes.

Her real subject is how Patmore knows anything. She places him between idealism and realism, drawing on William James's "wild data" and Arthur Lovejoy's problem of where the image of a distant star is actually located. Patmore refuses to split reality into body and soul, shadow and substance. "In Patmore's world, the wild data continue to behave in a wild manner," and "even the nouns act like verbs." That last phrase could describe Young's own prose.

One passage speaks straight to the whole collection: memory implies a doubleness, "that the past, in being known, still keeps its distance." That is Riley's problem with the old sweetheart and Old James's problem with Indianapolis, stated as philosophy. It is also hard to miss that Patmore's best-known poem is The Angel in the House, and Young's own 1945 book on the New Harmony utopias is Angel in the Forest. The title looks like a deliberate echo.

"Memorial Speech in Honor of Mark Van Doren" (first part)

The speech reads Van Doren's Collected and New Poems: 1923–1963 through its imagery, starting with the old bestiaries whose emblematic beasts became, in later writers, "minute epiphanies of revelation." She hears in Van Doren "the muted undertone of a doubting intellect," but finds that his images build "a mystical lighthouse" toward a vanished world, so real in memory "that one may knock upon the door of a house which is already gone." In his poems "the skeptic thus meets with the mystic."

She pairs him with his hero Don Quixote, noting that Sancho's realism, in trying to correct his master, keeps falling for the illusions itself. Realism in Van Doren is valuable only when it "collaborates with the fading vision of the ideal." Part 6 stops in the middle of her reading of "Old Whitey," a poem about a dead horse turned to cloud, and her answer to whether Van Doren can prove the horse is gone: "The point of all his poems is that he cannot."

Across part 6

Here Young's underpinnings come into view. The academic essays show her working out, in scholarly terms, the positions her magazine pieces state with more flair: that reality is not split into matter and spirit, that the mind's "wild data" count as real, and that the unconscious is the modern name for the mystic's eternity. The two public pieces, on the Wandering Jew and on Van Doren, turn that philosophy into a moral stance for a century of camps and bombs. What survives, in her view, is what is remembered and imagined, whether that is a destroyed city under an Alpine meadow, a house already gone, or a horse that became a cloud.
muses-part-9:
Inviting the Muses, Part 9

← Part 8 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Parts 10 and 11 →

Part 9 covers the end of "The Anarchic Principle," then "Excursus on War," "Plumbing the Irrational," "Comfort's Work," "Joseph Smith, Mormon Prophet," "Metaphysical Fiction," the Sartre review, and most of "An Indiana Book." The 1945 pieces show something new about Young: three of them appeared in Conscientious Objector, the pacifist paper, which places her plainly on the side of war resisters in the last year of the war.

"The Anarchic Principle," conclusion (Sewanee Review, 1945)

The rest of the roundup is quick sorting. Elizabeth Hardwick's The Ghostly Lover is "scrupulously well done." A novel satirizing advertising fails because "satire, to be effective, must be intellectual." In Harry Sylvester's book about the New Mexico Penitents, the best scene is not the flagellation but priests playing cards, and Young ends dryly: "Ace, it seems, even when the players are priests, takes all."

"Excursus on War" (Conscientious Objector, 1945)

A review of Henry Miller's Murder the Murderer, a book whose publisher printed a disclaimer of responsibility for its views. Young defends Miller's right to speak ("there is nothing in the least immoral in what Miller has to say") and observes that after every war "a wave of conscientious objection seems always to start," while only the brave object during one, against the mentality of "Remember Pearl Harbor." Yet she finds Miller "a good deal less radical and less thoughtful than Alex Comfort." Miller still believes in a unity "God-given in nature" and in a guilty superman and innocent little men; his flaw is "romantic individualism, which also blows trumpets and waves flags." Comfort's The Power House, by contrast, shows "the death of individualism" in a mechanized civilization conditioning everyone. What Young wants from a pacifist is not heat but reason, "positive, forceful." It is a principled, unsentimental position.

"Plumbing the Irrational" (Conscientious Objector, 1945)

A short art review of Howard Mitcham at the Jane Street Gallery, a cooperative started by men from Civilian Public Service, the program for conscientious objectors. Young reads his painting through her usual philosophy: "Elephants dissolve into smoky light beams," "the red rose is not red," and there is "no absolute standard available to us." Mitcham "makes a game of our terror," and his art "evades the total logic of nonentity, populating vacuums with extraterrestrial refugees." The atomic bomb appears again, with its "diseased atoms in contagion," and she argues that only "the myth of infinite distended variety" can answer "the spiritual vacuity which our unthinking technicians have presented to us."

"Comfort's Work" (Conscientious Objector, 1945)

Young returns to Comfort a third time, reviewing his poetry collection The Song of Lazarus while complaining that The Power House never found its American audience. The Book-of-the-Month Club passed it over for Young'un, "the story of a little pioneer girl who made her own party dress." She suspects readers feared the novel encouraged conscientious objection, then writes one of the sharpest lines in the book: "Now that, since the atomic bomb, every man is a conscientious objector, or almost every man, that fear should certainly have dissolved like the doomed cities of Japan." She compares Comfort to the public Shelley and calls his poems "elegies for the human race."

"Joseph Smith, Mormon Prophet" (Nation, 1945)

Young had praised Fawn Brodie's No Man Knows My History in "Complex Life," and here she treats Smith's life as proof that America is anything but plain: "Nothing could be more baroque." He founded a church "by a series of accidents" that no one could have predicted. Her tone is amused and sly: unlike most angels of the time, Moroni "was not in favor of an arid celibacy," and "for every wife, another star in heaven." She gives Emma Smith her due, noting she "astutely objected to all this carnality." Set beside "Horse Utopia," it is another portrait of a male visionary building a world that serves him, though Smith gets more wonder than judgment.

The ending is mythic. Smith is killed at thirty-nine, and as a man rushes forward to cut off his head, "the sun came out from behind the cloud, and the people fled silently away." Young takes Brodie's title literally: he remains "unknown, unknowable," a mystery "even to himself."

"Metaphysical Fiction" (Kenyon Review, 1947)

McCullers has appeared throughout the book, and this is Young's full reading of The Member of the Wedding. She insists it is not what it first seems, "a study of turbulent adolescence," but "a curiously spiritual book" built on "carefully erected symbols." Frankie wants to join her brother's wedding in order "to break down all barriers of atomic individualism," which Young compares to "a union of all the nations," and Berenice tells her such a dream is possible "only inside her own creative head."

Her details are well chosen. Berenice married three times looking for her dead first husband, once for a man's thumb and once for the coat she had pawned. Berenice's ideal world has Black and white people living "equally and freely" and includes that lost husband. The three characters play three-handed bridge with cards missing from the start. The "wedding of three" echoes Riley's triangle in "The Old Sweetheart," all three loving each other and held apart. The ending turns on Frankie announcing that she "just loves Michelangelo," and Young's last line is perfectly flat: "Either she will grow up, or she will not grow up."

"To Be or Not" (Tiger's Eye, 1947)

The only truly scathing review so far, of Sartre's The Age of Reason. Young's objection is not to its pessimism but to its thinness. "The thesis that life is meaningless is, in itself, quite meaningless," she writes, since meaninglessness would need rich paradox, dream, and contradiction to be shown. Instead she finds "blank, empty, unvisionary pages" marked only by "the guilty thumbprints of Jean-Paul Sartre," characters who "live as paper dolls," and writing "all too near the slick," like a Hollywood version of France. Dreiser, in her view, knew "more of life's phantasmagoric base" than Sartre, and Sartre's pessimism is "only the reverse of greeting-card optimism," the same phrase she used against Merton's weaker poems. The complaint that there is "no buzz, no boom of reality" echoes her Moore essay's "buzzing and booming and blooming of existence," borrowed from William James.

"An Indiana Book" (first part)

A review of John Bartlow Martin's history of Indiana, and Young is on home ground. Martin hunts for the Hoosier "type," and she answers that "the 'type' is always a laziness of vision" and that Indiana "has given birth to many individuals but to no types." She teases him for insisting Hoosier is an insult, suggesting the habit might come from his being "born in Ohio," and offers a lovely correction: in Indiana people speak of "the outside world," not from isolationism "but through recognition of the interior world," where "the distance between Indianapolis and heaven" may be "shorter than that between Indianapolis and Cincinnati." Still, she calls it "an utterly delightful book" with a fine eye for "the strangest birds in Indiana's history." Part 9 breaks off in Martin's survey of Riley and Lew Wallace's Indianapolis.

Across part 9

The war pieces reveal Young's politics more directly than anything earlier: a pacifist who wants conscientious objection grounded in reason rather than romance, and who reads the atomic bomb as the end of every comfortable certainty. Her literary judgments follow the same line. She values McCullers and Comfort for their depth of symbol and their refusal of easy wholeness, and she dismisses Sartre not for doubting meaning but for writing doubt without any texture. The Indiana review returns to the argument of "The Midwest of Everywhere": individuals are real, types are a failure to look.
muses-part-1:
Inviting the Muses, Part 1

Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 2 →

Part 1 covers the front matter, the Publisher's Note, and the Stories section through the first two pages of "Old James," so that story breaks off mid-scene.

Front matter and the Publisher's Note

The book is the 1994 Dalkey Archive edition, assembled by Steven Moore while Dalkey was preparing its reissue of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. His note lays out the editorial logic plainly. There are three sections (stories, essays, reviews), each arranged roughly chronologically. Four pieces were previously unpublished, one story and three essays, and because Young could not recall when she wrote them, the story went first in its section and the essays toward the end of theirs. Surviving typescripts were used to check published versions, which let Moore restore a paragraph of "An Afternoon with Marianne Moore" that Vogue's editors had cut. He credits Martha J. Sattler's bibliography as the thing that made the collection possible.

The contents page shows how wide her short prose ranged: Midwestern place essays, a visit with Marianne Moore, Mari Sandoz, Edward Young's Night Thoughts, Coventry Patmore, a memorial speech for Mark Van Doren, and reviews touching Caruso, Joseph Smith, Anaïs Nin, and a book on the "Endless House." The mix of mysticism, Americana, and literary portraiture is already visible before a single story starts.

"My Grandmother's Foot" (previously unpublished)

This is the piece most recognizably in the voice of Miss MacIntosh. The narrator admits the grandmother is "a construct of my imagination," then insists in the same breath that everything "is based on factual, uncolored reports and can be sworn to." That double claim, invention and testimony held together, is the story's engine. Young's sentences keep correcting and extending themselves ("or, more specifically"), and the family is built out of doublings: the father's luck being "the exact reverse" of his character, the mother facing "not one but two sinister separations," the elephant "multiplying by bifurcation," and the mother herself "merely doubled like the bifurcating elephant."

The mother, drugged and kept "like a Sleeping Beauty in a glass cage," neither dead nor alive, reads as an early sketch of the opium-dreaming mother in the novel. Against the parents, who love "inanimate objects, even a fence post, as substitutes for reality," the narrator sets the Jewish grandmother as "the great sanity of vision, the capacity for merely human life."

The plot is comic and grotesque in equal parts. The grandfather is torn apart in a pogrom and "scattered all over the corn fields," with no way to be reassembled on Resurrection Day. The grandmother's amputated foot is buried "in a Fourteenth Street shoe box," and when the rabbis exhume it to reunite it with her body, they find "a baby's hand, so small and blue." The father then searches a hospital's "morgue of missing members" and picks a foot with a bunion, possibly the wrong one. The repeated phrase "miscarriage of justice" carries a quiet second meaning once the baby's hand appears.

The ending turns the whole joke toward war: "When I see whole cities dissolving under the impact of high explosives, I do think of my grandmother's foot." The question "Should we really devote ourselves to the great business of scattering each other?" makes the story a meditation on bodily wholeness against mass violence, and on Jewish history as both suffering and the source of an unbreakable gaiety. The final image, "A lost foot," becomes something the narrator and "humanity itself" are searching for.

"The Dead Women" (American Prefaces, 1943)

This one is spare and realist, written in close third on Leda, a pregnant young woman who prepares bodies for her father-in-law's funeral business. It moves through three months, each with its own corpse.

In October it is an old country woman. Leda decides against rouge so that "God might recognize her," and so she "might know herself, with the kinks in the bones of her back." In November it is a young woman who died after a wild night, and here the prose slips into present tense as Leda imagines the saloon, the nickel in the slot, the dance going on. This time Leda does use rouge, "as if there would be a dance tonight, after all." In December the body is an old man found frozen in a shed with his feet in cold ashes, and the title's promise of women breaks. The third "dead woman" seems to be Leda herself, or what she carries. She has already said she "felt like two women, herself and someone else."

The father-in-law is loud, jovial, and relentlessly about birth: the Guernsey's twins "black as midnight," the teasing "I hope you don't fool Tom that way," the story of Tom crawling into coffins as a baby. His repeated question, "Have you felt it kicking yet?", gets deflected in October and November. In December no one asks, and the story ends: "But she knew. But she was sure now." Leda walks "heavily toward the stairway, passing alone under the sprig of green holly," the same spot where he always kisses her. The dripping faucet and the Christmas party with no gifts sharpen the sense that she is keeping time alone. The ending never says outright what she knows, but everything points toward a death inside her that the cheerful household cannot hear.

Feet recur here too: the crippled daughter "who has only one foot" bringing asters on a paper heart, and the father-in-law limping from a calf stepping on him. Read alongside the first story, the motif links the two across what seems a long gap in time and style.

"Old James" (opening only)

What appears sets up an Indianapolis stockbroker during the Depression and his secretary, Miss Greenwood, who enjoys his inattention because "in that fact lay her only freedom." She draws Greek faces in her shorthand book and sings hymns over the typewriter. James spends his days on the phone telling anyone who will listen about hollyhocks supposedly descended from Anne Hathaway's garden, the number of cows in Indiana, and old farm boundaries from when Sixteenth Street "was known as Tinker." Visitors ask whether he is "Expecting to go somewhere," which already hints at a man stalled on the edge of some departure. The local-history cataloguing looks forward to the Indiana material in the essays.

Across part 1

The ordering Moore chose puts the mature, digressive, comic-mystical voice first and the plainer 1943 story second, so part 1 almost runs backward through her development. What holds steady is the concern with the body as something that must be kept whole, the closeness of birth and death, women whose inner lives go unnoticed by the people around them, and a humor that sits right next to the macabre without canceling it.
muses-part-2:
Inviting the Muses, Part 2

← Part 1 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 3 →

Part 2 covers the rest of "Old James," the end of the Stories section, and the whole of the first essay, "The Midwest of Everywhere."

"Old James" (Kenyon Review, 1944)

The story turns out to be about authorship as much as about its title character. Old James, an Indianapolis stockbroker, is dictating his autobiography to his secretary, Miss Greenwood, and she quietly supplies whatever he leaves out. She adds "the portrait of Jesus Christ with the woolly lamb in his arms" to a church scene "which seemed rather too hurried in its realism," and he never objects to "these surreptitious additions to his life." He leaves the chronology for her to sort out and, when she looks bored, tells her to "add the details yourself." The pages end up read back to him "as if they were legal and sworn to before witnesses," which echoes the narrator of "My Grandmother's Foot," whose invented grandmother is also somehow sworn to.

His life, as it comes out in pieces, is a string of abandoned selves: a newspaperman who knew the streets and "a few domestic tragedies," a long-haired poet and "rival to James Whitcomb Riley," then a banker "almost overnight" after marrying a rich woman who "abhorred the poet in him." He apologizes for both poetry and banking. The nostalgia is lush and specific (crab apple orchards under the post office, a poultry house that was once a Greek Orthodox church, "a narrow angel, transparent as light"), and Young lets it be beautiful while making clear what it costs. He makes more money during the Depression than in normal times by buying up stocks that widows bring in "like so many soap coupons." He writes a law to protect property owners that collapses over the meaning of "emergency" and "act of God." He orders a thousand Chinese elms to plant a forest, and parasites eat them. He writes epitaphs for his club friends while "Hitler's armies were already gathering." Miss Greenwood keeps those files too, but "she filled in no blank spaces here," declining to add what she knows about men like Pierre Smith-Allen, who "thought more of his horses than of the girls at his glove factory."

The real center is Miss Greenwood. "Part of it was her story," Young writes. She is the one who notices the living pigeons, the skaters, the colts "splotched with their first golden hairs, like the impressions of maple leaves." The salesmen blame her for his "aberrations," he never notices her "faded dress, her tired look," and she is never paid for the extra work. When she finally leaves for Chicago with "a pasteboard box and a bag of oranges," she writes him about "riots in steel mills," her first private thought, and he answers with a form-letter acknowledgment. The blank on his side stays blank.

His death is handled with dry comedy: "Some say Hitler killed him, but others say it was just old time catching up with him." At the funeral, nobody remembers anything he said. Miss Greenwood, too poor to attend, "filled in this last blank space" by imagining it. The ending moves into present tense and asks the question the whole story has been building toward. "His left hand knew of the wild geese flying. It knew not of bombers over China." She cannot say how responsible he was "for the world's disaster," since she was "herself a collaborator." Published in 1944, that word carries its full wartime weight. The story indicts nostalgia as a way of not seeing, while admitting that the person who helps write the fantasy is implicated too.

"The Midwest of Everywhere" (Mademoiselle, 1945)

The essay opens with a thesis that is also a joke: "The Middle West is probably a fanatic state of mind." Young refuses the region as plain, flat, or ordinary. She is "sick of" the Andy Hardy picture and agrees with Sinclair Lewis's Main Street "only from his particular perspective." To critics who say the Midwest has no Main Stream, she replies that it has none "because it is oceanic," touching every shore. Her Midwest includes Xanadu, Byzantium, and "twelve unseen moons shining over the planet Jupiter."

The method is a catalogue of marvels, each told as plain fact: a dead whale in a boxcar in an Indiana cornfield, a dwarf driving Percherons, a sow at the wheel of a stalled Ford with fourteen piglets, a man who died in his sleep and was seen the next day mowing the grass and mentioning "his daughter's eczema." There is a village of old people deafened by malaria, which they pronounce so lovingly "you would think it was Miranda," and another where spirits like Pocahontas and Lincoln can be consulted for twenty-five cents. From New Harmony she passes along Charlie Chaffin's report of a nine-foot hoot owl that "made a noise like a flat tire while flying and had a bell around its neck," and his children named Thoughtless and Imadaisy, who do not exist.

That last detail is the key. Much of what she describes is absent or invisible: the children who aren't in the county, the old doctor's Chevrolet that cannot be seen though it is parked between a hearse and a milk truck, the doctor himself rising "out of his deathbed, as it were, to go deliver imaginary babies." The region's truest life, for her, is the unseen one. She calls herself "a good Heraclitean and lover of the flux" and hopes "the lower elements will never be got rid of," against a hostess who is proud of cleaning them out.

Underneath the comedy is the same darkness as the stories. Mark Twain "felt the coldness of the universe," and Riley "drank to forget the children," which sits sharply beside Old James, the former Riley rival, who insists he never drank in a dark room to forget the people he wrote about. She defines the Midwest finally as "a wild, hazardous, romantic experience of the individual and human character in juxtaposition with the coldness of the universe." The last line widens it to "the Egypt of Indiana, the Indiana of Egypt, the Russia of everywhere, the human soul."

One passing phrase dates the essay: the spirit-consultation signs are compared to fishing worms sold "in Negro shanty towns along a flower-infested railroad track," tossed off as local color in a way that sits uneasily beside her praise for the overlooked.

Across part 2

The two pieces read almost as a pair. "Old James" shows a man whose sentimental past blinds him to the present and to the woman beside him, while the essay argues for a vision that sees the marvelous in the ordinary without looking away from the cold. Both are built on blank spaces and what fills them, and both keep the war just offstage, in bombers over China and in the question of who collaborates in the world's disaster.
muses-part-3:
Inviting the Muses, Part 3

← Part 2 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 4 →

Part 3 covers four essays: "Complex Life and Complex Letters," "An Afternoon with Marianne Moore," "Mari Sandoz," and "Horse Utopia." Together they shift the collection from fiction into Young's public voice as a critic and portraitist in the late 1940s.

"Complex Life and Complex Letters" (Vogue, 1946)

This is a manifesto, and it reads like a defense of the novel Young was then deep inside writing. It opens: "Literature is our night life, our dream life, and the sun may not rise tomorrow." She pictures God as "the greatest fiction writer of them all," whose sentences are "replete with the most baroque imagery, and quite circumlocutious, and even a little long-drawn." The joke has a point. If creation itself is baroque, a plain style is not more truthful, only more limited.

Her target is the "commonsense critic," with J. Donald Adams named as the most eminent. These critics want literature "simple, plain, sensible, healthy, unassuming, underwritten, comfortable," and they believe it is enough to say "The cat was on the mat." Young answers that such a literature has never existed. Even Pilgrim's Progress has "its wild Gothic elements," nursery rhymes carry buried violence, and "an honest literature, from Job to Richard Wright, has even been a little morbid in spots." She lines up the writers she considers honest: Faulkner, Welty, Stead, McCullers, Robert Penn Warren, Stein, Joyce, Broch, Mann's The Transposed Heads. Against them she sets the mass-produced "average" book turned out "with the efficiency of Willow Run," and she singles out William Maxwell's The Folded Leaf as having "one neat insight per page, timed like a metronome."

Two moments carry real weight. When American reviewers attacked Grimm's fairy tales as a "German orgy of brutality," Young notes that "Goering and Goebbels were sensible," which turns the charge around: the atrocity came from the orderly, rational side, not from the disorderly dream world. And she points to sheep and goats being placed on ships for the atomic tests in the Pacific, asking "How can literature be of the modern world and not a crazy thing?" The essay closes with a parody of critics scolding Hawthorne, Melville, and Kafka, ending flatly: "The cat is on the mat, and that's the end of that."

There is a thread here back to "Old James," where the blank spaces were where the truth hid. The commonsense critics, she says, would prefer "even the blank page."

"An Afternoon with Marianne Moore" (Vogue, 1946)

This is the piece the Publisher's Note mentioned, where a paragraph cut by Vogue was restored. It is almost certainly the parenthetical beginning "Actually, although cut out by editorial scissors," which explains that Moore had borrowed from Yeats and let the line be quoted as hers. Young attaches this to "real toads in imaginary gardens," but in Moore's own notes to "Poetry" the Yeats debt is for "literalists of the imagination," while the toads are Moore's. Young seems to have blurred the two, which may be one reason an editor cut it.

The essay starts on the subway to Coney Island in winter, with Brooklyn's "spires like huge, inverted ice cream cones" and a boardwalk "Niagara Falls of pasteboard," then settles Moore into that landscape as the poet who "gives voice to marvels." The portrait is precise and affectionate: the narrow head and pale blue eyes, the apartment full of ivory mice and a baby ebony sea horse, the mixed furniture ("We mix our furniture systematically because we cannot help it"), and Moore's mother, whose remark "Let us have done with the umbrella of our contagion" shows the household talking the way the poems sound. A misshapen strawberry becomes "a strawberry that's had quite a struggle" and then a poem.

Young reads Moore through her own convictions. Moore's speech seems to reveal "the secret heart of things," but then "there is no secret heart, no simple solution but another problem." Everything in the poems "zigzags." The book reprints "The Mind Is an Enchanting Thing" in full because Young takes its phrase "conscientious inconsistency" as the key to Moore. She repeats the argument from the previous essay almost word for word: the dull is falsely called "good, old American," when America "has been, if anything, the land of crazy unreason." Moore becomes the proof, "a true pioneer in a wilderness of thought."

The ending lingers on Moore as collector: notebooks "as small as prayer books," envelopes labeled "lizards, Goths, elephants, cosmetics," a box of feathers, and a final gift offer: "She offered me a bluebird's foot." After "My Grandmother's Foot," it is hard not to notice.

"Mari Sandoz" (Flair, 1950)

A short profile built on the idea that Sandoz carries "the look of the land as it was." Young opens by making her "sand-colored like the Nebraska hills," like a bird camouflaged for protection, and sees her as "a passionate archaeologist of the Old West," interested in the psychology of the frontier as much as its events. She reads the gunfighters and outlaws as "the paranoids of the past," and Old Jules as a parable for "the frontiers of all the world," with readers writing to Sandoz from the Arctic, China, and "the inner isolations of Brooklyn."

The best detail is the map on her wall, pasted on cheesecloth so it won't tear in the wind, showing the old names and dried streams as they ran before irrigation, twenty-one years in the making. It is Old James's lost Indianapolis made rigorous and useful. The piece ends on a list of Sandoz's frontier skills (delivering babies before ten, sewing up her own wounds, molding bullets) and the note that she "has never, she says, learned to balance a teacup."

"Horse Utopia" (Flair, 1950)

This is the strangest piece so far. It describes the Lazy VV Ranch in Colorado, run by bean magnate Lynn W. Van Vleet as a preserve for Arabian horses and a summer gathering of guests who may not mention their professions, religions, or politics. The horse material is sincere: the breed's hardiness in blizzards, cowboys riding purebreds on mountain trails, the Mitanni clay tablets on horse training from about 1350 B.C.

The human side is harder to read. Van Vleet insists on the title "Boss," which Young calls "delusively simple." He is "the Prospero of this scene," and even the Continental Divide "seems only a cardboard backdrop of illusion." His utopia restores men's "ancient dignities" away from "valleys of petticoat domination": women wear Levis, may not wear lipstick, must wait on the men and catch their fish, and those who rebel face "a New England ducking stool." Young reports all of this without open comment, and the essay ends right on the ducking stool.

For a writer whose nonfiction book, Angel in the Forest, was about the utopian communities at New Harmony, the piece reads as another study in a man's dream of order imposed on others. Van Vleet belongs with Old James: a rich man with a private vision who assumes everyone else will fill in around it. Whether the magazine format kept her from saying so directly, the flat final image lets the reader judge.

Across part 3

The essays make explicit what the stories implied. Young's central belief is that reality is stranger and more complex than common sense allows, and that American life in particular is a land of marvel rather than plainness. Moore and Sandoz are her models, women who collect, map, and preserve the particular against the general. Van Vleet is the counterexample, the benevolent despot of a tidy utopia. Running under all of it is the war and the bomb, which, in her view, made the case against the "sensible" once and for all.
muses-parts-10-and-11:
Inviting the Muses, Parts 10 and 11

← Part 9 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part

Parts 10 and 11 close the Reviews section and the book. They run from the end of the Indiana review through Capote, Marianne Hauser, Doris Lessing, Frederick Kiesler, two pieces on Anaïs Nin, a Sherlock Holmes roundup, and a final review on Poe, followed by the index. Where part 9 was clustered in the 1940s, these reviews spread across three decades, from 1948 to 1977.

"An Indiana Book," conclusion

The review ends with Martin's section on Debs and the Hapgoods, "men in revolt" against capitalism. Debs was the subject of Young's own unfinished biography, so it is fitting that he is the last figure mentioned in her last piece on Indiana.

"Tiger Lilies" (Kenyon Review, 1948)

Young reads Capote's Other Voices, Other Rooms as she read McCullers, as symbolic rather than realist. His characters are not "the supposed normal" but "a confluence of signs," each "the aberrant fragment of self," "a piece of the unconscious" in "a world of curved mirrors." She notes that "love is equated with death," that "everyone is doing, too, a disappearing act," and that the book happens "at the intersection between two traffic lines, the real and unreal." She closes on the marsh where tiger lilies grow "the size of a man's head," concluding that "this landscape is also psychic, a mystery."

"Comedy in a Tragic Show" (New York Herald Tribune Book Review, 1958)

Marianne Hauser's The Choir Invisible concerns a bank clerk with a blood cancer who becomes a choir director, trying to make "heavenly music on this earth." Young takes up the book's premise that when we are about to die "we begin to live," and notes his dying brings back the figures of his childhood. Her favorite pairing is a spiritualist who believes she was once a Roman officer and once a nun, "in deadly rivalry with the prosperous undertaker to whom mortality is necessity." She calls it "a book not about death but about life." The undertaker's trade recalls "The Dead Women," though here it is played for comedy.

"The Darkest Part of Africa" (Washington Post Book World, 1966)

A review of the third and fourth books in Doris Lessing's Children of Violence series. Young's reading is that "Africa is thus the true heroine" and that Lessing's white settlers miss everything by refusing to know "the African brother," cutting themselves off through "tribal taboos and totems," "curfew laws," and master-and-servant relations. She adds a sharp reversal: Lessing may doubt the Black African misses much by staying outside a white world "capable of more violence than was ever dreamed by primitive man." Her judgment on Martha, who joins a communist movement she only half understands, fits Young's own pacifist logic from 1945: the novel is "criticism not only of reality but of idealism when it begets violence."

"The 'Endless House': A Man-built Cosmos" (Architectural Forum, 1967)

On the journals of architect and sculptor Frederick Kiesler, published after his death. Young is drawn to his sense of creation as something that happens through him, as when ink drops seemed to guide his hand. She describes his sculpture of a horse a man may crawl into and emerge "born again," and repeats the etymology from "The Artist as Wanderer": the horse means "mare, water and mother." Kiesler's link-upon-link vision of a universe bound by "cosmic love" and his endless house with meadows on its roof are the kind of total work Young herself pursued. Her closing line serves as an epitaph: "It may be hoped that his end is his beginning."

"Anaïs Nin" (Voyages, 1967) and the Nin Reader review (New York Woman, 1973)

The first piece reviews the second volume of Nin's diary. Young sees her as not only lost in the labyrinth but also as its builder: "the minotaur" and "also Minos and is also Daedalus, the architect of the maze." She asks whether "a seashell know[s] its own spiralings," and answers that this diary is "the seashell writing its many rooms." The familiar creed returns: "style is thinking."

This essay also matters for what Young does with Nin's views on gender. Nin argues that the woman artist creates "in her own womb" and that man invented woman out of fear. Young quotes her at length but concludes as she did in "Feminine Sensibility": "Perhaps the problems are greater than the differences between men and women writers," rather lying between "the mediocre and true literary insight." She places Nin "with men of great gifts," with Hawthorne, Poe, and Firbank.

The second review, of The Anaïs Nin Reader and its introduction by Anna Balakian, is the piece the Publisher's Note says was unknown until Young's assistant sent it in. It praises Balakian for showing that Nin's diary and fiction "feed each other constantly," and it takes one more swipe at literalists who "seem somehow to wish to be the geniuses of the blank page and usually call themselves, for this very good reason, realists." The blank page has been her enemy from "Complex Life" in 1946 to here.

"The Great Detective" (New York Times Book Review, 1975)

A cheerful roundup of seven Holmes books. The motif Young keeps returning to is that Holmes cannot die. Doyle killed him at Reichenbach Falls, but "Sherlock could not stay dead," and the public forced his resurrection, which Doyle managed partly because "he did not believe that he himself would ever be extinguished." She treats Doyle's stories as "pre-Freudian psychodramatic confessions, just as all real fiction is." She enjoys Samuel Rosenberg's theory linking Moriarty to Nietzsche, Nicholas Meyer's The Seven-Per-Cent Solution, John Gardner's Victorian thieves' slang, and Robert L. Fish's parody The Memoirs of Schlock Homes, "a delightful crime which he is bound to survive."

"Defending an Injured Reputation" (New York Times Book Review, 1977)

The last piece in the book is a review of John Carl Miller's Building Poe Biography, on John Henry Ingram, a London post office clerk who spent his evenings rescuing Poe from Rufus Griswold's slanders. Young is unusually fierce toward Griswold, "this hack," "the mud-throwing, very unreverend Reverend," who set out to leave Poe lying "in the muck and mud until the angel of resurrection should blow his conch." She notes that nearly every figure Ingram wrote about "had left a reputation that needed redemption from slander."

The emotional center is Marie Louise Shew Houghton, the nurse at the Fordham cottage, who bought Virginia Poe's "coffin, her grave clothes, and Edgar's mourning," taught Poe to eat fish and clams for brain power, and burned the letters in which he called himself a "Lost Soul." The book's final lines are about the Poes' cat, Caterina, "so nervous and 'possessed'" after Virginia's death that the nurse feared her, and later found dead: "Mrs. Houghton was almost glad."

It is a strange, quiet ending, and a fitting one. Houghton belongs with Miss Greenwood and Dorothy Caruso, the women in this book who tend the famous man, keep his memory, and decide what to preserve and what to burn. The collection that opened with a family resurrecting a grandmother's foot closes with a man's reputation being raised from the grave.

The index

The index is a names-only list, and it works as a map of Young's mind. The longest runs belong to Riley, Alex Comfort, Marianne Moore, Nin, Patmore, Poe, and the Wandering Jew essay's painters. William James, Proust, Joyce, Sterne, Swedenborg, and Melville recur across widely separated pages, confirming them as her steady sources. Debs appears at the start of the book, in "On Teaching," and in the Indiana review. The range is part of the point: Pancho Villa, Crazy Horse, Pocahontas, Hitler, Goebbels, Innocent III, and the Abbé Sicard sit alongside Dryden and Mallarmé. Edward Young is listed, while Marguerite Young, naturally, is not, and neither is Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, which shadows almost every page.

The collection as a whole

Read end to end, Inviting the Muses shows remarkable consistency across more than fifty years. From the 1935 Poetry reviews to the 1989 teaching essay, Young holds to a few convictions: reality is stranger and more complex than common sense admits; the dream, the irrational, and the invisible are part of the real; style is thinking, and the blank page is not honesty but poverty; and what survives, whether a doll, a remembered house, a reputation, or a grandmother's foot, survives through memory and imagination. The war runs beneath much of it, and her pacifism gives the philosophy moral weight. The recurring figures, the detached hand or foot, the triangle of lovers, the woman who takes dictation from a great man, the horse, the resurrection, tie the stories, essays, and reviews into something close to a single long work, which is exactly the kind of book she spent her life defending.
muses-part-5:
Inviting the Muses, Part 5

← Part 4 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 6 →

Part 5 finishes "The Old Sweetheart," covers "The World of Silence" and the title essay "Inviting the Muses" in full, and ends on the first page of "The Artist as Wanderer."

"The Old Sweetheart," conclusion (Mademoiselle, 1951)

The woman in the forest turns out to be the emotional center of the search. Unaware that McClanahan had already given Riley her tintype, she sends him one herself, "the shadow of her hand," wrapped with a ribbon and a lock of her hair. Young lays out the triangle with real delicacy: she loves Riley next to McClanahan, McClanahan loves Riley next to her, and Riley loves her after McClanahan, "all three separated by space." When they finally meet there is no disappointment, but she is dying, and she belongs to the wanderer. McClanahan comes back, they marry, Riley stands as best man, and she lives two years before becoming "their sacred memory."

Then Young lets comedy back in. Ella Wheeler Wilcox, another correspondent, meets Riley at last and he scolds her fashionable gown and her bang: would Mrs. Browning have dressed that way? Wilcox snaps back that Mrs. Browning "would have looked better with a bang than with those dreadful corkscrew curls in that old tintype." The poet is still searching for the girl in the poem even after he has met the real woman. He greets another literary editor with "Where are your corkscrew curls?"

The ending is Young's answer to her own question. Asked by a reporter on the telephone where his wife is, Riley says she might be in heaven, might be anywhere, that he might never have seen her, that "he might be talking to her even then, that she might be at the other end of the wire." The old sweetheart was never one woman. She was the search, the Muse, the ideal that no living person could be. Young handles this with more sympathy than she gave Old James, but the pattern is the same: a man who loves a figure in his head more than anyone who can walk into the room.

"The World of Silence" (Flair Annual, 1952)

This is the most ambitious essay so far, part reporting and part meditation on what it means to perceive. Young opens with Condillac's statue, a marble figure given the senses one at a time until it wakes into consciousness, and concludes that the world is built out of "our dreaming senses." The deaf, in her image, are statues complete except for one sense, missing "the footsteps in the ruined garden."

Robert Owen appears early, deaf in old age and holding long debates on socialism with spirits whose voices he "distinctly heard," publishing everything they said. For the author of Angel in the Forest, which dealt with Owen's New Harmony, it is a telling choice: the utopian who can hear only the voices he imagines.

Her best insight comes in one line: "The tragedy of those born deaf is not that they do not hear but that others hear." The problem, in other words, is social exclusion. From there the essay traces a history of cruelty, with deaf children thrown into pits in Sparta, into the Tiber, into holes in the ice, confined in imperial Japan, and "extinguished" in Nazi Germany. She does not let America off either. The first deaf education in the colonies, in 1776, went to the aristocratic Bolling family, with the teacher bound for five thousand dollars not to reveal his method, "the spirit was exclusive," while the poor deaf went unnoticed. In modern New York, she notes, some deaf people still live without any language at all.

The middle of the essay favors lip-reading and oral schooling, which was the dominant view of her time and is now strongly contested by Deaf communities who see sign as a full language. Yet Young's heart is plainly with the signs. She calls their rhythms "the counterpart of music," says they exist "all in the present tense," and suspects that for the deaf "time may be an illusion, a human construct." She describes Plains sign language and a Greenwich Village coffee shop where an Indian and a deaf painter discuss "Kantian metaphysics, baroque architecture, Virginia Woolf, Stalin's Russia" entirely by hand. Some of her claims show their age, such as her assertion that Chinese writing rests on pictures and that Semitic traders brought Egypt "the sense of time," and a passing generalization about Jewish deaf and criminality.

The essay's recurring word is amputation. The deaf man's life is "amputated from hearing," his isolation "a real amputation." After the grandmother's foot and the tintype of the hand, the collection's body-part motif now carries real weight: a missing sense treated as a missing member that society either restores or buries.

Its most moving pages are religious. A lay rabbi signs the stories of Noah's ark and Jacob's ladder, and Young raises a hard psychiatric question: how does a man with no language describe "his guilt complex if he has not even one small word?" At St. Ann's, meeting at St. Mark's in the Bowery, the service is signed, and "the hearer feels, in this church, his difference from others." Then comes a deaf Hamlet, "to be or not to be, which is the problem of the silence." The essay ends on the signs for mother, ocean, and burial: "the hands lowered slowly to the ground, the earth which is the mother."

"Inviting the Muses" (Mademoiselle, 1965)

The title essay is a look back at Young's teaching, first at Iowa and then at the New School, Columbia, Fairleigh Dickinson, and Fordham. It opens with one enormous sentence that runs from a Quonset hut in the snow through seals, penguins, frozen butterflies, mailboxes lost in drifts, and tin roofs drumming in the rain. That sentence is not self-indulgence. It is a demonstration of what she teaches, which she names at the end as "the dragnet sentence," where students drag the waters of memory and association and bring in whatever haul there is.

Her creed is compact. Talent is "almost a commonplace," like dreaming, but most people are stopped by self-criticism before anything reaches the page. The great writer "has no tollkeeper at the gate" and lets even the ridiculous through, trusting that the final form will make it cohere. She throws out the "beginning and middle and end" formula and asks instead for "memory and observation, dream and reality, conflict and character." Two definitions carry over directly from "Complex Life and Complex Letters": "Form is that which keeps the reader reading. What is style? Style is thinking." Twenty years after her fight with the commonsense critics, her position has not moved an inch.

There is humor in her picture of the poets next door, arguing all night over a raindrop and suspicious of prose, and real generosity toward students who later told her the long sentence was the first time they felt "the wonder of being a writer." The essay ends: "For literature is that which is memorable."

"The Artist as Wanderer" (opening only)

The first page sets up the next essay's terms: the artist as "a dedicated dreamer exploring the dream," asking whether the dream is real or reality the dream. She works through Pasternak's poems "The Waves" and "Finale" and a derivation of Mary from the word for both sea and horse.

Across part 5

The three complete pieces all turn on the same question from different angles: how a person reaches what they cannot directly perceive. Riley reaches toward a sweetheart who exists only in words, the deaf reach a world through the hand and eye, and the writing student reaches the unconscious through the long sentence. In each case Young favors the path through imagination and the body over the plain, sensible route, and the hand keeps reappearing as the instrument, whether it holds a Chinese fan in a tintype, signs the Book of Genesis, or casts the dragnet.
muses-part-8:
Inviting the Muses, Part 8

← Part 7 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 9 →

Part 8 finishes the Woolf and Porter review and covers four more reviews: Dorothy Caruso's memoir of her husband, Broch's The Death of Virgil, a large poetry roundup called "Our Person Our World," and the first half of "The Anarchic Principle," a fiction roundup led by Alex Comfort. Nearly all of it dates from 1945, the last year of the war, and the war runs under every piece.

"Fictions Mystical and Epical," conclusion (Kenyon Review, 1945)

Young's verdict on Katherine Anne Porter sets her against Woolf. Porter's great theme is "the continuity of the individual's experience," and she "rejects the artificiality of chaos, even as an abstraction." She is an intuitionist who believes "life and its values are not fictions." Young borrows Aquinas's argument that a universe with both angels and stones is better than one with angels alone, and delivers a fine summation: "Miss Porter has realized the angel at the border, but she has chosen the phantasmagoria of stone." Porter "does not see life itself as a hallucination," and is "the unpretentious critic of a defective material, human nature."

Young clearly stands closer to Woolf, yet she honors Porter fully. Her last point is that Porter's stories, though carefully shaped, seem to be "fragments of some larger, though absent whole," which gives them "an epic state of mind." That is the reverse of Young's own practice, a single epic built of fragments, and she recognizes the kinship.

Enrico Caruso (New York Times Book Review, 1945)

A warm, generous review of Dorothy Caruso's memoir, written twenty-three years after the tenor's death. Young's central claim is that the book, though "not a work of art," approaches that stature because its subject does. Caruso becomes "an autonomous character, a literary one," and she repeats a line from "Complex Life": "Perhaps, in this case, God must be considered the greatest writer, for here the facts are more fabulous than any average fiction."

The quoted letters in broken English are the heart of it, especially Caruso on a train to Denver confessing "a sentiment of fraidness," feeling "like a boy without protection." Young also delights in the plain details: his proudest honor was a medal from the New York Police Department, and his favorite pleasure was cards with an Italian restaurant keeper on Forty-seventh Street. She notes that "a stone-deaf man could enjoy this book," a phrase that looks ahead to "The World of Silence." And she praises the widow as a biographer who "seems not so much a writer as one who takes down in shorthand the speech of her husband, living or dead," never inventing traits he lacked. It is Miss Greenwood's role again, this time filled honestly. The last line: "he was himself the great work of art, the masterpiece."

"A Poet's Last Hours on Earth" (Broch, The Death of Virgil)

Broch's novel was one of the books Young had held up in "Complex Life" as the opposite of Maxwell's metronome, and here she gives it full attention. She stresses that Broch began it "in a Nazi prison, as a private preparation for death," and finished it as an American citizen at Princeton. The book is a deathbed in which Virgil "re-creates the world" in the moment of extinction, and she makes it universal: "We are the only God we know of." Brundisium, the city he is carried through, becomes "a symbol of the mob, wherever the mob coagulates."

Her closest American comparison is Melville, since both writers share "the night which circles in its immense space, the loneliness of man, the impossibility of any simple statement." The book "fits into no pigeonhole," is "not one diamond but a mountain of diamonds," and she hopes it will be "a corrective to our fundamentalism, our departmentalism." That second word appeared in the Midwest essay too; departmentalized knowledge is one of her persistent enemies.

"Our Person Our World" (Partisan Review, 1945)

The roundup covers Allen Tate, Richard Eberhart, Allan Dowling, Charles Butler, Thomas Merton, Robert Frost, Herbert Read, and Conrad Aiken, and it opens with an attack on "glib" reviewers who file every poet under Auden, Yeats, Hopkins, or Eliot. Her larger thesis is that "our age is devoid of one informing myth," but the death of myth comes with "the birth cry of an art which integrates new worldviews." Science keeps moving "from elephant as elephant to elephant as light beams," yet poets need not retreat to dogma, since science "may also have its symbolic uses, just like the old saints who ran after their heads after decapitation." Then, simply: "Imagination does not cease."

Tate gets the most admiring treatment. His centaur descending into hell with a "notched, amazing beard" shows there is no border between the earthly and the transcendent: "Heaven is a beard shaped like a notched arrow!" For Tate, she says, "the search is everything and not the object searched for," which is the lesson of Riley and the old sweetheart in another key. From Eberhart she takes the phrase "the beautiful disrelation of the spiritual," the same phrase she used, in quotation marks, in "The Midwest of Everywhere" the same year. His war poems grasp that "what was our religion is now our long-range artillery."

Her judgments of the others are pointed. Dowling expects agreement about "the word God, for example, and no further exploration necessary." Merton "writes as if he were two men, a Catholic monk and a man of this world," and the worldly one "is the stronger poet"; she adds the striking thought that "the extreme of mysticism is in this case the extreme of skepticism." Frost's A Masque of Reason shows God still "inept," and Frost, having distrusted theory, "ceases thinking about the whole damned subject." Aiken's hopeful ending receives one dry line: "Such a faith cannot be argued with, naturally." She saves her warmth for Herbert Read, "a dignified humanist of the first water," for whom the cosmos depends on "man, the pitiful incident."

"The Anarchic Principle" (first half)

This roundup centers on Alex Comfort's The Power House, a war novel, and Young puts Comfort in a line with Sterne and Joyce as writers who work from "the anarchic principle that reality is given to us only through our sensations." For them, "the best of reality is an opinion" and "the accident is the only absolute." She defends Comfort's crowded detail, the "children's hands like pink rats' claws," against readers who call it extraneous, because in this view reality is made of "minor episodes" rather than "eyeless seraphim."

Her most searching point is about the enemy. In modern war "one never sees his enemy, his enemy being, alas, everywhere," and she dwells on the French officer Vernier dreaming that he is Ritter, the German who spared him. It carries forward the question at the end of "Old James" about who collaborates in the world's disaster. Part 8 then runs briefly through Denton Welch, Feike Feikema, and William Sansom, and breaks off as she reaches Maxwell's The Folded Leaf, calling it "the least pretentious" and "the most baffling." Given her mockery of the same book in "Complex Life" a year later, the next page should be worth reading.

Across part 8

These reviews show that Young's standards are philosophical before they are stylistic. She rewards writers who accept a world without fixed certainty, whether they are skeptics like Tate and Comfort or visionaries like Broch, and she regards the two as closer than they look, since in Merton and in Van Doren alike "the skeptic meets the mystic." She is cool toward anything that settles the question too early, be it Dowling's God, Aiken's staircase of light, or Frost's shrug. And in every piece, 1945 presses in: the Nazi prison, the long-range artillery, the enemy who turns out to be oneself.
muses-part-7:
Inviting the Muses, Part 7

← Part 6 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 8 →

Part 7 finishes the Van Doren speech, covers the last two essays, "Feminine Sensibility" and "On Teaching," and opens the Reviews section, running through the early Poetry reviews, Jean Stafford's Boston Adventure, and most of a double review of Virginia Woolf and Katherine Anne Porter.

"Memorial Speech in Honor of Mark Van Doren," conclusion (previously unpublished)

The rest of the speech follows the same line: Van Doren's poems deal with fugitive things like a fallen barn that "have no history," and gain enchantment precisely "because they will be snatched away by time or change or inventive progress." Young casts him as a Prospero watching the island fade, knowing that Ariel and Caliban will outlast "the evocative magician." "Reality may be hidden but is not lost," she writes, and she reads his Indians as "the slain people" who are "also the phantoms of undying consciousness, that which cannot be slain." The speech ends on "the dream of a house, a house where the dead live." It is a fitting close to the essays proper, since that could describe much of what Young wrote.

"Feminine Sensibility" (Harvard Advocate, 1975)

A single page, and one of the most direct statements in the book. Young flatly says she does not "think that there is any difference between the works of men and women writers." Her reasoning is Jungian: a woman writer uses her animus and a man his anima, so "these sexual differences dissolve, bearing no relation to art." She turns the usual metaphor around by noting how many men have described their books as children and their writing as labor, citing Sterne and his "all-knowing embryo," and she says "the maternal is that by which the cosmic form is made to evolve from the chaos."

She also answers Woolf's A Room of One's Own without naming it outright. Women were not more protected than men but "less protected," "less in charge of their own fate," and "have not yet attained their liberation." Yet no writer is truly protected, "with or without a room of his own," because "the fact that he or she is a writer shows that he or she is unprotected, exposed to that reality from which others veil themselves by convention and habit." Coming from the author of a thousand-page novel largely about women, written over eighteen years, the essay reads less as theory than as self-description.

"On Teaching" (Review of Contemporary Fiction, 1989)

The latest piece in the collection, and a companion to "Inviting the Muses." Young describes her own work as prose "in a lyric form" or "epic form," and describes her Debs biography in progress as the story of "the failed millennial continent of America," a lost earthly paradise that socialism hoped to restore. She calls that project "history as a poem."

Her advice is to read poems first, because "a novel is an extension of metaphor," grounded in close observation of both dreams and outward events, which keeps a writer from "mechanical fantasies and inventions which simply creak with cleverness." The reading list is generous and revealing: Browning's The Ring and the Book, Dante, Blake, Coleridge, Eliot, Pound, Williams, Hopkins, Yeats, Melville, then Flannery O'Connor, Cynthia Ozick, William Gass, Anne Tyler, James Merrill, and biographies of Dalí, Freud, Jung, and others. Her central text is William James's Psychology, to be read beside Henry James's notebooks, with the note that William "wrote psychology like a novelist" and Henry "wrote novels like a psychologist." William James has now appeared in the Night Thoughts essay, the Patmore essay, and here, which makes him the closest thing she has to a single philosophical source.

The early reviews (Poetry, 1935–36)

These are Young at about twenty-seven, and the surprise is how strict she is. Reviewing Mrs. Hickler's Lower than the Angels ("Domestic Fables"), she praises "a combination of the fabulous with the domestic," which is her own later territory, but keeps her expectations cool. Mary Britton Miller's Intrepid Bird ("Leaning Backward") gets sharper treatment: four sonnets contrasting sparrows and doves are "heavy cargo for birds to carry through fifty-six lines," and on the dedication poem about a bird singing on a branch, "one only wishes the branch had been a little higher, a little more precarious." Florence Ripley Mastin's Cobwebs of Cable ("Uncertain Measures") is credited with extending human nature "beyond the prescriptions of the Marxian legislators," but she asks for poems where "every word of which must seem inevitable in its relation to the whole."

The young critic who scolds "stereotyped diction" and demands organic unity is recognizably the same writer who would later defend Proust's page-long paragraphs. What she wanted was not brevity but necessity.

"The Dusty Interiors of Boston" (Kenyon Review, 1944)

The Stafford review is one of the best pieces in the book. She admires Boston Adventure as "provocative" and "delightful," written "as if an insect recorded those minutiae which escape the average eye," with "a relentless capacity for fact" like Marianne Moore's octopus. But she diagnoses the world it depicts: a Boston where "the tragedy being that there is no tragedy," where "the irrational must be excluded," put out "to whine like an old dog in the dark," and where "God, to be real, would have to appear in a high silk hat." She adds a pointed parallel: the Greeks drowned the man who discovered irrational numbers.

The review is fair to Stafford in a way that is easy to miss. Young sees that the author is not waving "the red flag" and that behind the irony lies "much covert love" for a dying society, embodied in Miss Pride, "checkmating herself at chess throughout eternity, because her father did before her." She places the novel among English comedies of manners from Sheridan and Richardson to Thackeray and Austen, and she ends by saying popular novels like St. Elmo and Tempest and Sunshine deserve "a serious study." Two decades later in "Inviting the Muses" she would hold up those same titles as examples of forgotten bestsellers, so her view of them clearly shifted with context.

"Fictions Mystical and Epical" (Woolf and Porter)

Young reads Woolf's A Haunted House as philosophy, not mood. She places Woolf among "the philosophers of sensationalism," Locke, Hume, Berkeley, and Bergson, and calls her "of the order of grand mystic" whose impressionism is "the result of a grand intellectual discipline." In Woolf "there is a journey, but there is hardly a journeyer," and she ties Woolf to John Stuart Mill's definition of matter as the permanent possibility of sensation, the same Mill she cited in "Complex Life and Complex Letters." She grants that such a view "has never been popular," then concludes, "Mrs. Woolf may have, however, the final word."

With Porter's The Leaning Tower, she focuses on the Texas stories where "the conservation of the past was the great dream," and on the title story's papier-mâché tower in 1931 Germany, broken and mended, suggesting "the persistence of an older value." One sentence about the servant Nannie, noting "no disparagement then of the feudal order," is left unclear in its sympathies, and part 7 stops before Young finishes her judgment.

Across part 7

This section shows Young's whole career in a few dozen pages, from the precise young critic of 1935 to the teacher of 1989 handing students a reading list. The constants are her demand that language be necessary, her belief that reality includes the irrational and the invisible, and her refusal of anything that closes the door on either, whether that is a Boston drawing room, a gendered theory of literature, or a creaky plot. The Stafford and Woolf reviews also show that her sympathy extends to writers quite unlike her, as long as they see clearly.
muses-part-4:
Inviting the Muses, Part 4

← Part 3 · Inviting the Muses: A Reading, Part by Part · Part 5 →

Part 4 covers "The Doll People" in full and the first half of "The Old Sweetheart," which breaks off mid-story as Riley falls for a woman he has never met.

"The Doll People" (Mademoiselle, 1950)

On its surface this is a magazine feature about American dolls. Underneath, it is Young's argument that small, overlooked objects carry a nation's history better than official records. Johnny Gruelle, a political cartoonist, is said to have made a truer "commentary on American life" with Raggedy Ann than with any cartoon, because "everything that happens in the great world is reflected in the little."

The rag doll is her hero: "the oldest doll in America, the original folk doll," sewn from scraps in a scrap bag and "far from perfect, for she was the doll of a pragmatic people who were far from perfect themselves." Her face might be cut from old underwear, her features painted in pokeberry juice, and sometimes, "in the rush of creative events, her nose was forgotten." That detail is Young's kind of comedy, and it also restates her aesthetic from "Complex Life": the imperfect, improvised thing is the honest one.

She reads the doll trade as cultural history. American doll bodies were long fitted with European heads, "a commentary on the intellectual scene, much of our culture also coming from abroad." Only when submarine warfare cut off German doll heads in 1917 did Gruelle revive Raggedy Ann, a doll whose head, "though simple, was her own." There are good anecdotes: pirates who board a ship for gold and find only breakable doll heads; Edward and Wallis dolls made the same size "so that they should not seem conspicuous"; quintuplet dolls sold at birth and at six months to create "the illusion of growth"; Grace Putnam Storey, who modeled a doll on a newborn at a Salvation Army shelter and had to market it "against the obstacles of masculine resistance." One line records "old mammy dolls with nut-brown faces" appearing in the postwar South, and Young passes over the image without comment, the same kind of unexamined period note seen in the Midwest essay.

The essay's second half moves from dolls to Indiana's literature of childhood. Raggedy Ann is linked to Riley's "Little Orphant Annie" and the Raggedy Man, and here Young makes a sharp point about nostalgia. The rag doll represents "a past which may never have been what we think it was," and her colors are "scraps of an illusion." The proof is the real Orphant Annie, Mary Alice Smith. Riley, not knowing where she was, "killed her off in the grand old nineteenth-century manner, just with a stroke of his pen," giving her a death of a broken heart. She turned up after his death, alive on an Indiana farm with the husband who had not died in the war, too busy "shooing the chickens off the porch" to know she had become a legend. It is the plainest statement yet of a theme running through the collection: the story told about a person and the actual person rarely match, and the actual person usually has other things to do.

The ending turns darker. Young brings in Capote and McCullers's The Member of the Wedding, "where John Henry, the child like a little old man, a child who soon will die, plays with a doll." The last line is "And thus we see the impermanence of people, the permanence of things, even of dolls." Set against "My Grandmother's Foot," where the parents love "inanimate objects" as "substitutes for reality," the thought has turned over. Here objects are not a substitute for life but what survives it.

"The Old Sweetheart" (first half)

Riley has now appeared in every part of the book: Old James's poetic rival, the children's poet who "drank to forget the children," the creator of Orphant Annie. This essay finally gives him full attention, and it reads like a chapter from a biography in progress. It is framed as a detective question, "Who was the old sweetheart of James Whitcomb Riley?", and Young warns at once that the search "must take us into the night of the soul." Riley, she notes, asked the same question in his poem.

She builds the portrait from the inside out. His mother wrote poems in the household ledger, believed in fairies, and had heard Swedenborgian ideas from her friend Johnny Appleseed. Her death, when he was not quite twenty-one, drew "something like a lens" over his eyes. Outwardly he was a clown and mimic; his violin was his sweetheart. He later bought back his boyhood home and imagined it furnished, and when Greenfield restored it as a memorial, his poems were the most accurate guide, down to "the pheasant-feather fan that was used to sweep away the ashes." Life was reconstructed from art, which is the reverse of what realist critics expect.

Young names his method directly as a "Proustian dedication to the remembrance of things past," and sees marriage as its enemy: "Should not his wife be rivaled by that greatest love, the past?" That puts Riley alongside Old James, another Indianapolis man preferring memory to the present, though Young treats Riley with far more tenderness.

The candidates follow one at a time, each tied to a keepsake in "the old hair trunk": Nell, who believed in his gifts; Adda, with hair "as black as the midnight shadows," one of the girls passing west on the National Road; and a school-teaching poetess who wanted marriage and a roof, and who could not wait for a poor, sometimes drunk poet. Young gives her a fair hearing. "Who would pay for the firelight?" is a real question, not a sneer. The comedy of his luck is kept, too: a father at the door growling that his daughter "hain't goin' with you. She's got the measles." The famous poem itself, she says, was written in the margins of Blackstone while he studied law, and his poems were stuffed in his hat, his cuffs, the soles of his shoes, falling out of his umbrella "like a flurry of snowflakes."

Part 4 stops just as the strangest candidate arrives: a young woman in a remote forest, introduced by a wandering friend, McClanahan, whom she loves hopelessly. Riley never met her. What he fell for was a tintype of her hand, "satin-cuffed, holding between its long fingers a folded Chinese fan." After the grandmother's foot, the baby's hand in the shoe box, and Moore's bluebird foot, the collection's fascination with the detached body part comes back once more, now as the object of a love that exists only in letters.

Across part 4

Both essays are about the gap between the made thing and the living one. The rag doll and the old sweetheart are both assembled from scraps, and both stand in for a past that may never have existed as remembered. Young is drawn to that longing, and she writes it with real affection, but she keeps setting the real person beside the legend: Mary Alice Smith churning butter, the schoolteacher asking who will pay for the firelight. The permanence she grants to things always comes with a reminder that people moved on.

our-darling-part-6:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 6: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

← Part 5 · Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part · Part 7 →

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). Part 6 completes Susan Strehle's essay on women's time, then gives two of the book's most theoretical pieces: Miriam Fuchs's “Liquescence as Form” and Steven Shaviro's “Exorbitance and Death.” Together they make the collection's strongest case for why Miss MacIntosh, My Darling matters and why the academy has resisted it. Only material that illuminates Young and her work is kept below; quoted phrases from the book are marked with quotation marks.

Time without history

Strehle finishes by showing how thoroughly the novel dissolves historical time. Vera's quest is deliberately diffuse; she vanishes for hundreds of pages, and the long bus ride yields none of the adventures a traditional journey promises, because Young's world rests on the premise that “every heart is the other heart,” so hero and villain, self and other, cannot be cleanly opposed. The patriarchal counter-figure is the gospel salesman Bonebreaker, who speaks for linear striving and consulting his watch so that “every minute counted,” and who flees, struck speechless, when Miss MacIntosh reveals her baldness and her missing breast. Miss MacIntosh instead teaches Vera an ahistorical sense of time, in which death is not a culmination but an ongoing, echoing loss. Strehle sets Young apart from her male contemporaries in the postmodern epic, Pynchon, Barth, Coover, and DeLillo, who pack their books with the elections, wars, and news of the century. Young does the reverse: her coastal starting point and her Indiana ending go unnamed, and history is drained away so that the book can be told entirely from within what Kristeva calls women's time.

Liquescence as form

Fuchs builds her essay from the novel's sheer physical scale, which she takes from Bernard Bergonzi's review: eighteen years of work, some 3,449 pages in typescript, three and a half pounds in the hand. She turns that into her governing metaphor. Just as oil stirred into water divides into suspended particles before rising again, Vera narrates by mixing her recollected figures into small peculiar particles, Miss MacIntosh's bald head, Esther's swollen womb, Mr. Spitzer's double vision, and restirring them whenever the mixture thickens. In this liquid world objects and identities transform without stable boundaries: Catherine insists her lawyer Joachim is an umbrella stand, a pear becomes a glove becomes a basket of peaches, and borders are no more than “the thinnest line thinner than the thinnest thread.” There is almost no clearly delineated action; Vera's quest is openly illogical, “seeking for [Miss MacIntosh] in all those places where she was not,” pursuing a woman already dead and dissolved into ocean and objects. Fuchs reads this as Young's refusal to let the text be reduced to what can be understood and controlled, an embrace of what Alice Jardine calls the “categorically unrepresentable.” When plot does resurface, late and abruptly, through mad Dr. O'Leary, then Esther Longtree's hundred-and-sixty-five pages, then the stone-deaf man arriving eight pages from the end, it only skews the structure further: when Young uses plot, Fuchs argues, she does so to negate its legitimacy. A footnote records a striking fact: John Gardner was Young's pupil at Iowa and wrote his first two novels in her class, and she helped him find his narrative style; he called her novel extraordinary for breadth of mind and verbal genius.

Feminine writing and the dispersal of patriarchy

Both Fuchs and Strehle place the novel as a rare achieved example of the “feminine writing” that Hélène Cixous theorized: prose that wrecks partitions and refuses closure, that in Cixous's phrase “starts on all sides at once,” twenty or thirty times over, rather than driving from origin to conclusion.
