Fuchs argues that Esther Longtree's endless, possibly imaginary pregnancy is the perfect figure for a book that will not move toward climax or birth, and that the whole novel evokes a matriarchal world of mothers, would-be mothers, and daughters in which patriarchal law is dispersed and diluted, its fathers unnameable, its hangman mocked by children. Even the ending refuses to close: Vera reports in the conditional that Esther “would hang” her lunch sign, an act that has not yet happened and may not, suspending the book between action and inaction. Crucially, Fuchs stresses that for Young these feminine qualities, sympathy, nurture, patience, cross gender lines; they surface most movingly in Mr. Spitzer, the aging lawyer trying to comprehend the collapse of the old hierarchies and slowly yielding to the richness of female sentience.

Exorbitance, and why the academy resists it

Shaviro's essay is the boldest defense in the book. He describes entering the novel without guideposts, overwhelmed by its page-long sentences and infinite variations, so that the reader's disorientation mirrors Vera's own. He calls it a “delirious phantasmagoria of memories,” an epic lament of loss whose space of absence is nonetheless “infinitely full rather than infinitely empty.” His central claim is that the book induces a pre-interpretive delirium in the reader, a passion, and that this is exactly why it sits poorly in the academy. Academic criticism is built for modernist abstruseness, self-reflexivity, and formal intricacy, all of which Young supplies, but it cannot handle passion that threatens the critic's distance and mastery. The novel is, Shaviro insists, “as carefully and deliberately crafted as any great twentieth-century work,” yet it is anti-formalist and not metafictional; rather than folding back on itself it “expends itself to infinity.” This “ex-orbitance” marks a mutation in English-language modernism. Where Joyce, Pound, and Nabokov generate scholarly industries devoted to mastery, Young creates a different audience, a community of readers bound by a shared experience rather than a fraternity of scholars, and she feels none of the elitist male modernist compulsion to impose order on chaos, subverting instead the very dualisms, subject and object, male and female, individual and society, on which that modernism feeds. He notes, tellingly, that the book contains almost no dialogue, only multiple monologues, because dialogue would imply a reconciliation this radically pluralistic world does not allow.

A celebration of ordinary life

Shaviro closes on the novel's philosophy of the real, which he reads as its deepest achievement. Young grants every experience its own reality: a delusion or a hallucination is an actual event, and in Vera's words “even the unreal things were real,” including the ignored, the rejected, and the lost. The real is embedded in the imaginary rather than opposed to it, every actuality produced by a movement of desire, and the fact that all desires are disappointed does not cancel this but confirms it, since the unreality of failure is itself perfectly real. Death saturates the book to the point of obsession, yet even death is not conclusive; there is no final harmony and no return to silence, only an open, forever-varied passage. Shaviro's last point is the one worth keeping: for all its extravagance, Young's vision is not transcendent or otherworldly. What the novel offers is a vivid perception and a celebration of something available to everyone, at every moment, in ordinary life.
our-darling-part-1:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 1: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part · Part 2 →

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). This covers the front matter, Fuchs's introduction, Martha J. Sattler's chronology, and the first tributes. What follows keeps only the material that sheds light on Young and her work. Fond praise with nothing behind it has been left out. Quoted phrases from the book are marked with quotation marks.

The shape of a life

Young was born in Indianapolis on August 26, 1908, daughter of Chester Ellis Young and Fay Knight Young. Her parents separated in 1911, and she and her younger sister were raised by their maternal grandmother, Marguerite Herron Knight. She began writing poems as a child and joined a young authors' league at eleven. After the University of Indiana she took a BA in English and French from Butler University in 1930, the same year her poems first appeared in Poetry. She earned an MA at the University of Chicago in 1936, studying Elizabethan and Jacobean literature under Robert Morss Lovett, Ronald S. Crane, and T. V. Smith, and sitting in on Thornton Wilder's seminar alongside Gertrude Stein and Paul Goodman.

Two teaching facts matter for her place in American letters: at Shortridge High School in Indianapolis her students included Kurt Vonnegut, and at the University of Iowa in the mid-1950s she taught John Gardner. Her first book, Prismatic Ground, appeared in 1937, followed by Moderate Fable (1944) and Angel in the Forest (1945), her account of the utopian communities at New Harmony, Indiana. Her monumental novel Miss MacIntosh, My Darling was published by Scribner's in 1965, roughly two decades after the first forty pages, then titled “The Worm in the Wheat,” were accepted by the editor Maxwell Perkins. She spent her later decades on a vast biography of the socialist Eugene V. Debs, setting aside an earlier biography of the Indiana poet James Whitcomb Riley to do it.

The literary company she kept is part of the record: early readers and editors of her work included Mark Van Doren and Albert Erskine; she met Mari Sandoz and Anaïs Nin in the 1940s, formed a lasting friendship with Nin, spent time at Yaddo with Carson McCullers and Truman Capote, and served as fiction editor of the journal Tiger's Eye. In Rome in the early 1950s she met Princess Marguerite Caetani, whose review Botteghe Oscura published her story “The Opium Lady.”

How she worked

Fuchs draws out a working method that explains the strangeness of Young's output. Young completed major portions of her narratives long before they reached print, and she said in 1988 that “All the books were written together, from the beginning.” Her books were not sealed off from one another; Fuchs describes borders in her work as no more than “the thinnest line,” thinner than a thread of starlight. The same preoccupations run through her journalism of the 1940s and 1950s as through the novel: utopias, the Midwest, dolls, horses, the world of sounds, and the realm of the deaf.

Amy Clampitt records the pivot from poet to novelist in Young's own account. Having begun Angel in the Forest as verse, Young found she “couldn't fit in all the facts, which are fabulous,” and inclusiveness became her method. Clampitt reads this drive to take in the concrete, the peculiar, and the local as what made it so hard for Young to stop writing Miss MacIntosh. John J. Stephan's memory of visiting Young's hotel room in Rome makes the method physical: a “paperscape” of unopened onion skin, ridges of typescript, and crumpled discards, with a New York editor eager to publish and unable to pry the manuscript loose.

What the critics actually argue

Anna Balakian places Young among the innovators who turn the regional into the mythic. She argues that Miss MacIntosh breaks the ordinary rules of how myth is thought to form, deliberately sowing new myths, and she puts the novel beside Proust's work as something the era has not yet caught up with. For years Balakian taught a course, “The Metamorphosis of the Novel,” that ran from Dostoevsky to Young, and she notes that Young's reputation was spreading abroad faster than at home.

Clampitt's essay is more than reminiscence. She reads Young as a distinctly Midwestern imagination shaped by the flat interior, “the depressed middle,” and she ties Young's suspicion of authority to that landscape and to her sympathy for Debs. The detail Clampitt keeps returning to, a passage on George III in his madness idly picking out a note on a harpsichord, she offers as typical of how Young undercuts power.

Fuchs's introduction usefully summarizes the scholarly essays that follow. Charles Ruas traces Young's epic imagination across Angel in the Forest, the unpublished Riley biography, and the Debs project, treating them as chapters of American history. Suzanne Oboler reads the novel's largesse as an argument about diversity and multiculturalism in American culture. Martha Sattler emphasizes its turn toward female personages and a female culture. Fatima Shaik attends to its language, poised between “the flimsy” and “the sublime.” Susan Strehle argues the novel replaces linear historical time with what Kristeva called “Women's Time.” Steven Shaviro finds a phantasmagoria that “expends itself to infinity” yet celebrates the ordinary. Fuchs's own reading treats the book's world without exclusions as a rare instance of genuinely “feminine” writing.

The real people inside the fiction

Young insisted she did not invent the characters she wrote about, and the chronology names several living models. Minna Weissenbach, to whom Young read as a young woman in Chicago, became “The Opium Lady.” The artist Howard Mitcham was the model for the stone-deaf man in Miss MacIntosh. Stephan's family, who ran Tiger's Eye from Bleecker Street a few doors from Young, watched the character Mr. Spitzer take shape; a 1948 note in the journal already predicted the novel was “reaching epic proportions.”

One small cultural trace is worth keeping: Anne Tyler used Miss MacIntosh as her wandering hero's traveling companion, and a hardback copy turns up in the film of her novel The Accidental Tourist, tucked into the hero's suitcase.

In her own words

Fuchs closes with Young's answer to a question she used to put to her students, about why anyone chooses to write prose fiction: “They want to be known and loved beyond their time. Here was I, this was what I thought, this was what I felt.”
our-darling-part-3:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 3: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

← Part 2 · Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part · Part 4 →

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). Part 3 completes Jean Petrolle's essay, then gives Reinhard Friederich's account of rereading the novel, Erika Duncan's essay on Esther Longtree, and the opening of Miriam Fuchs's essay on Young's utopias. This is the most critically dense stretch of the book so far. Only the material that illuminates Young and her work is kept below; personal digression and pure praise are left out. Quoted phrases from the book are marked with quotation marks.

Imagination makes reality, so fictions have stakes

Petrolle closes her reading by drawing the ethical edge out of the novel's premise. If imagination and language actually produce the reality a person lives in, then the fictions a culture chooses matter. She distinguishes two kinds of fiction-maker in the book. Catherine Cartwheel knowingly creates her own fictions and so lives inside beautiful ones; Miss MacIntosh accepts the culture's ready-made fictions, the supposed facts of geography, history, science, and morality, without recognizing them as fictions at all, and so cannot escape the ugliness they impose on her, down to her belief that her own baldness is ugly. From this Petrolle raises the book's implicit challenge to the inherited canon: if writers, readers, and dreamers determine reality by incantation, why keep telling the old stories in which only men are adventurers and only women are raped. She places Young in a modernist strand marked by formal experiment and dense self-reflexive texture, alongside H.D., Joyce, Anna Kavan, Nabokov, Proust, Dorothy Richardson, and Woolf, and finds its philosophical cousins in Wittgenstein, Santayana, Dewey, and Mead, thinkers who put imagination and language at the center of being.

How the novel is built, and how to read it

Reinhard Friederich's essay is the most useful firsthand account of what reading Miss MacIntosh is actually like. He had failed to finish the fourteen-hundred-page novel four or five times over twenty-five years, always stalling partway. What finally worked was reading fast, a “leap-and-linger” motion that matched the book's own central movement, the rapid bus journey through night and day carrying interlaced memories and dreams. He describes the prose as a cumulative, symphonic thing, “a fractal method of harmonizing variations” that refuses to be recapitulated or excerpted, so that reading dissolves into a kind of seeing. His governing term is the novel's “life-world,” a totality that has to be taken in whole before analysis is possible, and he ranks the book with Tristram Shandy, Broch's Death of Virgil, Williams's Paterson, Murasaki's Genji, and Dostoevsky. Within that flow he singles out the novel's range of registers: the frog-musician grotesque, which opens as a tall tale in the American vein of Twain and Faulkner before turning meditative, and the hangman's tale, evidence of Young's “terse precision” when she wants it. His conclusion is thematic as well as technical: in this book loss is what creates splendor, and nothing concludes so much as it opens. He ends by placing Young with Whitman, Sandburg, and Dickinson, and even with Bessie Smith and Charlie Parker, as a maker of a democratic and difficult joy.

Esther Longtree and pregnancy as an epic subject

Erika Duncan's essay centers on Esther Longtree, the novel's perpetually pregnant woman, forever carrying the never-to-be-born and the shadow child. Setting aside Duncan's personal frame, the critical claim is striking: she argues that Young may have written serious literature's first full exploration of pregnancy, and that it could only be done inside an epic of this scale. Duncan reads the roughly hundred-page Esther section as the fruition of everything seeded across the earlier thousand pages, built by doubling and told largely in reverse, so that the murder that would explain everything surfaces only long after the reader feels its weight. She connects it to Adrienne Rich's Of Woman Born: it is precisely Esther's near-unconscious killing of her one live-born child that opens the many-sided treatment of the pregnant psyche, widening to take in all who have borne children and all who never have. Duncan also supplies a working detail, that while writing the novel Young was immersed in her biography of James Whitcomb Riley, “the little orphan Annie poet,” and drawn to figures like Fourier, the apostle of universal love who died alone with only his cats. The essay's closing sickbed scene yields two of Young's own lines: that the whole enterprise is “all a matter of research,” and, in Duncan's phrase, that Young was always “an opponent of the medium and the mean.”

Utopia, loss, and the value of the incomplete

Miriam Fuchs's essay reads all of Young's work as utopian in a particular sense: it enacts both the longing for an ideal and the impossibility of reaching it. Young fills her books with bungled jobs, confused messages, lost causes, and abandoned paradises, from the failed communities of George Rapp and Robert Owen at New Harmony in Angel in the Forest to Miss MacIntosh walking off into the Atlantic, leaving behind a corset, a red wig, and glassless spectacles. Fuchs argues that for Young partial success is the only success there is, and that her characters' broken visions are, in the novel's own words, “more complete in their incompletion than if they had been whole.” She points to a revealing habit: Young has said she never managed to finish the story of a flour miller trying to pass his thumbprint to his son, so she has folded it into each successive manuscript, never telling it whole, because the whole version would be the illusion. Creation is always flawed, and Young enacts the flaw rather than hiding it, echoing the undertaker in Angel in the Forest who warns that no one can remove the flaws from the universe without destroying it.

Against binary logic and the single self

Fuchs frames Young's deepest subversion as an assault on the either/or categories of Western thought, the fixed oppositions of masculine and feminine, order and chaos, self and other. In Young's world every soul is also the other soul, so nothing is singular; her characters are mutable, never fully themselves and never quite the other either. Fuchs aligns this with Hélène Cixous's critique of how fiction “fetishizes” a single privileged self, and reads Catherine Cartwheel's dissolving first person, the wealthy opium addict who says she is eating herself, is the divan and the mirror and Brooklyn Bridge, as prose that refuses to settle on any coherent subject. Passages like this run for chapters, doubling and multiplying their images rather than resolving.

Her own claim, and her place outside the canon

Fuchs uses Young's own words to explain why the late turn to biography is no departure. Young insists the clean lines separating poetry, prose, fiction, nonfiction, realism, and experiment belong “not to writers, but to critics,” because the poetry of nonfiction is as fabulous as any poetry she could write in fiction. Fuchs is candid that this refusal of category has cost Young her standing: as an experimental writer who is also a woman, she is twice removed from the mainstream, and despite William Goyen's 1965 praise of the novel as a work of “stunning magnitude and beauty,” she remains neglected by critics and unsanctioned by the canon. The book gathers the counterclaims of her admirers: Duncan calls the work an epic elegy for all creation, and Balakian ranks Young among the most innovative novelists of the age, what Gertrude Stein was to its beginning but, in Balakian's phrase, “so much more human, more poetic, visionary.”
our-darling-part-2:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 2: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

← Part 1 · Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part · Part 3 →

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). Part 2 runs from the close of John J. Stephan's recollection through the tributes by Peter Marchant, Rob Wynne, Michael and Betty Higgins, Caroline Sandoz Pifer, Gail Cohen, LaVerne Harrell Clark, and Lee Harrod, and into Jean Petrolle's critical essay. Only the material that illuminates Young and her work is kept below; fond praise without substance is left out. Quoted phrases from the book are marked with quotation marks.

Her teaching and her aesthetic

Peter Marchant's account of her Iowa workshop is the clearest window in this section onto how Young thought about writing. When he pruned his story to its bare action, she made him restore everything he had cut, telling him he had crossed out the best parts and left only surface. Her editorial instinct ran directly against realist tidiness: she told him the “logistical realities” did not matter and that a detail's factual impossibility was beside the point if it belonged to the character's inner life. Her standing advice was to stop hiding behind easy, realistic action, to “explore the phantasmagoric below the surface,” and to let the unconscious take over. Asked by his class why people write, students offered money, fame, and being unheard at home; Young's answer was that they all wrote “because you want to be loved.” Marchant notes that she gave her students more time and energy than she gave her own work, even while she was deep in Miss MacIntosh.

The method and philosophy of the novel

Several contributors try to name what Young was actually doing in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. LaVerne Harrell Clark quotes a letter Young wrote for Clark's anthology Focus 101 in which Young described her own governing thesis: that there is no reality except, realistically, its unreality, a thesis carried by musicalizations, rhapsodies, and symbolizations that double back on themselves in an oceanic tumult. Clark points back to the early poem “That Chance” in Moderate Fable (1944), whose lines about “deviation from the law / In lonely items of the real” she reads as the same principle underlying the novel's prose. She cites the novelist William Goyen, who called the book's method “classification through amassment” and described it as a mammoth epic and a massive dream, and she reports that Kurt Vonnegut championed the book as the work of a genius.

Clark also records a telling gesture about the book's form. At the end of her Tucson visit Young handed Clark ten or more hotel keys she had carried off during her travels and asked her to mail them back. Clark reads this as Young demonstrating what she believed about prose: that there is no real end, no closure adequate to any ending. Young's own resistance to finishing bears this out. Clark notes the novel was “eighteen years in the making primarily because of its epic dimensions,” and Stephan's memory of the Rome manuscript, a “paperscape” the author would not surrender to an eager editor, shows the same reluctance to close.

Jean Petrolle's essay is the most sustained reading here. She frames the novel as a “magical metaphysic,” a world in which imagination, in the forms of dream, language, and fiction, does not merely describe reality but creates it. She draws on the novel's own voices: Mr. Spitzer's conviction that “Nothing lived except through imagination,” and his sense of standing at a hedge between overlapping worlds. Petrolle argues that the book's dense intertextuality, its kinship with Nabokov, Woolf, Proust, and Joyce, mirrors that multiplicity of worlds, and that Vera Cartwheel's dreaming and shifting speech enact the same idea, that words and dreams construct reality. She places the novel's excess, what the critic Steven Shaviro called its “exorbitance,” in the company of Proust's Recherche.

Poetry and prose as one continuum

Clark's tribute makes plain that Young did not treat the border between poetry and prose as fixed. Young was the first prose writer Clark scheduled for the University of Arizona Poetry Center, over a board that wanted only poets, and Clark's own argument for her was that Miss MacIntosh is in effect a long poem. At the reading itself Young insisted on reading from her poetry collections, Prismatic Ground and Moderate Fable, rather than from the novel, and tried to persuade Clark that the two were of a piece, that the line between poetry and prose in her work was not real.

Influences and kinship

Lee Harrod's recollection of the 1988 Trenton conference turns on Robert Browning. After her reading, what Young wanted to discuss was not her own characters but Browning, whose well-thumbed book, she said, had nurtured her and served as a source of many voices. The connection is pointed: Browning's dramatic monologues, many-voiced and often neglected by critics, stand behind the chorus of voices in her own work. Melville is another touchstone; Stephan recalls reading Moby-Dick aloud with her, and the whale surfaces again in Harrod's parting scene. Clark and Petrolle between them name a wider company for the novel, Joyce and Faulkner for its style, Proust and Nabokov and Woolf for its world.

The world of the novel: voices and music

Rob Wynne's account of producing Miss MacIntosh for WBAI radio catalogs the novel's cast and texture. Among its characters are Miss MacIntosh, Vera Cartwheel, Mr. Spitzer, Mr. Chandelier, the Opium Lady, Old Doc, Cousin Hannah, the Frog Musician, the Bible Salesman, the Arctic Explorer, the Hangman, and Esther Longtree, the carrier of life and death. For the broadcast Wynne assigned each major figure a sound or musical leitmotif, using Mozart's “Adagio for Glass Harmonica” for Miss MacIntosh herself, so that the ethereal, dreamy instrument announced her arrival. His premise was that the book's language is so poetic that concrete sounds could underline it, an outside reader's confirmation of how musical Young's prose is.

Reception, milieu, and later work

Fragments across these tributes sketch the novel's standing and the life around it. Contemporaries called it the distinctive novel of its decade and, in the pianist Wayne McEvilly's phrase, the Great American Novel, with excerpts appearing in well-known journals before the book was complete. Gail Cohen describes the salon Young kept at Pennyfeather's restaurant in Greenwich Village and mentions plans, never realized, to stage Miss MacIntosh as a play. Her teaching spanned the New School for Social Research, Fordham, and Seton Hall. And through the later chapters she is at work on the multivolume biography of Eugene V. Debs, having set aside her study of the Indiana poet of her childhood, James Whitcomb Riley.
our-darling-part-4:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 4: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

← Part 3 · Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part · Part 5 →

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). Part 4 completes Miriam Fuchs's essay on Young's utopias and then gives three more scholarly essays: Lillian S. Robinson on narrative and redemption, Peter G. Christensen's William Jamesian reading of Angel in the Forest, and Charles Ruas on the epic imagination. This is the densest critical stretch of the book, and the Ruas essay is the fullest account so far of how Young understood her own project. Only material that illuminates Young and her work is kept below. Quoted phrases from the book are marked with quotation marks.

The utopian pattern, completed

Fuchs finishes her argument by showing how deeply the theme of glorious failure runs through Young's whole imagination. She points to the giraffe poem in Moderate Fable, where Young celebrates a creature that survives “beyond the curve of probables,” and to a whole menagerie of anomalies, the unicorn, the deer-footed mouse, the flytrap flower, that stand for imperfection as the condition of existence itself: it is in confusion, Young writes, that “our only existence [is] possible.” These oddities are kin to the misfits of Miss MacIntosh, the blind painter and the one-legged dancer, the culture's dispossessed. Angel in the Forest is her tribute to two more failures, the utopian communities of George Rapp and Robert Owen at New Harmony, and Fuchs reads the book's meaning as fluctuating rather than fixed: the more failures Young chronicles, the more ubiquitous utopia becomes, so that utopia is constituted by all its collapsing attempts rather than by any single achieved one. Fuchs adds a useful compositional fact from Young herself: Angel began as sixty ballads, was rewritten in blank verse, and took its final prose form over roughly three years, a “poetic compilation of individual portraits and collective histories.” The governing law is that there must always be a flaw, the flaw that heightens the crystal, and the unfinished tale of the flour miller, folded into book after book, is its emblem. What is “no-place” and many places in Angel becomes an “everyplace” in Miss MacIntosh, whose only landscape, Vera says, is the soul's. Fuchs ends on the image of Cousin Hannah's forty locked trunks and forty keys, always one key too many or too few, the mystery that cannot be solved, and on Young's decision to break off her twelve-hundred-page novel abruptly, because no single revelation could ever contain her utopia.

A whole world made of stories

Lillian Robinson borrows a phrase from her own review of Margaret Atwood to name what Young achieves: “a book that is a whole world,” and, more rarely, one with a woman's inner life at its center. She maps the novel's cosmos as three layers, a limited or forgetful God at the top, the solid middle earth of geography and government where Miss MacIntosh herself is rooted, and the individual mind as microcosm of the whole. What binds those layers is narrative: the book is made of hundreds of stories, a patchwork quilt of them. Robinson sets it against the encyclopedic tradition of Dante, but marks the crucial difference in the ending. Where Dante's quest rises to divine love, Young's ends on one more small constituent story, the restaurant sign reading “Bee bak in a whale,” a deliberately unimportant line that turns the reader back into the text rather than up toward perfection. For Robinson the point is that Young lets women's stories matter simply as stories, an assurance she says rarely coexists with the creation of a comprehensive fictional world. She also reads the heroine's birthplace, What Cheer, Iowa, as the flat middle of the country, a “Plantation without the Providence,” standing for the plain and ordinary against which the novel's cosmic theology pushes.

Politics, prophecy, and Angel in the Forest

Robinson and Christensen together bring out the political spine of Young's work. Robinson argues that Miss MacIntosh is intentionally incomplete, one part of a larger whole that includes Angel in the Forest and the forthcoming Debs epic, “Prelude in the Golden Key”; these more explicitly political books share the novel's visionary character. She names Young's antecedents precisely: Blake, building a New Jerusalem against the dark Satanic mills, and Bunyan, whose Pilgrim's Progress is Miss MacIntosh's favorite text and lends its title to the Robert Owen chapter of Angel. Debs is prized as a prophet and seer; Robinson calls Eugene Debs in prison Young's moral equivalent of Jesus on the Mount. Cousin Hannah carries the same visionary charge into the suffrage struggle, her battles fought as much in literature as in electoral politics. Christensen reads Angel in the Forest through William James's Varieties of Religious Experience. He shows Father Rapp as the ruin of belief turned tyrannical, a man who listens to no voice but his own until, in Young's words, “As vice-regent of the Deity, Father Rapp left nothing to the Deity.” Rapp's obsession with apocalypse and election, his retributive religion, even the killing of his own son, all fail the everyday human world, and Young links his apocalyptic fire to real industrial devastation. Owen, opposing imperialism with social harmony, is the counter-figure, and Christensen ties Young's mockery of aggressive Christian empire to James's own anti-imperialism. His conclusion is that Angel is less a study of religious psychology than “a defense of socialism with a human face,” placing society over the individual through Young's own image: stop thinking about flour, the individual, and think about bread, the collective.

How Young placed herself

Charles Ruas's essay is the clearest record of Young's own account of her lineage and method. She described herself as belonging to a tradition of “objective imagination,” reaching back to Milton and Spenser and forward through a novelistic line she claimed as her own: Balzac's human comedy, and more especially Sterne, Gogol, Dickens, Melville, and Dreiser. Pointedly, she distanced herself from Gertrude Stein, arguing that Stein practiced automatic writing while her own repetition and incantation grew out of writing poetry, and she claimed instead to be a disciple of William James and his pluralism, with a debt to Henry James for sensibility. Her strongest statement of method is an alliance with Browning: like him, she said, “I don't believe in inventing characters,” pointing to The Ring and the Book, built from history, as her model. Ruas lays out the novel's architecture, circling the disappearance of Miss MacIntosh around four archetypal figures, the governess, the Opium Lady, Mr. Spitzer, and Esther Longtree, each an archetype large enough to contain its own opposite; a proposed paperback edition would have subtitled its volumes Inquest, Opium, Twin, and Mule. Young defined her character-making as projection: she pours into the heightened image of a figure everything she thinks it is and might become, and insists that even a minor character must have a problem, or it is only “a name on a page.” Ruas closes on the scale of the ambition, noting the chapters given to the last passenger pigeon and the monarch butterfly's migration, Young's reach toward geological time, and her acceptance, echoing McCullers's line that “the novel is the epic of modernity,” of her generation's challenge to write the Great American Novel, an American epic modeled on Joyce's epic of Dublin.
our-darling-part-7:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 7: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

← Part 6 · Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). This final part contains the two conversations that close the book, a long interview conducted by Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs on 23 March 1988 and a brief conversation with Fuchs at St. Vincent's Hospital on 1 June 1993, followed by the contributors' notes. Because these are Young's own words, this is the most valuable section in the book for understanding her aims. Only material that illuminates Young and her work is kept below; quoted phrases are marked with quotation marks.

Everything she wrote is a search for utopia

Young traces the origin of Angel in the Forest to an accidental encounter with coal miners from the Ozarks living a wandering life that reminded her of Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath; talking with them led her to write about New Harmony. From this she draws a general principle: “Every real book is, no matter what the subject,” based on social consciousness, and a good writer cannot avoid it. Asked to describe her own obsession, she gives the clearest statement of her whole project: all her work explores the human desire for utopia, and the structure of every book is the search for utopias lost and rediscovered, true of Miss MacIntosh, Moderate Fable, Prismatic Ground, Angel in the Forest, and the Debs manuscript alike. Underlying all of it is the recognition that there is no single reality, and yet, as she puts it, the beauty is that you go on walking toward a utopia that may not exist, “on a bridge which might end before you reach the other side.”

The flour miller and the passage of the soul

In her own voice Young confirms the detail the critics kept circling. She was first inspired to write about New Harmony by an account of a flour miller who tried to pass his thumbmark to his son, a son who then killed himself. She wrote a short story about it that failed because it was too difficult, and ever since she has folded that flour miller and his thumb into everything she has written, because it is “the thing I never could write, the idea of identity and passage of the soul.” She explains that the recurring objects in Miss MacIntosh, a coin becoming a drachma becoming a poker chip, are references to transmutation, transmigration, metempsychosis, resurrection, and loss of identity. She also names the unfinished novellas she still hoped to publish, several built around Mr. Spitzer, including one about his effort to reach King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, to find a pony that had supposedly belonged to Queen Victoria, which she calls “a quest for something that cannot be found.”

Genre belongs to critics, and she is traditional, not experimental

Young insists the distinctions between poetry and prose, and between fiction and nonfiction, belong “not to writers, but to critics.” She finds no real difference between fiction and biography, holds that the poetry of nonfiction is as fabulous as any poetry in a novel, and says the novel as poem differs from the lyric only in length. She has never altered her style in anything she wrote, would never write realistic prose, and has been willing to go years without publishing, because “the style is the writing.” Strikingly, she rejects the label of experimentalist and calls herself traditional, placing her work in a Grand Tradition that runs back through Sterne, Gogol, Dickens, and Poe to Don Quixote, and rooted in the Bible, Saint Augustine, and, she stresses, the poetry of Joseph Smith and the Mormons. She denies being influenced by Joyce and resents the common claim that she echoes Eliot, explaining that she and Eliot merely studied the same sources at the University of Chicago, where she majored in epic literature under Robert Morss Lovett and read Tom Jones thirteen times in Ronald Crane's class. Miss MacIntosh has no beginning, middle, or end, she says, simply “because life has no beginning, middle, or end.”

“I don't make up anything”

The 1993 hospital conversation confirms, from Young herself, the Browning credo the earlier essays reported. Pressed on whether the stone-deaf community and the doctor who delivered imaginary babies could really be true, she answers flatly that they are: she lived in the house with the doctor, knew him, knew Dr. O'Leary and his violin, the man who could not hear the telephone ring and who told Esther Longtree she would never die in childbirth. “I don't make up anything,” she says. “I always know if it didn't happen.” When Fuchs presses on the strangeness of these recollected details, insisting they seem somewhat improbable, Young holds her ground, replies that they were all true, and finally turns the question back: “Well, what is the truth?” This is the same conviction that surfaced throughout the tributes, that she transcribes a real if transfigured world rather than inventing one.

Debs, Riley, and obsession as the engine

Young explains the turn to Eugene Debs as a matter of utopia: knowing what she knew about utopia, the only question was why not Debs, who spoke to ordinary people in poems and images drawn from The Arabian Nights, Poe, Don Quixote, and Dickens. She did not choose him, she says; “He chose me.” The path ran through James Whitcomb Riley, the poet of her Indiana childhood and, she notes, Debs's drinking companion; their conversations about how to reach utopia drew her from the Riley biography, nearly finished, into the Debs project, which grew from a short book into a three-volume epic of some 2,400 pages. She frames obsession as the precondition of all writing: if you have no obsessions, don't write. Debs was obsessed, Riley was obsessed, her characters are obsessed, and so are the historical figures in the Debs book, among them Emma Goldman and Margaret Anderson. She describes a lost book on the art of presenting a whole life in three or four pages, a method she adopted, and recalls the punishing regimen behind Miss MacIntosh: teaching from nine to four, sleeping an hour, writing from six until midnight, night after night. Mark Van Doren, she notes, named this quality in his introduction to Angel in the Forest, calling her effort to capture illusion an “unkillable concern.”

The rage against women, and her own neglect

Young is candid about the reception of her work. At the time she did not resent the attention paid to male experimental writers, because she always believed many of the great writers were women, naming Kay Boyle, Katherine Anne Porter, Christina Stead, Katherine Mansfield, Anna Kavan, and Jane Bowles, and because she thought of herself not as a woman or a man but as someone “doomed to be a writer.” But after Miss MacIntosh she found herself the victim of brutal male reviewers whose tone was “sometimes hysterical,” who suggested that had she married she never would have written such a book, when, as she says of Kay Boyle, one could have “a baby with every book.” She grants that William Goyen and some other men wrote beautiful reviews, but she has come to believe “there is a rage against women” that she did not notice at the time because she was absorbed in teaching and writing. She adds a practical afterthought: the novel would have sold far more copies had it been published one volume at a time.

Her closing self-definition

The book ends on Young's own answer to the question she used to put to her students, why anyone writes. Her reply, which Fuchs also placed at the front of the volume, is that people write to be known and loved beyond their time: “Here was I, this was what I thought, this was what I felt.” A few facts from the contributors' notes round out the record: Charles Ruas conducted the Paris Review interview with Young in its Winter 1981 issue and situated her among peers such as Capote, Tennessee Williams, Burroughs, Morrison, and Sontag; Martha Sattler completed a full descriptive bibliography of Young's work for Dalkey Archive; and Ann Tyler credits Miss MacIntosh as having proved helpful to her own The Accidental Tourist.
our-darling-part-5:
Marguerite Young, Our Darling, Part 5: What It Reveals About Young and Her Work

← Part 4 · Marguerite Young, Our Darling: What It Reveals, Part by Part · Part 6 →

Source: Marguerite Young, Our Darling: Tributes and Essays, edited by Miriam Fuchs (Dalkey Archive Press, 1994). Part 5 gathers five scholarly essays on Miss MacIntosh, My Darling: Erika Duncan on the novel as elegy, Suzanne Oboler on the American dream, Martha J. Sattler on woman's experience, Fatima Shaik on the subconscious, and the opening of Susan Strehle on women's time. They converge on two claims, that the book is an American epic and that it narrates female experience in a new way. Only material that illuminates Young and her work is kept below; quoted phrases from the book are marked with quotation marks.

An epic elegy for all creation

Erika Duncan reads the novel as an elegy and locates its origin precisely: Miss MacIntosh was begun in the shadow of the atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and it becomes an ode to humanity's futile search for perfection through which the beauty of the flawed, striving soul is revealed. She hears its keynote already in the poem “Death by Rarity” in Moderate Fable, a lament for extinct birds built on the idea that “rarity precedes extinction,” a celebration of the singular thing never to be known the same way again. Duncan is especially good on Young's technique. Where ordinary narrative builds a sense of place and plot from escalating outlines of what is, Young's prose works by a rapid, kaleidoscopic falling away of possibilities, a visible disappearance of all that might be but is not, so that reading becomes a matter of seeing patterns emerge from a tapestry in which every sentence holds infinite possibility. Beneath the twelve hundred pages she finds a single simple duality: Vera Cartwheel is torn between her opium-addicted mother, who lives in a stationary world of preserved beauty and waking dream, and the nursemaid Miss MacIntosh, the mover and doer who searches only for tangible reality and so must drown. What Duncan calls Young's particular genius is simultaneity, the capacity to sustain overtly allegorical figures without losing their human warmth, so that the psychological and the philosophical do not cancel each other. The quest ends not in despair but in Esther Longtree gathered at the wedding as “our love, all our loves.”

The American epic and its cultural reality

Suzanne Oboler frames the novel as a study of American cultural reality and pairs it, pointedly, with García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, published the same year, 1965. Both books break the boundaries of their cultures by reorganizing time and space, yet one became a touchstone of Latin American identity while Young's remains neglected. Oboler's central argument is that Young treats American reality as irreducibly plural: it resembles, in Young's own image, “a hawk rather than a tamed canary easily caged in definitions.” The book journeys through the country's inherited institutions to expose common sense itself as the deepest American illusion, and it insists that a nation's culture is not external to its people but exists in how they interpret their daily lives, so that culture becomes the collective “organization of illusion, of memory.” Oboler ties this to Young's self-description in the Ruas interview, “I'm a pluralistic person,” a pluralism she sees expressed even in Young's layered Afghan and Latin American street dress. She sets the novel against the 1870 to 1930 span of American history and its ambivalence about electric modernity, and reports Young's own rueful line about the eighteen-year labor: “If I had known it was going to take me so long to finish, I might never have started it.”

An epic of woman, and women's time

Martha Sattler reads the same epic as a study of the nature and inner life of woman, organized around motherhood, the one thing only a woman can do. The novel opens with a pregnant wife who resists her own condition; Vera's mother assigns her child to a governess and retreats into opium; and at the center stands Esther Longtree, “the mother of us all,” a tragic figure of endless pregnancy whose births may all be imagined, whom Sattler links to Oriana Fallaci's Letter to a Child Never Born. Sattler catalogs the book's women as archetypes across class and age: the abandoned Catherine Cartwheel escaping into her own dream world; Miss MacIntosh the old maid, her scars hidden under a red wig, betrayed by the gospel salesman Bonebreaker; and Cousin Hannah the great suffragette, whose forty locked trunks turn out to hold forty unworn wedding dresses, a secret hunger for love beneath the public cause. Susan Strehle sharpens this into a formal claim using Julia Kristeva's essay “Women's Time.” Against linear, historical, teleological time, the time of conventional narrative with its beginnings and endings, Kristeva sets a female temporality of repetition and eternity, of cycles and gestation. Strehle argues that at every level, from its nonlinear syntax to its inversion of linear plot, Miss MacIntosh replaces historical time with this female subjectivity, which is exactly why the twelve-hundred-page book lacks the tidy progression critics expect. She is candid about the cost: the novel struck early reviewers as “unreadable,” drew as much condemnation as praise, and sank into obscurity while keeping an underground readership.

The poetry of the subconscious

Fatima Shaik, herself a fiction writer, reads the novel as poetry drawn straight from the subconscious. She argues that Young gives herself over to the wisdom of her deepest dreams, trusting that the poetic speech of the inner mind will yield universal wisdom out of particulars. In Shaik's account the prose works by association, one flashing image linked to the next until phrases close back on their beginnings like smoke rings, carrying recurring polarities of yin and yang, angel and devil, light and dark. Its method is to include everything, even what Young calls “trumpery and frumpery and junk,” so that seemingly chaotic rhyming runs of words lead into profound pronouncements, the book moving easily “from the flimsy to the sublime.” Shaik describes this as the transcription of an inner chant, a private rhythm that every reader can sense, which is why the dense continuity of the language nonetheless reads effortlessly. The unifying drive she finds beneath it is toward wholeness, the reconciliation of opposites, two halves of a divided heart made one.
harp-post-03-the-tailor-and-the-poet:
Chapter 3. The Tailor and the Poet

← Chapter 2 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 4 →

Why a biography of an Indiana railroad man spends sixty pages in Germany and Paris

On page 22 of Harp Song for a Radical, Daniel Debs is waiting in New York. It is 1849. He has crossed the Atlantic ahead of Marguerite Bettrich, the mill girl he loves, and has already been swindled out of most of his inheritance by a confidence man. He is staying at the Shakespeare Hotel on Duane Street, a lodging house full of French and German radicals who fled Europe after the failed revolutions of 1848.

A reader expects the book to stay with Daniel. Instead, Young notices another guest at the Shakespeare Hotel, the wandering German tailor and prophet Wilhelm Weitling, and follows him. She follows him back to his birth in Magdeburg, into a Swiss prison, into a Hamburg bookshop where he meets the poet Heinrich Heine, and then to Brussels, where Karl Marx pounds a table at him. Daniel Debs does not return for a long time. Eugene will not be born for another hundred and sixty pages.

Most readers will find this the hardest stretch of the book to accept. It is also where Young demonstrates what she is doing.

The tailor

Weitling was, in Young's blunt word, a bastard. His father was a young French artillery officer who marched into Russia with Napoleon and never came back. His mother was a housemaid. As a boy, he helped his grandmother peddle matches and chicory coffee to Cossack soldiers. At twelve he was apprenticed to a tailor, and at eighteen he took to the roads as a wandering journeyman.

Young traces his politics to a child's question in a cathedral. Looking at the two thieves crucified beside Christ, he wondered why they were never thieves of mines and mills, and why instead they were always "petty thieves of bread crumbs for their starving children" (27). Those who stole a country's wealth from the poor were never punished, or were fined less than they had gained.

This is Reality Is Constructed where the law decides which taking counts as theft, and the law is made by the people doing the larger taking. Weitling's answer was childlike and exact. He wanted coins stamped not with the heads of kings but with a hammer, an anvil, or a saw, and with words saying what the coin would buy: one loaf of bread, one pound of meat (32). Money, which presents itself as a fact of nature, turns into an agreement the moment someone proposes changing the picture on it.

Young is not sentimental about him. He was vain, grandiose, and half persuaded he was the returning Christ. He threw his tailor's scissors into Lake Zurich, swearing never to sew again, "But alas, he was to be pursued by scissors the rest of his life, even unto his grave" (29). His certainty was total: "Utopia was that which was outside of history. It came because it must" (32). Young records that sentence without endorsing it. Everything else in her book argues against it.

She also records his generosity. He believed that "There was no such thing in nature as a bastard left upon a rock, for all children were the same in the eyes of God" (28). The Margins Reveal the Truth could hardly be more personal. The illegitimate tailor, sorted from birth into the lowest box, is the one who sees that the boxes are man-made.

The crime of the open mouth

In June 1843, Zurich police arrested Weitling at three in the morning. He was jailed "for having committed no crime but the crime of spreading his anarchic socialist or communist messages" (32). His prison chapters are among the most painful in the book. He hears knocking in the walls. He is sure an Austrian detective watches him through two peepholes. He refuses a clean nightshirt in case the jailers mean to hang him by its sleeves, and he refuses water in case it is poisoned. He writes poems with titles like "Forty-eight Hours in the Dark" and "Do Not Despair."

When he is finally sent home in chains, Young sums up the case in a single line: "He had committed no crime but that of failure to keep his big mouth shut" (38).

That line explains why Weitling belongs in a life of Debs. Nineteen pages earlier, Young described Debs as "one of the jackass Socialists who would not keep their mouths shut" (4). The two sentences rhyme deliberately. Seventy-five years before Woodrow Wilson jailed Debs for a speech, a Swiss court jailed a German tailor for a pamphlet. The prison at the start of the book has a floor beneath it, and Weitling's cell is one of the layers.

This is The Past Doesn't Go Away as structure. Young is showing that Debs's fate was not a strange American accident. It had been rehearsed, in other languages, by people whose names his admirers would never learn.

The poet

After his release, Weitling went to Hamburg to see his prison poems through the press. In the bookshop of his publisher, Julius Campe, he found Heinrich Heine, home from Paris on a rare visit to his mother.

Young stages the meeting as comedy. Weitling, in a red cap and red shoes with their soles tied on by rope, flops onto a bench and props his bare legs up one at a time, scraping away the prison mold and the sores. He lectures the startled poet on the coming kingdom of heaven. Heine, fastidious and fragile, dislikes being slapped on the back by strangers "lest he who was so fragile should be knocked over" (47). He later complained to Marx about the tailor's "nauseating familiarity" (51).

Heine is the other half of the utopian temperament, and Young gives him more room than anyone else in Part One. He wanted plenty for everyone. His theory was that "there would be plenty in this world for everybody if only there were fair play" (51), wine and roses and bread for all. He saw clearly how the rich "raised up a barricade of laws by which to protect themselves from the starving poor" (51). He also feared the leveling that radical politics might bring, and he "came increasingly to view communism as that which would cut down the very flower of civilization" (51).

Young does not resolve that contradiction, because Heine did not. She describes a man with "space for many selves including the masks of himself and his double" (40), whose "horizons were never made of a choice between the Either on the one hand and the Or on the other" (49). Of his inner life she writes, "Illusion might be reality, and reality might be illusion" (49). This is Not One Self given a face. Heine is not confused. He is several people at once, and he does not pretend otherwise.

One of the Heine poems Young retells looks straight ahead to Debs. A white horse in a farmyard watches a steam locomotive rattle past, trembling, and understands that there is no future for horses. Men's hearts are hard, and once they no longer need horses, no one will feed them (50). Young places the poem thirty pages before Debs's birth. The boy who will shovel coal into that locomotive has not been born yet, but the machine and the fear it brings are already on the page.

Heine spent his last eight years on what he called his mattress grave in Paris, paralyzed and nearly blind. Young reports that he meant to ask God why He had given him such a sense of humor and then such suffering, and that he considered bringing God to trial before the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (56). He died on February 17, 1856. Debs was three months old.

The theorist

Marx enters the story as Heine's friend and Weitling's enemy. In Brussels in 1846, Weitling announced at Marx's table that all their theory was unnecessary, because he had already worked everything out. Marx rose and brought his fist down so hard that the wine goblets and candlesticks jumped. Arousing fantastic hopes in workers, he declared, could lead only to their ruin (69).

Young treats this as the famous quarrel it was, and she lets each man score his points. To Marx and Engels, Weitling was a windbag. To Weitling, Marx was an excellent future lexicographer who would never found a world anyone could live in. Engels suspected Weitling of wanting money, and Young cannot resist the irony: "Money, it seemed, was required in order to found a moneyless utopia" (68).

What interests Young most about Marx is not his theory. She is drawn to his poverty and his grief. She describes a family pawning its china, a father who cannot afford paper and stamps for the articles he sends to Horace Greeley's New York Tribune, and the death of his small son Edgar. Of Marx's mourning she writes, "He could not dismiss a bundle of pink sand to nonbeing, of course" (59). Of Jenny Marx, "She was never to be consoled" (60). This is Grief Doesn't End. The prophet of historical necessity is, in these pages, a father who cannot get over his son.

Young also notes something about Marx that turns back on her own book. Marx believed "his writings could be published only when they were an artistic whole so well rounded that he could see the entire pattern" (52). Marx never finished Capital. Young never finished Harp Song. The man who wanted the finished whole and the woman who wrote in spokes both died with the work open on the table.

Three kinds of certainty

By the end of this stretch, Young has set three figures side by side. Weitling is sure by instinct, Marx is sure by science, and Heine is sure of nothing. Weitling believes utopia "came because it must." Marx's Hegelian inheritance, as Young puts it, held not so much "that what was rational would be but that what was rational must be" (53). Heine, meanwhile, knew early that the revolutionaries "would not live to realize their dreams of the dawn which was to come" (46).

Young sides with none of them, and her refusal is a position. The distrust of the frozen blueprint, the principle this study calls Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary, is how she separates the dream from the dreamers' certainty. Of Weitling's American Zion, which he never built, she writes that it "took a long time dying as in a dream that never really dies as some other dreamer must take over the dream, which transcends the individual" (48–49).

That sentence is the hinge of Part One. Weitling fails. His dream passes on to someone else. Young has just spent sixty pages showing whose hands it will pass through on its way to a boy in Terre Haute.

The vibrating string

In the middle of the Heine chapters, Young quotes a long passage from Denis Diderot about how the mind works. Thought, as she summarizes it, "depended upon associations of images streaming at random through the dreamer's mind like the music caused by the vibrations of strings" (49). One string sets another vibrating, and "an idea once aroused may sometimes set vibrating a harmonic at an inconceivable distance."

This is as close as Young comes to explaining her own method, and it may explain her title. A harp is a set of strings that sound one another. Weitling's cell in Zurich and Debs's cell in Atlanta are strings far apart that vibrate together. The white horse and the locomotive, Marx's lost son and Heine's mattress grave, the tailor's coins and the fireman's wages all sound in sympathy. The digressions are not a failure of focus. They are the instrument.

The crossing point

Weitling sailed for America late in 1846, went back to Europe for the revolution of 1848, and returned to New York in 1849, to the Shakespeare Hotel, where Daniel Debs was waiting for his bride. Young never claims the two men spoke. She puts them under the same roof and lets the reader feel the weight of it.

That hotel is the Crossing Point in its most literal form. Everything Young has traced so far, from the Napoleonic officer lost in the snow to the crucified thieves and the Brussels table, arrives at one address in lower Manhattan. Beneath the future Debs lies the ground these people packed down. Daniel will name his son after two French writers of social conscience, Eugène Sue and Victor Hugo. The boy will inherit the dream along with the names.

Checking the record

Young's broad outline holds. Weitling was born in Magdeburg in 1808, ten years before Marx, the illegitimate son of a French officer. He published Guarantees of Harmony and Freedom in 1842 and was arrested in Zurich in June 1843. The Brussels confrontation with Marx took place in 1846 and was recorded by the Russian visitor Pavel Annenkov, as Young says. She is also right that Heine described religion as a kind of opium before Marx made the phrase famous. Heine's meeting with Weitling in Campe's shop is real, and Heine told his own version years later in his Confessions, with the same tactless scene of the tailor tending the marks on his legs.

A few points need care:

  • Weitling's prison poems. The collection was published in German as Kerkerpoesien (Prison Poems). Young's English title shifts from "Wounds and Balsam" (39) to "Wounds and Blossoms" (43) within four pages, the kind of inconsistency an editor would normally catch.

  • Heine and baby Jenny Marx. Young sets this rescue in Brussels, with Heine turning the child upside down to dislodge a fish bone (52). The more common account places it in Paris in 1844, with Heine saving the infant from convulsions by calling for a warm bath.

  • Edgar Marx's death. Young places it after Heine's death, which would put it in 1856. Edgar died in April 1855, ten months before Heine.

  • Owen's "phalanstery." Young calls New Harmony Robert Owen's "phalanstery" (30). That was Fourier's term for his planned communities. Owen used different language, though Young, who wrote Angel in the Forest about New Harmony, would have known that. She may be blurring the utopias on purpose, as she often does. The blur still needs pointing out.

In the next chapter, Weitling heads west into the American interior, where the Icarians, the Rappites, and Robert Owen's New Harmony are waiting. It is ground Young had covered once before, in Angel in the Forest, and she comes back to it here.
harp-post-12-the-detective-and-the-miner:
Chapter 12. The Detective and the Miners

← Chapter 11 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 13 →

Allan Pinkerton, the Molly Maguires, and the law as a trap

The chapters from about page 396 to 474 form the longest set piece in the book, and Debs is barely present in them. Young tells the life of Allan Pinkerton, the Scottish radical turned detective, and the destruction of the Molly Maguires, the Irish coal miners of Pennsylvania who were hanged on the testimony of his agent. Debs appears at the margins, as the young editor watching and as the old man remembering.

The Chartist who changed sides

Young first mentioned Pinkerton back in Part One, as a young Chartist agitator in Scotland who came to America "in the year of the gold rush" (29). Here she fills in the story. He fled Britain after the Chartist cause failed, settled near Chicago, and built the most famous detective agency in the country. He guarded Lincoln and ran intelligence for the Union Army. Then he became the railroads' and mine owners' private police.

Young's judgment is that Pinkerton's "social philosophy not bound by loyalty to principles" had simply "reflected the colors of the surrounding world" (399). The man who had marched for workers' rights became their most effective enemy. This is Not One Self in its darkest version, a man whose selves were bought and sold.

She also records the violence that trailed the agency: the lynching of the Reno brothers in Indiana after they were captured, and the 1875 raid on the James family farm in Missouri, where an incendiary device thrown by detectives killed Jesse James's eight-year-old half-brother, whom she calls "Little Archie" (426). Pinkerton believed in phrenology, measuring skulls to judge character (440). Young lets that detail speak for itself.

The law as a mine without an exit

The heart of these chapters is the case of the Molly Maguires, a secret society of Irish miners in the Pennsylvania coal fields. Pinkerton's agent James McParlan infiltrated them, and on his testimony, in trials prosecuted by Franklin Gowen, president of the Reading Railroad, which also owned the mines, a series of men were convicted of murder and hanged.

Young's verdict comes in one sentence: "The law was made into a mockery of law" (449). She compares McParlan's plot to "the design of the mines which had no exit for them" (449). The railroad owned the mines, hired the detective, and led the prosecution. The miners were caught in a legal structure built as tightly as the shafts they worked in.

This is Reality Is Constructed at its most lethal. The courtroom, the jury, and the gallows looked like justice, and they were built by the same company that paid the miners' wages.

What Debs remembered

Debs kept a private calendar of labor's martyrs, and the Mollies were on it (398). Years later, in the socialist paper Appeal to Reason, he wrote of the executed men: "Not one of them betrayed the slightest evidence of fear or weakening, not one of them was a murderer at heart" (399). He did not claim they were saints. He called them "ignorant, rough and uncouth," the products of their conditions.

Young notes that McParlan's career did not end in Pennsylvania. Three decades later, the same detective led the investigation that charged the western miners' leaders William Haywood, Charles Moyer, and George Pettibone with murder in Idaho. Debs defended them passionately (441). They were acquitted.

This is the Crossing Point again, with the same man standing at both ends. The detective who hanged the Mollies in 1877 came for the Western Federation of Miners in 1906, and the young editor who watched the first case became the old agitator who fought the second.

What the lens shows

Young gives these chapters to people Debs never met because they are part of his inheritance. The Margins Reveal the Truth belongs to the miners, who saw the law's machinery from underneath. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act is Debs's calendar, a list kept for decades of names the country preferred to forget.

Checking the record

  • The number hanged. Young refers to "nineteen official executions" in 1877 (462), and her list of names includes John Kehoe, who was hanged in December 1878. Twenty men connected with the Molly Maguires were hanged between 1877 and 1879, ten of them on a single day, June 21, 1877.

  • John Kehoe's pardon. Young does not mention it. In 1979, Pennsylvania granted Kehoe a posthumous pardon, an official acknowledgment of the doubts she raises.

  • The Reno lynching. Young implies that Pinkerton's men took part. The Renos were seized from jail in New Albany, Indiana, in December 1868 by vigilantes. How far Pinkerton's agency was involved remains disputed.

  • McParlan and Haywood. Accurate. McParland, as the name is often spelled, directed the 1906 investigation in Idaho.
harp-post-07-a-boy-in-a-breaking-nation:
Chapter 7. A Boy in a Breaking Nation

← Chapter 6 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 8 →

Dred Scott, John Brown, the Lincoln funeral train, and Young's portrait of Mary Todd Lincoln

The chapters covering Debs's childhood (pages 198 to 262) contain surprisingly little of Debs. Young surrounds the boy with the nation's great quarrels and lets him stand at the edge of the picture: a small figure spinning a top, walking to Sunday school, reading his schoolbook. The foreground belongs to Dred Scott, John Brown, Abraham Lincoln, Andrew Johnson, and, at greatest length, Lincoln's widow.

The method is the same one Young used in Part One. The boy is shaped by events he barely understands, and the book shows those events so that a reader can feel their weight on him.

Two burials

Young introduces Dred Scott through his graves. Debs was "not quite three years old" when Scott was first buried, and older when Scott's body was dug up and moved (202). The Supreme Court decision that bore Scott's name had declared that a Black man could claim no protection from the Constitution. Young describes the chief justice reading it for three hours in a voice so faint that many words were lost, in a courtroom where "justice was blind and deaf and dumb even more than if it had been a stone" (204).

John Brown enters the same way, through a child's memory. On the day Brown was hanged in December 1859, four-year-old Eugene was spinning a top (203). He grew up hearing his father repeat that for Victor Hugo, "John Brown had been a greater man than George Washington" (204). Decades later, Young notes, admirers would call Debs "the second John Brown, the second Abe Lincoln, and the first Debs there ever was" (210).

This is The Past Doesn't Go Away at the scale of a single childhood. The boy did not choose his heroes from a list. They were pressed into him by his father's talk at the grocery counter, before he could read.

The schoolbook that left things out

Young is sharp about what the boy was taught. McGuffey's readers, the standard schoolbooks of the era, taught children that "Socrates died like a philosopher but that Jesus Christ died like a god" (221). They taught property rights through little moral tales. They said nothing about the Fugitive Slave Act, Dred Scott, or John Brown, even in the middle of a war over slavery. In McGuffey's world, "The struggles for freedom in the McGuffey's Acropolis were always of the remote past" (221).

This is Language Shapes What's Possible applied to a child's education. A schoolbook that puts every struggle for freedom in ancient Greece or Rome teaches, without saying so, that freedom is already won. Young notes that the boy's religious life ran on different lines. His Catholic mother and freethinking father let the children choose their own church or none, and "Debs's church would always be, it has been said of him, a church without walls" (219).

The joke as a safety valve

Young's Lincoln is a joker. "Jokes had provided a safety valve through which the steam could escape and without which old Abe would have blown up like a riverboat or a train" (213). For Lincoln, she writes, the joke was "the language of the skeptic brain transmuted by the faithful heart" (213). It is the same double vision she found in Debs and Twain, humor carrying grief rather than denying it.

When Lincoln's body went home to Springfield by train in 1865, Young describes towns so draped in mourning that there were "rivers of black crepe streaming across this continent" (216). The ten-year-old in Terre Haute was living in a country that was grieving along its railroad lines.

The black widow

The longest portrait in this stretch belongs to Mary Todd Lincoln, and it is one of the most compassionate in the book. Young follows her through widowhood: the debts, the long fight for a pension from a Congress that had hated her husband, the humiliation of William Herndon's lectures claiming Lincoln had never loved her, the deaths of her sons. In 1875, at her son Robert's request, a Chicago court declared her insane, and she was sent to a private asylum in Batavia, Illinois. A later court declared her sane. Young notes bitterly that some people would believe the first verdict "but not the reversal which had declared that she was sane" (256).

Young does not sanctify her. She says plainly that Mrs. Lincoln's "social consciousness" had shriveled "to so thin a thread that she could see little or no connection between her struggles and those of the sufferings of the blacks and the reds" (249). This is Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act at work. Young stays in the room with a difficult, grieving, sometimes selfish woman without either excusing or condemning her.

Then comes the thread that ties the portrait to Debs. Robert Todd Lincoln, the son who had his mother committed, would become "the future most important cog of the Pullman empire and lawyer for George Mortimer Pullman" (254). He later served as president of the Pullman Company. Mrs. Lincoln wrote to him in fury that he had "injured himself, not her" (255). Two decades later, Debs would lead the great strike against Pullman.

This is the Crossing Point, reached by an unexpected road. The same family that gave the country its emancipator would give Pullman his lawyer. Young does not draw the moral. She lets the dates carry it.

What the lens shows

These chapters are about inheritance. Not One Self appears in a boy formed at once by a Catholic mother, a freethinking father, a Protestant Sunday school, and a war. Grief Doesn't End runs through the Lincoln household. Reality Is Constructed shows in a schoolbook that erased the living struggle for freedom and a court that could erase a woman's sanity at her son's request.

Checking the record

  • The Dred Scott decision. Young places it "the very day after" Buchanan's inauguration (198). Buchanan took office on March 4, 1857. The decision came on March 6, two days later.

  • Scott's second burial. Young places Debs at "about nine years old" and the nation in the middle of the war when Scott's body was moved (202). The reburial took place in 1867, after the war, when Debs was eleven.

  • The Lincoln pension and trial. These are accurate. Congress passed the widow's pension in July 1870. The Chicago insanity hearing took place in May 1875, and it was reversed in June 1876. Robert Todd Lincoln did become Pullman's lawyer and, after Pullman's death, president of the company.
harp-post-01-the-unfinished-harp:
Chapter 1. The Unfinished Harp

The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 2 →

Reading Marguerite Young's last book, Harp Song for a Radical, as a philosophy of the open ending

Marguerite Young spent roughly the last twenty-five years of her life writing a biography of Eugene Victor Debs. Debs was the locomotive fireman from Terre Haute who became the country's best-known socialist and went to prison twice for his convictions. Young did not finish the book. When she fell ill, she was writing the chapter on the Pullman strike of 1894, which sent Debs to jail for the first time. That strike was meant to close the book. She died in 1995. Knopf published what she left in 1999, edited by her friend Charles Ruas, as Harp Song for a Radical: The Life and Times of Eugene Victor Debs.

The book runs close to six hundred pages, and in all of them Debs never becomes the man most people have heard of. There is no Socialist Party and no presidential campaign. There is no Atlanta Penitentiary, and no courtroom speech with its famous line, "while there is a soul in prison, I am not free." The narrative follows him to about 1888. He is in his early thirties, a union officer and magazine editor with a wife, a house, and a local name. Then the book wanders off to Whistler, Gogol, and Dostoyevsky, and stops. The climax it was building toward survives as one paragraph in an Editorial Note at the back.

How the book reached print

Young wrote in near seclusion. Ruas explains that "no one was allowed in her apartment for years on end" while she was composing. During one of her hospital stays, her building was renovated, and "the different drafts of her enormous work became mixed together." Friends helped her collate a single draft, which Ruas photocopied. She kept writing and revising through her illnesses. At the end, her niece moved the contents of her New York rooms to a house in Indianapolis and rebuilt them down to the details, and Young was nursed there.

So the book in print is several things at once. It is Young's last intention, a reassembly by friends, and an edition shaped by an editor after her death. The seams show. The front matter calls the World War I law the "Alien and Sedition Act." The Editorial Note names Debs's union the "American Railroad Workers Union" instead of the American Railway Union. These are small slips, but they are reminders that other hands finished what she could not.

What kind of book this is

By ordinary standards, Harp Song is badly out of proportion. Heinrich Heine and the German utopian Wilhelm Weitling take up some sixty pages before Debs's parents ever reach Indiana. Then come the French Icarians, Brigham Young's Mormons, and Mark Twain's brother Orion. Later, the Pinkerton detectives and the Molly Maguires fill about seventy-five pages in which Debs nearly disappears.

Young did this on purpose. She told Ruas her method: "I simply build the landscape, the time-scape, and there's the little boy." Ruas describes the structure as "spokes radiating from a center," and says she deploys "a series of multiple consciousnesses" before arriving at the record of events. The digressions are the method.

Young also named her subject across every book she wrote. "I believe that all my work explores the human desire or obsession for utopia, and the structure of all my works is the search for utopias lost and rediscovered." Then she added the sentence this study is built on: "All my writing is about the recognition that there is no single reality. But the beauty of it is that you nevertheless go on, walking towards utopia, which may not exist, on a bridge which might end before you reach the other side."

The lens

This study reads Harp Song through a philosophy that runs through Young's work. It can be stated as eleven ideas, and several of them are visible from the first pages.

The unfinished as honesty. A book about a man who never reaches his destination was written by a woman who never reached hers. Ruas says the book "stands by itself, a complete creation, without having been entirely finished." The study takes that seriously. The missing ending is not only an accident. It shows how Young thought about any story that claims to be closed.

Time as layers. The past in Young's work is not behind her characters. It lies beneath them, pressed into the present like rock. That is why Heine's Paris and Weitling's wanderings sit under Terre Haute, and why Debs's father names his son after Eugène Sue and Victor Hugo. Young writes that Debs believed socialism "had been sleeping in the womb of time long before it was born." Calling any arrangement inevitable hides the people who built it, and Young's long detours put those builders back in view.

Seeing the invention. On her first page, Young describes capitalism as an institution treated "as sacred as if it had been handed down by God to man, probably along about the time of the eviction of Adam and Eve and the fencing of the Garden of Eden." That joke carries a whole argument. Money, property, and the law that jailed Debs are agreements held in place by repetition. Seeing them as built is the first step out from under their spell.

The plural self. Young's Debs is a crowd rather than a statue. He is the "Abel who would be branded Cain," a man with "ten hopes to your one hope and ten loves to your one love." He is gentle and stubborn, "one of the jackass Socialists who would not keep their mouths shut." Young never resolves him into one thing, and the study does not either.

The view from the edges. Ruas says Young's great subjects were "the misfit, the wrecked, the impossible, and the forgotten." Her book is crowded with failed communes, cranks, convicts, and prophets who were right too early. The people who do not fit the categories are the ones who see them most clearly.

Language as a building material. Young calls Debs "an Aesopian fabulist" who spoke in the worn coins of common speech. She believed Americans of every party shared a common tongue of poetry: "They all spoke in metaphors. And Debs was one of the great lovers and users of metaphors." Her own sentences, long and circling and piled with clauses, resist the flat voice that claims to speak from nowhere.

The sacred ordinary, and a tension inside it. Young places Debs's hoped-for world "here upon this earth and not upon some other star beyond time, beyond space." Still, many of her utopians promised a distant paradise that justified sacrifice now. The study watches that tension closely. Young seems to have known it well. She said that "out of every dreamer something good comes. It might not be heaven on earth, it might only be an eight-hour day." The eight-hour day is a very ordinary kind of sacred.

The remaining ideas arrive later in the book. The witness who stays in the room with pain returns when the narrative reaches Kate Debs, the strikes, and Dostoyevsky before the firing squad.
