Grief as permanent weather is there too. So is the crossing point, where each person stands between everyone who came before and everyone who will come after. That last idea may be the deepest reason Young spent her final decades on a railroad fireman from Indiana.

How this study works

The chapters follow the book in order, in fifteen parts. They begin with the prison scene that opens the book and end with the strike it never reached. Every quotation from Young or Ruas appears in quotation marks with a page reference. Where Young's history can be checked against later biographies, it is, because a writer who distrusted final answers deserves a reader who checks the facts too.

Young once said a mature person is someone who has "examined all the illusions of life" and yet goes on. Harp Song for a Radical is that kind of walk, on a bridge that ends in midair. This study follows it as far as it goes.
harp-post-08-firing-the-engine:
Chapter 8. Firing the Engine

← Chapter 7 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 9 →

A paint scraper, a fireman's cab, a death on the rails, and a brotherhood

At fourteen, in the spring of 1870, Eugene Debs left school. Young says he did so "with considerable grief" (263). The family grocery was failing, and the boy went to work. The chapters from page 262 to about 282 follow him from the paint shop to the locomotive cab and back, and then into the union that would shape the next twenty years of his life.

Fifty cents a day

His first job came through a friend of his father's, Pierre Solomon, a French painter of boxcars who decorated engines with roosters, eagles, and owls. Solomon got Eugene hired at the railroad paint shop, where "Debs's diurnal pay had been fifty cents" (264). He had to pay a dollar, two days' wages, for his own paint scraper.

He kept it. Years later, as a labor leader, he hung that scraper on his office wall (264), proof to anyone who doubted that his hands had ever been blackened. Young treats the tool almost as a relic. It is The Sacred Is Here in a single object, a scraper that cost two days' pay and stayed with him for life.

The fireman's cab

He was promoted to fireman by accident, when the night fireman showed up too drunk to work (264). The job meant shoveling coal on moving engines in all weather. Young describes the winter runs: the young fireman "frozen by glacial cold on one side and his eye fried like an egg by the burning heat on the other side" (265). "The pay was measured not by time but by mileage" (265). Delays and breakdowns cost the railroad nothing and the worker everything.

Young adds a sly joke about his reading habits. The fireman did not read Plato's Republic on the job. He knew that a fireman caught reading philosophy would give the owners all the excuse they needed. At night, though, he read constantly: French and German poets, Shakespeare, and chapter after chapter of Les Misérables (266).

When the depression of 1873 cost him his place, he went to St. Louis. There he bunked with an engineer in a railroad flophouse, sleeping on a mattress of cornstalks, reading late and taking care to "shield with his red fireman's cap" the lamp so the light would not wake his roommate (272). He also reported home that he had killed thirty-seven bedbugs in a few minutes one night (268).

The man under the wheels

The turning point in these chapters is a death. Young reports a letter in which Debs, answering his mother's anxious question about a young man named Stewart killed near Terre Haute, blamed the dead man for his own fate. Young notes that this was the "first and last time" Debs would blame a worker for his own death (268).

Then she tells what really brought him home. It was not his mother's fear, she says, but the horror of watching a fellow worker who, "while working on a wheel had been knocked down, mangled, and mutilated" under the moving train (272).

Young follows this with one of her most biting passages, a mock version of the kind of notice the railroads issued about their dead. "Answered not to any name." "Was killed by error of his own and not the management" (273). The official language made every death the worker's fault. This is Reality Is Constructed in its coldest form. The accident report, like the "act of God" in Part One, turns a system into a single careless man.

Debs had written that very sentence about Stewart. The book shows him learning never to write it again.

The billing clerk and the brotherhood

Back in Terre Haute, Debs became a billing clerk for Herman Hulman's wholesale grocery, one of the largest businesses in town. Out of his first pay, he bought a five-year subscription to the New York Herald (273).

He still longed for the cab. In 1875, when Joshua Leach, grand master of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, came to Terre Haute, the grocery clerk stepped out of the crowd and asked to join. Leach, an Irish immigrant who had fired engines on the Erie, took him in, prophesying that he had signed up "a young towhead who would do his duty and make his mark" in the brotherhood (277). Debs became secretary of the new Vigo Lodge.

The brotherhood's magazine, which Debs would soon help edit, recorded the dangers of the trade with grim precision. Young quotes its list of the causes of wrecks: "flying switch, runaway engine or train, careless stopping or switching, bad switching, cattle on track, snow or ice, washout, landslide" (280). It reported a worker in Jersey City whose foot caught in the rails and who threw himself under the wheels rather than live crippled (283). Young's summary is simple: "Debs was not and would never be a worshiper of the capitalistic gods of terminus" (283).

What the lens shows

This is the section where the book's philosophy becomes a job. The Margins Reveal the Truth is literal here, the view from the fireman's side of the cab. Grief Doesn't End appears in the dead brakeman and the widow's-benefit rolls. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act appears in the magazine's patient lists of the dead, which Debs would keep compiling for years. The young man who once blamed a dead worker learns to record the dead and refuse the verdict.

Checking the record

  • The date he left school. The book contradicts itself. The chronology in the front matter says Debs began working in the railroad shops in 1869. The text says spring 1870 (263), which matches the standard accounts.

  • Why he left the cab. Most biographers give weight to his mother's fears and to the layoffs of the 1873 depression. Young acknowledges the mother but insists the decisive cause was witnessing the accident. Both may be true. Her version is an interpretation, not a settled fact.

  • Vigo Lodge. Accurate. The Terre Haute lodge of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was founded in February 1875, with Debs as its secretary.
harp-post-15-what-the-song-never-reached:
Chapter 15. What the Song Never Reached

← Chapter 14 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical

The Pullman strike, the missing volumes, and what Young's philosophy makes of an unfinished life

Harp Song for a Radical is the life of a man who is not yet the man it is about. The Debs of history led the Pullman strike of 1894, went to jail, read Marx in his cell, and came out a socialist. He helped found the Socialist Party and ran for president five times, the last time in 1920 from the Atlanta Penitentiary, jailed for a speech against the First World War. The Debs of Young's book is a union secretary and magazine editor in his early thirties. Everything else lives in the front matter, the opening chapter, the Editorial Note, and one small phrase at the end: "As will be seen."

This final chapter asks what that gap means.

The strike in a single paragraph

The Pullman strike was meant to close the book. Ruas says so in his introduction. Young was writing that chapter when she first fell ill. What survives is one paragraph in the Editorial Note on page 581. It records that Debs was sentenced to six months "for contempt of the federal injunction stopping the strike against the Pullman Palace Car Company" and that in jail "Debs first read Marx and reread old favorites, notably Victor Hugo's Les Misérables." That paragraph is Ruas's, not Young's. It gets even the union's name wrong.

Young's book does not contain the strike, but it contains everything the strike was built from. The court injunction had its first rehearsal in 1877. Robert Todd Lincoln, Pullman's lawyer, grew up in the Lincoln chapters. The Gatling gun that the injunction improved on appeared in the graveyard in Indianapolis. The dream of one big railroad union was Debs's "Ultima Thule of labor federation." Every layer is in place. Only the event is missing.

Where the missing books would have gone

The book's last sentence before the Afterword promises that Debs's elegiac sense would continue "for as long as he lived and perhaps long afterward. As will be seen." Ruas describes the scope of the published book as "the period of American history that formed the historical Debs." Together, those lines point to more books: at least one covering the strike, the prison, and the birth of the Socialist Party, and very likely another for the long campaigns, the war, and Atlanta.

What exists is the foundation. Young spent twenty-five years on the ground floor of a house she did not live to build.

The lens, one last time

This study has read the book through eleven principles of a philosophy that I believe runs through her work. Young never named or alluded to this. Here is what I believe each has found.

Not One Self. Debs is never one thing in these pages. He is his father's reader and his mother's revolutionary, Riley's drinking partner and Kate's absent husband. He is the man who once blamed a dead fireman and never did again, and the cautious union man who would become the most jailed radical in the country.

Reality Is Constructed. The book keeps exposing built things that pass for natural ones: the "act of God," the railroad accident report, the watermarked reference letter, the court that declared Mary Lincoln insane, and the law that hanged the Mollies.

Grief Doesn't End. Dead sisters, dead brakemen, dead sons of Marx and of Pierce, Heine on his mattress grave. None of them are redeemed. Young lets the grief stand.

Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act. Young stays in the room with Mary Lincoln, Lucy Harris, and the Mollies, and with Debs's own lapses, including his silence on Haymarket.

Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary. Every blueprint in the book fails: Icaria, Communia, Harmony, Zion. The dream passes on anyway.

Unfinished Is Honest. The book itself is the proof. It is unfinished, and it is honest.

The Margins Reveal the Truth. Convicts voting, a skeptical wife, a scorned suffragist walking through a mob, a Polish barber paying dues for a colony that no longer exists. The margins see the seams.

The Past Doesn't Go Away. Nothing starts fresh. The Icarians move into the Mormons' ruins, New Harmony is written over Harmony, and Debs is born on top of Colmar, Paris, the Shakespeare Hotel, and a Rappite mortgage.

Language Shapes What's Possible. McGuffey's readers leave out the living struggle. Twain wears a mask. Young's own sentences, long and circling, refuse the flat voice of official history.

The Sacred Is Here. A grocery scale, a paint scraper, a tailors' burial fund, and the eight-hour day that Young said might be all that comes out of a dream. That is enough.

The Crossing Point. Weitling and a Debs baby buried in the same Brooklyn cemetery. Robert Todd Lincoln between the Emancipator and Pullman. McParlan between the Mollies and Haywood. A young man in Terre Haute standing where all of it meets.

A tension to leave open

It would be too neat to say that this philosophy I call Radical Immanence simply confirms Debs's. Debs believed in a coming transformation. In the Afterword, Young quotes his faith that "Out of the misery of the past would surely rise the civilization of the future" (579). That is a promise of a distant arrival, and the principle this study calls The Sacred Is Here distrusts exactly such promises.

Young does not resolve this, and she may not have wanted to. Her own statement of faith, quoted in the first chapter of this study, was different from Debs's. She believed in walking "towards utopia, which may not exist, on a bridge which might end before you reach the other side." Debs believed the bridge reached the other shore. Young believed in walking it anyway. The book holds both.

The record, in sum

Across these chapters, the "Checking the record" sections have turned up a consistent pattern. Young's large outlines are usually right, and her small details are often wrong. There are misdated revolutions and court decisions, a Chinese reformer's name and a poet's name confused, William Jennings Bryan put in the place of William Cullen Bryant, two Harmonies merged into one, a union's name garbled in the editor's own note. At least once, in 1877, she chose her subject's comfort over the harder truth. Some errors are clearly hers. Others show how thinly the manuscript was checked after her death.

None of this makes the book less valuable. It makes it what it is: a great, flawed, unfinished work by a writer who believed that flawed and unfinished were honest conditions, not failures to hide.

The last image

Young ends with Norman Thomas's picture of Debs after death, a tall man in a gray suit, "walking the star belt," with "this world always half in darkness" (580). It is an image of someone still walking and still keeping watch, with no arrival in sight.

That is also a fair picture of the book. It never reaches Pullman, Atlanta, or the end of Debs's road. It walks as far as it can and stops mid-stride, with the next step already promised: "As will be seen."

harp-post-05-the-beehive-and-the-buttonh:
Chapter 5. The Beehive and the Buttonhole

← Chapter 4 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 6 →

Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, Mark Twain, and the death of Wilhelm Weitling at the close of Part One

Part One of Harp Song for a Radical ends on page 178. Its last sixty pages do two things. They build a portrait of the Mormon Zion, from Joseph Smith's golden plates to Brigham Young's desert beehive, seen partly through the eyes of a young Mark Twain. Then they follow Wilhelm Weitling, the wandering tailor who has carried Part One on his back, to his grave in Brooklyn.

Eugene Debs is still not born, at least not on these pages. By the time Weitling dies in 1871, the real Debs is fifteen and already working in the railroad shops of Terre Haute. Young never mentions this, but the dates carry the point. One dreamer is being buried while the next is shoveling coal.

Plates of sand and gold

Young's Joseph Smith is a comic figure, and she tells his story in a mock-epic voice that neither believes nor quite debunks. The golden plates, in one version she passes along, "had started out as about forty pounds of gleaming wet sand wrapped in his shirt" (120). In the retelling they grow heavier and heavier, at one point reaching "twelve hundred tons," then shrink until they "might shrink to the size of a watch or a moth or an eyelid" (120). The Book of Mormon, she writes, was a book "which some people thought was real and some people thought was a fraud" (121). She leaves both camps standing.

This is Not One Self applied to a prophet. In the previous section, Young called Smith's gift "the pluralistic art of infinite camouflage" (94). She does not try to peel the masks away to find the real man underneath. The masks are the man.

She also sets Smith beside the real gold hunters of his century. "For with all the sand in the world," she writes, "Joseph Smith had nothing to see but an idea in his mind" (122). The true builders of empire were the rising tycoons of coal and oil and steel, who "were well on the way to building their great pyramids of power which no poor gypsy could possibly overturn" (122). The contrast cuts both ways. Smith's gold was an idea, and so, in the end, was theirs. Money, property, and corporate power are also agreements held in place by belief and repetition. The tycoons' myth simply had the law and the militia on its side. This is Reality Is Constructed, told as a comparison between two kinds of treasure hunt.

The wife who doubted

The most striking pages in the Smith chapters belong to a minor figure. Martin Harris, a prosperous farmer, financed the translation of the plates and hoped to grow rich publishing them. His wife, Lucy, did not believe a word of it. Young reports, from Lucy Harris's own later account, that her husband beat her for her doubt, striking her with the butt end of an ox whip and chasing her around the garden (126–127).

Young takes her side in a single sentence: while some angels are angels of forgetfulness, "others may be the angels of memory, particularly if they are in communication with an abused wife who cannot forget one iota of his assaults upon her" (127).

When Harris lost the first pages of the manuscript, suspicion fell on Lucy, who was thought to have burned them. Young clearly enjoys her reply. She would neither confirm nor deny it, and she told her husband that Joseph Smith "should put on his magical spectacles and go peek for it" (129).

This is The Margins Reveal the Truth at its sharpest. In a story crowded with prophets, angels, and seer stones, the clearest eyes belong to the skeptical wife nobody listened to. Young gives her the last word.

Then, in the middle of the lost-manuscript story, Young breaks into a passage that sounds like a sermon of her own:

"Have a care about the next dead dog you may see on the road. Do not give it a kick. It may be the lost bible and may suddenly whine." A few lines later: "Have a care about the next pile of dung. It may speak with an angel's voice to a poor man, for it is also made with gold" (129).

It is The Sacred Is Here stated as Young ever states it. If there is holiness anywhere, it is in the roadside and the barnyard, not in golden plates hidden in a hill. Young does not mock the hunger for revelation. She simply points it at the ground.

The beehive

Brigham Young gets gentler treatment. Young gives him a hard childhood. He had "not exceeded a period of eleven days" of formal schooling (148). He carried his shoes in his hands to church so as not to wear them out on the road, putting them on only at the door. Left alone with his sister while their father searched for grain, the small boy shot a robin in the snow and baked it into a pie to keep them both alive (149).

As leader, Young's Brigham is practical to the bone. He told the handcart immigrants they "should not search the sky for the angelic beings who actually, of course, thickened the air about them but should dig ditches for irrigation and dig holes for the planting of the turnip" (144). Arriving in the desert, he announced, "We have been kicked out of the frying pan into the fire, out of the fire into the middle of the desert floor, and here we are and here we will stay" (144). In one of the book's sweetest scenes, a little girl on his knee tells him, "Mr. Young, your eyes look exactly like the eyes of my father's sow" (145). He gets up and goes out to the pig shed with her to study the sow's face.

Young does not hide the darker side of the kingdom, the violence, the polygamy, the power of one man. She does locate the source of the persecution precisely: "It was always because of their success that the Mormons were threatened by the Gentiles" (153). This echoes her earlier point that utopias die either because they fail with money or because envious neighbors destroy them when they succeed.

She also names the method of their destruction in a phrase that looks backward and forward at once. Joseph Smith's lynching in the Carthage jail, carried out while officials stood aside, followed "this tool pattern for the illegal lynch murder which was permitted or instigated by the legal authorities themselves and which had been used before and would be used again" (154). A page later, Weitling travels home through the Allegheny Mountains, which Young notes will be the scene of the Molly Maguire hangings in the 1870s. This is The Past Doesn't Go Away working as foreshadowing. The frame-up of Tom Mooney in the opening chapter, the Molly Maguires to come, and Debs's own prosecutions all rest on this layer.

Twain at the gate

In August 1861, Samuel Clemens rode into Salt Lake City by stagecoach with his older brother Orion, whom Lincoln had just appointed secretary of the Nevada Territory. Clemens would write it up a decade later in Roughing It, and Young follows his account closely.

Twain found the city "a land of enchantment and goblins and awful mystery" (141). He was struck that there were no loafers or drunkards, that clear streams ran down every street, and that everyone was busy. The Mormon emblem fit perfectly, he thought: "It was a representative of a Golden Bee Hive, with the bees all at work" (142). The brothers called on Brigham Young, who talked politics with Orion and ignored the younger brother's attempts to join in. As they left, he patted Sam on the head and asked Orion, "your child, I presume? Boy or girl?" (146).

Young enjoys all this, and then she quietly corrects it. Twain's jokes about Brigham's "homely" wives, she says, were an "acidulously comic portrait, which showed largely his own biases" (146). She adds what Twain left out: that in this city orphans were taken in rather than left to sleep in gutters, and that Brigham reportedly adopted two starving Native children he found in the desert and raised them as his own (141). She calls Twain's narrator, Mr. Johnson, a "comic mask concealing the tragic mask of the future Mark Twain" (150).

The chapter closes with William Dean Howells's review of Roughing It, and his sentence could describe Young's own book. Out West, Howells wrote, "all existence there must have looked like an extravagant joke, the humor of which was only deepened by its nether side of tragedy" (153). In the opening chapter, Young said Debs had a "comic sense which must sustain a larger tragic sense." Here she finds the same double vision in Twain. The joke and the grief are not opposites. Each makes the other deeper.

The tailor's last years

The final four chapters of Part One return to Weitling, and they are among the most tender in the book.

Communia collapsed. The dam he had built with such joy washed out. Accused of misusing the workers' funds, he cleared himself before a judge in Dubuque, never went back to the colony, and returned to New York as a jobbing tailor. "Upon the cobwebbed window of his shop in New York was hung a sign advertising Zion" (160). He still wore his red cap and red shoes at the bench. Young calls him "the unforgettable forgotten man" (160).

Engels, looking back years later, said Weitling "carried a recipe for the realization of heaven on earth ready-made in his pocket and was convinced that everybody intended to steal it from him" (161). Young quotes it and does not dispute it. Then she shows what the rest of his life was actually like.

He married Caroline Todt, a locksmith's daughter half his age who made straw bonnets and nursed the sick. They had five sons and a daughter. He named the boys after his heroes, including the French revolutionary Gracchus Babeuf and the astronomer Tycho Brahe, and they all quietly shortened their names. The daughter, Caroline Johanna, grew up to head a nursing program at Hunter College (167). He rescued a street dog that boys were stoning to death, and his wife stitched its torn ear back on. They named it Filou (164–165). He spent years on a universal language and a new map of the heavens.

He also invented a buttonhole and embroidery attachment for sewing machines, meant to spare the eyesight of women who punched eyelets by hand. He patented several improvements in 1861, and the big sewing machine companies used the ideas without paying him. Young notes that no investor could be found who saw "a future in saving the eyes of poor women" (168). Meanwhile, the government was backing a different kind of invention: "The eye puncher which was promoted by the government in the never-ending Civil War was, of course, the great Gatling gun" (171). Which machines get built and which get stolen is not a natural fact. It reflects who holds the money. Weitling put it in a letter to a friend: "Heaven save humanity from such republics of the money bags" (171).

For a while he worked at Castle Garden, the immigration station, writing letters home for new arrivals who could not write. He refused to take part in the practice of steering newcomers into the Union Army (169). This is Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act in its humblest form. The failed prophet spends his days guiding the hands of strangers as they sign their names with an X.

In 1868 he fell on the ice in his yard. The injured big toe was amputated, and his health never recovered. On January 24, 1871, he went out to a banquet of the Workers' International, hosted by his old friend Friedrich Sorge. Twenty years earlier, Sorge had played the fiddle under streetlamps to draw crowds for Weitling's pamphlets (175). That night Weitling suffered a stroke. He died the next day.

His union, the Journeyman Tailors' Protective and Benevolent Union, had kept up his dues when he could not, and it paid for the hearse and the grave at Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn, which spared him a pauper's burial. Young calls it "A surely admirable example of human solidarity" (176).

What the ending shows

The shape of Part One now becomes clear. Weitling began as a messiah who knew the way to paradise. He ended as a tailor buried by his union's burial fund. That is exactly what the Philadelphia workers had set up back in 1847 with their dues of three cents a week. Utopia never arrived. The coffin money did. For this study, that is The Sacred Is Here made concrete. The real achievement of the utopian century was not the colony on the prairie. It was ordinary people pooling pennies so that none of them would go into the ground alone.

Young also lets Weitling's work stay unfinished. The New York Times notice mentioned "his unfinished treatise on moon and sun and stars" (176). It is hard not to hear an echo of Young herself, who died with her own great book unfinished. The obituary she quotes from a German-language paper could stand as her epitaph for every dreamer in Part One: "Men ceased to believe in him, and the waves tossed him upon the beach." And then: "Throw no stone at him, for he proved to be a man amidst the storms of life, and his driving motive was something higher than ambition and selfishness" (177).

Marx gets his say too. In an 1877 letter to Sorge, he dismissed the returning tide of utopian socialism as "silly, stale, and basically reactionary" (178). Young lets the verdict stand in the record, but she gives Weitling the more important line: "Perhaps his travels were not over and there were metamorphoses yet to come" (175). That is Unfinished Is Honest in one sentence. A life that ends unfinished may still be passing something on. Part Two begins with the boy who will receive it.

Checking the record

Young follows her sources closely in these chapters. The scenes in Salt Lake City come directly from Roughing It, and Weitling's last years follow Carl Wittke's 1950 biography, which she names (166). Marx's letter to Sorge of October 19, 1877, and Engels's 1885 recollection of Weitling are real. Weitling died in New York on January 25, 1871, the day after the International's banquet, as she describes.

Several points need correcting or flagging:

  • Twain's trip. Young dates it 1862 (139). The Clemens brothers crossed the plains in the summer of 1861 and reached Salt Lake City that August.

  • The lost manuscript. Young gives it "one hundred and seventeen pages" (129). The usual count is 116.

  • The two Harmonies. Young places Emma Hale's family home "in Economy" and describes Smith's digging ground as "the former Rappite stamping ground" (117). Emma Hale grew up in Harmony, in Susquehanna County in northeastern Pennsylvania. Rapp's Harmony was in Butler County, in the western part of the state, and Economy was the Rappites' later town near Pittsburgh. Young, or someone preparing her manuscript, merged two places with the same name. Given how much of her life she spent writing about Harmony, the slip is almost poignant.

  • "Dialectical Materialism." Young twice treats this as the title of a book by Marx and Engels, saying it was published in the year Smith died (154, 157). No work of theirs bears that title, and the phrase came into wide use only later.

  • Governor Boggs. Young describes the Carthage killing as arranged through the agreement of Governor Ford of Illinois and Governor Boggs of Missouri (154). Lilburn Boggs issued his notorious order against the Mormons in 1838, but he had left office by 1844.

  • The wrong Bryan. Young writes that "William Jennings Bryan of the New York Evening Post" worked in his garden in Roslyn, Long Island, during the Civil War (171). The poet and editor who lived in Roslyn and ran the Evening Post was William Cullen Bryant. William Jennings Bryan, whom Debs would campaign for in 1896, was born in 1860. It is the kind of error an editor would have caught easily, and it shows how thinly this manuscript was checked.

Next chapter: Part Two opens, and Young finally turns to Daniel Debs, the Alsatian father who named his son after Eugène Sue and Victor Hugo.
harp-post-13-the-long-strike:
Chapter 13. The Long Strike

← Chapter 12 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 14 →

1877, the railroads, the troops, and the young man in the warehouse

In July 1877, after years of wage cuts, railroad workers walked off the job across the country. The strike spread from West Virginia to Pittsburgh, Chicago, and St. Louis. Federal troops were sent in, and dozens of people were killed. It was the first great national strike in American history. The chapters from about page 475 to 545 tell its story and the story of the labor struggles leading up to it.

The uncivil civil war

Young sets 1877 inside a longer pattern. She begins with the eight-hour strikes in New York in 1872 and the police attack on unemployed workers in Tompkins Square in 1874, where a young cigar maker named Samuel Gompers was in the crowd (480). She had called the 1877 strike, back in the Gatling chapter, part of an "uncivil civil war" (197), in which federal troops were used to put down "what was called an insurrection inspired by Karl Marx, a man of whom few had heard" (197).

The phrase links 1877 back to the Civil War of Debs's childhood. For Young, the war between North and South had ended and the war between rich and poor had simply taken its place. That was exactly what Daniel Debs had predicted.

Terre Haute's strike

Young documents the strike on June 1877, the firemen of Vigo Lodge on the Vandalia line had suffered wage cuts of "twenty-three percent between 1873 and 1876 and ten percent between August 1876 and May 1877" (539). They asked the line's president, Riley McKeen, for a fifteen percent raise, gave him one night to answer, and prepared to stop the trains (539–540).

When the national strike came, President Hayes sent federal troops, including to Indianapolis and Terre Haute. In Indianapolis, Benjamin Harrison, then a Republican lawyer and former general, helped organize a citizens' committee against the strikers. Debs would later recall this as "the first in which the powers of the federal courts had been evoked to break a railroad strike" (538). Afterward, he said, "Upon the railroads the mere suspicion of belonging to a union was sufficient grounds for instant discharge" (538).

The watcher

Young calls the strike's long history something "of which Debs was the magnetized witness, the watcher on many fronts" (506). She places him during the summer of 1877 still "confined in the warehouse" (542) as Hulman's billing clerk, while the brotherhood's magazine was edited by others. In 1878, he became its associate editor (545).

That placement is significant, and it raises the most important historical question in these chapters. It is taken up below.

Utopia for the munitions makers

Near the end of this stretch, Young turns the book's central word inside out. War, she writes, "would be a state of perpetual utopia for munitions makers and military men" (544). The perfect society exists after all. It belongs to the people who sell the guns.

It is the sharpest single sentence in the book about The Sacred Is Here and its enemy. Every dream of a distant perfect world can be claimed by someone. Young's point is that the utopia of the arms dealer is already here, paid for by the people who die in it.

What the lens shows

These chapters bring together everything the book has built. The layers of The Past Doesn't Go Away are the Mollies, the Pinkertons, the Gatling guns, and the Tompkins Square clubs. Reality Is Constructed appears as the courts, which here begin to replace the army as labor's great opponent. The Crossing Point is Debs's own recollection that 1877 was the first time the federal courts were used to break a strike. In 1894, an injunction from those same courts would destroy his American Railway Union and send him to jail.

Checking the record

  • Debs's own position in 1877. This is the largest gap in Young's account. By the standard record, Debs did not support the 1877 strike. At the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen's convention in Indianapolis that September, he defended the union against charges that it had backed the walkout, and the brotherhood's magazine condemned the strike. Young's placement of him in the warehouse, as a watcher rather than a participant, softens this. It is the clearest example in the book of a biographer protecting her subject. It is also, arguably, a place where Young's own principle of honest incompletion would have been better served by the harder truth: that the future leader of the Pullman strike began as a cautious union man who opposed a strike.

  • The 1876 election. Young writes that the Republicans "had stolen the office" from Samuel Tilden (539). The disputed election was settled by a special commission and a political bargain. "Stolen" states a view many historians share, but not all.

  • Troops at Terre Haute. Accurate. Federal troops were sent to Indianapolis and Terre Haute in July 1877.
harp-post-06-born-on-a-grocery-scale:
Chapter 6. Born on a Grocery Scale

← Chapter 5 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 7 →

Daniel and Marguerite Debs, the Alsatian inheritance, and a town that was not Nowhere

Part Two of Harp Song for a Radical opens on page 179 under the book's own title, "Harp Song for a Radical." After nearly two hundred pages of German tailors, Paris poets, and prairie utopias, Young finally turns to the Debs family. The first thing she tells about them is a burial.

In 1849, Daniel and Marguerite Debs, newly married in New York, lose their first child, a daughter who "could not breathe and had died almost immediately" (181). The baby is buried in the Greenwood graveyard in Brooklyn, "where one day the socialist tailor Weitling would be buried" (182). Part One ended with Weitling lowered into that same ground. Part Two begins with a Debs child placed in it first.

Young makes the connection deliberately, and then adds a detail from the future. Years later, when Eugene Debs was a presidential candidate beloved in the New York tenements, he went looking for his lost sister's grave at Greenwood. Young writes that had he known Weitling lay there too, he would have left flowers, since "his constant habit was to visit the graves of dead children and poets and socialists, he being that kind of permanently elegiac fellow" (182).

That sentence tells a reader what kind of hero this book will have. He is a man who goes looking for graves.

The mill girl and the book lover

Young sketched the parents' story briefly back in Part One (pages 18 to 22), and it is worth recapping it here. Daniel Debs grew up in a tall old house in the shadow of the cathedral in Colmar, in Alsace, the son of a prosperous mill owner. He was sent to school in Paris, where he read French romantics, skeptics, and revolutionaries. Marguerite Bettrich was a poor girl who beat flax and spun thread in his father's mills. His father forbade the match. Daniel would not give her up.

Young's comment on the romance is one of her quietest and most important lines: "Perhaps revolution was always love, love of common humanity, love of the poor" (19). She does not make Daniel a theorist. His radicalism starts with a refusal to accept that a mill owner's son and a mill girl belong to different kinds of people.

Marguerite, Young notes, hesitated for a sensible reason. She "had feared that in America there might be the injustices that there were in France" (19). She was right. Daniel sailed ahead of her in 1848, the year of failed revolutions. On the voyage and in New York, a confidence man talked him out of most of his inheritance, "the French equivalent of six thousand dollars" (20). He met his bride at the dock with roses in his hand and very little money.

The long way to Terre Haute

What follows is a story of repeated loss. After the first baby died, the couple decided to leave the city for Cincinnati. Daniel shipped their linens, silver, and china from Colmar down the Ohio River by flatboat. The flatboat broke loose in a flood and drifted away. "It was never reported as found among the lost" (182). The last physical pieces of their old life simply float out of the story.

They ended up instead in Terre Haute, Indiana, a Wabash River town where Daniel had heard there were many French speakers. What they found was mud and hogs. Hogs on their way to the slaughterhouse were "sometimes so thick in the unpaved clay streets that they were like a heavy tide" (182), and the river itself was sometimes clogged with slaughtered animals.

Daniel had the hands of a scholar, hands that "had not handled an ax but rather the rare leathers of old books" (183). He took work laying railroad ties. After two fourteen-hour days, "the palms of his hands so blistered and bleeding, that he could not hold the handle of the pick" (183), the foreman sent him home. He moved from job to job. A second daughter was born and died before she could be named. A third, Marie Marguerite, survived. The family went back east, where Louise was born, and then west again to Terre Haute.

With "the forty dollars that were left of their earthly capital" (184), they opened a grocery in the front room of a shack in the factory district. Daniel, who had learned from his father how to butcher a hog, worked the chopping block. Eugene Victor Debs was born on November 5, 1855, in the back room of that store, "which had a scale upon which to weigh him" (184).

It is a perfect image for this book. The future labor leader was born among the goods, and weighed on the same scale as the hams and flour. Young refuses to see destiny in it. The future, she writes, was then as always "a permanent enigma wrapped around with mysteries that might or might not unwind themselves" (184).

A town that was somewhere

Young pauses over the history of Terre Haute, and the pause is instructive. The site had once attracted French Jesuits who dreamed of a wilderness paradise of priests and converts. Later, General William Henry Harrison built Fort Harrison nearby and made war on the Native nations of the region, driving them west. The town itself was laid out in 1816, a short time after Father Rapp founded Harmony farther down the same river.

Then Young adds a dry, telling sentence: "This county was not that which should have been called Nowhere" (188).

The word "utopia" means "no place." Part One was a tour of Nowheres, Icaria and Communia and Zion and Harmony, each built as a model of the perfect society and each falling apart. Terre Haute is the opposite. It was built by speculators and settlers, with no angel's footprints and no founding vision. Its county lines were surveyed and recorded. Its streets were full of hogs.

This is The Sacred Is Here in its plainest form. After two hundred pages of paradises, the book's hero is born in a real place, messy and unplanned, among ordinary people trying to make a living. Young still sees the layers beneath it. Under the grocery lie the Jesuits' dream, the Native dead, Harrison's fort, and the Rappite mortgage from Part One. The Past Doesn't Go Away never stops. But this time the top layer is somewhere.

Books on the shelves

The Debs grocery was not a prosperous business, and Young makes clear why. In hard years, when customers had no money, Daniel gave credit or simply handed out a loaf of bread. The shelves "were sometimes better stocked with Daniel's books than with the provisions" (186). Between customers, he read French poetry aloud while Marguerite rocked the cradle at her feet.

He named his son for the two writers he had loved since his student days in Paris, Eugène Sue and Victor Hugo. Young describes what those writers meant to him. They believed that "the lowliest beings of the dust, were a species of divinity" (186), that the poorest people carried within them the living spark of redemption. The name itself was an inheritance, a philosophy handed to a baby.

Then Young records something unexpected. When the old Debs was asked where his revolutionary convictions came from, he did not credit his father's library, with its Rousseau, Voltaire, Saint-Simon, Sue, Hugo, and Heine. "He said quite simply that his mother had taught him to be a revolutionary when he was a little boy at her knee" (186).

Young agrees with him. Marguerite Debs, she says, "was and always had been an instinctive socialist" (186). She was the woman who put up preserves for the store and did not mind her husband wrapping hog jowls in paper printed with revolutionary poems. This is Not One Self at the root of Debs's character. He had two inheritances, his father's books and his mother's practice, and he claimed the second. The theory came from Daniel. The habit of care came from Marguerite.

It may be worth noting that the writer who tells this story was also named Marguerite. Young makes nothing of it. Readers may.

Blaming God instead of a rod

Young sets Debs's birth against the national scene, and one story from the White House stands out. In January 1853, before his inauguration, President-elect Franklin Pierce lost his only surviving son, Benjamin, in a railroad accident. Young notes that "the railroad powers would rather have blamed God than a rod" (185). According to Young, Pierce's grieving wife found comfort in believing the accident was an act of Providence meant to free her husband for the nation's work, and Pierce had his lawyer defend the railroad against the other victims' suits.

This connects back to the opening chapter, where Tom Mooney's father dies of coal-dust lungs, a death the mine owners preferred to call one of the "acts of God." It is Reality Is Constructed again. Calling a disaster an act of God is a way of hiding the people who could have prevented it. A broken rod has an owner. God does not answer lawsuits.

Hog cars full of boys

Debs was five when the Civil War began and ten when it ended, and Young tries to see it through his eyes. Terre Haute, she admits, was not a town especially moved by the suffering of enslaved people. Many of its families came up from the South. Daniel hated slavery, but he also saw something his neighbors missed. The deepest division in the country, he believed, "was not the division between North and South but the division into the rich and the poor" (191). He predicted, correctly in Young's view, that the war would widen that division.

When young Eugene asked why the war was called civil when it was so cruel, he got the answer other Hoosier fathers gave: it was not civil, and not polite. Children of the time, Young notes, pictured the Mason-Dixon Line as a chalk line drawn across the country (191). A boundary that decided who could be owned was, to a child, something anyone could draw.

What stayed with the boy was a single image. "What had mainly impressed him as to the uncivil Civil War were the hog cars packed not with hogs but with boys on their way to the South" (191). Many of them were poor Butternuts, as Southern-born Hoosiers were called. The draft let a prosperous father pay a poor boy to go in his son's place. Young's verdict is blunt: "The most expendable of all the products of the North were men" (192).

This is The Margins Reveal the Truth seen by a child. In a town that shipped hogs to slaughter by rail, the boy watched the same cars carry boys away.

Young balances this with gentler memories. Daniel took his son into the meadows and taught him the names of birds and bees. The boy "had learned to recognize all the wild birds and their songs, which he could accurately imitate throughout his life" (191). Daniel was known around town as the bloody mushroom hunter, because he knew exactly which mushrooms were safe to eat. The war was on the railroad. The father was in the woods, teaching the difference between what nourishes and what kills.

The doctor and his gun

The last chapters of this stretch belong to Dr. Richard Jordan Gatling, an Indianapolis physician who invented the rapid-fire gun that bears his name. Young describes his public reasoning, that a weapon terrible enough would make war unthinkable, as "the humanitarian mask of Dr. Richard Jordan Gatling's idea" (193).

She stages his demonstration in an abandoned Indianapolis graveyard, where one turn of the crank shot every quail out of the long grass. Then she reaches back to Part One. Gatling's patent made him rich, while Weitling, whose buttonhole machine was designed to "punch holes for buttons and not holes in men" (196), died in poverty. The country rewarded the invention that killed and ignored the one that would have spared poor women's eyes.

Young then carries the gun forward through time. Gatlings were turned against strikers at the McCormick works, at Homestead, and in mining towns from Appalachia to Coeur d'Alene and Cripple Creek. And she gives the older Debs, looking back on the Pullman strike of 1894, a bitter line: "the rapid-fire injunction would seem to him a great improvement over the great Gatling gun" (197).

That quip is the Crossing Point of this section. Debs was born into the age of the machine gun, and he would come of age in the age of the court injunction, when a judge's order could break a strike more efficiently than bullets. The weapon changed from a gun to a piece of paper. The people it was aimed at stayed the same.

What the lens shows

These pages turn the book from the dream to the ground. Grief Doesn't End runs through them in the two dead daughters, the lost china, and a father's bleeding hands, none of it resolved or redeemed. The Sacred Is Here is in the grocery scale, the shelves of books, and the mushrooms. Reality Is Constructed shows in the act-of-God excuse and the draft that sold one boy's life for another's. Part One is pressed underneath, from Colmar and 1848 to the Shakespeare Hotel and the Weitling grave, and it has finally surfaced as a boy in a back room in Indiana.

Checking the record

Young's family history agrees with the standard accounts. Eugene Victor Debs was born in Terre Haute on November 5, 1855. His parents had ten children, six of whom survived, and the family's Terre Haute grocery is well documented. Richard Gatling did live in Indianapolis, patented his gun in 1862, and saw it adopted by the Army in 1866. The Chicago Tribune did suggest strychnine as a remedy for tramps during the upheavals of 1877, as Young reports.

Several points need correcting or flagging:

  • Tecumseh at Tippecanoe. Young writes of Harrison's "cowardly attack upon the utopian philosopher Tecumseh and his sleeping red men when they had already surrendered" (187). At the Battle of Tippecanoe in November 1811, Tecumseh was away in the South. The fighting began with a pre-dawn attack on Harrison's camp by warriors following Tecumseh's brother, Tenskwatawa, known as the Prophet. Young's sympathies are clear, but the facts run the other way.

  • Lincoln's repeating gun. Young writes that Lincoln ordered ten "Union Repeating Guns" in October 1861, and she places the order in the middle of her Gatling chapter (194). The Union Repeating Gun, sometimes called the coffee mill gun, was a different weapon, sold by J. D. Mills, and it predated Gatling's invention. Lincoln's order was real. It was simply not an order for Gatlings.

  • The death of Benjamin Pierce. Young says the boy was killed "about a month after the election" (185). The accident happened on January 6, 1853, about two months after Pierce's election.

Next chapter: a boy in a breaking nation. Dred Scott, John Brown, and the Civil War reach Terre Haute, and Young paints one of her most sympathetic portraits, of Mary Todd Lincoln.
harp-post-14-whistler-gogol-dostoyevsky:
Chapter 14. Whistler, Gogol, Dostoyevsky

← Chapter 13 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 15 →

An ending in Russia, and an Afterword that finally speaks in Debs's voice

The last chapters of Harp Song for a Radical (pages 546 to 576) leave Indiana and never come back. Young tells the stories of the painter James McNeill Whistler's mother, of Whistler's father, who built a railroad for the czar, of Nikolai Gogol, and finally of Fyodor Dostoyevsky, arrested in 1849 for belonging to a Fourierist study circle and led out to be shot.

For a biography of Debs, it is a strange place to stop. For this book, it may be exactly the right one.

The mother in the painting

Anna Whistler is best known as the seated figure in her son's 1871 painting Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1. Young notes that it was revered in pious homes and mocked in saloons, where sometimes "the face of Susan B. was substituted for hers" (546).

Young's Anna Whistler is a missionary. In Russia, where her husband, Major George Washington Whistler, was building the railroad from St. Petersburg to Moscow for Czar Nicholas I, she handed out Bible tracts to railroad workers and soldiers "right under the nose of the czar" (546). She believed that her husband's railroad was "God's mask" for her own mission of converting Russians (547).

The czar himself, in a story Young repeats, drew the line of the railroad with a ruler, showing Major Whistler "the way the railroad should be laid as straight and shining as a thread" (562). Serfs laid the rails. Strikes were forbidden.

Death before life

Young then turns to Gogol, whose novel Dead Souls satirized a Russia where serfs were bought and sold even after death. The critic Vissarion Belinsky had hoped the book would stir Russians toward reform. When Gogol retreated into religious conservatism, Belinsky wrote him a furious open letter. Young's summary of the Russian situation is a single line: "Death, it seemed, had preceded life" (558).

That letter led directly to Dostoyevsky's arrest. He read it aloud at a meeting of the Petrashevsky circle, a group of young men studying Fourier's utopian socialism. A police informer had been planted among them. Young makes the parallel explicit, comparing the informer to the Pinkerton agents "the American czars of railroads and mills and mines would employ" (560).

In the spring of 1849, the police rounded up the circle. Dostoyevsky and others were sentenced to death, taken to a square in St. Petersburg, and prepared for execution. At the last moment, a messenger announced that the czar had commuted their sentences to hard labor in Siberia, "through the infinite clemency of the czar" (568). The whole scene had been staged. Young calls it "this macabre joke" (568).

Why end here

Ruas wrote in his introduction that Debs's imprisonment is "anticipated by the unforgettably harrowing scene of Dostoyevsky being led to his near execution." That is the first reason for the Russian ending. The book that began with Debs in prison ends with another radical led out to die for belonging to a reading group.

The second reason is the date. Dostoyevsky was arrested in 1849, the year Daniel Debs arrived in New York and Weitling returned there. Major Whistler died of cholera in St. Petersburg that same April. The Russian ending loops back to the moment where Part Two began. It is The Past Doesn't Go Away made into a circle.

The third reason is the railroad. Dostoyevsky, Young notes, used to go down to watch the new St. Petersburg railway station being built (554). The railroad the czar drew with a ruler, the railroad Anna Whistler's husband built, and the railroad Debs would fire engines on are, in Young's imagination, one line.

Just before the Afterword, she brings in Thoreau's famous question from Walden about the railroad ties: "Did you ever think what those sleepers are that underlie the railroad? Each one is a man" (576). And then comes the book's last sentence before the Afterword. How long would Debs's elegiac sense last? "It would continue for as long as he lived and perhaps long afterward. As will be seen" (576).

"As will be seen." The book promises more, and there is no more.

The Afterword

The Afterword, only four pages long, is the one place in the book where Debs speaks at length. Young quotes his essays on the forgotten early labor organizers, the pioneer who "ended his career a nameless outcast" and "filled an unknown grave" (578). She quotes his faith: "No strike has ever been lost, and there can be no defeat for the labor movement" (578). And she quotes his list of the people who do the world's work, who "dug its canals, made its road beds, laid its rails and operates its trains" (578).

She notes that from his earliest reading, The House of the Dead, Dostoyevsky's account of his Siberian prison years, was among his favorite books, a world "he would see at large and magnified in America from the 1870s onward, long before he knew that he would be a prison bird" (577).

The book ends with Norman Thomas's image of Debs after his death, a tall man in a gray suit "walking the star belt," with "this world always half in darkness" (580).

What the lens shows

The ending is Unfinished Is Honest as structure. The book promises "as will be seen" and then stops. It is also the Crossing Point on a world scale. Russia and America, the czar and the railroad king, the Fourierist study circle and the Terre Haute lodge are all shown as parts of one century. Debs is the man standing where all these lines cross, though he is barely on the page.

Checking the record

  • Debs and the B&O. Young calls Debs a "former fireman for the old B & O" (550). Debs fired engines on the Terre Haute and Indianapolis line and, briefly, on a line out of St. Louis. He never worked for the Baltimore and Ohio.

  • The Russian dates. Accurate in the main. The Petrashevsky circle was arrested in the early hours of April 23, 1849. Major Whistler died in St. Petersburg in April 1849. The mock execution took place that December.

  • Whistler's Mother. Painted in 1871, as Young indicates.
harp-post-10-kate:
Chapter 10. Kate

← Chapter 9 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 11 →

A marriage history has judged harshly, and Young's attempt at fairness

Kate Metzel Debs has had bad press. Debs's devoted younger brother Theodore disliked her, and later writers, most memorably Irving Stone in his 1947 novel Adversary in the House, cast her as a cold, social-climbing wife who stood in her husband's way. The chapters from page 316 to about 352 are Young's attempt to see her more fairly. They do not make her a heroine. They make her a person.

The girl at the ironing board

Young gives Kate a hard start. Her father, a German immigrant of mechanical talent, died young. Her mother married a widower with children of his own, John Jacob Bauer, and moved the family to Terre Haute (316). Kate stayed home helping with the younger children.

Debs first saw her through a kitchen window at night, "leaning above an ironing board" (318). Asked years later why he married her, he said there was no mystery beyond love itself: "quite simply, he had fallen head over heels with the girl" (318). Kate said she had been drawn by "his electrifying power and his brilliance of mind" and that he had awakened her interest in woman suffrage, though she had no wish to be in public. "She had been content to stay behind the scenes. She had polished the hearthstones" (318).

Theodore's view and Young's

Young lays out the case against Kate through Theodore, for whom she was "a self-adorning clotheshorse" (319). He believed she had schemed to catch his brother. Young grants that Kate "was never to accompany him on his missions in behalf of brotherhood" and was "not the wild duck" some would have chosen for him but "a very domestic duck" (318).

Then she pushes back. Theodore, she writes, should have stopped to consider what it meant to be married to a man who was never home. Her sympathy lies with the wife left behind, and she pays close attention to the hours. Theodore himself said that short working hours "were as unknown to Debs... as if he had been the citizen of another planet" (348). Tenants in his office building called him "the man who never sleeps" (348).

Kate kept "the porch light burning in expectation of his return" (350). Young's chapter on her nights alone begins with a sharp question about woman's work and whether it was ever done (345). This is Grief Doesn't End in a domestic key. The marriage was loving and also lonely, and Young refuses to resolve it into either.

The child who never came

The Debses had no children. Young states that "The couple had desired a large family" (332), and then offers a cautious speculation, marked as such. Kate may have feared being left a widow with small children if her husband died on the rails or in a strike, as so many railroad widows had been (335–336). Young does not know, and she says so by hedging. It is a guess from inside the fear of a railroad wife, and she offers it as nothing more.

The crane in the watermark

In the middle of the Kate chapters, Young describes something Kate learned about her husband's world: the blacklist. Railroads would dismiss a union man with a glowing letter of reference on company stationery. Held to the light, the paper showed a watermark of a crane. A crane "with broken legs" meant the man's union had been broken and he could be hired. A crane "standing upright on its legs" meant he belonged to an active union and must not be (345).

It is the clearest image in the book of Language Shapes What's Possible. The letter said one thing in ink and another in the paper itself. A worker carried his own sentence of unemployment from town to town without being able to read it.

Money in a grocery sack

Young ends this stretch with a detail about Debs and money that says as much as any speech. He never used a bank. He carried the union's remaining coins in an old grocery sack to his brother-in-law's drugstore and kept them in the safe (339). Kate, Young suggests, worried with good reason about a husband who gave away what little came in.

What the lens shows

Not One Self here belongs to a marriage. Kate was domestic and cultured, supportive and resentful, loved and left alone, all at once. Young refuses Theodore's single verdict and Stone's melodrama alike. This is Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act applied to the woman at the edge of the great man's story, whose view from the porch is as real as his view from the platform.

Checking the record

  • The marriage. Debs married Kate Metzel on June 9, 1885, as the book's chronology says.

  • Kate's reputation. The harsh image of Kate owes much to Theodore Debs's accounts and to Irving Stone's novel. Later historians, including Nick Salvatore, have drawn a more balanced picture, closer to Young's.

  • The watermark blacklist. Young presents the crane watermark as fact. Blacklisting of union railroad men was real and widespread. The specific crane watermark belongs to railroad labor lore and is hard to document. It is best read as a story workers told, which Young, characteristically, did not separate from the record.
harp-post-02-starting-at-the-prison-door:
Chapter 2. Starting at the Prison Door

← Chapter 1 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 3 →

How Harp Song for a Radical begins at the end, and why Young built it that way

Most biographies begin with a birth. Marguerite Young's biography of Eugene Victor Debs begins with a prison cell. Its first sentence says Debs "took the long leap to the Ultima Thule of prison," and for the next several pages he is an old man in convict's clothes, jailed by a president who promised peace. The birth in Terre Haute does not arrive until page 184.

This is the first of Young's large choices, and it shapes everything after it. The reader of Harp Song knows from the start how the story ends: in a cell, in 1920, with Debs running for president from the Atlanta Penitentiary. Suspense about the outcome is gone. What remains is the slower question of how the ground under that cell was laid, layer by layer.

The end, first

The opening chapter (pages 3 to 11) is set mostly during the First World War. Woodrow Wilson has sent Debs to prison under the Espionage Act for speaking against the war. Young treats Wilson's reasoning as a piece of logic that appears solid because it is repeated. Wilson, she writes, "believed that in order to have universal peace the way must be prepared by universal war" (3). She does not argue with the sentence. She sets it down and lets it sound as strange as it is.

This is the principle of Reality Is Constructed at work. War fever, patriotism, and the law that jailed Debs all present themselves as facts of nature. Young keeps showing the seams. She passes along a joke of the period about the secretary of war, Newton D. Baker: the office needed not a man named Baker but "a man named Butcher" (10). She calls the president "wood-headed Woody Wilson" (4). The puns are not decoration. They are how she refuses the official language of the moment.

She also goes further than a historian usually would. "Indeed, it may be that Wilson wanted Debs, with his smashed utopian dreams, to suffer as he suffered," she writes (5), picturing Wilson's face twitching as he staggers after his own dream of world peace. She offers this only as a "may be." It is speculation, and she marks it as speculation. It still says something about her method: the jailer and the jailed are both utopians, and both are breaking.

The uncounted votes

The most moving pages of the opening concern the 1920 election. Debs ran from inside the Atlanta Penitentiary, "old and puny gentleman who might never live to be released" (5), and won his prison district easily. The convicts' votes could not legally be counted. Young writes that Debs remembered them anyway as "the most precious straws that had been cast" (5), and that he laughed about it with tears running down his cheeks.

Here The Margins Reveal the Truth becomes literal. The men with no legal voice at all gave Debs his most unanimous victory. The ballot box, one of the country's most trusted inventions, turns out to have a floor beneath it where people vote and nothing is recorded.

Young does not let this become a tidy triumph. In the same pages she writes that the old Debs, in his cell, "experienced in the darkness of the prison cell, where he wore a convict's garb, the sense of despair that had always been the twin of hope" (6). Then she widens it: "Hope and despair were two of the most famous twins of the nineteenth century" (6). This is Grief Doesn't End. Young will not present Debs as a saint who never doubted. He had, she says, a "comic sense which must sustain a larger tragic sense than most people know" (5). The laughter and the tears arrive together.

The first spoke: Tom Mooney

Before the opening chapter ends, Young leaves Debs entirely for several pages to tell the life of Tom Mooney. This is the first of the book's many long detours, and it shows how the book works.

Mooney was a labor organizer convicted of the 1916 Preparedness Day bombing in San Francisco, on evidence that included perjured testimony. Young goes back to his father, a Knight of Labor and coal miner in Indiana, shot in the leg by a strikebreaker, who later died of miner's lung. She follows Tom as a boy sorting rags beside his widowed mother in a Holyoke paper mill, then as an iron molder working stripped to the waist so that no shirt would catch the sparks. She finds him standing before a Rembrandt in Rotterdam, where a stranger starts talking to him about socialism. He once said, "I suppose the urge to serve the labor movement was born in me" (9).

Mooney rode Debs's campaign train, the Red Special, in 1908, and asked what he could do for the cause. Debs, perhaps seeing something hawklike in him, answered, "Go and read more books" (10). Young describes Mooney as a man who saw everything in black and white, and who was "always right by being left" (10).

Mooney matters here as Debs's shadow. He is another son of labor, jailed by wartime panic, with the Haymarket executions of 1887 hanging behind his case. Debs, as Young draws him, is a crowd of selves, gentle and stubborn at once. Mooney is one self, fixed and certain. Placing them side by side is Not One Self principle in action. The book's hero is defined partly by the man he told to go and read.

Ruas describes Young's structure as "spokes radiating from a center." Here that structure becomes visible for the first time. The center is the prison. Mooney is the first spoke.

The poet who died the same day

Chapter 2 opens on a coincidence that Young handles with great care. On the same day as the San Francisco bombing, July 22, 1916, James Whitcomb Riley died in Indianapolis. Riley was the Hoosier poet of "Little Orphant Annie" and "When the Frost Is on the Punkin," and a longtime friend and drinking companion of Debs.

Young sets the bomb and the poet's death on the same page, violence beside nostalgia. The country was grieving a writer of lost childhood on the very day it was stepping toward war. At the center of Riley's work was Little Bud, the imaginary boy who was really Riley himself. Young notes that Bud, "having never been born, could never die" (11).

Old and ill, isolated as friends deserted him for the war, Debs wrote an elegy for Riley as part of his collection "Pastels of Men." Young could have let the elegy stand on its own. Instead she keeps the real man in view beside the sentimental one. Riley carried popcorn in one pocket for Little Bud, "but in the other pocket was something for Pa," and it was a bottle. She recalls that he had once worked the Wizard Oil medicine wagon, reciting poems about little red hens and then selling bottles of opiate cure-alls to country crowds. Debs's elegy leaves these things out. Young does not.

This is Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act at work. Young stays in the room with the whole of Riley, the sweet and the shabby together, and does not rush to wrap him up.

Then she gives Debs a question that could stand as the motto for the book. Considering what was real and what was unreal, Debs asked who could say that "the child world of the Little Bench-Legged Poet was not after all the real world" (16). Young, who said all her writing was about "the recognition that there is no single reality," lets the question stand without an answer.

She calls Debs and Riley "both Don Quixotes in quest of the golden world of happiness and harmony and peace" (16). They never agreed on politics. Riley claimed he voted only once in his life, meaning to vote Republican, and his hand slipped. Yet Young sees them walking the same road. Riley looked for paradise backward, in childhood. Debs looked for it forward, in a transformed society. Riley's death, she writes, seemed to many to mark the death of "that American innocence which, of course, had never been unless in dreams" (16). The phrase "of course" carries a whole philosophy. The golden age never existed, and Young says so in two words.

A childhood without documents

Chapter 3 finally turns toward Debs's own childhood, and Young begins it with a confession. What socialist children learned of his early years came from Henry Schnitkind's popular biography, which borrowed from the old stories of mother and child, "for which there was no documentation" (17).

Young then tells those stories anyway, and marks them clearly as legend. Debs's mother, Marguerite, whom the children called Daisy, explains that the dew is God's tears, wiped on a handkerchief of grass, and that "Earth is the marble God spins" (17). When the small boy first hears of a baby's death, he stamps his foot and scolds God. When he hears the night express, Daisy tells him the sparks flying up are "golden bees flying out of a beehive" (17). The locomotive fireman he will become is already in the scene.

This is Language Shapes What's Possible handled honestly. Every biography of a famous person grows a myth around the childhood, because the real record is thin. Young does not pass the myth off as fact, and she does not throw it away either. She hands it over labeled, and trusts the reader to hold both at once: this is not what happened, and it is part of who Debs became. That is Unfinished Is Honest in practice. She marks the gap instead of filling it.

What the opening teaches

By page 18, Young is ready to go back to 1848, to Colmar in Alsace, where Debs's father fell in love with a mill girl. The opening chapters have set out everything the reader needs to read the rest of the book.

The first lesson is The Past Doesn't Go Away. Young starts at the top layer, the prison in 1920, and then digs. Mooney's father's strike, the Haymarket hangings, Riley's lost Indiana, and Daisy's stories all lie beneath the cell. Nothing in Debs's end was inevitable, and Young's digging puts back in view the people who built each layer.

The second lesson is that Young's detours are the argument. Mooney, Riley, and the myth of childhood are each a way of seeing Debs from the side. A reader who wants only Debs will be frustrated for five hundred pages. A reader who accepts the crowd will find that Debs is inside all of it.

Checking the record

Young's history is often right in surprising places. Riley did die on July 22, 1916, the same day as the San Francisco bombing, so that pairing is fact and not invention. John Swinton's 1894 account Striking for Life, which she cites, is real, and Mooney did ride the Red Special in 1908.

Several claims need correcting or flagging:

  • Mooney's time on death row. Young writes that Mooney spent "more than two decades on death row." His death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment in 1918, after Wilson asked California's governor to intervene. Mooney spent about twenty-two years in prison, not on death row, and was pardoned in 1939.

  • Ingersoll as "Speaker of the House." Robert Ingersoll appears as "Republican Speaker of the House" (12). Ingersoll never held that office. He was famous as a Republican campaign speaker, and the capital letters may be an editor's or a typist's error that changed the meaning. It is a small example of how other hands shaped this book.

  • Wilson and Riley. The scene of Wilson weeping over Little Bud and dancing a jig as Little Orphant Annie comes without a source. It is best read as legend, the kind Young loved to repeat.

Next chapter: Heinrich Heine and Wilhelm Weitling, and why a biography of an Indiana railroad man spends sixty pages in Germany and Paris before his parents ever reach America.
harp-post-11-hoosier-company:
Chapter 11. Hoosier Company

← Chapter 10 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 12 →

Riley, Nye, the Tall Sycamore, and the politics of an Indiana town

The chapters from about page 353 to 400 are the warmest in the book. They return to James Whitcomb Riley, whose death opened the first chapter, and they show Debs among the friends and rivals of his Indiana years: the humorist Bill Nye, Senator Daniel Voorhees, and the Republican general who would become president, Benjamin Harrison.

The poet in the pub

Young sets one scene in an Irish pub in Terre Haute's railroad district. When Debs and Riley walked in together, there was "always something of an uproar of joy as suddenly the workmen coming in for drinks realized that the great poet was among them, whereas the presence of Debs was taken for granted" (379). Debs was one of them. Riley was a celebrity.

Young is candid about Riley's drinking. His touring partnership with Nye broke down amid newspaper jokes like "Riley Leaves Nye for Rye" (380). Kate Debs, she notes, worried about the gossip when the two men were seen together. Riley, for his part, wrote to Nye after one visit: "Have latterly returned from a brief visit to Debs, at Terre Haute" (381), and passed along Debs's greetings.

In 1886 Riley published "Regardin' Terry Hut," a comic tribute to the town, and in it he wrote the lines about his friend that would follow Debs for the rest of his life. Debs was "a man 'at stands / And jes' holds out in his two hands / As warm a heart as ever beat" (385).

Three sycamores

Young traces a local title through three men. The "Tall Sycamore of the Wabash" was first William Henry Harrison, the Indian fighter, then Senator Voorhees, and "the last Tall Sycamore would be Debs" (385). It is a small joke with a real point. The same Indiana soil produced the general who drove out the Native nations, the Democratic senator who made his career in Washington, and the labor leader who would run for president from a prison cell.

Debs campaigned for Voorhees and for the Democrats in these years. At a rally in 1888 he spoke against the Republican candidate, Benjamin Harrison. Young reports the charges that had followed Harrison since the railroad strike of 1877: that he had said a dollar a day was enough for any workingman (390), and that he had boasted he would wade through the blood of strikers (391). She presents them carefully as accusations "continually resurrected" against him. Later, Debs would conclude that "Harrison had been Carnegie's man, root and branch." Then he added a question that shows where his thinking was headed: "But whose man was Cleveland?" (396).

That question marks a turning point. Debs was beginning to suspect that both parties answered to the same owners.

The silence of 1886

Young does not hide a moment when Debs fell short. In 1886, when the Haymarket anarchists were arrested in Chicago after a bomb killed several policemen, Debs's voice was "stifled by various fears for his Firemen's Brotherhood" (353). He did not defend them. The union was fragile, public hysteria was enormous, and he stayed quiet.

Young records this without excuse and without condemnation. It is Grief Doesn't End in a different form, a refusal to tidy up the hero's record. The Debs who would later defend every persecuted radical in America was, at thirty, still weighing the safety of his own organization.

Toward federation

By the late 1880s, the separate craft brotherhoods were failing in strikes, often because one union's men would run the trains when another's walked out. Debs began to dream of joining them all. Young says he was traveling toward "what he would call the Ultima Thule of labor federation" (374).

The phrase echoes the first sentence of the book, where Debs "took the long leap to the Ultima Thule of prison." Ultima Thule means the farthest edge of the known world. Young uses it for both the prison cell and the united union. That repetition is The Past Doesn't Go Away as structure. The road to one farthest edge leads to the other.

What the lens shows

These chapters are about friendship across disagreement. Riley never shared Debs's politics. Voorhees was a party man. Nye was, in Young's phrase earlier, of the right wing. Debs loved them anyway. The Sacred Is Here lives here in the pub, the rally, and the bread-and-butter poem, in a politics that grows out of local affection rather than theory.

Checking the record

  • "Regardin' Terry Hut." Accurate. Riley's poem appeared in the Indianapolis Journal in 1886 and in his 1887 collection Afterwhiles.

  • Harrison's alleged remarks. The "dollar a day" charge dogged Harrison in several campaigns. He denied it, and it was never proved. Young is right to present it as an accusation.

  • Debs and Haymarket. Young's account of his silence in 1886 matches the historical record. His public defense of the Haymarket men came much later.
harp-post-04-back-to-new-harmony:
Chapter 4. Back to New Harmony

← Chapter 3 · The Unfinished Harp: Reading Harp Song for a Radical · Chapter 5 →

Weitling's tour of America's broken utopias, and Young's return to her own ground

In 1945, Marguerite Young published Angel in the Forest: A Fairy Tale of Two Utopias, her history of the two communities that took turns on the same stretch of Indiana riverbank. The first was Father George Rapp's celibate Harmony Society. The second was Robert Owen's rational New Harmony, built in the houses the Rappites left behind. That book made Young's name as a prose writer.

Half a century later, in her last book, she comes back to this ground. She does not come back head on. She arrives sideways, riding along with Wilhelm Weitling as he tours the American interior looking for a place to build the workers' paradise. Rapp and Owen, who once filled a whole book, appear here as ruins, rumors, and bad advice. That change in scale is the most interesting thing about these chapters (roughly pages 72 to 115). Young is treating her own earlier subject as one layer among many.

The peddler of paradise

Weitling reached New York late in 1846 expecting to edit a German workers' paper. It had already gone bankrupt. So he set out west with a bag of pamphlets, by train to Pittsburgh, by boat down the Ohio and the Mississippi to New Orleans, and even into Texas, founding workers' clubs as he went.

Young's account of this journey is comic and very little of it concerns grand theory. The Philadelphia workers' association he helped found collected dues of "three cents a week" (76). The money paid for doctors and medicine, for coffins and gravediggers, for a building and loan fund, and for a singing society. Utopia, on the ground, looked a great deal like burial insurance and a choir.

The recruiting went badly. In Cleveland, many of the German workers he addressed drifted off to "a picnic with harps and flutes and songs" in the woods six miles away, and he signed up only fourteen members (82). In Chicago, "Brother Weitling was able to bring into his harvest only one member, and that was a brewer" (84). In Wisconsin, he learned that many farmers saw hard currency once a year, a single silver dollar at harvest, and lost it at once to debts at the country store (84–85).

Young is laughing at Weitling here, but she is not sneering. The harps win against the pamphlets, and it is hard to blame the picnickers. This is The Sacred Is Here taking its revenge on the grand plan. People who had worked all week wanted music and grass more than a lecture about the future.

Communia
